grammarNotes: Come stai? uses the second person singular informal form of stare (to be). The verb stare conjugates based on formality and number: stai (informal singular), sta (formal singular), state (plural). Unlike English, Italian distinguishes between informal and formal registers when greeting.
learnerNotes: Register is crucial in Italian: use Come stai? with friends and family, Come sta? with professionals and strangers. The verb stare (to stay/be) changes form significantly with person and formality level. Note that Come va? is colloquial and unsuitable for first meetings or formal contexts—save it for established relationships.

exampleSentences.english: How are you? (informal singular)

englishTranslation: I can't wait / I look forward to
grammarNotes: This is an idiomatic expression using the verb vedare (to see) in first-person singular present tense. Literally it means 'I can't see the hour,' expressing impatience. It can be used standalone as an exclamation or paired with prepositions: 'di' + infinitive (non vedo l'ora di andare) or 'che' + indicative clause (non vedo l'ora che inizi). The expression does not conjugate when used as a response.
learnerNotes: This is one of the most common ways Italians express eager anticipation; far more natural than the literal 'non posso aspettare.' Remember that it combines with 'di' before infinitives and 'che' before full clauses—don't use 'per' or 'a.' Note that in informal speech you may hear it shortened to just 'non vedo l'ora!' as a standalone exclamation without additional context.

exampleSentences.italian: La settimana prossima esce la nuova stagione di Westworld. – Lo so, non vedo l'ora!
exampleSentences.english: Next week the new season of Westworld comes out. – I know, I can't wait!

exampleSentences.italian: Non vedo l'ora di cominciare il corso di danza domani, mi divertirò un sacco!
exampleSentences.english: I can't wait to start my dance class tomorrow, I'll have lots of fun!

exampleSentences.english: What a boring conference, it's never ending. I can't wait to go back home.

exampleSentences.english: I can't wait to go on vacation.

exampleSentences.english: I'm looking forward to seeing Paola again tonight.

englishTranslation: Who cares? / Who gives it importance?
grammarNotes: This is an idiomatic expression using the pronoun 'chi' (who) with the reflexive pronoun 'se' and the verb 'importare' (to matter/be important). The construction 'se ne importa' literally means 'does it matter to oneself.' The phrase functions as a fixed expression and doesn't require conjugation changes in typical usage.
learnerNotes: The standard form 'Chi se ne importa?' is appropriate in most contexts, while 'Chi se ne frega' is distinctly more informal and casual—reserve it for friends or relaxed settings. Both expressions can be softened by adding 'Ma' at the beginning (e.g., 'Ma chi se ne importa!') to sound less aggressive. The shortened forms 'chissene' and the single-word 'chissenefrega' represent the emphatic doubled 's' sound in speech and are primarily written representations of spontaneous language.

exampleSentences.italian: Luca si sta sfogando di nuovo su Facebook… – Ma chi se ne importa!
exampleSentences.english: Luca's venting on Facebook again… – Oh, who cares!

exampleSentences.italian: Ha detto che sono stupido. – E chi se ne frega di cosa dice. Non dargli retta!
exampleSentences.english: He said that I'm stupid. – Who cares what he says. Don't pay any attention to him!

exampleSentences.italian: È uscito il film su Chiara Ferragni. – Ma chissene!
exampleSentences.english: The film about Chiara Ferragni is out. – Who cares!

exampleSentences.italian: Ci siamo lasciati per la terza volta… – E allora? Perché non accettate che tra di voi non funziona?
exampleSentences.english: We've broken up for the third time… – And your point is? Why don't you just accept that things aren't working out between you two?

englishTranslation: Now, remember… / Please… / Now, listen to me… / Don't forget… / Please make sure… / I'm counting on you… / …got it?
grammarNotes: Mi raccomando is the reflexive form of the verb raccomandare (to recommend/entrust). The reflexive raccomandarsi means to plead with, to beg, or to implore. Mi raccomando functions as a set phrase used to emphasize the importance or urgency of a request, and can stand alone or introduce a clause. It expresses the speaker's faith in the listener to fulfill the request.
learnerNotes: Mi raccomando is never used to give orders; it's a friendly suggestion or encouraging hint where the other person has the choice to comply. The phrase can stand alone and carries different meanings depending on context—use it to stress urgency and appeal to trust rather than authority. Be aware that raccomandato/a as a noun has a slightly negative connotation, implying someone obtained a position through nepotism or connections.

exampleSentences.english: I pleaded with them but it was useless.

exampleSentences.italian: Pietro si è raccomandato con Laura di venire con lui.
exampleSentences.english: Pietro begged Laura to come with him.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi raccomando, non fare sciocchezze!
exampleSentences.english: Now remember, don't do anything silly, okay?

exampleSentences.english: Now, listen to me, boys, don't drink tonight. You have the exam tomorrow!

exampleSentences.english: I'm begging you, don't touch anything!

exampleSentences.italian: Guarisci presto, mi raccomando!
exampleSentences.english: Please get better soon!

exampleSentences.italian: Ci vediamo presto! Mi raccomando!
exampleSentences.english: See you soon! Take care!

grammarNotes: Ti amo is the first-person singular present tense of the verb amare (to love). The pronoun 'io' is typically omitted. The verb conjugates regularly in most tenses: present (amo), passato prossimo (ho amato), passato remoto (amai), imperfetto (amavo), and future (amerò). Ti is the indirect object pronoun meaning 'you' (informal singular).
learnerNotes: Ti amo is reserved for romantic partners, spouses, and children; using it with friends is unusual unless expressing very deep affection. For platonic relationships, prefer ti voglio bene instead. The verb amare is regular in all tenses except the informal passato remoto form amò (he/she loved), making it straightforward to conjugate for different time references and subjects.

exampleSentences.english: I love you, my love.

exampleSentences.english: I love you for what you are.

exampleSentences.english: I love you too!

italianTerm: Posso avere il conto per favore?
englishTranslation: Can I have the bill please? / May I have the bill please?
grammarNotes: The phrase uses the present indicative first-person singular 'posso' (can I) + infinitive 'avere' (to have). The definite article 'il' precedes the masculine noun 'conto' (bill). 'Per favore' is an adverbial phrase meaning 'please.' The conditional tense 'potrei' can replace 'posso' for greater politeness, equivalent to 'may' in English.
learnerNotes: Always add 'grazie' when using shorter versions like 'Il conto, grazie' to avoid sounding rude. You can increase politeness by using the conditional 'potrei' instead of 'posso,' or by adding 'mi scusi/chiedo scusa' at the beginning. Note that 'cortesia' means courtesy and is more formal; 'favore' and 'piacere' are neutral and commonly used in both spoken and written Italian.

englishTranslation: What is your name? / What do you call yourself?
grammarNotes: This phrase uses the informal second-person singular (tu) form of the verb chiamare (to call). The structure is 'Come' (how) + 'ti' (yourself, indirect object) + 'chiami' (you call). The formal equivalent is 'Come si chiama?' using the Lei form. For plural groups, use 'Come vi chiamate?' (voi form).
learnerNotes: Remember that 'Come ti chiami?' is informal—use 'Come si chiama?' with older people, authority figures, or formal situations. The reflexive verb 'chiamarsi' is essential for name-asking in Italian; don't confuse it with the transitive 'chiamare' (to call someone). The polite intonation-based form 'E tu ti chiami…?' is a clever way to ask without directly asking, useful when you've forgotten a name.

exampleSentences.italian: E tu, come ti chiami? – Mi chiamo Giulio…te l'ho già detto mille volte!
exampleSentences.english: And you, what's your name? – My name is Giulio…I've already told you a thousand times!

exampleSentences.italian: Lei come si chiama? – Mi chiamo Giovanni Agnelli ma i miei amici mi chiamano Gianni.
exampleSentences.english: What is your name? – My name is Giovanni Agnelli, but my friends call me Gianni.

exampleSentences.italian: Come vi chiamate?

exampleSentences.english: And your name is…? – Paolo, pleasure to meet you!

grammarNotes: The phrase demonstrates Italian's formal/informal distinction. 'Lei' (formal you) takes third-person singular verb conjugation 'parla'. The subject pronoun can be omitted as the verb conjugation indicates the subject, though including it sounds more polite in first encounters. Italian has three second-person forms: Lei (formal singular), tu (informal singular), and voi (plural).
learnerNotes: Always use 'Lei' (capitalized) with strangers, shop staff, or elderly people—this is essential for politeness in Italian. The verb 'sapere' (to know) offers a useful alternative when asking about ability: 'Sa parlare inglese?' emphasizes capability rather than the simple act of speaking. Remember that omitting the pronoun is grammatically correct and common, but including it in first encounters sounds more courteous.

grammarNotes: This phrase uses the informal second-person singular form 'hai' (you have). In Italian, age is expressed with 'avere' (to have) rather than 'essere' (to be), literally translating as 'how many years do you have.' The verb conjugates based on formality: 'hai' (informal singular), 'ha' (formal singular), 'avete' (plural). The response uses 'Ho' + number + 'anni' (I have + years).
learnerNotes: Critical: Use 'avere' (to have), never 'essere' (to be)—'Quanti anni sei?' is incorrect. Do not use 'quanto sei vecchio' as this insults the listener by implying they are very old. Remember that 'anni' (years) is different from 'ani' (anuses)—a common spelling mistake that drastically changes meaning.

englishTranslation: Where is…? / Where can I find…?
grammarNotes: Dove si trova uses the reflexive verb trovarsi (to be located) in the third person singular. The plural form is Dove si trovano for multiple items. The phrase is passive in nature; the active alternative Dove posso trovare (where can I find) uses posso (I can) to shift to first person. Both are grammatically correct but differ in formality and tone.
learnerNotes: Dove si trova is more passive and formal, suitable for asking about locations and places; use it with strangers or in formal contexts. Dove posso trovare is more active and friendly, making it better for casual interactions. When asking about a person you know, use the informal dov'è; for someone you don't know, prefer dove posso trovare or ask about their office/location instead (dove si trova l'ufficio di…?) to sound more polite.

englishTranslation: Who knows! / Goodness knows! / I wonder / Perhaps / You never know
grammarNotes: Chissà is an abbreviation of 'chi lo sa' (who knows it). The accent on the final à indicates stress falls on the final syllable. When used standalone, it functions as an interjection expressing uncertainty. Within sentences, it can be combined with pronouns (chi, che cosa) to create comparative expressions.
learnerNotes: Chissà and chi lo sa are not always interchangeable in full sentences—chissà is more subjective ('I wonder'), while chi lo sa is more objective ('Who knows?'). Use boh for very casual responses between friends, but chissà is safer in more varied contexts. Remember that chissà can translate to several different English expressions depending on context (wonder, perhaps, you never know), so focus on the uncertainty meaning rather than word-for-word translation.

exampleSentences.italian: Chi è quel ragazzo? – Boh, chissà!
exampleSentences.english: Who's that guy? – Who knows!

exampleSentences.italian: Chissà quando arriveranno! Sono già le otto!
exampleSentences.english: I wonder / Who knows when they'll arrive! It's already eight!

exampleSentences.english: I wonder if Marco went to buy bread.

englishTranslation: Merry Christmas / Happy Christmas / Good Christmas
grammarNotes: Buon Natale is an invariable greeting phrase. The adjective 'buon' (good) is in the apocopated masculine form before the masculine noun 'Natale' (Christmas). Indirect object pronouns (a te, a Lei, a voi) can follow to specify the addressee. The phrase does not conjugate.
learnerNotes: Note that Americans say 'Merry Christmas' while British English uses 'Happy Christmas,' but Italians use 'Buon Natale' (literally 'Good Christmas'). The indirect object pronouns (a te, a Lei, a voi) are optional additions for clarity. The verb augurare (to wish) conjugates normally, so choose the appropriate pronoun form based on formality and number of addressees.

exampleSentences.english: Merry Christmas!

exampleSentences.italian: Buon Natale a te e alla tua famiglia!
exampleSentences.english: Merry Christmas to you and your family!

exampleSentences.italian: Auguri di Buon Natale!
exampleSentences.english: Good Christmas Wishes / Merry Christmas!

exampleSentences.english: I wish you a Merry Christmas! (formal singular)

exampleSentences.english: I wish you a Merry Christmas! (plural)

englishTranslation: Have a good trip! / Good journey!
grammarNotes: This is an interjection/exclamation composed of the adjective 'buon' (good) agreeing with the masculine singular noun 'viaggio' (trip/journey). No verb is required in Italian, unlike English which typically includes 'have.' The expression functions as a standalone well-wish without needing grammatical completion.
learnerNotes: Use 'Buon viaggio!' specifically for the journey/travel itself, not the destination stay. For holidays or time spent at a location, use 'Buone vacanze!' instead. Note the gender/number agreement: 'buon' (masculine singular) matches 'viaggio' (m.s.), while 'buone' (feminine plural) matches 'vacanze' (f.p.). This phrase requires no verb—it stands alone as an exclamation.

exampleSentences.italian: Buon viaggio, Alice! Ci vediamo tra una settimana!
exampleSentences.english: Have a good trip, Alice! See you in a week!

relatedExpressions.meaning: Have a good vacation! (used for time spent at a destination or during school holidays)
Have a good trip and a good vacation! (combined greeting)
Journey/Trip (specifically the journey itself, not activities at destination)

englishTranslation: No problem! / There isn't a problem
grammarNotes: This is a fixed expression using the third-person singular present tense of 'essere' (c'è = there is) with the negation 'non'. The structure 'non c'è + noun' literally means 'there isn't a [noun]'. It is invariable and does not change based on gender or number of the speaker or listener.
learnerNotes: This is an essential expression for daily conversations and a reliable go-to response when someone thanks you or apologizes. 'Nessun problema' is equally common and interchangeable—choose whichever feels more natural to you. Note that many Italians now use the English phrase 'no problem' in informal speech, so you have flexibility if you forget the Italian version.

exampleSentences.italian: Caspita, ho dimenticato il regalo per Anna… – Non c'è problema. Lo prendiamo al ritorno.
exampleSentences.english: Darn, I forgot Anna's present… – No problem. We'll get it on our way back.

exampleSentences.italian: Grazie per avermi accompagnato a casa. – Nessun problema. È stato un piacere.
exampleSentences.english: Thanks for taking me home. – No problem. It was a pleasure.

englishTranslation: It is what it is! / That's how it is / That's how things are!
grammarNotes: È così is a fixed expression combining the verb essere (to be) in third person singular present tense (è) with the adverb così (so/like this). The phrase functions as a complete thought and doesn't require additional conjugation. It's often modified by preceding it with ormai (by now) or following it with e basta (and that's it).
learnerNotes: È così expresses resignation or acceptance of an undesirable situation—use it when you want to convey 'I'm not happy about this, but I've accepted it.' The expression is very common in everyday Italian speech and conveys a slightly fatalistic or resigned tone. Note that purtroppo (unfortunately) often accompanies this phrase to emphasize the reluctant acceptance.

exampleSentences.italian: Il calcio femminile è meno seguito. – Si, purtroppo è così.
exampleSentences.english: Fewer people follow female football. – Yes, unfortunately it is what it is.

exampleSentences.italian: Ormai è così. Non posso farci niente.
exampleSentences.english: At this point, it is what it is. I can't do anything about it.

exampleSentences.italian: Non voglio più pensarci. È così e basta!
exampleSentences.english: I don't want to think about it anymore. This is how it is, and that's all there is to it.

exampleSentences.italian: È così è un peccato ma è così.
exampleSentences.english: That's how it is it's a shame but that's how it is.

exampleSentences.italian: È così, mi dispiace ma è così!
exampleSentences.english: That's how it is I'm sorry but that's how it is!

exampleSentences.italian: È così, non ha senso ma è così.
exampleSentences.english: That's how it is it doesn't make sense but that's how it is.

relatedExpressions.meaning: at this point, it is what it is
this is how it is, and that's all there is to it

italianTerm: Mi piacerebbe… / Mi farebbe piacere… / Vorrei…
englishTranslation: I would like… / It would please me… / I would like to…
grammarNotes: Mi piacerebbe and mi farebbe piacere derive from the verb piacere (to like/to please) and use the conditional form to express wishes or desires. Vorrei is the conditional form of volere (to want) and functions both as a polite expression of desire and as a courteous request. Vorrei is more commonly used for ordering at restaurants or cafés, while mi piacerebbe sounds unnatural for obligatory situations (e.g., using the bathroom).
learnerNotes: Choose Vorrei when ordering food/drinks or making polite requests in restaurants—it's the most natural register for service interactions. Use Mi piacerebbe or Mi farebbe piacere for expressing genuine wishes or desires about leisure activities. Avoid mi piacerebbe for obligatory or unpleasant situations (as the article humorously notes for bathroom use); in such contexts, vorrei is always appropriate.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piacerebbe andare al cinema questa sera.
exampleSentences.english: I would like to go to the cinema this evening.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi farebbe piacere bere una birra fresca.
exampleSentences.english: I would like to drink a cold beer.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei fare un viaggio in India.
exampleSentences.english: I would like to travel to India. (Desire)

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei usare il bagno.
exampleSentences.english: I would like to use the bathroom. (Polite request)

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei un cappuccino.
exampleSentences.english: I would like a cappuccino.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei un caffè.
exampleSentences.english: I would like a coffee.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei qualcosa da bere.
exampleSentences.english: I would like a drink.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei un bicchiere di vino.
exampleSentences.english: I would like a glass of wine.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei una pizza.
exampleSentences.english: I would like a pizza.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei un panino.
exampleSentences.english: I would like a sandwich.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei un tavolo per due.
exampleSentences.english: I would like a table for two.

It would do me pleasure… (literal); I would like…

grammarNotes: This is a fixed idiomatic expression composed of the definite article 'il' (the), the adjective 'dolce' (sweet), the infinitive verb 'fare' (to do/make), and the pronoun 'niente' (nothing). The phrase functions as a noun and does not typically conjugate. Gender and number agreement apply only to the article 'il' relative to the implied noun.
learnerNotes: This expression is rarely used seriously by native Italian speakers and is primarily encountered in English-language media and tourism contexts. It has become a cultural stereotype about Italian lifestyle rather than an authentic everyday phrase. Be aware that using it seriously in Italian may sound affected or ironic; it is much more common to hear English speakers employ it when describing idealized Italian living.

exampleSentences.italian: Il dolce far niente traduce come 'la dolcezza di non fare nulla'.
exampleSentences.english: Il dolce far niente translates as 'the sweetness of doing nothing.'

exampleSentences.italian: Mentre gli americani lavorano troppo, gli italiani sanno apprezzare il dolce far niente.
exampleSentences.english: While Americans work too hard, Italians know how to appreciate the sweetness of doing nothing.

relatedExpressions.meaning: the sweet life (another clichéd Italian expression about lifestyle)

grammarNotes: Carino is a masculine singular adjective; carina is feminine singular. Gender agreement depends on the person being addressed. Subject pronoun tu is optional with sei but becomes necessary when using the subjunctive sia in dependent clauses. Plural forms are carini (masculine) and carine (feminine).
learnerNotes: Carino/carina is primarily used for children or pets; using it with adults can sound insufficiently complimentary or sarcastic. When expressing an opinion with a verb like penso, use the subjunctive sia instead of sei and always include tu. Note that carino can mean either 'cute' (physically) or 'sweet/kind' (character-related) depending on context.

exampleSentences.italian: (Tu) sei carino/a!
exampleSentences.english: You are cute!

exampleSentences.italian: (Tu) sei molto carina stasera.
exampleSentences.english: You're looking very cute this evening.

exampleSentences.italian: (Io) penso che tu sia carino.
exampleSentences.english: I think you are cute.

exampleSentences.italian: I gatti sono molto carini quando sono piccoli.
exampleSentences.english: Cats are very cute when they are small.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi hai fatto un disegno? Ma come sei carino.
exampleSentences.english: You drew me a picture? How sweet you are.

relatedExpressions.meaning: cute (singular); also sweet or kind when describing character

grammarNotes: The phrase breaks down as: Io (I, optional) + non (negation) + lo (it, direct object pronoun) + so (know, first person singular present). The subject pronoun 'io' is optional in Italian when context makes the subject clear through verb conjugation. It becomes necessary only for emphasis or when contrasting with another subject.
learnerNotes: Note the distinction between 'non lo so' (definite, possibly dismissive) and 'non saprei' (expressing genuine uncertainty or lack of expertise). The direct object pronoun 'lo' is essential here—saying just 'non so' without 'lo' changes meaning slightly. Be aware that 'che ne so io?' carries an annoyed or exasperated tone, so use it only when appropriate to the context.

exampleSentences.italian: Io non lo so ma lui lo sa benissimo.
exampleSentences.english: I don't know but he knows very well.

exampleSentences.italian: Come funziona questa macchina? Non lo so.
exampleSentences.english: How does this car work? I don't know.

exampleSentences.italian: Non ho la minima idea di chi sia quel signore lì.
exampleSentences.english: I have no idea who that gentleman is.

exampleSentences.italian: Chi ha preso le mie chiavi? – E che ne so io?!
exampleSentences.english: Who took my keys? – How should I know?!

exampleSentences.italian: Sai a che ora passa il pullman oggi? – Boh!
exampleSentences.english: Do you know what time the bus comes today? – Boh!

exampleSentences.italian: Mmm, non saprei. Non mi intendo di macchine…
exampleSentences.english: Hmm, I don't know. Cars aren't my expertise…

relatedExpressions.meaning: I wouldn't know (expressing uncertainty or lack of conviction)
I have no idea / I absolutely have no idea
Why/How should I know? (irritated or nervous tone)
I don't know / I'm not sure (one-word interjection)

englishTranslation: I don't care / It doesn't interest me / I'm not interested
grammarNotes: This expression uses the indirect object pronoun 'mi' (to me) with the verb 'interessare' (to interest). The structure follows the pattern: Non + indirect object pronoun + interessare + subject. When the subject is a clause or infinitive, the verb remains in third person singular. Related synonyms use similar constructions with different verbs (importare, fregarsene).
learnerNotes: Non mi interessa is the safest and most polite way to express indifference in Italian. Be aware that Non me ne frega nulla is colloquial and should only be used with friends; it may sound rude to strangers or older people. Avoid the vulgar variants (fotte nulla) entirely in formal or unfamiliar contexts, though understanding them helps with comprehension of native speech.

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi interessa che tu voglia andare a casa. Dobbiamo rimanere qui.
exampleSentences.english: I don't care that you want to go home. We have to stay here.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa seria TV non mi interessa più di tanto.
exampleSentences.english: This TV series doesn't really interest me.

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi importa se non vuoi venire a teatro stasera.
exampleSentences.english: I don't care if you don't want to come to the theatre tonight.

exampleSentences.italian: Non me ne frega nulla di quel fannullone!
exampleSentences.english: I don't care one bit about that deadbeat!

exampleSentences.italian: Ho vinto alla lotteria! – Chissenefrega!
exampleSentences.english: I won the lottery! – Who cares!

relatedExpressions.meaning: I don't care / It isn't important to me (very close synonym)

relatedExpressions.expression: Non me ne frega nulla / niente

relatedExpressions.expression: Non me ne fotte nulla / niente / un cazzo
relatedExpressions.meaning: I don't care (vulgar, to be avoided)

relatedExpressions.expression: Me ne frego! / Me ne fotto!

englishTranslation: I can do it! / I can manage it!
grammarNotes: Ce la faccio is built from the pronominal verb farcela (to manage/succeed). It combines ce (pronominal particle, variant of ci when followed by another pronoun) + la (pronominal particle) + faccio (first person singular present of fare). Pronominal verbs in Italian modify the base verb's meaning through attached particles; farcela conjugates regularly in the present tense across all persons.
learnerNotes: Pronominal verbs are fundamental to Italian; farcela is one of the most frequently used. Note that ce replaces ci when followed by another pronoun (la in this case). The negative form Non ce la faccio! is equally common and useful in everyday conversation. Pay attention to the infinitive form farcela when looking up the verb, as dictionaries may not list ce la faccio directly.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei sicuro di farcela?
exampleSentences.english: Are you sure you can do it?

exampleSentences.italian: Sì sì, ce la faccio.
exampleSentences.english: Yes yes, I can do it.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei sicuro di poter finire tutto entro stasera?
exampleSentences.english: Are you sure you can finish everything by tonight?

exampleSentences.italian: Sì dai, ce la posso fare!
exampleSentences.english: Yes, I can do it!

exampleSentences.italian: Non ce la faccio a venire stasera. Ho troppi impegni.
exampleSentences.english: Sorry, I can't come this evening. I have too much to do.

exampleSentences.italian: Non ce la faccio più!
exampleSentences.english: I can't take it anymore! / I've had enough!

relatedExpressions.meaning: I can do it! (alternative form using potere)
I can't take it anymore! / I've had enough!

grammarNotes: Va bene is composed of the third-person singular present indicative of andare (va = goes) plus the adverb bene (well). It functions as an invariable expression used to affirm or accept proposals. The suffix -issimo can be added to bene to create va benissimo for emphasis.
learnerNotes: Do not confuse va bene (genuine acceptance, positive) with vabbè (reluctant acceptance, indifference, or resignation). Va bene shows enthusiasm or at least genuine agreement, while vabbè suggests 'whatever' or 'I don't really care.' Regional variations like va buono are common in everyday speech across Italy, so exposure to these alternatives is useful for listening comprehension.

exampleSentences.italian: Mangiamo fuori stasera? – Va bene.
exampleSentences.english: Shall we eat out tonight? – Okay.

exampleSentences.italian: Come va? – Va bene.
exampleSentences.english: How is it going? – Fine.

exampleSentences.italian: Vuoi venire? – Va bene.
exampleSentences.english: Do you want to come? – Okay.

exampleSentences.italian: Aspetta qui un attimo. – Va bene.
exampleSentences.english: Wait here a minute. – Alright.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono un po' in ritardo. – Va bene, non preoccuparti.
exampleSentences.english: I'm a bit late. – That's fine, don't worry.

exampleSentences.italian: Ci vediamo verso le otto? – Sì, va benissimo!
exampleSentences.english: See you at around eight? – Yes, that's absolutely fine!

exampleSentences.italian: Vuoi guardare un film? – Vabbè.
exampleSentences.english: Do you want to watch a movie? – Whatever.

exampleSentences.italian: Non posso prestarti il libro, scusa. – Vabbè, non fa niente.
exampleSentences.english: I can't lend you the book, sorry. – Oh well, it doesn't matter.

relatedExpressions.meaning: Whatever / Oh well (expresses lack of enthusiasm or resignation)
Fine (Neapolitan regional variation, widely used nationally)

grammarNotes: Italian expresses hunger using avere (to have) + the noun fame, rather than essere (to be) + an adjective like English. Ho is the first-person singular present tense of avere. This construction is typical for physical sensations and emotional states in Italian (ho sete, ho freddo, ho paura, etc.).
learnerNotes: Remember that Italian uses avere + noun for physical sensations rather than essere + adjective—this is a critical difference from English. Ho fame is neutral and appropriate in all contexts; the alternative expressions are more emphatic or colloquial. The childish variant voglio la pappa is endearing but register-specific; use only with children or in family contexts.

exampleSentences.english: I am in a hurry. (Literally: I have haste.)

exampleSentences.italian: Che fame che ho!
exampleSentences.english: How hungry I am!

exampleSentences.italian: Sono affamato!
exampleSentences.english: I'm starving!

exampleSentences.italian: Ho una fame da lupi!
exampleSentences.english: I have the hunger of wolves!

exampleSentences.italian: Non ci vedo più dalla fame!
exampleSentences.english: I can't see from hunger!

englishTranslation: Everything is going to be all right! / Everything will be ok!
grammarNotes: Andrà is the third person singular future tense of andare (to go). The structure is straightforward: andrà (will go) + tutto (everything) + bene (well/fine). This is a simple future affirmative construction commonly used for reassurance and encouragement.
learnerNotes: Andrà tutto bene became a viral rallying cry during the COVID-19 pandemic in Italy, often paired with rainbow symbols (arcobaleno). Note that andare in the future tense is regular: andrò, andrai, andrà, andremo, andrete, andranno. This expression carries emotional weight beyond its literal meaning and functions as both reassurance and solidarity.

exampleSentences.italian: Andrà tutto bene!
exampleSentences.english: Everything is going to be all right!

englishTranslation: I'm staying at home / I stay at home
grammarNotes: The phrase uses restare (to stay/remain) conjugated in first-person singular present tense. The pronoun 'io' is optional and often omitted in colloquial speech; the conjugation alone indicates the subject. Note: avoid the progressive form 'sto restando' with stative verbs like restare, as it is grammatically incorrect in Italian.
learnerNotes: Three verbs can express 'to stay': restare, stare, and rimanere are largely interchangeable here. The pronoun 'io' is often dropped in casual speech—focus on the verb conjugation to identify the subject. Remember: never use the progressive form 'sto restando' with restare, as it violates Italian grammar rules for stative verbs.

exampleSentences.italian: Io resto a casa.
exampleSentences.english: I'm staying at home.

exampleSentences.italian: Io sto a casa.
exampleSentences.english: I'm staying at home.

exampleSentences.italian: Io rimango a casa.
exampleSentences.english: I'm remaining at home.

grammarNotes: The phrase consists of 'siamo' (first person plural present of essere, 'to be') + the preposition 'con' ('with') + 'voi' (plural form of 'you'). The personal pronoun 'noi' ('we') is omitted because Italian verb conjugations explicitly indicate the subject; pronouns are only necessary for emphasis or contrast. This is a common feature of pro-drop languages like Italian.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'voi' is the plural 'you' in Italian; use 'tu' for singular. The verb 'essere' is highly irregular, so memorize its present tense conjugation early. In modern Italian, pronouns are often dropped in casual speech when the verb conjugation makes the subject clear, so don't be surprised to hear 'Siamo con voi' without 'noi'.

exampleSentences.english: We are with you!

exampleSentences.italian: Noi siamo con voi, ma voi non siete con noi!
exampleSentences.english: We are with you, but you aren't with us!

grammarNotes: Lavarsi is a reflexive verb conjugated with the reflexive pronoun (mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si) that agrees with the subject. The definite article le is used before mani (hands) instead of possessive adjectives in Italian. In the imperative, the reflexive pronoun attaches to the verb: Lavati (tu singular) or Lavatevi (voi plural).
learnerNotes: Note that Italian uses the definite article le mani instead of a possessive adjective (unlike English 'my hands'), which is the standard pattern for body parts when the possessor is clear from context. The imperative forms attach the reflexive pronoun directly to the verb: Lavati (not Ti lava!). The idiomatic expression 'lavarsi le mani di' mirrors English but requires the preposition di when specifying what one is disclaiming responsibility for.

exampleSentences.italian: (Io) mi lavo le mani
exampleSentences.english: I wash my hands

exampleSentences.italian: (Tu) ti lavi le mani

exampleSentences.english: Wash your hands! (singular)

exampleSentences.italian: Lavatevi le mani!
exampleSentences.english: Wash your hands! (plural)

exampleSentences.italian: Lavati le mani, Carlo! La cena è pronta!

englishTranslation: I don't feel like it! / I don't fancy it! / It doesn't sit well with me!
grammarNotes: This expression combines non (negation) + mi (indirect object pronoun 'to me') + va (3rd person singular present of andare). It literally means '(it) doesn't go for me.' The phrase can stand alone or be followed by di + infinitive. The construction is invariable and does not conjugate based on subject.
learnerNotes: This phrase expresses only momentary feelings or whims, not long-term decisions requiring serious thought. Use it naturally with the adverb tanto to soften the tone and sound less abrupt. Be careful not to confuse this with non ho voglia di (more general 'I don't want') or non me la sento di (which emphasizes lack of confidence or ability).

exampleSentences.italian: Vuoi mangiare fuori stasera? – No, non mi va.
exampleSentences.english: Do you want to eat out tonight? – No, I don't feel like it.

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi va di andare al lavoro.
exampleSentences.english: I don't feel like going to work.

exampleSentences.english: I don't fancy eating pizza.

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi va di vedere questa trasmissione.

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi va tanto di vedere un film.
exampleSentences.english: I don't really feel like watching a movie.

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi va di iscrivermi all'università.
exampleSentences.english: I don't feel like registering for university.

exampleSentences.italian: Ti va di prendere un caffè? – Sì, perché no?
exampleSentences.english: Do you feel like getting a coffee? – Okay, why not?

grammarNotes: Buona is the feminine form of the adjective 'buono' (good), agreeing with the feminine noun Pasqua (Easter). The expression can be modified with indirect object pronouns (a te, a Lei, a voi) to specify the recipient. The structure follows the pattern 'Buona [noun]' common in Italian greetings.
learnerNotes: Remember that Pasqua is feminine, so the adjective is 'buona' not 'buono'. The greeting Buona Pasqua is the most common and neutral way to wish someone Happy Easter in Italian; it's more natural than the longer Auguri di Buona Pasqua in everyday speech. Be careful to use the correct indirect object pronoun (a te/Lei/voi) based on formality and number when personalizing the greeting.

englishTranslation: We can do it! / We will get through this! / We will manage
grammarNotes: This expression is built from the verb farcela (to manage/succeed) combined with the first-person plural future tense. It consists of three components: ce (form of the 'ci' particle) + la (it) + faremo (we will do). The phrase functions as a motivational expression and requires understanding of future tense conjugation and pronominal particles.
learnerNotes: The particle ce (ci) + la combination can be tricky for learners; remember that la is the direct object pronoun 'it' referring to the implied task or situation. This expression became widely used during the COVID-19 pandemic in Italy as a rallying cry. Pay attention to the full conjugation of farcela across different persons, as the future tense endings follow regular -are verb patterns but with the pronominal particles always attached.

grammarNotes: The verb mancare (to miss/to lack) uses an indirect object construction: the person who is missed becomes the subject, and the person doing the missing becomes the indirect object (mi). The personal pronoun tu is typically omitted since the verb conjugation clarifies the subject. Conjugation varies by person: mi manchi (you singular), mi manca (he/she/it/formal you), mi mancate (you plural), mi mancano (they).
learnerNotes: Remember that mancare uses indirect object pronouns (mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi, gli) rather than direct objects—this is a key difference from English. The pronoun tu is almost always omitted in casual speech, but include it only for emphasis or clarity. Note that formal relationships (boss, shopkeeper) rarely trigger this phrase in Italian; it's reserved for people whose absence genuinely affects you emotionally.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi manchi tanto. Quando posso venire a trovarti?
exampleSentences.english: I miss you so much. When can I come and see you?

exampleSentences.italian: Tu mi manchi ma lui non mi manca.

grammarNotes: This is a fixed greeting expression. 'Buona' is the feminine singular form of the adjective 'buono' (good), agreeing with the feminine noun 'Festa' (celebration). The preposition 'della' is a contraction of 'di + la' (of the). The phrase can be modified by substituting 'buona' with 'felice' (happy) without changing the structure.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'Buona Festa della Mamma' uses the feminine form 'buona' because 'festa' (celebration) is feminine. The article states Mother's Day falls on the second Sunday in May in Italy and most Western countries. Note that 'mamma' is informal and affectionate; if writing formally, 'madre' might be used instead, though 'mamma' is standard for Mother's Day greetings.

exampleSentences.english: Happy Mother's Day!

englishTranslation: Have a nice day / Have a good day
grammarNotes: Buona giornata is an invariant greeting expression where buona (feminine) agrees with giornata (feminine noun). Unlike buongiorno, it is never used as a standard greeting—only when parting ways or saying goodbye. The expression can be intensified with ti/Le/vi auguro (I wish you) followed by una buona giornata or di passare una buona giornata.
learnerNotes: Do not confuse buongiorno with buona giornata: buongiorno is a standard greeting used when arriving or leaving any time of day, while buona giornata is exclusively a farewell used in the morning or early afternoon. Use ti auguro for informal singular, Le auguro for formal singular, and vi auguro for plural. The verb passare (to spend) is preferred over avere (to have) in the emphatic form ti/Le/vi auguro di passare una buona giornata.

exampleSentences.italian: Buongiorno. Come sta?
exampleSentences.english: Good morning! How are you?

exampleSentences.italian: Ci sentiamo domani. Buona giornata!
exampleSentences.english: We'll talk tomorrow. Have a nice day!

exampleSentences.italian: Buona giornata, Silvio! – Anche a te!
exampleSentences.english: Have a nice day, Silvio! – You too!

exampleSentences.english: I wish you a nice day! (formal)

grammarNotes: Grazie is the plural of the noun 'grazia' (grace/favour) and is used as an invariable expression. It can be followed by prepositions 'per' or 'di' (mostly interchangeable) to introduce a noun or verb. When followed by 'a', it means 'thanks to' and denotes consequence or reason. The verb form is 'ringraziare' (to thank).
learnerNotes: Grazie works for both positive and negative responses to offers—say 'Sì, grazie!' for yes please and 'No, grazie.' for no thank you. Note that 'grazie di tutto' and 'grazie di cuore' are fixed expressions where 'per' cannot substitute 'di'. Be aware that grazie can also be used sarcastically to mean 'of course' or 'no wonder' when responding to an obvious statement.

exampleSentences.italian: Ricordati di dire grazie, sempre.
exampleSentences.english: Always remember to say thank you.

exampleSentences.italian: Grazie di avermelo detto. Grazie per avermelo detto.
exampleSentences.english: Thank you for telling me.

exampleSentences.italian: Grazie della tua risposta. Grazie per la tua risposta.
exampleSentences.english: Thank you for your response.

exampleSentences.italian: Grazie di essere te stesso. Grazie per essere te stesso.
exampleSentences.english: Thank you for being you.

exampleSentences.italian: Grazie dei bellissimi fiori! Grazie per i bellissimi fiori!
exampleSentences.english: Thank you for the beautiful flowers!

exampleSentences.italian: Grazie alla generosità di Paolo, possiamo cavarcela anche questo mese.
exampleSentences.english: Thanks to Paolo's generosity, we can get through this month too!

exampleSentences.italian: Sì, grazie!
exampleSentences.english: Yes, please!

grammarNotes: Ciao ciao is the doubled form of ciao, used exclusively as a farewell. Unlike the singular ciao, which serves both as greeting and goodbye, ciao ciao functions only when saying goodbye. The repetition intensifies informality and affection, and may be repeated three or four times with pauses for emphasis, especially in phone conversations.
learnerNotes: Ciao ciao is strictly a farewell—never use it to greet someone at the start of a conversation. Remember that ciao and ciao ciao are only appropriate with people you know well and would address informally with tu; avoid using them with authority figures or in formal contexts. The etymology from Venetian s-ciào vostro ('I am your slave') reflects an old expression of availability and loyalty, not literal servitude.

exampleSentences.italian: Ciao Enrica, come stai?
exampleSentences.english: Hi Enrica, how are you?

exampleSentences.italian: Ciao Enrica, ci vediamo domani!
exampleSentences.english: Bye Enrica, see you tomorrow!

exampleSentences.italian: Ok, ci vediamo presto, ciao ciao…
exampleSentences.english: Ok, see you soon, bye bye…

exampleSentences.italian: Fai ciao alla mamma. Brava!
exampleSentences.english: Say hello/goodbye to mummy. Good girl!

to wave goodbye; to make the gesture of opening and closing one's hand in greeting

englishTranslation: Yes, I know / Yes, I know that
grammarNotes: The phrase combines Sì (yes) + lo (direct object pronoun 'it') + so (first person singular of sapere 'to know'). Personal pronouns like io are typically omitted in Italian unless necessary for clarification. The pronoun lo is essential when 'I know' stands alone or is followed by 'that'; it cannot be omitted as it can in English.
learnerNotes: The key distinction is that 'I know' requires lo when it stands alone or precedes 'that,' but omit lo when followed by a noun, verb, or clause (e.g., So che... 'I know that...'). Adverbs like già, bene, benissimo commonly accompany lo so to add nuance. Remember that personal pronouns (io, tu, lui, etc.) are optional and usually omitted unless emphasizing who is doing the knowing.

exampleSentences.italian: Giulia non viene oggi. – (Sì,) lo so.
exampleSentences.english: Giulia isn't coming today. – (Yes,) I know (that).

exampleSentences.italian: Lo so più che bene.
exampleSentences.english: I know more than well.

exampleSentences.italian: Lo so fin troppo bene.

englishTranslation: Hello, my name is… / Hi, I call myself…
grammarNotes: The verb 'chiamare' (to call) is reflexive here as 'mi chiamo' (I call myself). The personal pronoun 'io' is typically omitted in Italian. 'Ciao' is informal; use 'Buongiorno' or 'Buonasera' in formal contexts. The phrase structure is: greeting + reflexive verb + name.
learnerNotes: Avoid 'Il mio nome è…' for introductions—it's grammatically sound but sounds unnatural in conversation. In formal settings, replace 'Ciao' with 'Buongiorno' or 'Buonasera' and use the formal pronoun -La ending on 'conoscere.' The shorter form 'Sono [name]' is equally common and more natural in casual settings.

exampleSentences.english: Hello, my name is Matteo.

grammarNotes: This is a fixed greeting expression composed of the adjective 'buona' (good, feminine to agree with 'festa'), the noun 'festa' (celebration), and the possessive 'del papà' (of the dad). The structure follows the Italian greeting pattern of 'Buona + [occasion].' Gender agreement is required: use 'buona' for feminine nouns and 'buono' for masculine ones.
learnerNotes: Note that in Italy, Father's Day (Festa del Papà) is celebrated on March 19th, not in June like most English-speaking countries. Use 'Ti voglio bene' (literally 'I want well for you') for familial and platonic love; reserve 'Ti amo' strictly for romantic contexts. The greeting 'Buona Festa' follows a common Italian pattern—you can apply this structure to other celebrations like 'Buona Pasqua' (Happy Easter) or 'Buon Natale' (Merry Christmas).

grammarNotes: This expression combines the direct object pronoun 'ti' (you), the first-person present indicative 'amo' (I love from amare), and the contraction 'anch'io' (also I, formed from anche + io). The phrase can be inverted to 'Anch'io ti amo!' without changing meaning. Ti amo is exclusively reserved for romantic partners or deeply committed relationships.
learnerNotes: Critical distinction: 'Ti amo anch'io' is strictly for romantic partners in committed relationships, while 'Ti voglio bene anch'io' is the appropriate response for family, friends, and children. Using 'ti amo' with someone you're not romantically involved with can create awkward misunderstandings. Always ensure reciprocated feelings before declaring 'ti amo' to avoid the 'love bomb' effect.

englishTranslation: Enjoy your meal / Bon appétit / Good appetite
grammarNotes: Buon appetito is an invariable exclamation combining the adjective buon (good) with the noun appetito (appetite). It does not change form regardless of gender or number. The proper response is grazie, altrettanto (thanks, likewise) or grazie, anche a te/voi (thanks, and to you/you too).
learnerNotes: Buon appetito is said before eating, not after, and is extremely common in Italian restaurants and homes. While it historically signified gratitude toward the poor, today it's a standard greeting before meals across all social classes. Be aware that a small minority of modern Italians consider it outdated or prefer formal alternatives like prego, but it remains widely used and saying it is generally appreciated.

englishTranslation: You're so beautiful! / How beautiful you are!
grammarNotes: The expression combines the intensifier 'ma' (optional but emphatic) + 'come' (how) + 'sei' (are, 2nd person singular of essere) + 'bella' (beautiful, feminine). The feminine adjective 'bella' must agree with the female subject. The personal pronoun 'tu' is typically omitted in spoken Italian when context is clear.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'bella' must agree in gender with the person being complimented—use 'bella' for women and 'bello' for men. The 'ma' at the beginning is optional but adds emotional emphasis; it does not mean 'but' in this context. The personal pronoun 'tu' can be dropped in conversation since the subject is clear from context, so both 'Tu sei bella!' and 'Sei bella!' are equally correct and natural.

grammarNotes: Mi dispiace is an impersonal construction using the indirect object pronoun 'mi' (to me) with the verb dispiacere (to displease). It conjugates with essere in compound tenses. The construction often appears with a subordinate clause introduced by 'che' + subjunctive mood, as in 'Mi dispiace che tu non sia riuscita.'
learnerNotes: Be careful: mi dispiace expresses regret or sympathy about situations, NOT apology for personal mistakes—use scusa/scusami for that instead. Non mi dispiace ('I don't mind') is used for mild approval, a unique Italian usage not found in English's literal 'I'm sorry.' You may hear both mi dispiace and scusa together in the same sentence for emphasis.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi dispiace che tu non sia riuscita a superare l'esame.
exampleSentences.english: I'm sorry you didn't pass the exam.

exampleSentences.english: I'm sorry but the coffee has run out.

grammarNotes: Composed of stare (to stay) in informal singular imperative (stai) + zitto (silent/quiet, which agrees in gender/number: zitto/zitta/zitti/zitte). For plural use State zitti!. The formal imperative stia zitto exists but is rarely used in practice due to the inherent rudeness of the command.
learnerNotes: Stai zitto! is highly disrespectful and contentious—avoid using it in polite or formal contexts. The adjective zitto must agree with the subject in gender and number (zitto/zitta/zitti/zitte). For addressing multiple people or strangers, prefer milder alternatives like Silenzio! or Taci!, or use the formal imperative stia zitto when necessary, though its rudeness remains unchanged.

exampleSentences.english: Shut up, I can't hear anything!

englishTranslation: Have a nice evening! / Have a good evening!
grammarNotes: Buona serata is a fixed expression combining the adjective buona (fem. sing., agreeing with serata) and the noun serata (evening). It uses the subjunctive/imperative mood implicitly. The expression can be modified with indirect object pronouns (ti, Le, vi) and the verb augurare to intensify the wish.
learnerNotes: Buona serata is specifically used only when parting ways, not when greeting someone—use buonasera for that. The similar-sounding buonasera is more formal and serves double duty as greeting or goodbye. Remember that serata is feminine, so the adjective must be buona (not buono), and you can personalize it with pronouns (ti, Le, vi) plus augurare for emphasis.

englishTranslation: I want to be/stay with you
grammarNotes: Composed of voglio (first person present indicative of volere 'to want') + stare (infinitive 'to stay') + con (with) + te (you). The subject pronoun io can be omitted since verb conjugation identifies the subject, but is used for emphasis or distinction. Stare is preferred over essere in Italian for expressing relationships and cohabitation.
learnerNotes: Stare is the preferred verb for expressing romantic relationships and cohabitation in Italian, not essere. The phrase can indicate either short-term togetherness (tonight) or long-term commitment (forever) depending on context. Note that rimanere implies continuation of an existing relationship, while vivere emphasizes moving in together or a deeper commitment level.

englishTranslation: I'm lost / I have lost my way / I got lost
grammarNotes: This is a reflexive verb construction using the present perfect tense of 'essere' with the past participle 'perso/a'. Gender agreement is required: use 'perso' for masculine speakers and 'persa' for feminine speakers. The plural forms are 'Ci siamo persi' (mixed or all-male groups) and 'Ci siamo perse' (all-female groups). Can also be used in past tense: 'mi ero perso' (I had gotten lost).
learnerNotes: Remember that gender agreement is mandatory—use 'perso' or 'persa' depending on your gender, not based on who you're talking to. The phrase uses 'essere' (to be) as the auxiliary verb, so it follows the standard present perfect pattern for reflexive verbs. You can intensify this phrase by adding adverbs like 'completamente' or 'totalmente', and it's polite to start with 'Mi scusi' when asking for help on the street.

englishTranslation: Not bad! / Not bad at all!
grammarNotes: Mica male is a litote—a negative understatement expressing positive meaning. It consists of the adverb 'mica' (meaning 'not/at all/in the least') + the adjective 'male' (bad). Can stand alone or follow the verb 'essere' (to be). The phrase inverts literal meaning to convey approval or satisfaction.
learnerNotes: Mica male expresses strong approval through understatement—the literal 'not bad' actually means 'very good' or 'excellent.' This is typical of Italian litotes and may confuse learners expecting literal negation. Use it in informal conversational contexts; it sounds more natural and authentic than always using overtly positive expressions like 'Fantastico!' The synonym 'niente male' is equally common and interchangeable.

englishTranslation: It doesn't matter / Never mind / No problem / No big deal
grammarNotes: The phrase consists of the negation 'non' + the third-person singular present tense of 'fare' (to do/make) + 'niente' (nothing). It can be shortened to 'fa niente' in casual conversation. The word 'niente' can be replaced with 'nulla' (another word for nothing) without changing the meaning: 'Non fa nulla.'
learnerNotes: This is an essential reassuring phrase for daily conversation. Remember that 'fa niente' (shortened form) is very common in spoken Italian and sounds more natural than the full 'non fa niente.' Both 'niente' and 'nulla' are interchangeable synonyms for 'nothing,' so 'non fa nulla' means exactly the same thing as 'non fa niente.'

grammarNotes: The phrase requires the definite article 'la' before the noun 'vita'; omitting it is incorrect in Italian. Remember the grave accent on 'è' (is); without it, 'e' means 'and' instead. The superlative form 'bellissima' adds emotional emphasis; use it when expressing stronger conviction.

grammarNotes: Buon is the masculine singular form of the adjective 'buono' (good), agreeing with the masculine noun compleanno (birthday). The phrase uses buon rather than felice (happy), though felice compleanno appears in longer constructions like 'Ti auguro un felice compleanno.' Buon undergoes elision before vowels, becoming bu' in some contexts.

Note that 'felice' (happy) is rarely substituted directly for 'buon' in the main greeting, though it appears in longer phrases. For milestone birthdays, Italian numbers transform the adjective (sedicesimo, diciottesimo, trentesimo, etc.) — these ordinal forms must agree in gender/number with compleanno.

grammarNotes: This phrase combines the preposition 'di' (of) + 'dove' (where) + 'sei' (2nd person singular of essere). When stating origin, use 'Sono di + città' for cities, but 'Vengo da + articolo + paese/regione' for countries and regions (the definite article is mandatory: dal Canada, dalla Francia, dagli Stati Uniti). grammarNotes: Mangiamo is the noi (we) conjugation of the infinitive mangiare (to eat) in the present tense, formed by adding -iamo to the stem. When used as an imperative without the pronoun noi, it means 'let's eat.' The -iamo ending is characteristic of first conjugation (-are) verbs and can only attach to the noi subject, making the subject pronoun optional.
learnerNotes: The -iamo ending serves double duty: it can be declarative (we eat) or imperative (let's eat). When using it as an imperative suggestion, omit the noi pronoun—saying 'Mangiamo!' is more natural than 'Noi mangiamo!' Learn the softer alternatives (Ti va di mangiare? Perché non mangiamo?) to sound more conversational. Remember that -iamo only occurs with noi, so listeners always understand the subject without it being stated.

grammarNotes: Cucù is an exclamatory expression used in the context of the game 'il gioco del cucù' (the peekaboo game). It is not conjugated and functions as an interjection. The expression is typically pronounced in a high-pitched, playful voice when revealing one's face to an infant.
learnerNotes: Cucù is primarily used in childcare contexts and is not part of standard adult vocabulary. The expression is always accompanied by the physical act of covering and revealing one's face, making it a complete communicative gesture. Regional variations exist across Italy, so you may encounter different expressions depending on where you travel within the country.

englishTranslation: Trick or treat! / Little treat or little joke?
grammarNotes: This is an idiomatic expression used during Halloween. It consists of two noun phrases joined by 'o' (or). The suffix '-etto' is a diminutive that attaches to nouns to indicate something small or little: dolce (sweet) becomes dolcetto (little sweet/small treat), and scherzo (joke/trick) becomes scherzetto (little joke/trick). The question form is typically expressed with the rising intonation rather than inverted syntax.
learnerNotes: The diminutive suffix '-etto' is essential to understanding this expression; without it, you'd say 'dolce o scherzo' which sounds less playful. While 'dolcetto o scherzetto' is now standard in modern Italian Halloween culture, many Italians may not be familiar with it since Halloween traditions are relatively recent in Italy. Note that the expression functions as a complete sentence when used with rising intonation, similar to English.

italianTerm: Buon Halloween! / Felice Halloween! / Buona Festa di Halloween!
grammarNotes: All three expressions are greetings using different structures. 'Buon Halloween!' uses the masculine singular adjective 'buon' (short form of 'buono') before a borrowed English noun. 'Felice Halloween!' pairs the adjective 'felice' (happy) with Halloween. 'Buona Festa di Halloween!' uses 'buona' (feminine singular) agreeing with 'festa' (f.), followed by the prepositional phrase 'di Halloween.' The choice depends on context and formality level.
learnerNotes: Note that 'Halloween' is a borrowed English word in Italian, so it doesn't follow typical gender agreement patterns—use 'buon' (masculine singular) or 'buona festa di' (treating it as feminine through 'festa'). The phrase is rarely heard in everyday Italian life since Halloween is not a traditional Italian holiday; you'll encounter it mainly at parties or in younger, more international contexts. Be aware that 'Carnevale' (February) is the traditional Italian costume festival, so Halloween celebrations remain less deeply rooted than in English-speaking countries.

Alternative constructions use spostare or tirare as the main verb instead of tornare.

Note the gender and number agreement: 'lancette' (feminine plural) requires 'sono tornate' and 'spostate,' not 'tornati' or 'spostati.' Use the presente pro futuro (present tense for future) in everyday speech: 'le lancette devono essere spostate' is more common than the conditional form in colloquial contexts.

Remember that reflexive alternatives (mi sono preso/a, mi sono pigliato/a) must agree with the speaker's gender; use -o/-a for masculine/feminine. 'Cotta' literally comes from 'cooked,' reflecting the metaphor of feelings being 'cooked up' inside you—this is not a false cognate but a genuine etymological link worth remembering.

Pay attention to the placement of 'ci'—it's a pronoun that can move between positions (Non ci posso credere vs. Non posso crederci), both being equally correct. Remember that 'credere' takes 'a' with direct objects (credere a qualcuno) but 'in' when expressing conviction (credere in Dio).

Note that Italian uses the definite article 'il' before 'tempo' where English omits it—this is typical for Italian idioms. The verb 'volare' is regular; pay attention to the inversion in emphatic questions ('Come vola il tempo?') versus statements ('Il tempo vola quando...').

relatedExpressions.meaning: It's incredible how time flies (with introductory clause)

grammarNotes: C'era is a contraction of ci (there) + era (was), the imperfect tense of essere. Una is the feminine indefinite article (a), and volta means time/occasion. The phrase literally translates to 'there was a time.' Related forms include c'è (there is), ci sono (there are), and c'erano (there were).
learnerNotes: This is the quintessential opening phrase for Italian fairy tales and children's stories. The imperfect tense (c'era) is essential for storytelling about the past, so practicing this phrase helps reinforce that tense. Remember that volta can mean 'time' in the sense of 'occasion' or 'turn'—it's distinct from tempo (time duration) and ora (hour/time of day).

exampleSentences.italian: C'era una volta un castello dove vivevano un re e una regina.
exampleSentences.english: Once upon a time there was a castle where a king and queen lived.

relatedExpressions.meaning: And they lived happy and content (And they all lived happily ever after)

englishTranslation: Christmas is here! / Christmas has arrived!
grammarNotes: This is a compound expression using the present tense of essere (è) + past participle (arrivato). The verb arrivare takes essere as its auxiliary verb because it denotes movement. The past participle arrivato agrees in gender and number with the masculine noun Natale. The word order can be inverted to È arrivato il Natale without changing meaning.
learnerNotes: Use Natale è arrivato! when emphasizing the arrival or coming of Christmas; use Natale è qui when indicating physical presence only. The verb arrivare (to arrive) is preferred over essere qui (to be here) when discussing the temporal arrival of events or seasons in Italian. Note that arrivato must agree with the masculine singular noun Natale, so the ending is always -o for this phrase.

exampleSentences.italian: Natale è arrivato!
exampleSentences.english: Christmas is here!

exampleSentences.italian: È arrivato il Natale!
exampleSentences.english: Christmas is here!

exampleSentences.italian: Babbo Natale è qui.
exampleSentences.english: Santa Claus is here. (physically present in this location)

exampleSentences.italian: Babbo Natale è arrivato.
exampleSentences.english: Santa Claus is here. (has just arrived from elsewhere)

exampleSentences.italian: È arrivato Babbo Natale.
exampleSentences.english: Santa Claus is here. (inverted word order)

exampleSentences.italian: Natale è qui.
exampleSentences.english: Christmas is here. (acceptable but less common)

relatedExpressions.meaning: Christmas is here (denotes physical presence rather than arrival)

grammarNotes: Buon is the masculine singular form of the adjective 'buono' (good), used here to agree with the masculine noun 'anno' (year). When addressing specific individuals, the phrase can be modified with personal pronouns (a te, a Lei, a voi) or conjugated verb forms (ti auguro, Le auguro, vi auguro). The expression remains unchanged regardless of the speaker's gender.
learnerNotes: Use 'Buon Anno a te!' with friends and family, but switch to 'Buon Anno a Lei!' (with capital L) when addressing strangers, elders, or people of higher status—this formal distinction is crucial in Italian. 'Auguri!' is a versatile abbreviation that works for any context and can also mean 'good luck' beyond New Year. Note that 'Felice Anno Nuovo' is more common in written greetings (cards) than in speech, whereas 'Buon Anno' dominates casual conversation.

exampleSentences.english: Happy New Year to all!

exampleSentences.italian: Ti auguro un buon anno!
exampleSentences.english: I wish you a Happy New Year!

exampleSentences.italian: Le auguro un buon anno!
exampleSentences.english: I wish you a Happy New Year! (formal)

exampleSentences.italian: Vi auguro un buon anno!
exampleSentences.english: I wish you all a Happy New Year!

exampleSentences.italian: Buon anno a te!
exampleSentences.english: Happy New Year to you! (informal)

exampleSentences.italian: Buon anno a Lei!
exampleSentences.english: Happy New Year to you! (formal)

exampleSentences.italian: Buon anno a voi!
exampleSentences.english: Happy New Year to you all!

exampleSentences.italian: Buon anno, Marco! – Altrettanto!
exampleSentences.english: Happy New Year, Marco! – And to you!

exampleSentences.italian: Che questo 2023 sia pieno di gioia e soddisfazioni! Buon anno!
exampleSentences.english: May this 2023 be full of joy and satisfaction! Happy New Year!

exampleSentences.italian: Ti auguro tanta gioia e tante risate in questo nuovo anno!
exampleSentences.english: I wish you much joy and laughter in this new year!

exampleSentences.english: I wish you and your entire family a 2023 full of peace, health and prosperity. Happy New Year!

relatedExpressions.meaning: And to you / Same to you (response)

grammarNotes: Fai is the second person singular imperative of fare (to do/make). In formal address, use faccia instead. For plural (two or more people), conjugate to fate. The expression can be shortened informally to Con calma! The apostrophe form fa' is an alternative spelling of fai.
learnerNotes: This phrase can be used sincerely to reassure someone there's no rush, or sarcastically to criticize someone for being slow. Pay attention to context and tone to distinguish the two uses. Remember to conjugate fare correctly based on whether you're addressing one person (fai/faccia) or multiple people (fate). The formal faccia is essential when speaking to strangers or in professional settings.

exampleSentences.italian: Fai con calma, non c'è nessuna fretta!
exampleSentences.english: Take your time, there's no rush at all!

exampleSentences.italian: Fate con calma. Tanto siamo in anticipo.
exampleSentences.english: Take your time. We're early after all.

exampleSentences.italian: Si accomodi signor Rossi e faccia pure con calma, l'avvocato sarà da Lei fra qualche minuto.
exampleSentences.english: Please sit down and take your time, mister Rossi, the lawyer will be with you in a few minutes.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei ancora in pigiama? Prego, fai con calma! Dobbiamo solo uscire fra cinque minuti!
exampleSentences.english: You're still in your pyjamas? Please, take your time! We only need to go out within the next five minutes!

relatedExpressions.meaning: Take your time (literally: take your time)

relatedExpressions.expression: Prenditi il tempo che ti serve.
relatedExpressions.meaning: Take the time that you need

grammarNotes: This expression uses the conditional form 'vorrei' (I would like/I wish) combined with the imperfect subjunctive 'fossi' (were). The subjunctive is required after 'vorrei che' when expressing a wish about something that is impossible or unlikely to happen. The subject pronoun 'tu' can be omitted if context is clear.
learnerNotes: Do not confuse 'vorrei' (I wish/would like) with 'augurare' (to wish someone something good) or 'desiderare' (to strongly desire)—each has distinct uses. Remember that the imperfect subjunctive 'fossi' is required here because the wish is counterfactual (contrary to reality). This expression is common for expressing nostalgia or missing someone, particularly across distances like international friendships.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei che tu fossi qui.
exampleSentences.english: I wish you were here.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei che fossi qui.
exampleSentences.english: I wish (you) were here.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei poter guidare.
exampleSentences.english: I wish I could drive.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei che smettesse di piovere.
exampleSentences.english: I wish it would stop raining.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei aver studiato di più.
exampleSentences.english: I wish I had studied more.

exampleSentences.italian: Ti auguro una bella giornata.
exampleSentences.english: I wish you a nice day.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho sempre desiderato una vita migliore.
exampleSentences.english: I've always wished for a better life.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to wish someone something good (typically used with a direct object)
to wish in the sense of strong desire or craving; to desire
to make a wish (in a magical sense, as on a star or birthday candles)

grammarNotes: Alla is an articulated preposition combining 'a' (at/to) + 'la' (the feminine singular article). Prossima is the feminine form of the adjective prossimo (next/close), where volta (time) is omitted but implied from context. The full form is 'Alla prossima volta!' but the shortened version is more common in everyday speech.
learnerNotes: Alla prossima! is a natural, friendly closing phrase that works well in casual conversations. The word volta (time) is understood from context, so you don't need to say it—the shortened form is actually more common than 'Alla prossima volta!' Watch out: prossimo/a/i/e must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies; here it's feminine singular because volta is feminine. This expression is safe for all contexts but is most natural in casual, friendly speech.

exampleSentences.english: Bye guys, until next time!

exampleSentences.italian: Ci vediamo la prossima volta!
exampleSentences.english: See you next time!

exampleSentences.english: See you later!

exampleSentences.english: See you soon!

englishTranslation: Such is life! / That's life. / C'est la vie!
grammarNotes: The phrase combines the adverb così (like this/in this way), the present tense verb è (is), the feminine singular definite article la, and the noun vita (life). In Italian, vita requires the definite article when discussing life in general, unlike English. The word order can be rearranged to la vita è così with the same meaning.
learnerNotes: This phrase is used to express acceptance or resignation—both seriously and jokingly—when facing difficult situations. Remember that vita always takes the definite article la in Italian when referring to life generally, a key difference from English. The variation Così è fatta la vita is equally common and useful to recognize.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi spiace che non ti abbiano prolungato il contratto di lavoro. – Eh vabbè, pazienza, così è la vita! Cercherò qualcos'altro.
exampleSentences.english: I'm sorry that they haven't extended your job contract. – Yeah well, whatever, that's life! I'll look for something else.

exampleSentences.italian: godersi la vita
exampleSentences.english: to enjoy life

exampleSentences.italian: la vita è bella
exampleSentences.english: life is beautiful

relatedExpressions.meaning: Life is made like this (popular variation using past participle of fare)

englishTranslation: Good for you / It's alright for some / Whoop-dee-do
grammarNotes: Composed of three elements: 'buon' is the apocopated form of the adjective 'buono' (good) used before a singular masculine noun; 'per' is a preposition meaning 'for'; 'te' is the second person informal pronoun. The phrase requires no conjugation and remains invariable, though tone of voice dramatically alters its meaning from genuine to sarcastic.
learnerNotes: This phrase is deceptively simple in structure but highly dependent on tone and context for interpretation. While it can express genuine happiness, it is far more commonly used sarcastically to convey indifference, mild jealousy, or dismissal. Be cautious using this with native speakers in casual situations, as tone can easily determine whether you appear rude or friendly.

exampleSentences.italian: Mio padre mi ha regalato una Ferrari per Natale! – Buon per te.
exampleSentences.english: My dad gave me a Ferrari for Christmas! – Good for you…

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi non devo studiare quindi passo la giornata in montagna. – Buon per te. Io invece ho dieci compiti da consegnare…
exampleSentences.english: I don't have to study today so I'm spending the day in the mountains. – Good for you. I, on the other hand, have ten assignments to hand in…

grammarNotes: This is an exclamatory greeting phrase composed of the adjective 'buon' (good) agreeing with the masculine noun 'pomeriggio' (afternoon). The apostrophe in 'buon' indicates elision before a vowel. The exclamation mark signals its function as a farewell or welcome expression.
learnerNotes: While grammatically correct, 'Buon pomeriggio' is rarely used in everyday Italian conversation and sounds quite formal or artificial. Italians typically use 'Buona giornata!' in the afternoon instead, reserving 'Buon pomeriggio' for broadcast media. Don't worry about using this phrase naturally in casual settings—focus on 'Buona giornata!' and 'Buona serata!' for authentic communication.

exampleSentences.italian: Buon pomeriggio a tutti i nostri ascoltatori e ben ritrovati.
exampleSentences.english: Good afternoon everyone, and welcome back.

afternoon (the time period between noon and evening)

englishTranslation: Hello, my love! / Hi, my love! / Bye, my love!
grammarNotes: This expression combines ciao (an informal greeting/farewell), amore (masculine noun meaning 'love'), and mio (first-person masculine singular possessive adjective). Mio agrees with the masculine noun amore, not the gender of the person addressed. The phrase functions as an affectionate form of address and does not require the definite article il when used as direct address.
learnerNotes: Remember that ciao functions as both 'hello' and 'bye'—context determines meaning. When using amore with the definite article (il mio amore), it refers to the loved one as a noun phrase and is not used as direct address. Note that Italians use amore not only for romantic partners but also for children and family members, making it a versatile term of affection.

exampleSentences.english: Hello, my love! / Bye, my love!

grammarNotes: The expression uses avere (to have) rather than essere (to be), which is typical in Italian for physical sensations. 'Ho' is the first-person singular present indicative of avere, and 'sete' is a feminine noun meaning thirst. Italian frequently uses avere + noun where English uses 'to be' + adjective (e.g., ho fame = I'm hungry, ho freddo = I'm cold).
learnerNotes: Remember that Italian uses avere (to have) + noun for physical sensations where English uses 'to be' + adjective—this is a key structural difference. The formal alternative 'sono assetato' exists but is rarely used in everyday conversation; stick with 'ho sete' for authentic communication. Notice that intensity can be easily modulated by adding adjectives (tanta, molta, pazzesca) or idiomatic expressions, making this a versatile phrase for expressing different degrees of thirst.

grammarNotes: This phrase uses hai, the second person singular present indicative of avere (to have). The subject pronoun tu is dropped because it's clear from context. Un is the masculine singular indefinite article (shortened from uno via apocope). For formal situations, use Ha instead of hai with Lei.
learnerNotes: Remember that subject pronouns (tu/Lei) are typically omitted in Italian when context makes them clear, so "Hai un minuto?" naturally drops tu. Always use ha instead of hai when addressing someone formally (boss, client, stranger). The friendly response "Anche due!" is idiomatic—learners should memorize it as a fixed expression rather than trying to construct it logically.

exampleSentences.english: Do you have a minute?

grammarNotes: Che cosa is the literary form of 'what' (che = what, cosa = thing). Vuoi is the 2nd person singular present indicative of volere (to want). Regional variation exists: cosa alone is preferred in northern Italy and Sardinia, while che alone prevails in central-southern regions. The pronoun tu can be added for emphasis: Tu che cosa vuoi? or Che cosa vuoi tu?
learnerNotes: This phrase is very direct and can sound rude if used with people you don't know well—use Che cosa desidera? in formal situations instead. When said with an aggressive tone, it becomes an expression of annoyance. Note the regional variation: northern speakers prefer cosa alone, while southern speakers prefer che alone, but the full form che cosa works everywhere and is considered literary/standard.

exampleSentences.italian: Allora, Maria vuole un caffè, Marco dice che vuole un cappuccino. E tu, che cosa vuoi?

grammarNotes: Mi chiedo uses the reflexive verb chiedersi (to ask oneself/to wonder), conjugated in the present tense first person singular. The pronoun mi is attached to the verb stem. Perché is an interrogative adverb meaning 'why' and should not be confused with the conjunction perché meaning 'because'. The phrase can be expanded with noun clauses following perché.
learnerNotes: Remember that perché as an interrogative adverb (why) is different from perché as a conjunction (because)—context and intonation distinguish them. The reflexive verb chiedersi requires reflexive pronouns (mi, ti, si, ci, vi); pay attention to the pronoun changes across conjugations. In colloquial speech, Italians may add Ma (but) or pause/repeat perché for emphasis, which softens or dramatizes the expression.

grammarNotes: A presto is composed of the preposition 'a' (to/at) + the adverb 'presto' (soon). It functions as a standalone farewell expression and requires no conjugation. The phrase is invariable and used identically regardless of context or interlocutor number.
learnerNotes: A presto! is strictly informal and should only be used with close friends, family, or peers—avoid using it in formal or professional settings where arrivederci is more appropriate. The similar expression 'Ci vediamo presto!' is equally casual but slightly more explicit in meaning. Remember that 'presto' as an adverb can also mean 'quickly' or 'early' depending on context, but in this farewell expression it exclusively means 'soon.'

exampleSentences.italian: Ciao Marco, a presto!
exampleSentences.english: Bye Marco, see you soon!

grammarNotes: Parli is the informal second-person singular form of parlare (to speak). The subject pronoun tu is typically omitted in Italian but can be included for emphasis. The formal alternative is Parla italiano? (using Lei). Languages in Italian are not capitalized. Both 'Parli italiano?' and 'Parli l'italiano?' are grammatically correct, though usage varies by region.
learnerNotes: Use Parli italiano? with peers and younger people; use Parla italiano? with strangers, elders, or those of higher status. Remember that the direct object pronoun lo (it) is used in responses: 'lo parlo' (I speak it). Be aware that while both forms with and without the definite article are correct, regional preferences vary—some speakers find the article unnecessary while others expect it.
