to put pasta into boiling water
dried pasta (drained of water before sauce is added)
to have a finger in the pie, to be involved

relatedExpressions.expression: Vediamo di che pasta sei fatto!
relatedExpressions.meaning: Let's see what you're made of!
a different kettle of fish, a different character

grammarNotes: Felice is an adjective ending in -e, so it has only two forms: felice (singular, both masculine and feminine) and felici (plural, both masculine and feminine). The ending remains unchanged in the singular regardless of gender, changing only to mark plurality. This is a common pattern for Italian adjectives ending in -e.
learnerNotes: Felice and contento both mean 'happy,' but they differ in use: felice refers to a general state of being or character, while contento describes happiness about something specific and temporary. However, both are acceptable for short-term happiness. Note the false cognate: 'felicity' in English refers to appropriate phrasing or elegant style, whereas felice in Italian primarily means 'happy,' though it can also mean 'fitting' in certain contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Secondo un sondaggio, gli Italiani tendono ad essere molto felici.
exampleSentences.english: According to a survey, Italians tend to be very happy.

exampleSentences.italian: Penso che questa traduzione sia poco felice.
exampleSentences.english: I don't think this translation is very fitting.

exampleSentences.italian: Ero contento di sentire la voce dei miei genitori dopo un anno senza sentirli.
exampleSentences.english: I was happy to hear my parents' voices after a year of not hearing from them.

exampleSentences.italian: I bambini sono molto felici di vedere la mamma.
exampleSentences.english: The children are very happy to see their mother.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to have a talent in something/to have a skill (literally: to have the happy hand)

englishTranslation: power / can / be able to / be allowed to
grammarNotes: Potere functions as both a noun (masculine; plural: poteri) and a modal verb. As a modal verb, it is highly irregular in conjugation: posso, puoi, può, possiamo, potete, possono (present tense). When paired with essere or darsi, it functions as an adverb of doubt expressing possibility or likelihood.
learnerNotes: Potere is a highly irregular modal verb—memorize its conjugation early as it appears frequently in conversation. Distinguish between potere (ability/permission) and potenza (physical/mathematical power or superpower status); potenza is a noun only. When expressing doubt or possibility, use può essere che or può darsi che with the subjunctive in the dependent clause.

exampleSentences.italian: Il capo del governo ha il potere di sciogliere il Parlamento.
exampleSentences.english: The head of the government has the power (authority) to dissolve parliament.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mago ha usato i suoi poteri magici per trasformare il principe in una rana.
exampleSentences.english: The magician used his magic powers (special abilities) to transform the prince into a frog.

exampleSentences.italian: La Cina sta diventando una potenza economica e politica.
exampleSentences.english: China is becoming an economic and political superpower.

exampleSentences.italian: Posso richiamarti più tardi? Sono un po' impegnato adesso.
exampleSentences.english: Can (May) I call you later? I'm a bit busy right now.

exampleSentences.italian: Posso aspettare fino alle sette, dopodiché devo andare.
exampleSentences.english: I can (am able to) wait until 7, after which I have to go.

exampleSentences.italian: Può essere che (lui) non venga stasera.
exampleSentences.english: He may not come tonight.

exampleSentences.italian: Può darsi che mi richiamino domani.
exampleSentences.english: It's possible that they'll call me back tomorrow.

relatedExpressions.meaning: power (in mathematical, physical, or superpower contexts); force or intensity
it may be that / it's possible that

grammarNotes: Cugino is a masculine noun; the feminine form is cugina. The plural forms are cugini (masculine or mixed group) and cugine (all feminine). Like most Italian nouns ending in -o/-a, gender agreement affects both the article and any adjectives. Diminutive forms cuginetto/cuginetta exist for children.
learnerNotes: Remember that Italian distinguishes gender in family relationships more explicitly than English—always mark whether a cousin is male or female. The plural cugini can refer to a mixed group or all males, while cugine specifically means all females. Be aware that familial terms use different diminutives for children (cuginetto/cuginetta), which are common in spoken Italian but less formal than the standard forms.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho quattro cugine e solo un cugino.
exampleSentences.english: I have four female cousins and only one male cousin.

exampleSentences.italian: Roberto è un lontano cugino ma vado più d'accordo con lui che con il resto della famiglia!
exampleSentences.english: Roberto is a distant cousin but I get along with him better than the rest of my family!

relatedExpressions.meaning: second cousin / first cousin once removed
third cousin / first cousin twice removed

grammarNotes: Speranza is a feminine noun with plural form speranze. It derives from the verb sperare (to hope) and related adjectives include speranzoso (hopeful) and sperato (hoped for, long-awaited). The word does not have a cognate in English but resembles French espoir.
learnerNotes: Remember that speranza is feminine, so use la/una speranza and adjectives like speranzoso/speranzosa must agree in gender. In addition to 'hope,' speranza can mean 'chance' or 'possibility' depending on context—pay attention to surrounding words. The idiom "un filo di speranza" (literally 'a thread of hope') is commonly used in Italian to express a slim but real chance.

exampleSentences.italian: La speranza è l'ultima a morire.
exampleSentences.english: Hope is the last to die.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è speranza per il ragazzo ricoverato in ospedale ieri notte.
exampleSentences.english: There is a chance that the boy who was taken to hospital last night will recover.

grammarNotes: Pesce is a masculine noun with regular plural pesci. When capitalized as Pesci, it refers to the Pisces constellation and zodiac sign. The word shares etymological roots with English 'pescatarian' and derives from Latin piscis.
learnerNotes: Pesce is a false cognate with English 'piece'—it means fish, not piece. The plural pesci is irregular in formation. Note that 'pescatarian' uses the combining form pescetariano in Italian, not a direct translation. The Pesce d'Aprile tradition is culturally significant in Italy and worth remembering for cultural context.

exampleSentences.italian: Un pescetariano è una persona che mangia pesce, ma non bistecche, maiale o altri tipi di carne.
exampleSentences.english: A pescatarian is a person who eats fish, but not steak, pork or other kinds of meat.

relatedExpressions.meaning: April Fool's Day (literally 'April's Fish'); also used to mean an April Fool's prank

relatedExpressions.expression: essere come un pesce fuor d'acqua
relatedExpressions.meaning: to be like a fish out of water
to not know what to do

relatedExpressions.expression: non essere né carne né pesce
relatedExpressions.meaning: to be in a grey area, something not easily categorised
to be as fit as a fiddle (literally 'as healthy as a fish')

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural cucine. Has multiple meanings depending on context: the physical room, the cooking equipment/furnishings, the culinary tradition, or the stove itself. Gender agreement required with adjectives and articles (la cucina, una cucina nuova).
learnerNotes: Polysemy alert: cucina has four distinct meanings (room, equipment, cuisine, stove) depending on context—pay attention to surrounding words. When renting or buying property, 'senza cucina' means the apartment lacks kitchen fixtures, not that there's no kitchen room. Related verb cucinare (to cook) is regular; learn it early as it's frequently used.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho cucinato un pollo in cucina oggi.
exampleSentences.english: I cooked a chicken in the kitchen today.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo appartamento è semi-arredato e la cucina è nuova di zecca.
exampleSentences.english: This apartment is partly furnished and the kitchen is brand new.

exampleSentences.italian: La cucina italiana è la mia preferita in assoluto.
exampleSentences.english: Italian cuisine is my absolute favourite.

exampleSentences.italian: Mia nonna usa una vecchia cucina con quattro fornelli.
exampleSentences.english: My grandmother uses an old stove with four burners.

grammarNotes: Febbraio is a masculine noun (il febbraio) representing the second month of the year. Unlike English, Italian month names are not capitalized. The preposition 'a' is used to express 'in' a month: a febbraio (in February).
learnerNotes: Remember that Italian months are lowercase (febbraio, not Febbraio) unlike English. Use 'a febbraio' (in February) rather than 'in febbraio'. The zodiac signs associated with February are Acquario (Aquarius, roughly January 20–February 18) and Pesci (Pisces, roughly February 19–March 20).

exampleSentences.italian: Il primo giorno di febbraio
exampleSentences.english: The first day of February

exampleSentences.italian: Il compleanno di mia moglie è a febbraio.
exampleSentences.english: My wife's birthday is in February.

exampleSentences.italian: Febbraio è il secondo mese dell'anno.
exampleSentences.english: February is the second month of the year.

exampleSentences.italian: Febbraio ha 28 giorni.
exampleSentences.english: February has 28 days.

exampleSentences.italian: Gli anni bisestili hanno 29 giorni a febbraio.
exampleSentences.english: Leap years have 29 days in February.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural 'cuori'. Used literally for the anatomical organ and figuratively for emotions, thoughts, and as a term of endearment. Agrees with adjectives in gender and number (e.g., cuore infranto, cuori spezzati).
learnerNotes: Cuore is one of the most versatile and emotionally-charged words in Italian—use it both literally (the organ) and figuratively in idioms. Note that 'infarto' is the formal medical term for heart attack, but 'attacco di cuore' is the colloquial alternative. Many expressions with cuore mirror English idioms closely ('cuore d'oro' = 'heart of gold'), making them intuitive to learn.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mio cuore ha cominciato a battere così forte che non potevo respirare.
exampleSentences.english: My heart started beating so fast that I couldn't breathe.

exampleSentences.italian: Ti amo con tutto il cuore!
exampleSentences.english: I love you with all my heart!

exampleSentences.italian: Un battito del cuore
exampleSentences.english: A heartbeat

relatedExpressions.meaning: to wear one's heart on one's sleeve
to come to terms with something, to accept a situation for what it is
to have one's heart in one's throat

grammarNotes: Notte is a feminine noun with plural form notti. It agrees with feminine adjectives and articles (la notte, una notte, le notti). The adjective form notturno (nocturnal) is used when 'night' functions as an adjective in English (e.g., locale notturno = night club).
learnerNotes: Note that Italians often use sera (evening) where English speakers would say 'night,' especially when describing activities spanning evening into night hours. The expression notte in bianco has historical roots in medieval knighthood initiation ceremonies. Be careful not to confuse notturno (adjective, meaning nocturnal) with notte (noun, meaning night itself).

exampleSentences.italian: Buona notte Alice, e grazie ancora di tutto!
exampleSentences.english: Good night, Alice, and thanks again for everything!

exampleSentences.italian: Quando ero in Portogallo, ogni sera ero solito tornare a casa molto tardi.
exampleSentences.english: When I was in Portugal, I used to get home very late every night.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho passato una notte in bianco perché il bambino non ha smesso di piangere.
exampleSentences.english: I had a sleepless night because the baby wouldn't stop crying.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to sleep on it (sleep brings advice)
to make it through the night

grammarNotes: Mela is a feminine noun with regular plural mele. It derives from Latin mālum and forms the basis for related fruit names in Italian (melone, melagrana, mela cotogna, melanzana). The corresponding tree is called melo (masculine).
learnerNotes: Remember mela is feminine (una mela, le mele). The proverb 'Una mela al giorno toglie il medico di torno' is a common saying worth learning as a fixed expression. Note that melanzana (eggplant) contains mela but refers to a vegetable, not a fruit—this is a historical etymological quirk of Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Cerco di mangiare una mela ogni giorno.
exampleSentences.english: I try to eat an apple every day.

exampleSentences.italian: Una mela al giorno toglie il medico di torno.
exampleSentences.english: An apple a day keeps the doctor away.

relatedExpressions.meaning: bad apple (a corrupt or negative person with harmful influence)

relatedExpressions.expression: bianco e rosso come una mela
relatedExpressions.meaning: as white and red as an apple (describing a healthy, rosy complexion)

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural signorine. Derived from signora with the diminutive suffix -ina, literally meaning 'little lady.' Gender agreement applies when used as an address or descriptor. The abbreviation Sig.na is used in written correspondence before names.
learnerNotes: Signorina traditionally referred to unmarried women, but modern Italian increasingly uses signora for all women regardless of marital status, especially in professional contexts. In casual speech, Italian parents may jokingly call young daughters signorina. Be aware that the term is becoming less common in contemporary usage; when in doubt, use signora as it is more politically correct and widely accepted today.

exampleSentences.italian: L'ho conosciuta quando era una bambina, ma ora è diventata una signorina.
exampleSentences.english: I met her when she was a child, but now she has become a young woman.

exampleSentences.italian: Puoi smettere di fare la sciocca, signorina?
exampleSentences.english: Can you stop being silly, young lady?

exampleSentences.italian: Buona sera, signorina, buona sera.
exampleSentences.english: Goodnight, Miss, goodnight.

relatedExpressions.meaning: lady / woman (married or adult woman, now standard for all women)
abbreviation of signorina used in written correspondence

grammarNotes: Paese is a masculine noun with plural paesi. It has a dual meaning depending on context: either a large political entity (country/nation) or a small settlement (town/village). Some writers capitalize Paese when referring to a country for clarity. The word can also denote the inhabitants of a place collectively.
learnerNotes: Paese is a false friend for English speakers—it looks like 'passage' but means 'country/town.' Remember that context determines meaning: L'Italia è un paese (country) but Roma è una città (city) and Milano è un paese (town) would be less common—use città for larger urban centers. The idiom 'mandare qualcuno a quel paese' is colloquial and slightly rude, used when telling someone to go away.

exampleSentences.italian: L'Italia è un paese meraviglioso.
exampleSentences.english: Italy is a marvellous country.

exampleSentences.italian: Cantalupa è un paese vicino a Torino.
exampleSentences.english: Cantalupa is a town close to Turin.

exampleSentences.italian: Adoro il mio paese.
exampleSentences.english: I love my country. (or I love my town.)

exampleSentences.italian: Tutto il paese è andato alla festa.
exampleSentences.english: The whole town went to the party.

relatedExpressions.meaning: inhabitant of a town; rustic, rural, or simple
nation (synonym for paese when referring to country)
state (synonym for paese when referring to country)
It's the same the world over. (Literally: The whole world is a town.)
To tell someone to get lost. (Literally: To send someone to that town.)

relatedExpressions.expression: Paese che vai, usanze che trovi.
relatedExpressions.meaning: When in Rome do as the Romans do. (Literally: Country you go to, customs you find.)

grammarNotes: Marrone is both a noun and invariable adjective meaning the colour brown. Plural form: marroni. It agrees with the noun it modifies (un cane marrone, una casa marrone). The diminutive form marroncino means brownish or dull brown. For hair and eyes, Italians often prefer castano (chestnut brown) instead of marrone.
learnerNotes: Note that for describing brown hair (capelli castani) and brown eyes (occhi castani), Italians prefer castano over marrone, though marrone is not incorrect. The slang meaning 'testicle' and the idiom 'rompere i marroni' (to annoy someone) are colloquial/vulgar and should be avoided in formal contexts. Remember that marrone can function as both an adjective (invariable) and a noun with multiple unrelated meanings.

exampleSentences.italian: Il nostro cane è marrone scuro come il cioccolato.
exampleSentences.english: Our dog is dark brown like chocolate.

exampleSentences.italian: Le pareti sono diventate un po' marroncine dopo tutti questi anni.
exampleSentences.english: The walls have become a dull brown colour after all these years.

exampleSentences.italian: Sara ha i capelli e gli occhi castani.
exampleSentences.english: Sara has brown hair and brown eyes.

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi rompere i marroni!
exampleSentences.english: Don't break my balls!

exampleSentences.italian: Sì, lo so, ho commesso un marrone. Farò meglio la prossima volta.
exampleSentences.english: Yes, I know, I messed up. I'll do better next time.

relatedExpressions.meaning: chestnut brown (used for hair and eyes)
to make a blunder or mess up

grammarNotes: Latte is a masculine noun with plural form latti. It is commonly used in compound expressions to specify milk types (latte intero, latte scremato, etc.). The term also functions as a modifier in adjective forms: latteo (adjective describing white/creamy appearance) and lattiginoso (adjective describing milky consistency).
learnerNotes: Be careful with the false cognate: ordering 'un latte' in an Italian café will get you a glass of milk, not the espresso drink English speakers call a 'latte'—ask for 'latte macchiato' instead. The word latte also extends to plant-based milks (latte di soia, latte di mandorle), making it versatile for modern dietary needs. Related adjectives (latteo, lattiginoso) and noun derivatives (latticini, latteria) are useful for expanding vocabulary in food and dairy contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Posso avere un latte macchiato per favore?
exampleSentences.english: Can I have a latte, please?

exampleSentences.italian: Il latte contiene quantità significative di vitamine.
exampleSentences.english: Milk contains a significant quantity of vitamins.

exampleSentences.italian: Se spremete un pezzo di patata fra le dita, vedrete fuoriuscire un liquido lattiginoso.
exampleSentences.english: If you squash a piece of potato between your fingers, you'll see a milky liquid emerge.

relatedExpressions.meaning: espresso with milk (the drink commonly called 'latte' in English)

relatedExpressions.expression: avere ancora il latte alla bocca
relatedExpressions.meaning: to still have milk in one's mouth; to be young and inexperienced

grammarNotes: Cena is a feminine noun (la cena). It forms related words by adding suffixes: cenone (big supper, -one suffix for augmentation) and cenare (verb: to have dinner/dine). The phrase ora di cena means dinnertime and functions as a temporal expression.
learnerNotes: Cena is part of Italy's traditional four-meal daily structure (colazione, pranzo, merenda, cena). The verb cenare is regular (-are conjugation). Note that apericena is a modern, popular concept among students—a budget-friendly alternative combining drinks and substantial food for around €10, distinct from traditional light aperitivi.

exampleSentences.italian: Stasera torno a casa per cenare con la famiglia.
exampleSentences.english: Tonight I'm going home to have dinner with the family.

exampleSentences.italian: La cena è pronta.
exampleSentences.english: The dinner is ready.

exampleSentences.italian: È pronto in tavola.
exampleSentences.english: It's ready on the table.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho cominciato a preparare la cena alle 5.
exampleSentences.english: I started preparing the dinner at 5 o'clock.

relatedExpressions.meaning: portmanteau of aperitivo and cena; budget-friendly appetizer-dinner hybrid

grammarNotes: Arancione is both an adjective and noun describing the color orange. It agrees with the noun it modifies in gender and number (arancione, arancioni). Two common synonyms exist: arancio (also meaning orange tree) and aranciato (less common), which are largely interchangeable with arancione.
learnerNotes: Arancione, arancio, and aranciato are essentially interchangeable for the color orange—use whichever you encounter. Note that Italian kept older color terms for certain objects: pesce rosso (goldfish) and gatto rosso (ginger cat) literally mean 'red fish' and 'red cat' because orange wasn't named as a distinct color until the fruit arrived in Europe (11th–12th centuries). Don't confuse arancia (the fruit) with arancione (the color).

exampleSentences.italian: Questa arancia è più verde che arancione. Non sarà ancora matura.
exampleSentences.english: This orange is more green than orange. It probably isn't ripe.

exampleSentences.italian: La signora indossava un abito arancio scuro.
exampleSentences.english: The lady was wearing a dark orange outfit.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho comprato una maglietta di un bel colore aranciato acceso.
exampleSentences.english: I bought a nice bright orange-coloured shirt.

relatedExpressions.meaning: orange tree; also accepted synonym for the color
Sicilian fried rice ball, named for its orange-like appearance

grammarNotes: Oceano is a masculine noun with regular plural form oceani. It derives from Greek ōkeanos. In Italian, the word agrees with masculine articles (il, un, degli) and adjectives. Though oceano technically refers to the largest saltwater expanses, Italians often use il mare (the sea) colloquially to refer to oceans.
learnerNotes: Remember that oceano is masculine (l'oceano, un oceano). In everyday conversation, Italians frequently use il mare instead of oceano, so both terms are useful. The figurative use of oceano to describe vast quantities (oceano di sabbia) is common in poetic or descriptive contexts—note this expanded usage beyond the literal definition.

exampleSentences.italian: L'oceano più grande del mondo è l'Oceano Pacifico.
exampleSentences.english: The biggest ocean in the world is the Pacific Ocean.

exampleSentences.italian: Guarda quanto è grande il deserto. È come un oceano di sabbia.
exampleSentences.english: Look how big the desert is. It's like an ocean of sand.

exampleSentences.italian: Gli oceani coprono circa il 71% della superficie terrestre.
exampleSentences.english: The oceans cover approximately 71% of Earth's surface.

relatedExpressions.meaning: the sea (colloquial term often used for ocean)
ocean of sand (figurative: a large expanse)

grammarNotes: As an adjective, buio agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: buio (masc. sg.), buia (fem. sg.), bui (masc. pl.), buie (fem. pl.). As a noun, il buio is masculine singular and means 'the dark.' The adjective form is used for darkness related to light absence or figuratively for difficult periods, not for dark colours or shades.
learnerNotes: Buio and scuro are often confused: use buio only for absence of light or figurative meanings (dark period, troubled expression), and scuro for dark colours or objects (dark jacket, dark hair). Remember that buio as a noun (il buio) is masculine. The adjective form must always agree with the noun's gender and number.

exampleSentences.italian: vicolo buio
exampleSentences.english: dark alley

exampleSentences.italian: notte buia
exampleSentences.english: dark night

exampleSentences.italian: vicoli bui
exampleSentences.english: dark alleys

exampleSentences.italian: notti buie
exampleSentences.english: dark nights

exampleSentences.italian: Ho attraversato un periodo buio ma ora sto meglio.
exampleSentences.english: I went through a dark period but I'm better now.

exampleSentences.italian: Il giovane è diventato buio in volto quando ha aperto la lettera.
exampleSentences.english: The young man's expression became troubled when he opened the letter.

exampleSentences.italian: I bambini hanno paura del buio.
exampleSentences.english: The children are afraid of the dark.

exampleSentences.italian: Il ladro è uscito al buio con una tuta scura.
exampleSentences.english: The thief went out into the dark dressed in a dark outfit.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to take a leap into the unknown

relatedExpressions.expression: al buio tutti i gatti sono grigi
relatedExpressions.meaning: in the dark, beauty/good cannot be distinguished from ugliness/evil
to be in the dark, to have no clue

grammarNotes: Cipolla is a feminine noun (la cipolla). The plural is cipolle. Diminutive forms include cipollina (small onion) and cipollotto (spring onion). When used as an adjective in compound expressions like orologio a cipolla, it remains unchanged.
learnerNotes: Cipolla is essential vocabulary for food contexts and everyday Italian. Pay attention to the diminutive cipollina and cipollotto, which have specific culinary meanings. The idiomatic expressions vestirsi a cipolla and orologio a cipolla are culturally interesting but not essential for beginners—focus on the main noun and common varieties first.

exampleSentences.italian: Ci sono tanti tipi di cipolle in Italia.
exampleSentences.english: There are many kinds of onions in Italy.

exampleSentences.italian: In padella, fai appassire le cipolline in olio, rosmarino e sale.
exampleSentences.english: In a pan, lightly fry the small onions in oil, rosemary and salt.

relatedExpressions.meaning: Tropea red onion (famous sweet variety from southern Italy)
to wear layers (literally 'dress like an onion')

grammarNotes: Polpo is a masculine noun with regular plural polpi. In everyday Italian, polipi (plural of polipo) is often used colloquially for octopuses, but zoologically polipo refers to cnidaria (corals, jellyfish, sea anemones), not octopuses. The term applies to both the living creature and the culinary dish.
learnerNotes: Be careful not to confuse polpo/polpi with polipo/polipi—they are zoologically different creatures. While Italians use polipi colloquially for octopuses, polipo technically refers to polyps (corals, jellyfish, anemones). The synonym piovra carries strong figurative meanings related to greed and organized crime, useful for understanding Italian crime drama references like the TV series 'La Piovra.'

exampleSentences.italian: il polpo
exampleSentences.english: the octopus (singular)

exampleSentences.italian: un polpo
exampleSentences.english: an octopus

exampleSentences.italian: i polpi
exampleSentences.english: the octopuses (plural)

exampleSentences.italian: dei polpi
exampleSentences.english: of the octopuses

exampleSentences.italian: Il polpo ha otto tentacoli con ventose.
exampleSentences.english: The octopus has eight tentacles with suction cups.

relatedExpressions.meaning: common octopus; also figuratively: a greedy unscrupulous person or a criminal organization with wide influence
polyp (zoologically: cnidaria such as corals, jellyfish, sea anemones)

grammarNotes: Vecchio is a four-form adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: vecchio (masc. sing.), vecchia (fem. sing.), vecchi (masc. plural), vecchie (fem. plural). The word forms the basis of related nouns (vecchiaia = old age, vecchietto/a = old person) and the verb invecchiare (to age). When referring to people, the synonym anziano (elderly) is more polite.
learnerNotes: While vecchio is grammatically correct when describing people, it can sound impolite in formal contexts—use anziano instead. Colloquially, il mio vecchio (my old man) is an affectionate way to refer to one's father, similar to English. Note that un vecchio amico means a friend of long standing, not necessarily an elderly friend.

exampleSentences.italian: Voglio sostituire questo vecchio tavolo con uno nuovo.
exampleSentences.english: I want to replace this old table with a new one.

exampleSentences.italian: Tutti i vecchietti dicono che la vecchiaia è una brutta cosa!
exampleSentences.english: All old people say that old age is a terrible thing!

exampleSentences.italian: Ho offerto il mio posto sul treno alla signora anziana.
exampleSentences.english: I offered my seat on the train to the elderly lady.

relatedExpressions.meaning: my old man (colloquial, referring to father)
an old friend (one known for years)
to have a lot of experience (literally: to be old in the profession)
old fox (implying someone has acquired considerable skills and knowledge)
to be very old (literally: to be as old as a cuckoo)
to be very old (literally: to be older than the world)
to be very old (literally: to be older than parsley)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form conigli. The word refers both to the living animal and to rabbit meat (like English). The diminutive form coniglietto (little rabbit) is commonly used for the Easter Bunny to create a cuter image.
learnerNotes: Coniglio is notoriously difficult to pronounce for English speakers due to the 'gli' sound cluster. Unlike English where buck/doe distinguish rabbit sexes, Italian uses maschio di coniglio and femmina di coniglio. Note that lepre (hare) is feminine and much easier to pronounce—useful for distinguishing these animals in conversation.

exampleSentences.italian: Da piccolo avevo un coniglio che si chiamava Yo-Yo.
exampleSentences.english: When I was little I had a rabbit called Yo-Yo.

exampleSentences.italian: Non ho mai mangiato coniglio in vita mia.
exampleSentences.english: I've never eaten rabbit in my life.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei veloce come una lepre!
exampleSentences.english: You're as fast as a hare!

relatedExpressions.meaning: scaredy-cat / coward (literally: heart of a rabbit)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural ragni. Commonly used in compound expressions like ragno crociato (European garden spider), ragno violino (violin spider), and ragno d'acqua dolce (water spider). The term derives from ancient Greek arachne, as does the English 'arachnophobia.'
learnerNotes: Ragno is a high-frequency noun essential for nature vocabulary. Note the idiomatic expression 'sembra un ragno' for describing thin people—not literal translation. The phrase 'non cavare un ragno dal buco' is a useful but colloquial idiom expressing futile effort; learn it as a set expression rather than word-for-word. Be aware that Italy has about 1,600 spider species, mostly harmless, but two notable exceptions (ragno violino and tarantola) are worth knowing.

exampleSentences.italian: Mia zia ha la fobia dei ragni.
exampleSentences.english: My aunt has arachnophobia.

exampleSentences.italian: Mio figlio è così magro che sembra un ragno!
exampleSentences.english: My son is so skinny he looks like a spider!

exampleSentences.italian: Nonostante le sue indagini segrete, non cavò un ragno dal buco.
exampleSentences.english: Despite his secret investigations, he couldn't find anything.

relatedExpressions.meaning: spiderweb (two equivalent terms, ragnatela more commonly used)
he/she looks like a spider (idiomatic: describing someone as very skinny)

relatedExpressions.expression: non cavare un ragno dal buco
relatedExpressions.meaning: to not get a spider out of the hole (idiom: to fail to obtain results despite effort)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with irregular plural: uomo → uomini. When used to describe a specific type of man, it combines with adjectives or prepositional phrases (e.g., uomo d'affari, uomo della strada). Gender agreement applies when used with articles and adjectives (l'uomo, un buon uomo).
learnerNotes: Uomo is commonly used in colloquial speech to refer to a partner (boyfriend/husband) in informal contexts, which differs from English where 'man' sounds much more casual. The plural uomini is irregular and should be memorized. Be aware that uomo can mean both 'an adult male' and 'humankind/humanity' depending on context—context determines whether it's countable or abstract.

exampleSentences.italian: Quell'uomo si chiama Marco. Abita nell'appartamento sopra al mio.
exampleSentences.english: That man is called Marco. He lives in the apartment above mine.

exampleSentences.italian: Cinquantuno anni fa l'uomo mise piede sulla Luna.
exampleSentences.english: Fifty-one years ago man set foot on the moon.

exampleSentences.italian: Come sta il tuo uomo? Non lo vedo da un sacco!
exampleSentences.english: How is your man? I haven't seen him for ages!

exampleSentences.italian: C'è l'uomo del gas alla porta.
exampleSentences.english: The gas man is at the door.

relatedExpressions.meaning: man of practical skills but not very intelligent
man you can trust for delicate jobs
for a long time (as long as man can remember)

relatedExpressions.expression: Un uomo avvertito è mezzo salvato

grammarNotes: Soldi is the plural form of soldo (a medieval Italian coin) and is always used in the plural in modern Italian when referring to money. The singular soldo is rarely used except in idiomatic expressions. The diminutive form is soldini (little coins/small amount of money). Unlike the formal denaro (which is always singular), soldi is the everyday colloquial term.
learnerNotes: Remember that soldi is always plural in modern Italian—you cannot say 'un soldo' when referring to money in everyday speech. For formal contexts (banking, legal documents), use denaro instead. Watch out for the idiomatic expressions with soldo (singular), which typically appear in fixed phrases expressing worthlessness or poverty; these are important cultural expressions to recognize.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho risparmiato abbastanza soldi per comprare una casa.
exampleSentences.english: I've saved up enough money to buy a house.

exampleSentences.italian: Giuseppe è uno che sa fare soldi. Fattelo amico!
exampleSentences.english: Giuseppe is someone who knows how to make money. Make friends with him!

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei prelevare del denaro dal conto corrente.
exampleSentences.english: I wish to take out some money from my bank account.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be worthless (literally: not worth a soldo with a hole in it)
to earn some money, a few pennies
to make money, to earn a lot of money or become rich
of little value (used for people, ideas, works of art, etc.)
of little value (variation of da quattro soldi)
of little value (variation of da quattro soldi)

grammarNotes: Silenzioso is a four-form adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: silenzioso (masc. sing.), silenziosa (fem. sing.), silenziosi (masc. plur.), silenziose (fem. plur.). It can describe both physical quietness and personality traits.
learnerNotes: When describing people, silenzioso can carry different connotations: it may be a positive comment on discretion or a negative observation about social withdrawal. Pay attention to context clues and surrounding information. The phrase 'modalità silenzioso' on smartphones is a common, practical expression you'll encounter in daily life.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piace lavorare in questa stanza perché è molto silenziosa.
exampleSentences.english: I like working in this room because it is very quiet.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel ragazzo è molto silenzioso. Non parla mai.
exampleSentences.english: That boy is very quiet. He never speaks.

exampleSentences.italian: Maria è la vicina di casa ideale. È molto silenziosa, soprattutto di sera.
exampleSentences.english: Maria is the ideal neighbour. She's very quiet, especially in the evening.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural gioielli. Derived from Latin iocus (joke/jest). In plural form, gioielli can function as a mass noun translating to 'jewellery' or a countable noun for 'jewels'. The diminutive form gioiellino exists and is commonly used figuratively or as a term of endearment.
learnerNotes: Gioiello has a figurative sense meaning 'something precious' that extends beyond physical jewels—use it to describe people, cities, or prized possessions. The diminutive gioiellino is primarily figurative and works well as a casual term of endearment in Italian, so avoid overusing it to mean literally 'small jewel.' Note that gioielli (plural) functions as both countable ('jewels') and uncountable ('jewellery'), similar to English usage.

exampleSentences.italian: Mia nonna tiene tanti gioielli dentro una scatola nella sua stanza.
exampleSentences.english: My grandma keeps lots of jewellery inside a box in her room.

exampleSentences.italian: Torino è una vera città gioiello.
exampleSentences.english: Torino is a real jewel of a city.

exampleSentences.italian: Ciao gioiellino, come stai oggi?
exampleSentences.english: Hi little jewel, how are you today?

relatedExpressions.meaning: little jewel (diminutive; used figuratively or as term of endearment)

grammarNotes: Gattino is a masculine noun (plural: gattini) formed by adding the diminutive suffix -ino to gatto (cat). The feminine form is gattina (plural: gattine). Diminutive suffixes -ino/-etto/-otto are commonly used with animal names to denote offspring or express smallness and affection, and can apply to adult animals as terms of endearment.
learnerNotes: Remember that diminutive suffixes (-ino, -etto, -otto) add layers of meaning: they indicate smallness but also affection or tenderness. You can use gattino for actual kittens or as a term of endearment for an adult cat. The alternative micino is equally common in everyday speech, so both terms are worth learning for authentic communication.

exampleSentences.italian: Ma che bella gattina! Possiamo adottarla?
exampleSentences.english: What a beautiful kitten! Can we adopt her?

exampleSentences.italian: Tu sai come prenderti cura di un cucciolo di gatto?
exampleSentences.english: Do you know how to take care of a kitten?

relatedExpressions.meaning: female kitten; also used affectionately for adult female cats
alternative word for kitten (from micio, meaning cat)
cub; used for many baby animals including cats, dogs, bears, and wolves

grammarNotes: Timido is a regular adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: timido (masc. sing.), timida (fem. sing.), timidi (masc. plur.), timide (fem. plur.). It can also function as a noun to describe a shy person. The suffixes -one/-ona can be added to create timidone/timidona for emphasis.
learnerNotes: Remember that timido shares Latin roots with English 'timid,' making it a cognate—easy to remember! Beyond personality, timido also means 'faint' or 'weak' when describing actions lacking conviction or things lacking force (e.g., un timido tentativo). When used as a noun, use the definite article: 'il timido,' 'la timida,' 'i timidi,' 'le timide.'

exampleSentences.italian: Fin da bambino, sono sempre stato molto timido.
exampleSentences.english: Since I was a child, I've always been shy.

exampleSentences.italian: Pietro era il timido del gruppo.
exampleSentences.english: Pietro was the shy one in the group.

exampleSentences.italian: Dai, non fare la timidona. Fatti coraggio!
exampleSentences.english: Come on, don't be so shy. Show some courage!

exampleSentences.italian: un timido tentativo
exampleSentences.english: a feeble attempt

exampleSentences.italian: un timido raggio di sole
exampleSentences.english: a faint ray of light

grammarNotes: Polizia is a feminine noun (la polizia). The plural is polizie, though it is often used in singular form to refer to the police force collectively. A policeman is poliziotto (masculine, plural poliziotti); a policewoman is poliziotta (feminine, plural poliziotte). When used as an adjective, it is preceded by della (of the).
learnerNotes: Be careful not to confuse polizia (police) with pulizia (cleaning/cleanliness)—pronounce the 'o' in polizia very clearly to avoid misunderstandings. In Italy, there are multiple police forces with different jurisdictions; the most common are Polizia di Stato and Carabinieri. Remember that polizia is feminine, so use la polizia and adjectives must agree in gender (e.g., la macchina della polizia).

exampleSentences.italian: La polizia è responsabile di mantenere l'ordine e la sicurezza.
exampleSentences.english: The police are responsible for maintaining order and security.

exampleSentences.italian: I miei figli vogliono diventare poliziotti.
exampleSentences.english: My sons want to become policemen.

exampleSentences.italian: La macchina della polizia sta pattugliando le strade.
exampleSentences.english: The police car is patrolling the streets.

grammarNotes: Succo is a masculine noun with regular plural succhi. It agrees with articles and adjectives in gender and number (il succo, i succhi, un succo). The word has multiple semantic fields: beverage juice, figurative meaning (essence of an argument), and anatomical secretions.
learnerNotes: Succo has three distinct meanings: beverage juice, the essence/gist of something (figurative), and biological secretions. Be careful not to confuse succo (juice/liquid) with spremuta (freshly squeezed juice made on premises)—Italians make this distinction when ordering at cafés. Note that succulent (English) is a helpful cognate to remember the word's origin and meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: Bevo il succo ogni mattina a colazione.
exampleSentences.english: I drink juice every morning at breakfast.

exampleSentences.italian: No, non voglio il succo d'arancia…preferirei la spremuta.
exampleSentences.english: No, I don't want the orange juice…I'd prefer the freshly squeezed juice.

exampleSentences.italian: Il succo gastrico è una secrezione prodotta dallo stomaco.
exampleSentences.english: Gastric juice is a secretion produced by the stomach.

relatedExpressions.meaning: the takeaway message / the overall gist

grammarNotes: Marzo is a masculine noun (il marzo) and, like all Italian month names, is not capitalized in standard writing. It is invariable and does not change form in plural contexts. The article is typically used when referring to the month in a general sense.
learnerNotes: Remember that Italian month names are always lowercase unless at the start of a sentence, unlike English. Marzo derives from the Latin god Mars (Marte in Italian), which is a useful etymology aid. Note that zodiac signs born in marzo fall into two categories depending on the exact date: Pesci (March 1–20) or Ariete (March 21–31).

exampleSentences.italian: A marzo comincia a fare più caldo in Italia.
exampleSentences.english: In March it starts to get warmer in Italy.

grammarNotes: Ombra is a feminine noun with regular plural ombre. It agrees with feminine articles and adjectives (l'ombra, un'ombra, le ombre). The word has both literal meanings (physical shadows/shade) and figurative uses (spirits, suspicion, protection), so gender agreement remains consistent across all applications.
learnerNotes: Ombra is deceptively versatile—while beginners learn it primarily for physical shadows/shade, intermediate learners should recognize its figurative uses, especially in expressions involving suspicion or doubt. The phrase 'senza ombra di dubbio' (without a shadow of a doubt) is idiomatic and commonly used in both spoken and written Italian. Pay attention to prepositions: 'all'ombra' (in the shade), 'all'ombra di' (under the protection of), and 'fare ombra a' (to cast suspicion on).

exampleSentences.italian: L'albero proiettava un'ombra sul marciapiede.
exampleSentences.english: The tree cast a shadow on the footpath.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi sono seduto all'ombra per scappare dal sole rovente.
exampleSentences.english: I sat in the shade to escape from the scorching sun.

exampleSentences.italian: le ombre dei trapassati
exampleSentences.english: the spirits of the dead

exampleSentences.italian: un'ombra di sale
exampleSentences.english: a small amount of salt

exampleSentences.italian: vivere all'ombra di suo padre
exampleSentences.english: to live under the protection of his father

exampleSentences.italian: non c'è ombra del ragazzo
exampleSentences.english: there isn't a trace of him

exampleSentences.italian: fare/dare ombra a qualcuno
exampleSentences.english: to cast suspicion on someone

exampleSentences.italian: dissipare le ombre
exampleSentences.english: to clear up an ambiguous situation

exampleSentences.italian: prendere ombra (di qualcosa)
exampleSentences.english: to cast suspicion upon oneself

relatedExpressions.meaning: without a shadow of a doubt
to take offense / cast suspicion upon oneself

grammarNotes: Avventura is a feminine noun (plural: avventure). It derives from Latin adventurus meaning 'about to happen.' The word agrees with feminine articles and adjectives, as in 'un'avventura' (singular indefinite article) or 'le avventure' (plural definite article).
learnerNotes: English 'adventure' typically suggests excitement and risk, but Italian avventura has a broader semantic range including romantic flings. The phrase 'per avventura' is a fixed expression meaning 'by chance' or 'perhaps'—learn it as a unit. Be careful not to confuse avvenire (to happen / the future) with avventura, though they share Latin roots.

exampleSentences.italian: Il nostro viaggio in Galles è stato un'avventura.
exampleSentences.english: Our trip around Wales was an adventure.

exampleSentences.italian: È stata soltanto un'avventura per lui. Non cercava un rapporto serio.
exampleSentences.english: It was just a fling for him. He was not looking for a serious relationship.

exampleSentences.italian: Se per avventura capiti da queste parti, vienimi a trovare.
exampleSentences.english: If by chance you happen to be in the area, come and visit me.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to venture, to take a risk
by chance / maybe (synonym for per caso or forse)

grammarNotes: Regina is a feminine noun with plural regine. It agrees with feminine articles (la regina, le regine) and feminine adjectives. The word derives from Latin rex (king) and is cognate with English 'reign.' It can refer to female rulers, wives/mothers of kings, reproductive insects, or outstanding women/things in a figurative sense.
learnerNotes: Regina is a straightforward feminine noun easily remembered by its resemblance to English 'reign.' Note that it extends beyond literal queens to describe outstanding women or things (e.g., 'regina del rock'), making it useful for figurative expressions. The diminutive reginetta refers both to fairy tale characters and beauty pageant winners, so context determines the specific meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: Margherita di Savoia fu la prima regina consorte d'Italia.
exampleSentences.english: Margherita di Savoia was the first queen consort of Italy.

exampleSentences.italian: L'ape regina è la madre di tutte le api presenti nell'alveare.
exampleSentences.english: The queen bee is the mother of all the bees in the hive.

exampleSentences.italian: Penso che Gianna Nannini sia la regina del rock italiano.
exampleSentences.english: I think Gianna Nannini is the queen of Italian rock.

exampleSentences.italian: La rosa è la regina dei fiori.
exampleSentences.english: The rose is the most beautiful of all flowers.

relatedExpressions.meaning: queen consort (wife of a reigning king)
Queen of the Vineyards (a type of golden grape)
Queen of the Orchards (a type of peach tree)
young queen; beauty pageant winner (diminutive form)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural 'colori'. Derives from Latin 'color'. Used literally for colour and paint, and figuratively for complexion, vivacity, political opinion, and national flag colours. Related verbs include 'colorare' (to colour, paint, embellish) and 'colorire' (to colour with focus on change rather than artistic action).
learnerNotes: Colore has multiple figurative uses beyond the literal meaning of colour: it can refer to complexion (un brutto colore = poor complexion suggesting fatigue), political leaning (cambiare colore = change political views), and vivacity in performance. The related verbs 'colorare' and 'colorire' have distinct uses: colorare means to paint/colour artistically, while colorire refers to acquiring colour or making something more interesting. Pay attention to context when interpreting figurative meanings, especially in idiomatic expressions like 'dire tutti i colori' (let off steam).

exampleSentences.italian: Ci sono sette colori in un arcobaleno.
exampleSentences.english: There are seven colours in a rainbow.

exampleSentences.italian: Non posso finire di dipingere le pareti perché è finito il colore.
exampleSentences.english: I can't finish painting the walls because the paint has run out.

exampleSentences.italian: far colorire la cipolla
exampleSentences.english: to brown the onion

exampleSentences.italian: colorire un racconto
exampleSentences.english: to make a story more interesting

exampleSentences.italian: colorire in viso
exampleSentences.english: to tan or to blush

exampleSentences.italian: Un viso colorito
exampleSentences.english: a bright, vivid face

exampleSentences.italian: linguaggio colorito
exampleSentences.english: explicit language

exampleSentences.italian: un brutto/cattivo colore
exampleSentences.english: a terrible complexion

exampleSentences.italian: La tua recitazione è priva di colori.

exampleSentences.english: Daniele often changes his political opinion. I have no clue who he will vote for in this election.

exampleSentences.italian: I colori d'Italia sono il verde, il bianco e il rosso.
exampleSentences.english: The Italian colours are green, white and red.

let off steam, to talk freely without concern for decency or the feelings of others
to lead a busy life that is often reprehensible and dishonest, also used for kids when they make a big mess or a fuss
to have many diverse experiences in life
to change one's expression due to feelings of shame, anger or indignation
to colour, to paint, to embellish
to colour (with focus on change in colour rather than artistic action)

grammarNotes: Rosa is a feminine noun (plural: rose). As an adjective meaning 'pink', it agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. When used as an adjective to describe romantic or female-oriented media (un film rosa, un romanzo rosa), it remains invariable in this idiomatic sense. The word has multiple meanings: the flower/plant, the colour pink, romantic fiction, and a shortlist of qualified candidates.
learnerNotes: Remember that rosa as a colour adjective must agree with the noun (una camicia rosa, dei fiori rosa). The phrase 'film rosa' and 'romanzo rosa' are fixed Italian expressions for romantic media and don't translate literally—learn these as collocations. Be careful not to confuse rosa (pink) with rossa (red), a common mistake for beginners.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa rosa mi sembra più rosa che rossa.
exampleSentences.english: This rose looks more pink than red to me.

exampleSentences.italian: Trovo che i film rosa siano poco profondi.
exampleSentences.english: I find that chick flicks are shallow.

exampleSentences.italian: Maria vede tutto rosa.
exampleSentences.english: Maria sees everything through pink-coloured glasses.

relatedExpressions.expression: non è tutto rose e fiori

as fresh as a rose / as fresh as a daisy

the shortlist of players / a list or group of qualified people

grammarNotes: Stanco agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Masculine singular: stanco; feminine singular: stanca; masculine plural: stanchi; feminine plural: stanche. The reflexive verb stancarsi (to get tired/to tire oneself out) is commonly paired with this adjective to express becoming tired.
learnerNotes: Remember that stanco can express both physical/mental tiredness (mi sento stanco) and being fed up with something (sono stanco di...). The synonym stufo also means 'tired of / fed up with' and is interchangeable in the latter sense. Pay attention to gender agreement when using this adjective—use stanca with feminine nouns and stanchi/stanche for plurals.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi sento molto stanco oggi quindi non vado in palestra.
exampleSentences.english: I feel very tired today so I'm not going to the gym.

exampleSentences.italian: Ieri mi sono stancato dopo una lunga passeggiata.
exampleSentences.english: I tired myself out / got tired yesterday after a long walk.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono stanco di sentire le tue scuse.
exampleSentences.english: I'm tired of hearing your excuses.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to get tired / to tire oneself out

grammarNotes: Luna is a feminine noun (la luna) with plural lune. It agrees with feminine adjectives and articles. Related adjective lunare (lunar) is used to describe moon-related phenomena. The word forms the basis for lunedì (Monday), derived from Latin 'Lunae dies' (day of the moon).
learnerNotes: Remember that luna is feminine, so use la, una, and feminine adjectives (e.g., la luna piena, una luna calante). The word lunedì (Monday) is derived from luna but is masculine and always requires il/un. Be aware that lunatico (lunatic) has a negative connotation stemming from historical beliefs about lunar influence on mental health.

exampleSentences.italian: La luna impiega un mese per orbitare intorno alla terra.
exampleSentences.english: The moon takes a month to orbit around the earth.

exampleSentences.italian: Quante lune ha Saturno?
exampleSentences.english: How many moons does Saturn have?

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be in a bad mood, to wake up on the wrong side of the bed
to expect/ask for the moon, to expect too much

grammarNotes: Pigro is a regular adjective ending in -o that must agree with the subject's gender and number: pigro (masc. sing.), pigra (fem. sing.), pigri (masc. pl.), pigre (fem. pl.). It can function as a noun when referring to a lazy person. The augmentative forms pigrone (masculine) and pigrona (feminine) intensify the meaning ('lazy bones').
learnerNotes: Remember that pigro agrees with the subject just like any Italian adjective—don't forget the gender and number endings. The augmentative forms pigrone/pigrona are colloquial and affectionate, commonly used in spoken Italian. Synonyms like letargico, indolente, apatico, and svogliato offer variety, but pigro remains the most common everyday term for 'lazy.'

exampleSentences.italian: Sono troppo pigro per andare a correre tutti i giorni.
exampleSentences.english: I'm too lazy to go running every day.

exampleSentences.italian: Di' a quel pigro di spostarsi.
exampleSentences.english: Tell that lazy guy to move.

exampleSentences.italian: Dai pigrone, alzati o farai tardi!
exampleSentences.english: Come on lazy bones, get up or you'll be late!

exampleSentences.italian: camminare a passi pigri
exampleSentences.english: to walk slowly (lazy walk)

exampleSentences.italian: un pomeriggio pigro
exampleSentences.english: a lazy afternoon

grammarNotes: Pulito is the masculine singular form of the adjective, derived from the past participle of pulire (to clean). It agrees with gender and number: feminine singular pulita, masculine plural puliti, feminine plural pulite. The word changes its final vowel to match the noun it modifies.
learnerNotes: Remember that pulito has multiple figurative meanings beyond 'clean'—context is crucial. The related noun pulizia (cleanliness/cleaning) is commonly used in plural form (pulizie) even when referring to a single cleaning task. Watch for gender and number agreement when using pulito as an adjective modifying nouns.

exampleSentences.italian: È difficile tenere la casa sempre pulita!
exampleSentences.english: It's hard to keep the house clean all the time!

exampleSentences.italian: Le tue mani non sono molto pulite. Le hai lavate bene?

exampleSentences.italian: marmo pulito
exampleSentences.english: polished marble

exampleSentences.italian: un ragazzo pulito
exampleSentences.english: an honest guy

to get away with something; to avoid deserved punishment or overcome danger without harm
to send everyone away; to take everything away; to sweep away
to clean (usually a house or office)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural fiumi. Derived from Latin fluvius, cognate with English 'fluvial.' Can function as an adjective in compound expressions (e.g., riunione fiume = never-ending meeting). When used figuratively, it maintains masculine gender agreement.
learnerNotes: Remember that fiume is masculine (il fiume), so adjectives and articles must agree. The figurative use 'un fiume di + noun' is idiomatic and very common in Italian; it emphasizes abundance or overwhelming quantity. Don't confuse fiume (river) with ruscello (small stream) or torrente (torrent), which describe different types of water flows with distinct characteristics.

exampleSentences.italian: Il Po è il fiume più lungo d'Italia.
exampleSentences.english: The Po is the longest river in Italy.

exampleSentences.italian: Un fiume di gente ha invaso la piazza ieri sera.
exampleSentences.english: A flood of people swarmed the square last night.

exampleSentences.italian: La pagina Facebook del politico è stata inondata da un fiume di insulti.
exampleSentences.english: The politician's Facebook page was flooded with insults.

exampleSentences.italian: Mamma mia, non uscirò mai vivo da questa riunione fiume!
exampleSentences.english: Oh boy, there's no way I'm going to escape from this never-ending meeting alive!

relatedExpressions.meaning: small stream or creek (flowing from a spring or glacier)
torrent or slope stream (dependent on flood water, can dry up)

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural form mogli. Derived from Latin mŭlier (woman, wife, mistress). Forms diminutive mogliettina (wifey, little wife) as a term of endearment. Related terms include futura sposa/futura moglie (future wife), promessa sposa (promised bride, literary), and ex-moglie (ex-wife).
learnerNotes: The informal term donna (woman) can refer to wives among close friends, but use moglie in formal contexts. Note the distinction between futura moglie (neutral) and promessa sposa (literary/romantic). The diminutive mogliettina carries affectionate connotations and is typically used by husbands, not in formal or professional settings.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho conosciuto mia moglie dieci anni fa.
exampleSentences.english: I met my wife ten years ago.

grammarNotes: Virus is a masculine noun in Italian (il virus) with an invariant plural form (i virus). Despite identical spelling to English, Italian pronunciation differs significantly. The word derives from Latin virus, originally meaning the poisonous secretion of snakes and plants.
learnerNotes: Note that 'virus' is pronounced differently in Italian than English despite identical spelling—pay attention to the audio guide provided. This word became particularly relevant in contemporary Italian discourse during the COVID-19 pandemic. Related medical vocabulary like 'febbre', 'sintomi', and 'quarantena' are essential for health-related conversations in Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Il virus sta cominciando a circolare anche a Roma.
exampleSentences.english: The virus is starting to circulate in Rome too.

exampleSentences.italian: Italy joined the list of coronavirus-affected countries on January 30th when two positive cases were reported in Chinese tourists.
exampleSentences.english: Italy joined the list of coronavirus-affected countries on January 30th when two positive cases were reported in Chinese tourists.

exampleSentences.italian: The most common symptoms of the coronavirus include a fever (febbre), tiredness (stanchezza) and a dry cough (tosse secca).
exampleSentences.english: The most common symptoms of the coronavirus include a fever, tiredness and a dry cough.

englishTranslation: garbage can / trash can / rubbish bin
grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural form bidoni. Can be used standalone or modified with prepositional phrases (bidone della spazzatura, bidone dei rifiuti, bidone dell'immondizia) to specify the type of waste. Gender agreement applies to articles and adjectives modifying it.
learnerNotes: Bidone has multiple meanings: primarily a garbage can, but also slang for a decrepit old car. The expressions fare/dare/tirare un bidone (to scam or stand someone up) are idiomatic and should be learned as fixed phrases. Related synonyms include pattumiera (household bin), cestino (small paper bin), and cassonetto (large wheeled outdoor bin)—learn these distinctions for contextual accuracy.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho messo il sacchetto di plastica nel bidone della spazzatura.
exampleSentences.english: I put the plastic bag into the garbage bin.

to scam someone / to miss an appointment

englishTranslation: to grumble / to complain / to rumble
grammarNotes: Brontolare is a regular -are verb conjugated normally in the present tense (io brontolo, tu brontoli, lui/lei brontola, noi brontoliamo, voi brontolate, loro brontolano). It can describe both human complaining and natural sounds like thunder or digestive rumbling. The verb derives from Greek βροντάω (vrontáo), meaning to thunder, visible in the word 'brontosaurus.'
learnerNotes: Brontolare is useful for describing both literal complaints and onomatopoetic sounds (thunder, stomach noises), making it more versatile than a simple 'complain' verb. The noun brontolone/brontolona is colloquial and often used jokingly among friends. Note that while the verb describes the action, derived nouns like brontolio and brontolone add nuance for expressing frustration with complainers.

exampleSentences.italian: Mio padre non faceva altro che brontolare giorno e notte.
exampleSentences.english: My father did nothing but grumble day and night.

exampleSentences.italian: Dai, non fare il brontolone come al solito.
exampleSentences.english: Come on, don't be a grump as usual.

exampleSentences.italian: Si sentì un tuono brontolare in lontananza.
exampleSentences.english: Thunder was heard rumbling in the distance.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a complaint, gripe, or low rumbling sound
a grump or grouch; a person who complains constantly

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural battute. The word is highly polysemous with different meanings across contexts (acting, writing, music, sports, hunting). Gender agreement applies when used with adjectives or articles (una battuta, le battute).
learnerNotes: Battuta is highly context-dependent; the meaning changes dramatically depending on the field (acting, music, sports, writing). As a beginner, focus on the primary sense: a witty, spontaneous comment or joke. Don't confuse battuta (witty remark) with barzelletta (premeditated joke) or scherzo (prank/trick)—each has distinct connotations regarding preparation and intent.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho fatto una battuta sulla barba di mio fratello e si è offeso.
exampleSentences.english: I made a joke about my brother's beard and he got offended.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with regular plural pietre. Derived from Greek pétrā. Can refer both to large compact mineral masses and smaller fragments. The name Pietro (Peter) shares the same etymological root, providing a useful mnemonic device.
learnerNotes: Pietra and its synonym sasso are largely interchangeable, but sasso is preferred for water-smoothed stones and when describing smaller pebbles. Note that pietra preziosa (gemstone) is the standard expression—you would not say sasso prezioso. The idiomatic uses (avere un cuore di pietra, mettere una pietra sopra) are common in everyday Italian and worth memorizing.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo pavimento è in pietra.
exampleSentences.english: This floor is made of stone.

exampleSentences.italian: Il bambino ha lanciato una pietra contro la finestra.
exampleSentences.english: The boy threw a rock/stone at the window.

exampleSentences.italian: Chi è senza peccati scagli la prima pietra.
exampleSentences.english: Let him who is without sin cast the first stone.

to turn the page, to leave the past behind
to start the construction of a building, often with a ceremony
to not be able to swallow or stomach something

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural zaini. Uses the articles lo/un for singular (lo zaino, uno zaino) and gli/degli for plural (gli zaini, degli zaini). The diminutive form zainetto (small backpack) is commonly used to refer specifically to children's school backpacks.
learnerNotes: Zaino is a common everyday word for any bag with shoulder straps, not just hiking backpacks. Note that Italian has no dedicated verb 'to backpack'—use the phrase 'viaggiare con lo zaino in spalla' instead. The diminutive zainetto is frequently used when discussing school supplies or children's belongings.

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi serve una valigia. Lo zaino è più che sufficiente.
exampleSentences.english: I don't need a suitcase. The backpack is more than enough.

exampleSentences.italian: Non dimenticare lo zainetto quando vai a scuola, Beatrice!

relatedExpressions.expression: viaggiare con lo zaino in spalla
