to be swollen with pride (literally: to be full of wind)
to take full advantage of all circumstances (literally: to go where the wind blows)
to speak in vain (literally: to speak to the wind)
to waste something (literally: to throw something to the wind)
to go on happily, without problems (literally: to go with the wind in the stern)
What brings you here! (antiquated, used when an old acquaintance appears unexpectedly)

grammarNotes: Panino is a masculine singular noun (il panino). Its plural is panini. It is the diminutive form of pane (bread), formed with the -ino suffix. Related compound forms include panino imbottito and panino farcito (both meaning 'filled sandwich').
learnerNotes: Note that panini (the plural you likely encounter in English) is the correct Italian plural form. While 'sandwich' has entered Italian, panino remains the standard and far more frequently used term. Be careful not to confuse panino with tramezzino—the latter specifically refers to the American-style sandwich made with soft white bread and is typically served in Italian bars as an inexpensive snack.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho mangiato solo un panino a pranzo.
exampleSentences.english: I ate just a sandwich for lunch.

relatedExpressions.meaning: American-style sandwich made with white bread (pancarré), typically triangular and crustless

grammarNotes: Triste is an invariable adjective ending in -e, maintaining the same form for masculine and feminine singular subjects. The plural form is tristi for all genders. It commonly pairs with verbs like essere, sentirsi, diventare, rendere, and vedere to express emotional states or observations.
learnerNotes: Use essere triste for permanent states (Sono triste) and sentirsi triste for temporary feelings (Mi sento triste oggi). The verb vedere + triste translates literally as 'I see you sad' but means 'you look sad'—a common Italian construction. Synonyms like depresso, infelice, and malinconico exist, but triste is the most frequently used everyday word for sadness.

exampleSentences.italian: È una situazione molto triste per tutte le persone coinvolte.
exampleSentences.english: It is a very sad situation for everyone involved.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono triste di dovermene andare.
exampleSentences.english: I'm sad that I have to leave.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi sento triste oggi.
exampleSentences.english: I feel sad today.

exampleSentences.italian: Divento triste facilmente.
exampleSentences.english: I become sad easily.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi ha reso / fatto diventare molto triste.
exampleSentences.english: It made me very sad.

exampleSentences.italian: Ti vedo triste stamattina. È successo qualcosa?
exampleSentences.english: You look sad this morning. Did something happen?

exampleSentences.italian: Il ragazzo che abita sopra di noi ha sempre un'aria triste.
exampleSentences.english: The boy who lives above us always looks sad.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a sad air/vibe; to look sad

englishTranslation: gourmet / foodie / connoisseur of good food
grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural forms. Definite articles: il buongustaio (singular), i buongustai (plural). Indefinite articles: un buongustaio (singular), dei buongustai (plural). Formed from the compound buon- (good) + gustare (to taste) + -aio (agent noun suffix).
learnerNotes: Buongustaio differs semantically from mangione and golosone: while those terms focus on quantity of eating, buongustaio emphasizes refined taste and appreciation for quality food without overeating. The word can extend metaphorically to any domain of taste or expertise (e.g., cigars, wine, art). Note the irregular plural buongustai rather than buongustaios.

exampleSentences.italian: Lasciamo decidere al buongustaio che cosa ordinare.
exampleSentences.english: Let the gourmet decide what to order.

exampleSentences.italian: Marco è un buongustaio in fatto di sigari.
exampleSentences.english: Marco really knows his cigars.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a person who eats a lot
a person who cannot resist eating large quantities of certain kinds of foods

grammarNotes: Like all Italian adjectives ending in -o, morbido agrees with the noun it modifies. Masculine singular: morbido; feminine singular: morbida; masculine plural: morbidi; feminine plural: morbide. The word can also function as a noun meaning 'something soft.'
learnerNotes: Beware of the false cognate: morbido (soft) ≠ morbid (morboso in Italian). Both derive from the Latin morbus (disease) but diverged in meaning over time. In arts and photography, morbido describes delicate, harmonious tones and can be translated as 'soft' or 'subdued.' Remember gender and number agreement when using morbido as an adjective.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo gatto ha un pelo molto morbido.
exampleSentences.english: This cat has very soft fur.

exampleSentences.italian: La fotografia di Andrea è morbida e poco dettagliata, quasi surreale.
exampleSentences.english: Andrea's photography is subdued and not very detailed, almost dreamy.

relatedExpressions.meaning: soft little (diminutive form, e.g. coniglio morbidino = soft little bunny)
big soft (augmentative form, e.g. cane morbidone = big soft dog)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural squali. Because it begins with s + consonant, it takes the indefinite article uno (uno squalo) and definite article lo (lo squalo). Plural articles are gli and degli (gli squali, degli squali). The word derives from Latin squalus.
learnerNotes: Don't confuse squalo (shark) with squallido (run-down, sleazy), which are completely different words. Remember the s + consonant rule: uno squalo, lo squalo—this applies to many Italian words starting with s + consonant. The figurative use of squalo to describe an aggressive, exploitative person is common in business contexts, similar to English.

exampleSentences.italian: uno squalo
exampleSentences.english: a shark

exampleSentences.italian: lo squalo
exampleSentences.english: the shark

exampleSentences.italian: gli squali
exampleSentences.english: the sharks

exampleSentences.italian: degli squali
exampleSentences.english: some sharks

exampleSentences.italian: A differenza di altri pesci, lo squalo ha uno scheletro fatto di cartilagine.
exampleSentences.english: Unlike other fish, the shark has a cartilage skeleton.

exampleSentences.italian: Negli affari Nicola è un vero squalo.
exampleSentences.english: In business matters, Nicola is a real shark.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with regular plural form salse. Salsa is used for both prepared sauces and condiments. The related synonym sugo is also feminine and refers specifically to cooked, seasoned sauces. Both words are countable and take standard feminine article agreements (la salsa, delle salse).
learnerNotes: Note that sugo is a close synonym but refers more specifically to cooked, seasoned sauces, while salsa is broader. The idiom 'in tutte le salse' is useful for describing repetitive persuasion attempts. Be aware that salsa can also reference the dance style in Italian, so context determines meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: Sai mica dove posso comperare la salsa di pomodoro?
exampleSentences.english: Do you have any idea where I can buy tomato sauce?

exampleSentences.italian: Servono ottimi ingredienti per realizzare un buon sugo di pomodoro.
exampleSentences.english: You need excellent ingredients to make a good tomato sauce.

exampleSentences.italian: Glie l'ho detto in tutte le salse, ma non mi ha dato retta.
exampleSentences.english: I told him in every possible way, but he didn't listen.

relatedExpressions.meaning: in all possible ways; repeatedly presenting something in various ways to convince someone
to change something only in appearance, not substance

relatedExpressions.expression: salsa di pomodoro / salsa al pomodoro

relatedExpressions.meaning: green sauce (typically with garlic, capers, anchovies, parsley)

grammarNotes: Pecora is a feminine noun with plural pecore. The male is montone or ariete (ram), and the offspring is agnello (lamb) up to one year old. In figurative usage, pecora can be used as a derogatory term for a person, retaining its feminine gender or used generically with masculine plural pecorone (big sheep).
learnerNotes: Pecora has both literal and figurative meanings: literally it refers to a female sheep, but figuratively it describes someone silly, cowardly, or submissive who follows the crowd mindlessly. The diminutive pecorella is common and has multiple meanings (small sheep, faithful follower, or a small white cloud), so context is essential. Related terms like montone (ram) and agnello (lamb) are distinct and should not be confused with pecora.

exampleSentences.italian: La pecora sta pascolando sulla collina.
exampleSentences.english: The sheep is grazing on the hill.

exampleSentences.italian: Siete una massa di pecoroni! Ragionate con la vostra testa per una volta!
exampleSentences.english: You're a bunch of lemmings! Think for yourselves for once!

relatedExpressions.expression: Chi fa la pecora, il lupo la mangia
relatedExpressions.meaning: If you allow yourself to be weak, you will suffer harmful consequences

relatedExpressions.expression: Meglio un giorno da leone che cento da pecora
relatedExpressions.meaning: It's better to be brave than live in fear
big sheep; someone who mindlessly follows the crowd
little sheep; a faithful Christian follower; a small white cloud

grammarNotes: Per sempre is a two-word prepositional phrase composed of per (for) + sempre (always/still). It functions as an adverbial expression modifying verbs to indicate perpetual duration. The phrase remains unchanged regardless of subject or tense; the conjugation occurs only on the accompanying verb.
learnerNotes: Per sempre is one of the most common ways to express perpetual duration in Italian and should be memorized as a fixed phrase. Note that English uses the single word 'forever' while Italian requires two separate words. Be careful not to confuse per (for) with per favore (please); they share the preposition but have different meanings in context.

exampleSentences.italian: Chi vuole vivere per sempre?
exampleSentences.english: Who wants to live forever?

exampleSentences.italian: Spero che rimarremo amici per sempre.
exampleSentences.english: I hope we will be friends forever.

exampleSentences.italian: durare per sempre
exampleSentences.english: to last forever

exampleSentences.italian: vivere per sempre
exampleSentences.english: to live forever

exampleSentences.italian: tacere per sempre
exampleSentences.english: to forever hold one's peace

exampleSentences.italian: restare per sempre
exampleSentences.english: to stay forever

exampleSentences.italian: amare per sempre
exampleSentences.english: to love forever

exampleSentences.italian: Ci sarò per sempre nei tuoi occhi ovunque.
exampleSentences.english: I'll be there forever in your eyes everywhere.

exampleSentences.italian: Tu sei per me il bene più caro.
exampleSentences.english: You are the dearest benefit to me.

grammarNotes: Festa is a feminine noun (la festa) meaning 'celebration' or 'holiday.' Repubblica is also feminine (la repubblica). The phrase uses the preposition 'della' (di + la = della), a contraction showing possession. In Italian, national holidays are typically capitalized and referred to with the definite article.
learnerNotes: Festa della Repubblica is always capitalized and used with the definite article (la). Note that 'festa' can mean both 'celebration' and 'holiday/party,' while 'Repubblica' specifically refers to the form of government established in 1946. Be careful not to confuse festa (celebration) with Pasqua (Easter) or other religious holidays—Repubblica Day is secular and commemorates Italy's transition from monarchy to republic.

exampleSentences.italian: Ogni anno il 2 giugno, gli italiani celebrano la Festa della Repubblica.
exampleSentences.english: Every year on June 2nd, Italians celebrate Republic Day.

exampleSentences.italian: La Festa della Repubblica celebra il referendum istituzionale tenutosi un anno dopo la fine della Seconda Guerra Mondiale.
exampleSentences.english: Republic Day celebrates the institutional referendum held just a year after the end of the Second World War.

exampleSentences.italian: L'evento principale si svolge sempre a Roma.
exampleSentences.english: The main event always takes place in Rome.

exampleSentences.italian: Durante la cerimonia, viene cantato l'inno nazionale italiano.
exampleSentences.english: During the ceremony, the Italian National anthem is sung.

exampleSentences.italian: Poiché è una festa nazionale, molti negozi e uffici rimangono chiusi.
exampleSentences.english: Because it is a public holiday, many shops and offices remain closed.

relatedExpressions.meaning: Tricolour Arrows (Italian Air Force aerobatic team)

grammarNotes: Respirare is a regular -ARE verb conjugated as: respiro, respiri, respira, respiriamo, respirate, respirano in the present tense. It shares etymology with the English verb 'to respire' and is the standard Italian term for breathing. Related verbs include inspirare (to inhale), espirare (to exhale), aspirare (to inhale/breathe in), esalare (to exhale), and inalare (to inhale, medicinal context).
learnerNotes: The noun respiro (breath/breather) derives from respirare and is frequently used in set phrases. Be aware of the semantic distinction between respiro (the act of breathing) and fiato (the air expelled), as fiato is preferred in figurative expressions. The verbs aspirare, espirare, inspirare, esalare, and inalare all relate to breathing but have specific contexts: aspirare and inspirare both mean 'to inhale' but aspirare requires a direct object, while inalare is typically used for medicinal/gaseous contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Faccio fatica a respirare quando corro.
exampleSentences.english: I find it hard to breathe when I'm running.

exampleSentences.italian: Chiudi gli occhi, inspira, e poi espira lentamente.
exampleSentences.english: Close your eyes, breathe in, and then breathe out slowly.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho preso un fiore, l'ho avvicinato al naso e ne ho aspirato il profumo.
exampleSentences.english: I picked a flower, brought it to my nose and breathed in its scent.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to draw one's last breath; to die

grammarNotes: Facile is invariable in singular form (used for both masculine and feminine subjects: il libro facile, la canzone facile). The plural is facili for all genders (i libri facili, le canzoni facili). It can be followed by da/a + infinitive to express 'easy to do something.' When combined with essere + subjunctive clause, it expresses probability.
learnerNotes: Beware of the false cognate: English 'facile' means simplistic or superficial, while Italian 'facile' simply means 'easy.' Note the gender distinction: una donna facile means a promiscuous woman, but un uomo facile means an easygoing, amiable man—a significant semantic difference based on gender. The prepositions 'da' and 'a' can both be used with the infinitive (facile da fare/facile a fare) with subtle differences in usage.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural form cibi. Can function as both a mass noun and count noun, with the plural cibi used more freely than English 'food.' Commonly modified by adjectives like buono, cattivo, pesante, piccante, fresco, sano. Derived from Latin cibus.
learnerNotes: While cibare (to feed) is the formal verb derived from cibo, colloquial Italian strongly prefers dare da mangiare a instead. Note that alimento is a more formal/scientific synonym emphasizing nutritional value, whereas cucina can substitute cibo when referring to cuisines from specific countries (e.g., cucina messicana). Figuratively, cibo extends to intellectual or spiritual nourishment, as in the expression 'Art is food for the soul.'

exampleSentences.italian: Ho una passione per il buon cibo italiano.
exampleSentences.english: I have a passion for good Italian food.

exampleSentences.english: The mother fed her child.

exampleSentences.english: Art is food for the soul.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form inizi. Can denote both a point in time (l'inizio dell'anno) and a physical location (l'inizio della strada). Often used in plural when referring to prolonged periods or early stages (gli inizi del medioevo). Used in three verbal constructions: iniziare (to begin), dare + inizio (to give beginning), and avere + inizio (to have a beginning—strictly intransitive).
learnerNotes: Remember that inizio is masculine (il/un inizio) and its plural inizi is commonly used for extended time periods (gli inizi dell'estate). Be careful with avere + inizio: it's strictly intransitive, so you cannot say *avere inizio qualcosa; use dare inizio a instead. The related verb iniziare is much more common in everyday speech than the costructions with dare/avere + inizio.

exampleSentences.italian: L'inizio del film era interessante ma il finale era banale.
exampleSentences.english: The beginning of the film was interesting but the end was banal.

exampleSentences.italian: Sto per dare inizio ad un nuovo progetto.
exampleSentences.english: I'm about to begin a new project.

exampleSentences.english: The construction of the church began in 1678.

exampleSentences.italian: Gli inizi sono sempre difficili.
exampleSentences.english: It's always difficult at the beginning. (Lit: The initial period is always difficult.)

grammarNotes: Scodella is a feminine noun with regular plural scodelle. It can refer either to the physical bowl itself or to the quantity of food it contains (bowlful). Diminutive scodellina denotes smaller bowls, while scodellone refers to large bowls. Gender agreement applies to adjectives describing it.
learnerNotes: Scodella is the most generic word for bowl in Italian, but context matters: use piatto fondo specifically for soup plates, insalatiera for salad bowls, and tazza for cereal. Be careful not to confuse scodella with coppa (which refers to a cup or goblet) or insalatiera (which is specifically for salad and larger than typical eating bowls). Remember that scodella can mean either the container or the quantity it holds, depending on context.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho versato il brodo in una scodella di plastica.
exampleSentences.english: I poured the broth into a plastic bowl.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho mangiato due scodelle di zuppa.
exampleSentences.english: I ate two bowlfuls of soup.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural letti. Derives from Latin lectus. The diminutive form lettino refers to small beds, cribs, cots, and fold-up beds. Also functions as the past participle of leggere (to read).
learnerNotes: Note that 'letto' has multiple meanings: as a noun it means bed, but as the past participle of 'leggere' (to read) it means 'read.' The phrase 'andare a letto con i polli' is a distinctly Italian idiom with no English equivalent—it describes early sleeping habits, not anything inappropriate. Be careful not to confuse 'stanza da letto' (bedroom) with just 'stanza' (any room), though 'camera' alone often refers to a bedroom in casual Italian.

exampleSentences.english: Go to bed, it's late!

exampleSentences.italian: Gianni va sempre a letto con i polli perché si alza molto presto al mattino.
exampleSentences.english: Gianni always goes to bed early so that he can wake up early in the morning.

exampleSentences.english: Each room has sleeping accommodation for three people and an additional extra bed upon request.

exampleSentences.english: I read that book last week.

grammarNotes: As an adjective, caldo agrees with the noun in gender and number: caldo (m.s.), calda (f.s.), caldi (m.p.), calde (f.p.). When used as a noun, caldo means 'heat'. In weather expressions, use the verb fare rather than essere: Fa caldo (It is hot) rather than È caldo.
learnerNotes: Remember that Italian uses Fa caldo for weather expressions with the verb fare, not essere. The word caldo has many figurative uses beyond temperature: it describes passionate personalities (avere il sangue caldo), enthusiastic displays (una calda accoglienza), and recent events (una notizia calda). Importantly, unlike English slang, caldo does not mean 'attractive'—use figo, figa, or sexy instead.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with regular plural maledizioni. Composed of male (bad/evil) + dizione (speech/diction). Can function as both a literal supernatural curse and a figurative expression for any source of misfortune. The exclamation 'Maledizione!' is old-fashioned but still used.
learnerNotes: Maledizione as an exclamation (Maledizione!) is becoming old-fashioned; younger speakers prefer mannaggia or accidenti. The figurative sense (any source of misfortune) is common in everyday Italian, so don't assume it always refers to supernatural curses. Remember the feminine gender and plural form when using related verbs like avere, essere, and spezzare.

grammarNotes: Cielo is a masculine noun with plural form cieli. It agrees with adjectives in gender and number (e.g., cielo azzurro, cieli azzurri). The word has both literal (sky) and figurative (heaven/God) meanings depending on context.
learnerNotes: Note that cielo has dual meanings: literal (the sky) and figurative/religious (heaven/God), with the latter used in common exclamations and idioms. The expression 'a cielo aperto' (literally 'open sky') is essential vocabulary for describing outdoor activities. Be aware that 'intervento a cielo aperto' (open surgery) is a specific medical term that extends the metaphor into professional contexts.

exampleSentences.english: The sky is filled with clouds today.

grammarNotes: Fresco is a four-form adjective that agrees with gender and number: fresco (masc. sing.), fresca (fem. sing.), freschi (masc. plur.), fresche (fem. plur.). It can function as a standalone descriptor or within idiomatic expressions. The verb phrase 'mettere al fresco' and 'tenere in fresco' use the noun form of the word.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'fresco' has multiple meanings depending on context: temperature (cool/chilly), quality (fresh), and time (new/recent). Crucially, never say you want to eat 'al fresco' in Italy—this literally means 'in prison' due to historical cold cells, not outdoors. Use 'mangiare all'aperto' (eat outdoors) instead. The idiomatic expression 'stare fresco' is colloquial and means to be in trouble or difficulty.

grammarNotes: Turista is a masculine/feminine noun (invariant in form: il turista, la turista, i turisti, le turiste). It derives from English 'tourist' rather than Latin, making it a loanword. The related adjective turistico (touristic/touristy) agrees with the noun it modifies in gender and number.
learnerNotes: Turista is one of the few Italian words that comes from English rather than Latin, so it won't follow traditional Romance language patterns. Note that the plural turisti applies to both masculine and feminine groups. Be aware of 'turisti mordi e fuggi'—a colloquial expression describing tourists who visit briefly without engaging deeply with a destination.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa città è sempre piena di turisti in qualsiasi stagione.
exampleSentences.english: This city is always full of tourists no matter the season.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa è una destinazione turistica frequentata soprattutto nei mesi estivi.
exampleSentences.english: This is a popular tourist destination especially in the summer months.

grammarNotes: As an adjective, maleducato agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: maleducato (masc. sg.), maleducata (fem. sg.), maleducati (masc. pl.), maleducate (fem. pl.). The word can also function as a noun to describe an ill-mannered person. It is formed from the prefix male- (bad) + educato (educated/mannered).
learnerNotes: Maleducato is commonly paired with 'in modo maleducato' rather than the adverb form because it's easier to pronounce for native speakers. Note that while maleducato is neutral in register, related terms like scortese, sgarbato, volgare, and osceno offer synonyms with varying intensity—volgare and osceno carry stronger, more offensive connotations. False cognate alert: educato does not mean 'educated' in the academic sense, but rather 'well-mannered' or 'polite.'

exampleSentences.italian: A volte quel ragazzo è proprio maleducato con i suoi genitori.
exampleSentences.english: Sometimes that boy is really rude to his parents.

exampleSentences.english: He acted rudely towards me.

exampleSentences.italian: Quella ragazza è una gran maleducata!

grammarNotes: Vergogna is a feminine noun with plural form vergogne. It agrees with definite articles (la vergogna) and indefinite articles (una vergogna). The related reflexive verb vergognarsi means 'to feel ashamed,' and the adjective vergognoso means 'shameful/disgraceful.' In plural form (vergogne), it can euphemistically refer to private parts.
learnerNotes: Vergogna is highly versatile: use it with 'sentire/provare' for emotional shame, with 'essere' + article to describe someone/something as a disgrace, and as an exclamation (Vergogna!, Che vergogna!) to express disapproval. Be aware of register—Vergognati! is more forceful than the softer reflexive vergognarsi. The euphemistic plural vergogne is colloquial and should be avoided in formal contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Non provi neanche un po' di vergogna per quello che hai fatto?
exampleSentences.english: Don't you feel even a little bit ashamed for what you've done?

exampleSentences.italian: Non si dicono le bugie! Vergogna!
exampleSentences.english: You shouldn't tell lies! Shame on you!

exampleSentences.italian: Quel ragazzo è la vergogna della famiglia.
exampleSentences.english: That boy is a disgrace to his family.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel nuovo grattacielo è una vera vergogna!
exampleSentences.english: That new skyscraper is a real disgrace!

exampleSentences.italian: Copriti le vergogne! Ti vedono tutti!
exampleSentences.english: Cover your private parts! Everyone can see you!

grammarNotes: Scemo functions as both a noun and adjective. As an adjective, it agrees with the noun it modifies: scemo (masc. sing.), scema (fem. sing.), scemi (masc. plur.), sceme (fem. plur.). When used as a noun (the idiot/fool), it also agrees with the gender of the person being described.
learnerNotes: Scemo is a common colloquial insult and can be quite offensive; use with caution in real conversations. Note the diminutive tendencies in Italian speech—you may hear variants or emphatic forms in heated discussions. Related synonyms like cretino, stupido, and imbecille are largely interchangeable but may carry slightly different tones of offense or formality.

grammarNotes: Orso is a masculine noun derived from Latin ursus. It takes the definite article l'orso (singular) and gli orsi (plural), and indefinite articles un orso (singular) and (degli) orsi (plural). Like all Italian nouns, it requires gender agreement with adjectives and articles.
learnerNotes: Orso can be used both literally (for the animal) and figuratively to describe a grumpy, antisocial person. Note that diminutives orsetto and orsacchiotto are common in Italian and have distinct uses. Be aware that several idiomatic expressions with orso exist; 'vendere la pelle dell'orso prima di averlo ucciso' is particularly useful as it parallels English expressions about premature counting.

grammarNotes: Estate is a feminine noun (la estate). The plural form is estati. It can be modified by adjectives like estivo or d'estate to mean 'summer' as an adjective (e.g., vacanze estive = summer vacation). The word is used for both meteorological summer (June 1–August 31) and astronomical summer (starting with the solstizio d'estate).
learnerNotes: Remember that estate is feminine, so use la estate and adjectives must agree (estiva, not estivo, when modifying a feminine noun). The adjective form varies: use estivo/estiva/estivi/estive as a standalone adjective, but use d'estate in fixed expressions like 'vacanze d'estate' or 'giorno d'estate'. The peak vacation period Ferragosto (August 15) is culturally significant in Italy and many businesses close during this time.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with regular plural spiagge. Used with prepositions: alla/in spiaggia (to the beach), sulla spiaggia (on the beach), lungo la spiaggia (along the beach). Derived from the obsolete word piaggia meaning slope, shore, or land.
learnerNotes: Note the different prepositions: use 'alla' or 'in' spiaggia (to go to), but 'sulla' or 'lungo' la spiaggia (on/along). The expression 'ultima spiaggia' is idiomatic and means 'last resort' rather than a literal beach. Be aware that 'spiaggia rocciosa' (rocky beach) and 'spiaggia sabbiosa' (sandy beach) are common descriptive terms in Italian travel contexts.

grammarNotes: Frutta is a feminine singular collective noun (almost always used with definite article 'la') referring to fruit in general or a fruit course. Frutto is the masculine singular form for individual fruits (plural: frutti), used with both definite and indefinite articles. The feminine plural frutte exists but is rarely used.
learnerNotes: Remember that frutta is always feminine and typically paired with 'la'; using 'una frutta' is incorrect. Use frutto (masculine) when referring to individual fruits. Watch out for the idiom 'essere alla frutta'—it means someone is finished or has no prospects, not simply that they're eating fruit!

exampleSentences.italian: La frutta contiene tantissime vitamine.
exampleSentences.english: Fruit contains loads of vitamins.

exampleSentences.italian: Cerco sempre di mangiare un frutto dopo il pasto.
exampleSentences.english: I always try to eat a piece of fruit after my meal.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel cantante è alla frutta. Non ha più la voce di una volta.
exampleSentences.english: That singer has had it. He doesn't have the voice he once did.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be at the end of the road with no chance of comeback (idiom)
to arrive at the end of something or to arrive late

grammarNotes: Giardino is a masculine noun with plural form giardini. It derives from French jardin and Germanic roots (gart/garto). The diminutive form giardinetto refers to a small garden. When used as an adjective (e.g., città giardino), it describes places surrounded by greenery.
learnerNotes: Note that giardino can mean 'garden,' 'yard,' or 'park' depending on context; giardini pubblici specifically refers to urban parks. The related verb is fare giardinaggio (to garden), not simply 'giardinare.' Be careful not to confuse giardiniera (female gardener or pickled vegetables) with the masculine giardiniere (male gardener).

exampleSentences.italian: La casa è circondata da un giardino immenso.
exampleSentences.english: The house is surrounded by an immense garden.

exampleSentences.italian: Porto i bambini ai giardini pubblici dopo la scuola.
exampleSentences.english: I'll take the kids to the park after school.

exampleSentences.italian: L'Italia è il giardino d'Europa.
exampleSentences.english: Italy is the garden of Europe.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to garden / take care of the garden

grammarNotes: Cane is a masculine noun; plural is cani. The feminine form is cagna (bitch). Diminutives include cagnolino (small dog/puppy) and cagnone (big dog). It derives from Latin canis and is etymologically related to English 'canine.'
learnerNotes: Cane has important figurative uses in Italian: it describes cruelty or incompetence, and appears in many expressions meaning 'very bad' or 'miserable.' Be cautious with curse phrases like 'Figlio di un cane!' and expressions with cavolo/cazzo as they can be offensive. Note that some compound forms (alla cazzo di cane) are considered vulgar and should be avoided in formal settings.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piacerebbe adottare un cane nero.
exampleSentences.english: I would like to adopt a black dog.

exampleSentences.english: Dog pork!

grammarNotes: Squisito is a four-form adjective that agrees with the gender and number of the noun it modifies: squisito (masc. sing.), squisita (fem. sing.), squisiti (masc. plur.), squisite (fem. plur.). The absolute superlative form is squisitissimo/a/i/e, meaning 'extremely delicious/exquisite.' It also has an adverb form, squisitamente, which means 'exquisitely' or 'in an exquisite manner.'
learnerNotes: Squisito is distinct from delizioso (which means 'adorable' or 'charming' rather than specifically 'delicious'). Use squisito when praising food quality or describing refined, elegant aspects of people and objects. The adverb squisitamente can modify both verbs (cucinare) and adjectives (raffinata), making it a versatile intensifier for describing excellence.

exampleSentences.italian: Non c'è niente di meglio che mangiare un piatto squisito in un luogo squisito.
exampleSentences.english: There's nothing like eating a delicious meal in an exquisite location.

exampleSentences.italian: Grazie mille per la cena. Era tutto squisitissimo!
exampleSentences.english: Thank you very much for the dinner. Everything was absolutely delicious!

grammarNotes: Carino is a four-form adjective ending in -o that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: carino (masc. sing.), carina (fem. sing.), carini (masc. pl.), carine (fem. pl.). To express 'very cute,' use the adverb molto or the absolute superlative carinissimo. It functions both as a descriptive adjective for physical appearance and behavior, and as an exclamation of approval.
learnerNotes: Carino is one of the most frequently used adjectives in everyday Italian conversation and is far more versatile than 'cute' alone—it describes physical appearance, personality traits, actions, and even abstract concepts like jokes or thoughts. Remember that when used as a standalone exclamation (Carino!), it expresses genuine appreciation or approval. The diminutive form caro (dear) is its root, so carino carries an affectionate undertone even in neutral contexts.

exampleSentences.english: She has been very kind to me.

exampleSentences.english: Who's going to tell me a funny joke?

exampleSentences.english: How lovely! I'm going to buy it right away!

englishTranslation: fluffy / hairy / furry / fuzzy / woolly / shaggy
grammarNotes: Peloso is a regular adjective ending in -o with four forms based on gender and number: peloso (m. sing.), pelosa (f. sing.), pelosi (m. plur.), pelose (f. plur.). Like all Italian adjectives, it must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. It derives from the noun pelo (hair).
learnerNotes: Peloso has both literal and figurative meanings: literally it describes texture (fluffy, hairy), but figuratively it can describe a person who is self-interested, hypocritical, and lacks moral scruples. Note the synonyms irsuto, villoso, lanuginoso, and lanoso—these are more formal/technical alternatives. Pay attention to gender agreement when using this adjective in different contexts.

exampleSentences.english: a fluffy cat

grammarNotes: Natura is a feminine noun with regular plural form 'nature'. It corresponds directly to English 'nature' across multiple semantic fields: physical environment, inherent character, and essence of things. The adjective form is 'naturale' (natural), which agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies.
learnerNotes: Natura is a straightforward cognate with English, making it easy to remember. Note that 'pagare in natura' has both literal (barter) and colloquial sexual meanings—context is crucial. The phrase 'per natura' (by nature) and 'nella mia natura' (in my nature) are common idiomatic uses when describing inherent personality traits.

exampleSentences.italian: Noi esseri umani non esisteremmo senza la natura.
exampleSentences.english: We human beings would not exist without nature.

exampleSentences.italian: Non è nella mia natura essere disonesto.
exampleSentences.english: It's not in my nature to be dishonest.

exampleSentences.italian: Un agente segreto non può mai rivelare la vera natura del suo lavoro.
exampleSentences.english: A secret agent can never reveal the true nature of his work.

exampleSentences.italian: È morto per cause naturali.
exampleSentences.english: He died of natural causes.

relatedExpressions.meaning: against nature; unnatural, improper, or immoral
to pay with goods/merchandise instead of money; also has sexual connotation

grammarNotes: Colazione is a feminine noun; plural is colazioni. The adjective prima (first) is commonly paired with it as prima colazione (traditional term for breakfast). It derives from the French collatiòn and Latin collatiònem, meaning to contribute or bring together, originally referring to meals taken by Christian monks after evening meetings.
learnerNotes: Note that historically colazione meant any meal of the day (prima colazione = breakfast, seconda colazione = lunch), but today only prima colazione survives with this meaning; pranzo is now the standard word for lunch. At a bar/café, Italians typically order a cappuccino or espresso with a cornetto (croissant), which is different from the traditional home breakfast of caffè latte with bread and spreads. Be careful not to confuse colazione with cena (supper/dinner), which is eaten much later in the evening (7-9 p.m.) in Italy.

exampleSentences.italian: Non bisogna saltare la colazione perché è il pasto più importante della giornata.
exampleSentences.english: We shouldn't skip breakfast because it is the most important meal of the day.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai già mangiato? No? Allora andiamo a fare colazione al bar.
exampleSentences.english: Have you eaten already? No? Then let's go have breakfast at the café.

relatedExpressions.meaning: breakfast (literally 'first breakfast'); traditional term still used today
breakfast with solid food requiring a knife and fork
packed breakfast to take on a trip or class outing
working breakfast; quick lunch with colleagues discussing business

grammarNotes: Bocca is a feminine noun with plural bocche. It derives from Latin bucca (cheek). The word is used literally for the mouth of living creatures and figuratively for openings or entrances of objects and natural features. Common phrases require proper article and preposition agreement.
learnerNotes: Bocca is an essential body part vocabulary item and appears in numerous idiomatic expressions that are worth memorizing in context. Pay attention to prepositions: 'in bocca' (in the mouth), 'di bocca' (of/from the mouth), and 'della bocca' (of the mouth). The idiom 'In bocca al lupo!' (literally 'in the wolf's mouth') is commonly used like English 'break a leg' for wishing someone good luck, with the response being 'Crepi il lupo!' (may the wolf die).

exampleSentences.italian: Ho messo la gomma da masticare in bocca.
exampleSentences.english: I put the chewing gum in my mouth.

exampleSentences.english: Good luck on your exam tomorrow!

grammarNotes: Luglio is a masculine noun (il luglio) and, like all Italian month names, is not capitalized in standard written Italian, unlike in English. It is invariable and does not change form in plural contexts. The word derives from Latin iūlius, named after Julius Caesar.
learnerNotes: Remember that Italian month names are never capitalized, even at the beginning of a sentence—this is a key difference from English. Both idiomatic expressions featuring luglio relate to deception or exaggeration, so they're useful for advanced conversational contexts. Note that luglio has 31 days, making it one of the longer months, which may be worth remembering for practical contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: We have officially entered the first days of July
exampleSentences.english: We have officially entered the first days of July (i primi giorni di luglio)

exampleSentences.italian: Luglio is the seventh month of the year according to the Julian and Gregorian calendars.
exampleSentences.english: Luglio is the seventh month of the year according to the Julian and Gregorian calendars.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mese di luglio dura 31 giorni.
exampleSentences.english: The month of July lasts 31 days.

grammarNotes: Capelli is always plural when referring to hair on one's head; the singular capello refers to an individual strand. It is a masculine plural noun. Do not confuse with cappelli (hats), which sounds similar but has a double 'p' and brief pause in pronunciation.
learnerNotes: Capelli is always used in plural form for hair on your head, never as capello in this context. Be careful with the confusing similar word cappelli (hats)—listen for the double 'p' sound and brief pause. Many hair-related verbs use reflexive forms (pettinarsi, asciugarsi, acconciarsi), so ensure you conjugate the reflexive pronoun correctly.

exampleSentences.italian: I cappelli tendono ad appiattire i capelli.
exampleSentences.english: Hats tend to flatten hair.

exampleSentences.italian: Prima di uscire, mia sorella vuole sistemarsi i capelli.
exampleSentences.english: Before going out, my sister wants to do her hair.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be sick or tired of something/someone
to have a huge number of problems to deal with

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural mostri. Gender agreement applies to adjectives and articles (il mostro, i mostri). The word has multiple figurative extensions beyond its literal meaning, all maintaining the same gender and number rules.
learnerNotes: Do not confuse mostro (monster) with mostra (exhibition)—they sound similar but have completely different meanings. Mostro has rich figurative uses: it can describe something physically ugly, a cruel person, or conversely (with the construction 'un mostro di') a prodigy or genius. Pay attention to context to determine which meaning applies.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è un mostro sotto al mio letto!
exampleSentences.english: There's a monster under my bed!

exampleSentences.italian: Quel mostro merita di rimanere dietro le sbarre per il resto della sua vita.
exampleSentences.english: That monster deserves to stay behind bars for the rest of his life.

exampleSentences.italian: Hitchcock è un mostro sacro del cinema.
exampleSentences.english: Hitchcock is a cinematic genius.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a master/prodigy in a particular field (e.g., un mostro di bravura = a genius)
sacred monster; a person who has reached unsurpassed levels in a field, universally admired
derogatory diminutive: an ugly or misshapen person/animal; also a funny pet name for a cheeky child

grammarNotes: Carota is feminine (la carota). The plural is carote. When pronouns attach to infinitive verbs, the final 'e' of the infinitive is dropped: tagliarle (to cut them) instead of tagliare + le. Gender agreement applies to related adjectives: carote crude (raw carrots, feminine plural).
learnerNotes: Note that 'carota' as a descriptor for redheads (pel di carota, capelli color carota) is less common than capelli rossi in modern Italian. When attaching pronouns to infinitives, remember to drop the final vowel: bollirle (to boil them), arrostirle (to roast them). The idioms 'vendere/piantare carote' (to tell lies) are figurative and colorful—useful for intermediate learners but not as frequently used as dire bugie.

exampleSentences.english: I prefer to cut them into pieces.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai lavato e pelato le carote?
exampleSentences.english: Have you washed and peeled the carrots?

exampleSentences.italian: Le grattuggiamo e le condiamo con sale, pepe, limone e olio d'oliva.
exampleSentences.english: We grate them and season them with salt, pepper, lemon and olive oil.

to tell lies (lit. to plant carrots)

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with regular plural tempeste. Used literally for meteorological storms (characterized by venti forti, tuoni e fulmini, forte pioggia, ghiaccio, sabbia, neve, grandine) and figuratively for inner turmoil, conflict, or bombardment of questions/calls. Gender agreement required with articles and adjectives.
learnerNotes: Tempesta is highly versatile: use it literally for weather phenomena and figuratively for emotional upheaval or chaos. The idiomatic phrase 'C'è aria di tempesta' is useful for both literal and metaphorical contexts. Note that related terms like temporale, bufera, and tormenta each specify distinct storm types, so choose precisely based on context. Be aware this word appears frequently in Italian literature and news.

exampleSentences.english: The storm caused lots of damage.

exampleSentences.english: A storm is brewing! (Figuratively: a big argument is about to start)

englishTranslation: I don't know / dunno / no idea
grammarNotes: Boh is an invariable interjection that stands alone or can be followed by reinforcing phrases like non lo so or che ne so. It is often elongated as 'booooh' for emphasis. Unlike the standard non lo so, boh conveys a casual, dismissive tone and can imply disinterest or indifference depending on intonation.
learnerNotes: Boh is highly informal and should never be used with teachers, bosses, or unfamiliar older adults, as it conveys disinterest and lack of respect. While not offensive, it suggests you don't care about the answer. Elongating the sound ('booooh') emphasizes genuine confusion rather than apathy, making the tone crucial to interpretation.

exampleSentences.italian: Vieni alla festa stasera? – Boh, forse.
exampleSentences.english: Are you coming to the party tonight? – I dunno, maybe.

exampleSentences.italian: Sai mica dov'è la stazione? – Boh…
exampleSentences.english: Do you know where the station is? – No idea…

exampleSentences.italian: Perché sta lì in mezzo alla strada!? – Booooh!
exampleSentences.english: Why is he standing in the middle of the street!? – Noooo idea!

exampleSentences.italian: Tu sai con chi sta uscendo Marta? – Boh, e che ne so io?!
exampleSentences.english: Do you know who Marta is dating? – Nope, how should I know?

relatedExpressions.expression: Non ne ho la minima idea.
Non ne ho la più pallida idea.

grammarNotes: Testardo is a four-form adjective following the -o/-a/-i/-e pattern: testardo (masc. sing.), testarda (fem. sing.), testardi (masc. plur.), testarde (fem. plur.). It can function both as an adjective modifying a noun and as a noun itself to refer to 'a stubborn person.' The word derives from testa (head), reflecting the metaphor of hardheadedness.
learnerNotes: Testardo is a high-frequency adjective for describing personality traits. The etymological link to testa (head) appears in several synonyms like testone and 'avere la testa dura,' making them memorable as a word family. Remember that testardo can be used as both an adjective and a noun without changing form in the singular masculine.

exampleSentences.italian: Che ragazzo testardo!
exampleSentences.english: What a stubborn guy!

exampleSentences.italian: Con lui non si può mai ragionare!
exampleSentences.english: You can never reason with him!

exampleSentences.italian: Sei un gran testardo, lo sai!?
exampleSentences.english: You're a really stubborn person, you know!?

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be stubborn, hard-headed (literally: to have a hard head)

grammarNotes: Fragola is a feminine noun (la fragola). The plural form is fragole. It can function as a noun referring to the plant or fruit, and can also be used as an adjective (color fragola) to describe a strawberry-red shade, in which case it remains invariable or agrees with the noun it modifies.
learnerNotes: Remember that fragola is feminine (la fragola, le fragole), so adjectives and articles must agree. The diminutive form fragoline is useful for describing small or wild strawberries. When used as a color descriptor, fragola is typically invariable or placed after the noun with 'color' (un vestito color fragola), making it less flexible than standard adjectives.

exampleSentences.italian: Adoro mangiare le fragole con la panna!
exampleSentences.english: I love eating strawberries and cream!

exampleSentences.italian: Si è messa un vestito (color) fragola per la festa.
exampleSentences.english: She put on a strawberry coloured dress for the party.

englishTranslation: spicy / hot / sharp / risqué / saucy / racy
grammarNotes: Piccante is invariable in form: it remains piccante for singular (masculine or feminine) and piccanti for plural, regardless of gender. It derives from the French 'piquant' and is used both literally (for spicy food) and figuratively (for risqué or sarcastic comments). The diminutive form piccantino describes something slightly or moderately spicy/saucy.
learnerNotes: Remember that piccante has different meanings depending on context: with food, it means spicy/hot, but with cheeses it means sharp/strong in flavor. When describing a dish with many spices that isn't hot, use speziato instead. In figurative contexts (jokes, stories, conversations), piccante translates as risqué, saucy, or sarcastic, so be mindful of register when using it.

exampleSentences.english: spicy salami

exampleSentences.english: hot sauce

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural uccelli. The diminutive form uccellino means baby bird or fledgling. The augmentative uccellone means big bird (literal) or fool (figurative). Derived from Latin aucellus. Note: uccello is also vulgar slang for male genitalia.
learnerNotes: Uccello is a common beginner-level noun; memorize the plural uccelli. Be aware of its vulgar slang usage to avoid unintended offense. The verb uccellare (to fowl/catch birds, or figuratively to fool someone) and related forms like uccellone (big bird/fool) expand your vocabulary around this root. Many bird names have interesting etymologies and cultural references (e.g., Gazza Ladra, Pettirosso) that can help with retention.

exampleSentences.italian: L'uccello è entrato dalla finestra.
exampleSentences.english: The bird came in through the window.

exampleSentences.italian: Il criminale si è reso uccel di bosco insieme ad altri due detenuti.
exampleSentences.english: The criminal disappeared into the undergrowth along with two other prisoners.

relatedExpressions.meaning: one swallow does not make a summer (one instance doesn't indicate a trend)
to sing with a clear, limpid voice
bird of the woods (fugitive, runaway, or someone hard to catch)

relatedExpressions.expression: Ogni uccello canta il suo nido
relatedExpressions.meaning: Each bird thinks its own nest is beautiful (there's no place like home)
to be a bird in a cage (to be in captivity or lacking freedom)
