grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural form edifici. Derives from Latin aedificium, cognate with English 'edifice.' Can also mean 'argument/case' (legal) or 'framework/structure' (abstract). The related verb edificare (to build, construct, erect) is less commonly used than costruire.
learnerNotes: While edificio is formal and literary, the everyday word costruzione or the verb costruire are more commonly used in casual speech. Remember that edificio can have metaphorical meanings (an 'edifice' of an argument, a framework), not just physical structures. The word palazzo deserves special attention—it means both 'palace' and 'apartment building,' depending on context, and is more frequent than edificio in modern Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: L'edificio è crollato durante il terremoto.
exampleSentences.english: The building collapsed during the earthquake.

exampleSentences.italian: L'accusa ha demolito l'edificio della difesa.
exampleSentences.english: The prosecution demolished the defence's case.

exampleSentences.italian: Lo statuto va considerato come il mattone fondamentale su cui costruire l'edificio sociale.
exampleSentences.english: The statute must be considered the fundamental building block upon which social order is built.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a building of considerable size used for various purposes
an urban building intended for homes, offices and shops
to build, construct, or erect a building

grammarNotes: Bar is a masculine noun borrowed from English. The plural form is also 'bar' (invariant). It does not follow typical Italian noun declension patterns due to its foreign origin. Gender agreement applies to articles and adjectives: il bar, un bar, dei bar.
learnerNotes: Be careful with false cognates: Italian 'bar' means café/coffee shop, NOT a place that serves alcohol (which is called 'locale'). The word is borrowed from English but has a completely different meaning in Italian context. Bar culture in Italy involves quick counter service for espresso rather than sitting down, which differs from American coffee shop culture.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è un bar in ogni angolo della città!
exampleSentences.english: There's a coffee shop on every corner of the city!

exampleSentences.italian: Facciamo pausa pranzo? C'è un bar proprio qui sotto.
exampleSentences.english: Shall we have a lunch break? There is a café just downstairs.

relatedExpressions.meaning: coffee shop with an outdoor area
bar in the American sense (alcoholic drinking establishment)

grammarNotes: Broccolo is masculine singular (il broccolo); the plural is broccoli. English borrowed the Italian plural form broccoli to use as a singular uncountable noun. The word is a diminutive of brocco (shoot/sprout) derived from Latin broccus (projecting, pointed). In colloquial Italian, broccolo can also describe a stupid or clumsy person.
learnerNotes: Note that English uses 'broccoli' as both singular and plural (uncountable), but Italian distinguishes between broccolo (singular) and broccoli (plural). The figurative meaning—calling someone a broccolo as an insult—is colloquial and should be used cautiously. Pay attention to gender: broccolo is masculine, so use il, un, questo, etc.

exampleSentences.italian: Cuciniamo i broccoli al forno stasera.
exampleSentences.english: We're cooking baked broccoli this evening.

exampleSentences.italian: Ieri Maurizio ha fatto la figura del broccolo davanti alla ragazza che gli piace.
exampleSentences.english: Yesterday Maurizio came across as a real dolt in front of the girl he likes.

relatedExpressions.meaning: broccolini/baby broccoli (hybrid of broccoli and Chinese kale)
regional Italian names for broccolini (used in some regions)
to come across as foolish or clumsy

grammarNotes: Bicicletta is a feminine noun; plural form is biciclette. It can be abbreviated to bici (also feminine). The word was borrowed from French and shares etymological roots with English 'bicycle'. Gender agreement applies to articles and adjectives: una bicicletta nuova, le biciclette rosse.
learnerNotes: The abbreviation 'bici' is very common in everyday speech and should be used confidently at A2 level. Avoid confusing 'bici' with 'motocicletta' (motorbike/motorcycle) — they are distinct vehicles. The verb phrase 'andare in bicicletta' uses the preposition 'in' rather than 'su', which is typical for modes of transport in Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Andare in bicicletta fa bene alla salute.
exampleSentences.english: Bike riding is good for your health.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai voluto la bicicletta? E adesso pedala!
exampleSentences.english: You wanted the bike? So now pedal!

exampleSentences.italian: Antonio trova un lavoro che richiede una bici per girare le strade di Roma.
exampleSentences.english: Antonio finds a job that requires a bike to ride around the streets of Rome.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to ride a bicycle, to cycle, to go bike riding

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form 'orologi'. Derives from Latin 'horologium' and Greek 'hōrológion' (combination of 'ora'—hour and 'dire'—to say). Can be modified with descriptive phrases like 'orologio da muro' (wall clock) or 'orologio da polso' (wristwatch) to specify type.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'orologio' covers both wall clocks and wristwatches—use modifiers like 'da muro' or 'da polso' to be specific. Common verbs paired with 'orologio' include 'guardare' (to look at), 'caricare' (to wind up), and 'mettere avanti/indietro' (to put forward/back). The expression 'd'orologio' meaning 'exactly' is useful in time contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mio orologio segna le dieci in punto.
exampleSentences.english: My watch says that it is 10 o'clock on the dot.

exampleSentences.italian: Il concerto ha durato due ore d'orologio.
exampleSentences.english: The concert lasted exactly two hours.

relatedExpressions.expression: essere preciso come un orologio svizzero
relatedExpressions.meaning: to be as precise/punctual as a Swiss watch; to be extremely punctual, like clockwork
to stay with a watch in one's hand; to act with great punctuality and speed
to go/work like a clock; to work with extreme precision

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural passeggini. Derived from passeggio (walk/stroll). Distinguished from carrozzina (pram/baby carriage) by its upright seat design for older babies and toddlers rather than a cot-like structure. Adjectives describing types agree in gender and number with the masculine plural when used attributively.
learnerNotes: Distinguish passeggino (upright stroller for toddlers) from carrozzina (pram/cot-like carriage for newborns)—these serve different developmental stages. The word derives transparently from passeggio, making it easier to remember. Modern modular systems like passeggini duo/trio are increasingly common, so familiarize yourself with this contemporary vocabulary.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mio bambino adora andare a passeggio nel passeggino.
exampleSentences.english: My boy loves to go on a walk in the stroller.

grammarNotes: Sgridare is a regular -are verb derived from gridare (to shout/yell). It conjugates normally in all tenses. The related noun sgridata (feminine) means 'a scolding' or 'a telling-off' and is frequently used with verbs like fare, dare, prendere, ricevere, and beccare to express receiving or giving a scolding.
learnerNotes: Sgridare is straightforward to conjugate, but pay attention to the noun sgridata which is always feminine. The idiom 'dare una lavata di capo' literally means 'to give someone a head-washing' and is a vivid colloquial way to express a severe scolding. Note that rimproverare and redarguire are more formal alternatives, while fare la ramanzina and dare una lavata di capo are colloquial and colorful.

exampleSentences.italian: Se faccio tardi mamma mi sgrida!
exampleSentences.english: If I'm late mom will tell me off!

exampleSentences.italian: Sua moglie gli ha dato una bella lavata di capo quando è tornato a casa.
exampleSentences.english: His wife gave him a harsh scolding when he came home.

relatedExpressions.expression: dare una lavata di capo (a qualcuno)
relatedExpressions.meaning: to give (someone) a harsh scolding (colloquial idiom)

grammarNotes: Banca is feminine (la banca, plural: le banche). It derives from Germanic 'bank' meaning bench, but specifically refers to financial institutions and credit organizations. The masculine form banco exists but now retains its original meaning of desk or workbench, though it may still appear in proper names of defunct banks (Banco di Napoli, Banco di Roma).
learnerNotes: Remember banca is feminine (la banca, le banche). The adjective form is bancario/a (assegno bancario = bank cheque). Note that 'banca dati' (database) uses banca metaphorically to mean a storage facility for data, similar to how 'banca del sangue' means blood bank—this extended usage is common in Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Vado in banca ad aprire un conto.
exampleSentences.english: I'm going to the bank to open an account.

exampleSentences.italian: andare in banca
exampleSentences.english: to go to the bank

exampleSentences.italian: mettere in banca
exampleSentences.english: to put in the bank

exampleSentences.italian: depositare denaro in banca
exampleSentences.english: to deposit money at a bank

exampleSentences.italian: prelevare / ritirare denaro in banca
exampleSentences.english: to withdraw money from the bank

grammarNotes: Dormire is a regular -ire verb conjugating as: io dormo, tu dormi, lui/lei dorme, noi dormiamo, voi dormite, loro dormono. It follows standard -ire patterns with no irregular forms. The verb can be used literally (to sleep) or figuratively (to laze about, bore, neglect, postpone decisions).
learnerNotes: Dormire is often confused with its English cognate 'dormitory,' which helps with memorization. Note that 'andare a dormire' means both 'to go to sleep' and 'to go to bed'—context clarifies the distinction. The figurative uses (to bore, to neglect, to postpone) appear frequently in spoken Italian, so familiarize yourself with these extended meanings beyond the literal 'to sleep.'

exampleSentences.italian: I neonati dormono tante ore al giorno.
exampleSentences.english: Newborns sleep for many hours a day.

exampleSentences.italian: Vai a dormire subito!
exampleSentences.english: Go to bed right away!

exampleSentences.italian: In questa azienda si dorme invece di lavorare.
exampleSentences.english: At this company we laze about rather than work.

exampleSentences.italian: Il professore mi fa dormire con le sue lezioni antiquate.
exampleSentences.english: The professor is boring me with his outdated lessons.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mio dottorato di ricerca dorme da anni.
exampleSentences.english: I've neglected my PhD for years.

exampleSentences.italian: Non è una decisione da prendere alla leggera. Devo dormirci sopra.
exampleSentences.english: This isn't a decision to be taken lightly. I have to sleep on it.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to sleep with a clean conscience
to go to sleep / to go to bed
those who sleep don't catch fish (the early bird gets the worm)
to sleep between two pillows (sleep comfortably without worries)
to sleep with one's eyes open
to sleep on the laurels (rest on one's laurels)
to sleep on one's feet (daydream, space out)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form tramonti. Derived from the verb tramontare (to set, fade, wane), combining monte (mount) and the prefix tra- (beyond). The literal etymology 'to go beyond the mountains' reflects the sun disappearing behind a mountain range.
learnerNotes: Tramonto is commonly used both literally (the natural phenomenon at the end of the day) and figuratively (decline or end of something's power). The expression 'sul viale del tramonto' is idiomatic and poetic—avoid translating it word-for-word. Note that crepuscolo is a more literary alternative for 'dusk/twilight,' while tramonto is more colloquial for everyday use.

exampleSentences.italian: Che bel tramonto che c'è stasera!
exampleSentences.english: What a beautiful sunset there is this evening!

exampleSentences.italian: La festa in spiaggia comincia al tramonto. Ci vediamo lì!
exampleSentences.english: The beach party starts at sunset. See you there!

exampleSentences.italian: Gino ha novantadue anni. Ormai è al tramonto della vita.
exampleSentences.english: Gino is 92 years old. He is at the end of his life.

exampleSentences.italian: Quell'attore è sul viale del tramonto.
exampleSentences.english: That actor has passed his peak.

exampleSentences.italian: dall'alba al tramonto
exampleSentences.english: from dawn to dusk

relatedExpressions.meaning: at sunset; at dusk (used to indicate time of day)
at the end of one's life (figurative)
on the boulevard of sunset; in decline or past one's peak (poetic expression)
from dawn to dusk; all day long

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural bisogni. When expressing 'to need' in Italian, bisogno is paired with the verb avere (to have) plus the preposition di or conjunction che: ho bisogno di/che. By extension, bisogno can mean poverty or physiological needs (euphemism in plural form).
learnerNotes: Bisogno alone means 'need' as a noun, but to say 'I need X' you must use ho bisogno di X, not just bisogno. Don't confuse bisogno (noun) with bisognare (verb used only in 3rd person, like 'it is necessary'). In informal speech, use bisogno/avere bisogno; reserve necessitare and necessità for formal writing or urgent situations.

exampleSentences.italian: Sento il bisogno di mangiare qualcosa.
exampleSentences.english: I feel the need to eat something.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho bisogno di mangiare qualcosa.
exampleSentences.english: I need to eat something.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho bisogno che tu mi porti qualcosa da mangiare.
exampleSentences.english: I need you to bring me something to eat.

exampleSentences.italian: Bisogna ripassare il testo tante volte.
exampleSentences.english: It is necessary / essential to go over the text many times.

exampleSentences.italian: Bisogna stare attenti a non contrarre il virus.
exampleSentences.english: We must / need to / have to be careful not to catch the virus.

exampleSentences.italian: Il ragazzo necessita di cure mediche.
exampleSentences.english: The boy needs medical attention.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho la necessità di parlare con l'avvocato.
exampleSentences.english: I need to speak to the lawyer.

exampleSentences.italian: Non c'è bisogno di un permesso per entrare.
exampleSentences.english: There's no need for permission to enter.

exampleSentences.italian: Non c'è bisogno che i bambini si alzino presto.
exampleSentences.english: There's no need for the children to get up early.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mio cane ha fatto i suoi bisogni sul tappeto.
exampleSentences.english: My dog did its business on the carpet.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be a need for / to need
to be in need / in poverty
to be necessary / essential; to need / have to / must (3rd person only)

grammarNotes: As an adjective, arrabbiato agrees with the noun it modifies: arrabbiato (m.s.), arrabbiata (f.s.), arrabbiati (m.pl./mixed), arrabbiate (f.pl.). It is also the past participle of arrabbiarsi (to get angry) and fare arrabbiare (to anger someone). The word can function as an intensifier when placed after other adjectives (e.g., salato arrabbiato = extremely salty).
learnerNotes: Remember that arrabbiato must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies—this is essential for correct usage. Beyond the basic meaning of 'angry,' arrabbiato can intensify other adjectives or describe fanatical/persistent behavior, so context matters. Note the culinary use all'arrabbiata specifically indicates spicy dishes with chili peppers, not just any seasoning.

exampleSentences.italian: Mio papà è molto arrabbiato con mio fratello perché è tornato a casa tardi.
exampleSentences.english: My dad is angry with my brother because he came home late.

exampleSentences.italian: Spero che tu non sia ancora arrabbiato con me.
exampleSentences.english: I hope you aren't still angry with me.

relatedExpressions.meaning: hot and spicy (culinary term, e.g., penne all'arrabbiata)

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural form panetterie. Formed from pane (bread) + -eria suffix, which denotes a place where something is made or sold. The suffix -eria is productive in Italian and appears in other nouns like gelateria and pizzeria.
learnerNotes: Regional variation is important: panetteria, panificio, and forno all mean bakery but usage varies by region and city. Use 'Vado in panetteria' to emphasize the place or 'Vado dal panettiere' to emphasize the baker person. The -eria suffix is a useful pattern for recognizing similar places: pasticceria (pastry shop), gelateria (ice cream shop), pizzeria (pizza restaurant).

exampleSentences.italian: Vado in panetteria a comprare dei grissini.
exampleSentences.english: I'm going to the bakery to buy some breadsticks.

exampleSentences.italian: Hanno aperto un nuovo panificio vicino a casa.
exampleSentences.english: They've opened a new bakery near home.

exampleSentences.italian: Vado in panetteria.
exampleSentences.english: I'm going to the bakery.

exampleSentences.italian: Vado dal panettiere.
exampleSentences.english: I'm going to the baker (literally: to the baker).

relatedExpressions.meaning: baker (the person who works in a panetteria)
bakery (alternative term, often refers to shops or industrial facilities; regional variation)
bakery/oven (alternative term for shops or factories where bread is made; regional variation)

grammarNotes: Zia is a feminine noun with plural zie. It agrees with feminine articles and adjectives (la zia, una zia, le zie). When referring to an aunt by marriage, the term zia acquisita is commonly used to distinguish from a blood aunt.
learnerNotes: While zia primarily means 'aunt,' younger Italians use it colloquially as 'bro/sister' when addressing friends, especially in the phrase bella zia to express agreement. In Bologna and surrounding regions, zia can humorously describe someone who is slow, awkward, or clumsy—context is essential to avoid misunderstanding. Remember the plural zie follows regular feminine noun patterns.

exampleSentences.italian: Mia zia abita in Italia da dieci anni.
exampleSentences.english: My aunt has lived in Italy for ten years.

exampleSentences.italian: Ci vediamo alle 10 per una birra? – Bella zia, a dopo!
exampleSentences.english: Are we meeting for a beer at 10? – Sure sister, see you later!

relatedExpressions.meaning: great-aunt; aunt of one of your parents
colloquial agreement expression meaning 'nice uncle/aunt' or 'sure thing'; originated in Milan suburbs

grammarNotes: Ridarella is a feminine noun derived from the verb ridere (to laugh). It has accepted synonyms riderella and risarella, plus numerous dialectal variations (ridarola, risarola, ridariola). The masculine form ridarello/riderello also exists. When used as an adjective (e.g., occhi riderelli), it agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies.
learnerNotes: Ridarella is an informal, colloquial term commonly used in everyday Italian to describe uncontrollable laughter. Be aware that regional variations exist—your Italian friends may use riderella, risarella, or dialectal forms instead, so familiarity with synonyms is useful. When used as an adjective (riderello/riderella), remember to apply gender and number agreement like any other Italian adjective.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho la ridarella!
exampleSentences.english: I've got the giggles!

exampleSentences.italian: Mi è presa la ridarella!
exampleSentences.english: I've got the giggles!

exampleSentences.italian: Mi è venuta la ridarella!
exampleSentences.english: I've got the giggles!

exampleSentences.italian: Tu sei proprio un bimbo riderello, lo sai?!
exampleSentences.english: You really are a cheerful boy, you know?!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to get the giggles (literally: to make the giggles come to you)

relatedExpressions.expression: far venire la ridarella a qualcuno

grammarNotes: Presto is an invariable adverb with four main meanings depending on context. It often pairs with specific verbs (alzarsi, svegliarsi, arrivare, partire) when meaning 'early,' and appears in fixed expressions (il più presto, ben presto, presto o tardi) when meaning 'soon.' As an exclamation, it means 'quick,' and in the idiomatic phrase 'Si fa presto a...' it means 'easy.'
learnerNotes: Presto is a high-frequency word with multiple meanings; context is crucial for determining which translation applies. Common synonyms include fra poco/a breve (soon), veloce/in fretta (quick), and prima (earlier, especially in 'il prima possibile'). Remember that the English exclamation 'Presto!' used by magicians actually derives from Italian—a helpful mnemonic for this word!

exampleSentences.italian: Mi alzo presto al mattino.
exampleSentences.english: I get up early in the morning.

exampleSentences.italian: Sarò presto papà!
exampleSentences.english: I'll soon be a dad!

exampleSentences.italian: Faccio presto!
exampleSentences.english: I'll be quick!

exampleSentences.italian: Faccio il più presto possibile!
exampleSentences.english: I'll be as quick as possible!

exampleSentences.italian: Presto, chiama un'ambulanza!
exampleSentences.english: Quick, call an ambulance!

exampleSentences.italian: Si fa presto a criticare.
exampleSentences.english: It's easy to criticise.

exampleSentences.italian: Si fa presto a dire / fare…
exampleSentences.english: It's easy to say / do…

exampleSentences.italian: Si fa presto a fare amicizia con le persone quando si condivide la stessa passione.
exampleSentences.english: It's easy to make friends with people when you share the same passion.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural form bruchi. Like most Italian nouns ending in -o, it takes masculine articles (il, un, i, degli) and agrees with masculine adjectives. The word can extend beyond literal caterpillars to refer to insect larvae more broadly.
learnerNotes: While 'bruco' is the standard Italian word for caterpillar, note that it can also refer to larvae of other insects like beetles and worms in extended usage. In Tuscan dialect, the word takes on a metaphorical meaning referring to poverty, so context matters. The transformation process (uovo → bruco → bozzolo/crisalide → farfalla/falena) provides useful vocabulary for discussing metamorphosis.

exampleSentences.italian: Il bruco è diventato una farfalla.
exampleSentences.english: The caterpillar turned into a butterfly.

exampleSentences.italian: Il bruco mangia le foglie.
exampleSentences.english: The caterpillar eats leaves.

exampleSentences.italian: Il bruco forma un bozzolo.
exampleSentences.english: The caterpillar forms a cocoon.

relatedExpressions.meaning: The Very Hungry Caterpillar (children's book title)

grammarNotes: Intelligente is invariable in the singular form and works for both masculine and feminine subjects (un bambino intelligente, una bambina intelligente). The plural form is intelligenti for all genders. It agrees with the noun it modifies and can describe people, their expressions, objects, or technology.
learnerNotes: Note that intelligente does NOT change in the singular regardless of gender (unlike many Italian adjectives ending in -e). The plural intelligenti applies to all genders. English speakers: avoid saying 'telefono intelligente' for smartphone—Italians use the English loanword 'smartphone' instead. This adjective is useful for describing both people and objects with intellectual or advanced qualities.

exampleSentences.italian: Carlo è un bambino molto intelligente.
exampleSentences.english: Carlo is a very intelligent child.

exampleSentences.italian: Ci sono persone che credono di essere più intelligenti di quello che sono realmente.
exampleSentences.english: There are people who believe themselves to be more intelligent than they actually are.

exampleSentences.italian: Uno studente intelligente.
exampleSentences.english: An intelligent student.

exampleSentences.italian: Una domanda intelligente.
exampleSentences.english: An intelligent question.

exampleSentences.italian: Una faccia intelligente.
exampleSentences.english: An intelligent face.

exampleSentences.italian: Un'espressione intelligente.
exampleSentences.english: An intelligent expression.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel cane ha uno sguardo molto intelligente.
exampleSentences.english: That dog has a very intelligent look.

exampleSentences.italian: Una macchina intelligente.
exampleSentences.english: A smart machine / smart car.

grammarNotes: Canzone is a feminine noun (la canzone). The plural is canzoni. It derives from the verb cantare (to sing). Related diminutives include canzoncina (a cute or simple song) and canzonetta (a popular song or ditty). The broader term canto encompasses songs, bird calls, chants, and poems.
learnerNotes: Canzone is one of the most frequently used words in Italian culture and media. Beyond its literal meaning, canzone can refer figuratively to a recurrent, monotonous situation (la solita canzone = 'the same old story'). Learning common verbs paired with canzone (cantare, scrivere, mettere, incidere, rilasciare) will help you speak naturally about music. Note that canto is a broader term encompassing bird calls and poems, so it's not always interchangeable with canzone.

exampleSentences.italian: Tu sai chi ha scritto questa canzone? Mi è rimasta in testa!
exampleSentences.english: Do you know who wrote this song? It's stuck in my head!

exampleSentences.italian: Ogni giorno è la solita canzone!
exampleSentences.english: Every day is the same old story!

relatedExpressions.expression: Festival della Canzone Italiana di Sanremo

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form 'cosi'. Derives from 'cosa' (thing). Can substitute almost any noun when the speaker forgets or doesn't know the proper name. Often carries a pejorative or disrespectful tone, particularly when referring to people (lacking respect for not making the effort to learn their name).
learnerNotes: Use 'coso' carefully: while perfectly acceptable in casual speech, it sounds diminutive and disrespectful when applied to people, as it suggests laziness in learning their actual name. The verb 'cosare' works similarly for any verb you can't recall. Avoid in formal contexts or with people you want to show respect toward.

exampleSentences.italian: Dammi quel coso lì sul tavolo!
exampleSentences.english: Give me that thingy over there on the table!

exampleSentences.italian: Che stai cosando?
exampleSentences.english: What are you doing? (lit: What are you thingamabobing?)

relatedExpressions.meaning: thing/object/matter (the base word from which coso derives)
verb form: to substitute any verb you don't know or can't remember

englishTranslation: if necessary / perhaps / in the event that / should / by any chance / just in case
grammarNotes: Eventualmente is an adverb that expresses conditional uncertainty about whether an action or event will occur. It can introduce a subordinate clause with the subjunctive mood (e.g., 'Eventualmente non funzionasse...') or stand alone at the beginning of a sentence. It often implies a low probability or contingency, distinguishing it from the English false cognate 'eventually' which suggests certainty with unknown timing.
learnerNotes: Do NOT confuse eventualmente with the English word 'eventually'—this is a classic false friend. Eventualmente expresses uncertainty about whether something will happen, whereas 'eventually' suggests certainty with an unknown timeline. Eventualmente often pairs with the subjunctive mood in Italian. In many cases, it can be omitted or replaced with 'se' (if) or its synonyms without significantly changing the meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: Verrò a trovarti prima o poi.
exampleSentences.english: I'll come and visit you eventually. (There is relative certainty that I'll visit the person. I'm not sure when.)

exampleSentences.italian: Eventualmente verrò a trovarti.
exampleSentences.english: Perhaps I'll come and visit you. (I'm not sure if I'll visit the person or not.)

exampleSentences.italian: Eventualmente potremmo prendere il treno.
exampleSentences.english: If necessary, we could take the train.

exampleSentences.italian: La mattina sono impegnato; eventualmente passerò a trovarti nel pomeriggio.
exampleSentences.english: In the morning I'm busy; perhaps I'll stop by to see you in the afternoon.

exampleSentences.italian: Eventualmente non funzionasse la TV, potresti chiamare il tecnico.
exampleSentences.english: In the event that the TV doesn't work, you can call the technician.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa mostra è molto bella. Eventualmente ti interessasse, conosco una guida che ti può accompagnare.
exampleSentences.english: This exhibition is very interesting. Just in case you're interested, I know a guide that can accompany you.

exampleSentences.italian: Se eventualmente cambiassi idea, sai dove trovarmi.
exampleSentences.english: If by any chance you change your mind, you know where to find me.

relatedExpressions.meaning: if necessary / by chance / in case
in the event that / in case that
if anything / rather / if need be
if (can often replace eventualmente in many contexts)

grammarNotes: Liscio is a regular adjective that agrees with the gender and number of the noun it modifies: liscio (masc. sing.), liscia (fem. sing.), lisci (masc. pl.), lisce (fem. pl.). The ending changes follow standard Italian adjective patterns. Beyond its primary meaning of 'smooth,' liscio extends metaphorically to describe anything pure, uncomplicated, or undisturbed.
learnerNotes: Liscio has a broad semantic range beyond literal 'smoothness'—it describes things that are pure, uncomplicated, or free of obstacles (caffè liscio, acqua liscia). Learn the idiomatic phrases andare liscio come l'olio and passarla liscia, as these are frequently used in everyday Italian. In sports, liscio as a noun refers to a missed shot, which differs significantly from the adjective meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: I neonati hanno la pelle molto liscia.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with regular plural form scorciatoie. Formed from the verb scorciare (to shorten) + instrumental suffix -oia. Use the article una/le and adjectives in feminine form when modifying.
learnerNotes: The verb phrase is prendere una scorciatoia (literally 'to take a shortcut'), not 'fare una scorciatoia.' Beyond physical routes, scorciatoia can metaphorically mean a quicker way to achieve any goal. In computing contexts, it translates the English term 'shortcut' for keyboard commands.

exampleSentences.english: I know a shortcut that will save us a half an hour.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural sorrisi. Derives from the verb sorridere (to smile), which comes from Latin subridere. Can be used literally to describe a facial expression or figuratively to describe temperament, mood, or beauty.
learnerNotes: Note the diminutive forms sorrisetto and sorrisino carry negative connotations (insincere, forced, ironic), whereas the base word sorriso is neutral. The expression 'avere il sorriso sulle labbra' is idiomatic and means someone is habitually cheerful. Be aware that sorriso can shift from literal (physical smile) to figurative (beauty, serenity, temperament) depending on context.

grammarNotes: Fumo is a masculine noun with plural form fumi. It can refer to literal smoke from fires, cigarettes, or motors, as well as figuratively to deception or confusion. In the plural fumi, it describes states of mental confusion caused by alcohol, excitement, or passion.
learnerNotes: Don't confuse fumare (to smoke) with fumo (smoke itself). Remember that fumare works both transitively (fumare una sigaretta) and intransitively (il motore fuma), but fare fumo and emettere fumo are only intransitive. The figurative expressions—especially mandare in fumo and andare in fumo—are common idioms worth memorizing for intermediate-level Italian.

grammarNotes: Bivio is a masculine noun with plural form 'bivi'. It is commonly used with preposition 'a' (a un bivio) and frequently paired with verbs like essere, trovarsi, and arrivare to express both literal physical locations and figurative life decisions.
learnerNotes: Bivio is primarily used figuratively in modern Italian to describe important life decisions, similar to English 'at a crossroads'. Remember the preposition 'a' is required before bivio (a un bivio, not simply 'un bivio'). The plural 'bivi' is irregular—note the vowel change from -io to -i.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun (plural: puzze). The masculine variant 'puzzo' exists in dictionaries and is standard in Tuscany, but 'puzza' is more common in spoken Italian across northern regions. Gender agreement affects adjectives and articles used with this word.
learnerNotes: While 'puzzo' appears in standard dictionaries as the masculine form, you'll hear 'puzza' (feminine) far more frequently in everyday Italian, especially in the north. The verb 'puzzare' works both literally (something smells bad) and figuratively (something is suspicious/fishy), similar to English. Be aware that regional variation matters here—Tuscany is an exception where masculine 'puzzo' is more standard.

grammarNotes: Birichino is both an adjective and noun. As an adjective, it agrees with the noun it modifies: birichino (m.s.), birichina (f.s.), birichini (m.p.), birichine (f.p.). When used as a noun, it typically refers to a person (usually a child) and still follows gender/number agreement. A regional variant biricchino with double 'c' is accepted in some dictionaries.
learnerNotes: Birichino is primarily used for children or playful mischief, not serious wrongdoing; it carries an affectionate or light tone. Be aware that in northern and central Italy, the double-'c' variant (biricchino) is common in speech, though the single-'c' spelling is official. The word works both as an adjective (describing someone as mischievous) and as a noun (naming the mischievous person directly).

exampleSentences.italian: Lui è il bambino più birichino che io conosca!
exampleSentences.english: He's the most mischievous boy I know!

exampleSentences.english: Your daughter is a real little monkey!

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural zuccheri. In medical/health contexts, the plural zuccheri is often used instead of the singular (e.g., calo di zuccheri = low blood sugar). The word entered Italian via medieval Latin from Arabic sukkar.
learnerNotes: Zucchero has a figurative meaning beyond the literal food item: it can describe something or someone as sweet/lovable (e.g., 'Quella ragazza è uno zucchero'). Remember that in medical contexts, zuccheri (plural) is more common than the singular when discussing blood sugar levels. The word is masculine (lo zucchero), so use masculine articles and adjectives (zucchero bruno, not bruna).

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form impicci. Derived from the verb impicciare (to hinder, obstruct). Used with prepositions like 'in' (in un impiccio) or 'da' (da un impiccio) to express being stuck in or getting out of a situation. Commonly paired with verbs like trovarsi, mettersi, cavarsi, and liberarsi.
learnerNotes: Impiccio is commonly used in mafia-related contexts in Italian media (as seen in Suburra), so it carries associations with trouble and getting tangled up in dangerous situations. The word emphasizes both physical obstruction and abstract complications. Learn it alongside the verb impicciare and the common fixed phrases listed above, as these collocations are essential for natural usage.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural girasoli. The word is a compound of girare (to turn) + sole (sun), reflecting the flower's heliotropic behavior. Gender agreement applies to articles and adjectives: il girasole, un girasole splendido.
learnerNotes: Girasole is a transparent etymological compound—if you know girare (to turn) and sole (sun), you can understand why the flower has this name. Remember that semi di girasole and olio di girasole are common food-related expressions you'll encounter in Italian cooking contexts. Note that heliotropism is a real phenomenon but only occurs in young sunflowers, not mature ones.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è uno splendido girasole in giardino.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with regular plural form 'gole'. Derives from Latin 'gula'. Can refer to the anatomical throat, the neck area (less precise than 'collo'), or figuratively to gluttony. Gender agreement applies to adjectives and articles: la gola infiammata, una gola secca.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'gola' primarily means throat, while 'collo' is the more precise anatomical term for neck—gola can extend to cover neck area colloquially. 'Mal di gola' is the standard phrase for sore throat; note the masculine article 'il' with 'mal'. Be aware that 'gola' has multiple figurative uses in idioms, especially emotional expressions like 'cuore in gola' (heart in throat) and financial troubles 'avere l'acqua alla gola' (literally water at your throat).

grammarNotes: Borsa is feminine (la borsa); plural is borse. The diminutive borsetta refers to a smaller handbag or purse, while borsone is the augmentative for a large bag. Gender agreement applies to all articles and adjectives modifying it.
learnerNotes: Borsa has multiple meanings beyond 'bag'—it's also used in financial contexts (stock market, scholarship). Don't confuse it with sacco (large sack for bulk items) or sacchetto (single-use plastic bags). Note that borse can refer to under-eye bags when describing facial features, just like in English.

grammarNotes: As an adjective, curioso agrees with the noun it modifies: curioso (m.s.), curiosa (f.s.), curiosi (m.pl./mixed), curiose (f.pl.). It derives from Latin curiosus. Can also function as a noun (busybody, oddity) or exclamation.
learnerNotes: Curioso has multiple meanings depending on context: 'eager to learn' (positive), 'strange/unusual' (neutral), and 'nosy/prying' (mildly negative). Remember the four-form gender/number agreement pattern typical of Italian adjectives ending in -o/-a/-i/-e. The noun form can mean either 'busybody' (person) or 'oddity' (thing), so context is essential.

grammarNotes: Basilico is a masculine noun with plural form basilichi. In Tuscan dialect, it is pronounced with a double 's' (bassilico). The word must not be confused with basilica (a type of church), which sounds similar but has a different meaning and gender.
learnerNotes: Basilico is easily confused with basilica (church) due to similar pronunciation—pay attention to stress and context to distinguish them. As a masculine noun, remember basilico when using articles (il basilico, un basilico). This word is essential for cooking vocabulary in Italian and appears frequently in recipes and food discussions.

grammarNotes: Abbuffarsi is a reflexive verb that only exists in reflexive form (unlike its synonym rimpinzarsi). It conjugates regularly as a first-conjugation (-are) verb: mi abbuffo, ti abbuffi, si abbuffa, ci abbuffiamo, vi abbuffate, si abbuffano. The past participle is abbuffato/a/i/e, which agrees with the subject in gender and number when using essere in compound tenses.
learnerNotes: Abbuffarsi is distinctly colloquial and best used in informal contexts. Remember it always requires the reflexive pronouns (mi, ti, si, etc.)—there is no non-reflexive form. The related noun abbuffata is useful for saying 'a good feed' without using the verb: 'Che abbuffata!' (What a feast!)

grammarNotes: Quasi is a versatile adverb that can modify nouns, adjectives, other adverbs, and verbs. It is invariable and does not change form. When paired with negative expressions (niente, nulla, nessuno, mai), it translates as 'hardly' or 'barely.' When followed by subjunctive or past participle forms, it becomes synonymous with 'come se' (as if).
learnerNotes: Quasi is highly versatile: it primarily means 'almost,' but can also mean 'perhaps/maybe' or 'as if' depending on context. The doubled form 'quasi quasi' emphasizes uncertainty or half-serious intention and is not limited to expressions of anger. Remember that quasi paired with negatives (niente, nessuno, mai) shifts meaning to 'hardly/barely,' so 'quasi nessuno' means 'barely anyone,' not 'almost nobody' (though English accepts both translations).

grammarNotes: Sfinito is the past participle of sfinire (to exhaust), formed from the prefix s- + finire. As an adjective, it agrees with the subject in gender and number: sfinito (m.s.), sfinita (f.s.), sfiniti (m.p.), sfinite (f.p.). It typically describes physical or mental exhaustion resulting from strenuous activities or conditions.
learnerNotes: Sfinito conveys more intense exhaustion than the common adjective stanco (tired); use it for situations involving marathons, extreme heat, or illness. Remember it's an adjective that must agree with gender and number, unlike the invariable adverb molto (very). The related verb sfinire is less frequently used than the adjective form in everyday conversation.

exampleSentences.italian: Il corridore è arrivato sfinito al traguardo.
exampleSentences.english: The runner reached the finish line exhausted.

grammarNotes: Purtroppo is an invariable adverb derived from pure + troppo (with the final 'e' of pure dropped). It does not change form regardless of gender, number, or context. It typically appears at the beginning or middle of a sentence to express regret or disappointment about a situation.
learnerNotes: Purtroppo is the most common and neutral way to express 'unfortunately' in everyday Italian. Be aware that many native speakers mispronounce it as 'pultroppo' because the 'r' before 't' is barely audible, and this variant also exists in some Italian dialects—but stick to the standard 'purtroppo' spelling and pronunciation. The three synonyms (sfortunatamente, disgraziatamente, malauguratamente) carry progressively stronger and more serious emotional weight, so choose based on context.

exampleSentences.italian: Purtroppo, sì
exampleSentences.english: Yes, unfortunately

exampleSentences.italian: Purtroppo il viaggio è stato annullato.
exampleSentences.english: Unfortunately the trip has been cancelled.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun (il gomito) derived from Latin cubitus. Standard masculine plural is i gomiti, though feminine plural le gomita exists in some regions like Tuscany. Like many body parts, it can take both masculine and feminine plural forms despite being grammatically masculine.
learnerNotes: Gomito has figurative uses beyond anatomy: it can mean a sharp road bend (fare un gomito) and appears in the idiom alzare il gomito (drink excessively). Note the regional feminine plural le gomita, though masculine i gomiti is standard everywhere. The expression con le gomita/i gomiti means doing something hastily or poorly—useful colloquial phrase for B1 learners.

grammarNotes: Settembre is a masculine noun in Italian (il settembre). Unlike English, Italian month names are not capitalized. The word derives from Latin 'septem' (seven) because it was originally the seventh month of the Roman calendar. It can be modified by the adjective 'settembrino/a' to describe things associated with September.
learnerNotes: Remember that Italian month names are never capitalized, unlike in English. The adjective 'settembrino' agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies (settembrino/settembrina/settembrini/settembrine). Note that September has 30 days, which may help you remember the word in context using the mnemonic about which months have how many days.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mese di settembre dura 30 giorni.
exampleSentences.english: The month of September is 30 days long.

exampleSentences.italian: Settembre è il nono mese dell'anno.
exampleSentences.english: September is the ninth month of the year.

exampleSentences.italian: Chi nasce in settembre è del segno della Vergine o della Bilancia.
exampleSentences.english: Those born in September are either Virgo or Libra.

grammarNotes: Sangue is a masculine noun (il sangue). The related adjective sanguigno is used when describing blood-related things (e.g., gruppo sanguigno = blood group). It can be modified by adjectives to create figurative expressions like sangue caldo (hot blood) and sangue freddo (cold blood).
learnerNotes: Sangue is a high-frequency word with many figurative uses in Italian. Pay attention to expressions like sangue caldo/freddo which work similarly to English but may not be immediately obvious. The word appears in numerous idioms related to intensity, sacrifice, and family bonds—memorizing a few common ones will help with reading comprehension. Remember that sanguigno (not sangue) is used as an adjective before nouns (e.g., gruppo sanguigno, not gruppo sangue).

exampleSentences.italian: Domani mattina devo alzarmi presto per andare a fare l'esame del sangue.
exampleSentences.english: Tomorrow morning I need to get up early to go for a blood test.

exampleSentences.italian: I due soldati hanno combattuto fino all'ultimo sangue.
exampleSentences.english: The two soldiers fought to the death.

relatedExpressions.meaning: hot blood; in the heat of the moment
to be composed under trying circumstances

relatedExpressions.expression: dare / versare il proprio sangue (per qualcuno)

relatedExpressions.meaning: Good blood doesn't lie (proverb about inherited traits)
Wine is good for the soul
to get worked up about something
to demand something from someone who cannot or won't give it

grammarNotes: Masculine singular osso has two distinct plural forms: ossa (feminine, from Latin neutral plural, used for human bones collectively) and ossi (masculine, for individual bones or animal bones). The adjective osseo is preferred when describing bone-related concepts (e.g., midollo osseo = bone marrow). Gender agreement varies depending on context and whether the plural refers to human or animal bones.
learnerNotes: The dual plural system (ossa vs. ossi) can be challenging: use ossa for abstract or collective human bones, ossi for individual bones or animal bones. The figurative expressions (un osso duro, sputa l'osso) are very common in colloquial Italian and worth memorizing. Watch out for the adjective osseo in medical/scientific contexts rather than the noun form.

exampleSentences.italian: Ci sono 206 ossa nel corpo umano.
exampleSentences.english: There are 206 bones in the human body.

exampleSentences.italian: Mia mamma ha dato gli ossi al cane.
exampleSentences.english: My mom fed the dog bones.

exampleSentences.italian: Angelo è un osso duro. Non molla mai.
exampleSentences.english: Angelo is a hard nut to crack. He never gives up.

exampleSentences.italian: Dai Marco, non essere timido, sputa l'osso!
exampleSentences.english: Come on Marco, don't be shy, tell us!

relatedExpressions.meaning: a tough customer / a hard nut to crack
to lose weight / to reduce oneself to skin and bones
Put down the bone! / Don't touch that / Put it back
Spit out the bone! / Tell us what you're thinking

grammarNotes: Migliore amico is used for males, migliore amica for females. The plural forms are migliori amici (male) and migliori amiche (female). With possessive pronouns, gender agreement follows the noun being modified: il mio migliore amico (my best friend—male) or la mia migliore amica (my best friend—female), regardless of the speaker's gender. The adjective migliore can be shortened to miglior before singular nouns.
learnerNotes: Remember that migliore means both 'best' and 'better' depending on position: before the noun (il migliore amico = the best friend) or after (un amico migliore = a better friend). Be careful with possessive pronouns—the gender agrees with the noun being possessed (amico/amica), not the speaker. The apocope form miglior is common in speech before singular nouns.

exampleSentences.italian: Tu sei sempre stato il mio migliore amico.
exampleSentences.english: You've always been my best friend.

exampleSentences.italian: Non posso immaginare un'amica migliore di te.
exampleSentences.english: I can't imagine a better friend than you.

exampleSentences.italian: Gianni sarebbe stato un amico migliore per Luigi.
exampleSentences.english: Gianni would have been a better friend for Luigi.

exampleSentences.italian: Lui è il miglior amico che io abbia mai avuto.
exampleSentences.english: He is the best friend that I have ever had.

exampleSentences.italian: Lui è l'amico migliore che io abbia mai avuto.
exampleSentences.english: He is the best friend that I have ever had.

relatedExpressions.meaning: close friend (lit: friend of the heart)
best friend (apocope form of migliore amico)

englishTranslation: brimming / full to the brim / peak / summit / absurd / ridiculous
grammarNotes: As an adjective, colmo agrees with the noun it modifies: colmo (masc. sing.), colma (fem. sing.), colmi (masc. pl.), colme (fem. pl.). The phrase 'essere colmo di qualcosa' means to be full of or bursting with something. The related verb colmare means to fill to the brim or to shower someone with something. When used as a noun, colmo can mean peak or summit, though cima and vetta are more common synonyms.
learnerNotes: Colmo as an adjective (full/brimming) is straightforward, but the noun use and 'il colmo per/di…' expression are distinctly Italian. The latter forms the basis of a specific joke genre that relies on wordplay and double meanings—these are difficult to translate because English lacks an exact equivalent. Watch the gender and number agreement when using colmo as an adjective, and remember that colmo (noun) is less common than synonyms cima and vetta for physical peaks.

exampleSentences.italian: La tazza è colma di caffè.
exampleSentences.english: The cup is full to the brim with coffee.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mio cuore è colmo di felicità.
exampleSentences.english: My heart is bursting with joy.

exampleSentences.italian: Qual è il colmo per un computer? Non avere un programma per la serata.
exampleSentences.english: What is the most absurd thing for a computer? Not having a schedule for the evening.

exampleSentences.italian: Qual è il colmo per un politico? Cercare per la figlia un buon partito.
exampleSentences.english: What is the most absurd thing for a politician? Looking for a good marriage prospect for his daughter.

exampleSentences.italian: Qual è il colmo per un cane? Incontrare un osso duro!
exampleSentences.english: What is the most absurd thing that can happen to a dog? Meeting a tough cookie.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo è il colmo!
exampleSentences.english: This beats everything! / This takes the cake!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to burst or brim over with something
the most absurd / ridiculous thing for… (used in wordplay jokes)
This beats everything! / This takes the cake! (exclamation of surprise at excessive audacity)
to fill to the brim; to shower (someone with something)

grammarNotes: Spazzola is feminine (la spazzola) with plural spazzole. Diminutive spazzolina (little brush) and masculine spazzolino (toothbrush) follow standard Italian diminutive patterns. The augmentative spazzolone denotes a larger, more robust brush. Related verbs spazzolare (to brush) and reflexive spazzolarsi (to brush oneself) are regular first-conjugation verbs.
learnerNotes: Note that spazzolino specifically means toothbrush in Italian—use this instead of the generic spazzola when discussing dental hygiene. Italians prefer the phrase si lavano i denti (they wash their teeth) over spazzolarsi i denti. Be aware that pennello is the separate term for art/makeup brushes, not spazzola. The verb spazzolare has a colloquial second meaning of 'to devour' which appears in the idiom Che spazzola!

exampleSentences.italian: È difficile trovare una spazzola che sia perfetta per i miei capelli.
exampleSentences.english: It is difficult to find a brush that is perfect for my hair.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho dato una spazzolata veloce alle mie scarpe.
exampleSentences.english: I gave my shoes a quick brush.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to give something a quick brush
What an appetite! (from the sense of devouring food)

grammarNotes: Fulmine is a masculine noun with plural fulmini. It refers to the electrical discharge itself (lightning bolt), distinguishing it from lampo, which refers to the flash of light produced. The word can be used literally for weather phenomena or figuratively for speed, sudden events, or anger.
learnerNotes: Note the distinction between fulmine (the electrical discharge/bolt) and lampo (the flash of light)—this is crucial for precise expression. Fulmine has several figurative uses that are common in Italian: metaphors for speed, sudden events (colpo di fulmine), and anger. Be aware that 'fulmine di guerra' is frequently used ironically, so context is essential for interpreting its true meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono stato travolto da un grosso temporale con tuoni e fulmini mentre tornavo a casa.
exampleSentences.english: I got caught in a big thunderstorm with thunder and lightning while I was heading home.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel corridore è veloce come un fulmine.
exampleSentences.english: That runner is as quick as lightning.

exampleSentences.italian: Tra me e la mia ragazza è stato un colpo di fulmine.
exampleSentences.english: My girlfriend and I fell in love at first sight.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi domando se quel fulmine di guerra di Luca ha capito che cosa sta succedendo.
exampleSentences.english: I wonder if that bonehead Luca realises what is happening.

exampleSentences.italian: I suoi occhi lanciavano fuoco e fulmini.
exampleSentences.english: His/her eyes were full of anger.

relatedExpressions.meaning: flash of lightning (the light produced, not the discharge itself)
love at first sight (literally: a lightning strike)
a bolt from the blue; an unexpected or sudden event
someone who acts rapidly and decisively; often used ironically for someone slow on the uptake

grammarNotes: Capriccio is a masculine noun. Singular: il capriccio (definite) / un capriccio (indefinite). Plural: i capricci (definite) / dei capricci (indefinite). It follows regular masculine noun patterns and requires masculine article and adjective agreement.
learnerNotes: Capriccio has multiple meanings depending on context: with children it means tantrum (fare i capricci), with desires it means whim, and in romance it describes infatuation. The phrase 'a capriccio' means 'on a whim' and is commonly used. Note that while 'caprice' is the English cognate, 'capriccio' is the more versatile Italian term covering tantrums, whims, and unreliable behavior in objects or weather.

exampleSentences.italian: Non fare i capricci quando andiamo dai nonni!
exampleSentences.english: Don't be naughty when we go to your grandparents' house!

exampleSentences.italian: Giacomo non avrebbe tenuto con sé la foto di Maria se fosse stato solo un capriccio estivo.
exampleSentences.english: Giacomo wouldn't have kept Maria's photo if it was only a summer infatuation.

exampleSentences.italian: Il computer sta facendo di nuovo i capricci.
exampleSentences.english: The computer is playing up again.

exampleSentences.italian: Se fai qualcosa a capriccio, lo fai su un improvviso impulso.
exampleSentences.english: If you do something a capriccio, you do it based on a sudden urge.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to throw a tantrum / to be naughty
on a whim / based on a sudden urge
popular Italian pizza with mozzarella, tomato sauce, mushroom, ham, and artichokes

grammarNotes: Gallo is a masculine noun with regular plural galli. It derives from Latin gallus. Related feminine noun is gallina (hen). The word combines with other terms to form compound nouns (e.g., gallo cedrone, peso gallo) and idiomatic expressions.
learnerNotes: Gallo is often used idiomatically rather than literally—fare il gallo and essere il gallo della Checca both describe male behavior and are colloquial. The onomatopoeia chicchirichì differs significantly from the English 'cock-a-doodle-doo,' so memorizing both versions helps with cultural comprehension. Note that gallina (hen) is feminine, so gender agreement is important when discussing roosters versus hens.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel ragazzo fa il gallo con tutte le ragazze del quartiere.
exampleSentences.english: That young man flirts with all the girls in the neighbourhood.

exampleSentences.italian: Il gallo canta al mattino presto, prima del sorgere del sole.
exampleSentences.english: The rooster sings early in the morning, before sunrise.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to swagger, flirt, or act like a Casanova (lit: to do the rooster)
to be a lady-killer or Don Juan (lit: to be the rooster of Checca)
to wake up at the crack of dawn (lit: to wake up with the crow of the rooster)
super bantamweight boxing category (lit: super rooster)

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural 'macchine'. Derives from Latin 'machina' and Greek 'mekhos'. In Italian, compound terms are formed by adding 'macchina' + function descriptor (e.g., macchina fotografica). Context often allows shortening to 'macchina' alone when the type is clear.
learnerNotes: In spoken Italian, 'macchina' is more popular than 'auto' or 'automobile' for 'car'. Note that 'macchina' can refer to any machine or device, but contextually means 'car' in phrases like 'salire in macchina'. The diminutive 'macchinetta' describes small mechanical tools and implies quick, mechanical efficiency when used figuratively about actions.

exampleSentences.italian: Hanno costruito una macchina complicata con semplici materiali domestici.
exampleSentences.english: They built a complicated machine out of simple household materials.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi passi la macchina?
exampleSentences.english: Could you pass me the camera?

exampleSentences.italian: Ho comprato una macchina nuova perché quella vecchia si è rotta.
exampleSentences.english: I bought a new car because the old one broke down.

exampleSentences.italian: Quando si mette a lavorare, lei è una macchina.
exampleSentences.english: When she puts herself to work, she's a machine.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to get out of the car
small machine (diminutive; used for coffee makers, hair clippers, lighters, braces)
like a small machine (quickly and uniformly)

grammarNotes: Subito is an invariable adverb derived from Latin. It can be intensified by adding the suffix -issimo (subitissimo = very quickly) or by repetition (subito subito). When used as an answer to a command, it functions as a response adverb similar to English 'right away' in professional contexts.
learnerNotes: Subito is a high-frequency adverb essential for everyday Italian. Remember it's invariable (doesn't change form) and works with all verb tenses. Note that 'd'un subito' and 'fin/sin da subito' are fixed expressions—don't try to modify them. Be aware that 'subito' as a standalone response (like 'Subito, signore!') is professional/service register, commonly heard in restaurants and shops.

exampleSentences.italian: Torno subito.
exampleSentences.english: I'll be right back.

exampleSentences.italian: Si è addormentato subito.
exampleSentences.english: He fell asleep right away.

exampleSentences.italian: Si asciuga subito.
exampleSentences.english: It dries very quickly.

exampleSentences.italian: Subito a letto!
exampleSentences.english: Straight to bed!

exampleSentences.italian: Per favore vai all'ufficio postale. Questo pacco dev'essere spedito subito.
exampleSentences.english: Please go to the post office. This parcel must be sent right away.

exampleSentences.italian: Lo faccio subito subito!
exampleSentences.english: I'll do it right away!

exampleSentences.italian: Usciremo subito prima di mangiare.
exampleSentences.english: We will go out right before eating.

exampleSentences.italian: Usciremo subito dopo aver mangiato.
exampleSentences.english: We will go out right after eating.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho capito fin da subito che era timido.
exampleSentences.english: I realised right from the start that he was shy.

exampleSentences.italian: Cameriere, un'altra birra per favore. – Subito, signore!
exampleSentences.english: Waiter, another beer please. – Right away sir.

exampleSentences.italian: Ed è subito crisi! Il turismo crolla a causa del maltempo.
exampleSentences.english: And suddenly, a crisis. Tourism collapses because of the bad weather.

relatedExpressions.expression: fin da subito / sin da subito

relatedExpressions.meaning: and suddenly... (journalistic/advertising expression indicating sudden occurrence)

grammarNotes: Incinta is primarily used in its feminine form (plural: incinte). The masculine form incinto exists but is rarely used except in humorous or imaginary contexts. The adjective agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. It derives from Medieval Latin incincta.
learnerNotes: Incinta is always feminine in standard usage—don't use the masculine form in formal contexts. Italian offers several euphemistic expressions for pregnancy (stato interessante, dolce attesa) that are common in polite speech. False cognate alert: the word pregna exists but refers almost exclusively to pregnant animals, not humans.

exampleSentences.italian: Mia moglie è incinta di quattro mesi.
exampleSentences.english: My wife is four months pregnant.

exampleSentences.italian: Pietro aveva mangiato così tanto che sembrava incinto.
exampleSentences.english: Pietro ate so much that he looked pregnant.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be in an interesting state (euphemism for pregnant)
to be in sweet expectation (euphemism for pregnant)

relatedExpressions.expression: la mamma dei cretini è sempre incinta
relatedExpressions.meaning: the mother of idiots is always pregnant (proverb; equivalent to 'stupidity breeds stupidity')

grammarNotes: Invece is a linking word used to contrast ideas or present alternatives. When contrasting, it appears standalone without prepositions. When presenting alternatives, it is typically followed by 'di' (or a partitive article like del, della, degli) or the subordinate conjunction 'che'. The archaic form 'in vece' is still used, especially before possessive adjectives where it means 'in one's stead,' and the possessive can be inserted between 'in' and 'vece'.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'invece' without any preposition is used when simply contrasting two ideas. Use 'invece di' for alternatives (most common), but 'invece che' is required when the following clause contains a preposition like 'in ufficio.' The detached spelling 'in vece' is preferred before possessive adjectives and is technically required when the possessive comes between 'in' and 'vece.'

exampleSentences.italian: Pensavo fossimo in orario, invece mi sbagliavo!
exampleSentences.english: I thought we were on time but I was wrong!

exampleSentences.italian: Dovrei andare io ma non ho voglia. Vai tu invece!
exampleSentences.english: I should be the one to go but I don't want to. You go instead!

exampleSentences.italian: Alcuni amano il caldo, altri invece preferiscono il fresco.
exampleSentences.english: Some people like hot weather, whereas others prefer it cool.

exampleSentences.italian: Perché non vai a fare una passeggiata invece di rimanere sul divano tutto il giorno?
exampleSentences.english: Why don't you go for a walk instead of sitting on the couch all day?

exampleSentences.italian: Invece di comprarti un regalo preferisco darti dei soldi.
exampleSentences.english: Rather than buy you a present, I'd prefer to give you money.

exampleSentences.italian: Al mattino preferisco bere un caffè invece del tè.
exampleSentences.english: In the morning I prefer to drink a coffee instead of tea.

exampleSentences.italian: Si è iscritta Maria invece della sorella.
exampleSentences.english: Maria signed up instead of her sister.

exampleSentences.italian: Si è iscritta Maria invece che la sorella.
exampleSentences.english: Maria signed up instead of her sister.

exampleSentences.italian: Preferisco lavorare a casa invece che in ufficio.
exampleSentences.english: I prefer working at home rather than at the office.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono andato io in vece di mio fratello.
exampleSentences.english: I went instead of my brother.

exampleSentences.italian: È venuta mia sorella in vece mia.
exampleSentences.english: My sister came in my stead.

exampleSentences.italian: È venuta mia sorella in mia vece.
exampleSentences.english: My sister came in my stead.

relatedExpressions.meaning: instead of / rather than (most common modern form)
instead of / rather than (used with clauses or prepositions)

grammarNotes: Potente is invariable in the singular form for both masculine and feminine subjects (il muscolo potente, la donna potente). The plural form is potenti for all genders. It can also function as a noun meaning 'a powerful person or nation.' In colloquial youth language, it functions as an exclamation of admiration.
learnerNotes: Potente shares etymology with English 'potent,' making it an easy cognate to remember. Be aware that in youth slang, potente functions as an exclamation (like 'cool!'), which is quite different from its standard adjective use. The rare construction with 'a + infinitive' (potente a fare) is less common in modern Italian and may sound archaic to contemporary speakers.

exampleSentences.italian: muscoli potenti
exampleSentences.english: powerful muscles

exampleSentences.italian: un politico potente
exampleSentences.english: a powerful politician

exampleSentences.italian: una nazione potente
exampleSentences.english: a powerful nation

exampleSentences.italian: un odore potente
exampleSentences.english: a powerful smell

exampleSentences.italian: un discorso potente
exampleSentences.english: a powerful speech

exampleSentences.italian: un colpo potente
exampleSentences.english: a powerful blow

exampleSentences.italian: Un potente terremoto ha scosso la città.
exampleSentences.english: A powerful earthquake shook the city.

exampleSentences.italian: Che potente quel film!
exampleSentences.english: What a cool film!

exampleSentences.italian: È potente a fare qualcosa.
exampleSentences.english: He is capable of doing something.

exampleSentences.italian: Bisogna aiutare i poveri e lottare contro i potenti.
exampleSentences.english: We must help the poor and fight against the powerful.

englishTranslation: that is / namely / in other words / or rather
grammarNotes: Cioè is a fusion of the pronoun ciò (this/that) and è (third person singular present of essere). It is invariable and does not change form. In spoken Italian, it is pronounced quickly and may sound like c'è (there is), which can cause confusion.
learnerNotes: Cioè serves multiple functions: it introduces clarifications, corrections, examples, or specific details. In casual speech, it's overused as a filler word similar to 'like' or 'you know' in English—listen for native speakers using it to buy thinking time. Pay attention to context and pronunciation to distinguish cioè from the homophone c'è (there is), which are semantically very different.

exampleSentences.italian: Parliamo delle partite giocate dalla Juventus in casa, cioè a Torino.
exampleSentences.english: We're talking about the games played by Juventus at home, that is, in Turin.

exampleSentences.italian: Abbiamo imparato molto sui grandi felini, cioè leoni e tigri.
exampleSentences.english: We learned a lot about the big cats, namely lions and tigers.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho usato un chilo di farina, cioè tutto il pacco.
exampleSentences.english: I used one kilogram of flour, or in other words, the whole packet.

exampleSentences.italian: Ha risposto a tutte le domande, cioè, a quasi tutte.
exampleSentences.english: He answered all the questions, or rather, almost all of them.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho una domanda da farti. – Cioè…?
exampleSentences.english: I have something to ask you. – And that would be…?

exampleSentences.italian: Cioè… non volevo farlo ma non avevo altra scelta.
exampleSentences.english: I mean… I didn't want to do it but I didn't have a choice.

relatedExpressions.meaning: there is (easily confused with cioè in spoken Italian)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural cuscini. In Italian, a single term covers both English 'pillow' and 'cushion'—context or compound phrases (cuscino da letto, cuscino del divano) clarify which type. The diminutive cuscinetto refers to small pillow-like objects or technical bearings.
learnerNotes: Cuscino is a false cognate with English 'cushion'—while cushion typically refers to soft furniture, cuscino covers both pillows and cushions in Italian. Remember the synonym guanciale is old-fashioned and specifically for bed pillows; it derives from guancia (cheek). The idiom dormire fra due guanciali is more common than dormire fra due cuscini for the meaning 'to be carefree.'

exampleSentences.italian: I neonati dormono senza cuscino.
exampleSentences.english: Newborn babies sleep without a pillow.

exampleSentences.italian: Il pilota si è dovuto ritirare dal gran premio di Gran Bretagna per un problema al cuscinetto della ruota posteriore.
exampleSentences.english: The racing driver had to retire from the British grand prix because of a bearing problem in the rear wheel.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to sleep between two pillows; to be relaxed/not worry

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural form tuoni. Derives from the verb tuonare (to thunder). Should not be confused with tono (tone), which sounds similar but has a different meaning, though both share Latin origin from tonus.
learnerNotes: Tuono refers literally to the loud sound after lightning during a storm, but can also be used figuratively for any deep, resonant noise from cannons, volcanoes, or trains. Be careful not to confuse tuono (thunder) with tono (tone)—they sound similar but are completely different words. The plural tuoni is regular and commonly used when discussing multiple thunder sounds.

exampleSentences.italian: Il rombo del tuono segue il bagliore del lampo.
exampleSentences.english: The rumble of thunder follows the flash of lightning.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai sentito il tuono del cannone?
exampleSentences.english: Did you hear the roar of the cannon?

grammarNotes: Arachide is a feminine noun (la arachide) with regular plural form arachidi. It agrees with feminine articles and adjectives: le arachidi tostate (roasted peanuts). The word can refer to both the individual peanut and the peanut plant.
learnerNotes: Arachide is not commonly used in everyday Italian conversation; most Italians prefer one of the three synonyms (nocciola americana, pistacchio di terra, cece di terra). Note that peanut butter (burro di arachidi) is not a staple in Italy like it is in North America, so you may need to explain this product to Italian speakers. Remember the feminine gender and use appropriate articles: un'arachide, le arachidi.

exampleSentences.italian: Le arachidi sono il mio snack preferito.
exampleSentences.english: Peanuts are my favourite snack.

exampleSentences.italian: Sai dove posso comprare del burro di arachidi?
exampleSentences.english: Do you know where I can buy some peanut butter?

exampleSentences.italian: Non ne ho la più pallida idea!
exampleSentences.english: I don't have a clue!

grammarNotes: Magia is a feminine noun (la magia) with plural form magie. It derives from Latin magica and Greek magike. When used as an adjective, it often becomes magica (e.g., bacchetta magica), though some compound expressions use magia as a noun (e.g., spettacolo di magia).
learnerNotes: Note that magia is feminine (la magia, una magia), not masculine. The adjective form magica is commonly used in compound nouns (bacchetta magica, parola magica), but compound expressions with magia as a noun are also acceptable (spettacolo di magia). The idiom 'come per magia' is a useful conversational phrase meaning 'as if by magic' or 'suddenly.'

exampleSentences.italian: Nel medioevo, tutti credevano nella magia.
exampleSentences.english: In the Middle Ages, everyone believed in magic.

exampleSentences.italian: Harry Potter porta sempre con sé una bacchetta magica.
exampleSentences.english: Harry Potter always carries a magic wand with him.

exampleSentences.italian: Stavo bevendo in un locale quando, come per magia, mi sono ritrovato davanti a lui. Non lo vedevo da vent'anni!
exampleSentences.english: I was drinking at a bar when, as if by magic, I found myself in front of him. I hadn't seen him for twenty years!

relatedExpressions.meaning: as if by magic; suddenly and unexpectedly
the magic of the evening (figurative: delightful atmosphere)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural trucchi. Related verbs include truccare (to put on make-up), truccarsi (to put make-up on oneself, reflexive), and struccarsi (to remove make-up, reflexive). The noun truccatura and adjective truccato/a derive from the same root.
learnerNotes: Trucco is highly polysemous—its meaning depends on context. While 'make-up' is the most common modern usage, dictionaries often list 'trick' first historically. Watch the register: when referring to fraud or scams, trucco takes on a slightly negative connotation. The reflexive verb truccarsi (to put make-up on oneself) is more natural than the non-reflexive truccare in everyday speech.

exampleSentences.italian: Devo farmi il trucco prima di andare in onda.
exampleSentences.english: I need to put on my make-up before going on air.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi insegni qualche trucco di magia?
exampleSentences.english: Can you teach me some magic tricks?

exampleSentences.italian: Conosco un trucco per non pagare le bollette.
exampleSentences.english: I know a trick to not pay the bills.

exampleSentences.italian: È troppo bello per essere vero, dov'è il trucco?
exampleSentences.english: It's too good to be true, where's the catch?

grammarNotes: Topo is a masculine noun with plural topi. The diminutive forms are topino and the more popular topolino (also the Italian name for Mickey Mouse). The feminine form topa (plural tope) has both literal and slang meanings. Various compound expressions modify the base word to create figurative meanings.
learnerNotes: Beware of the false cognate: in Italian computing contexts, use 'mouse' (pronounced as English) for computer mice, not 'topo'—asking for 'un topo per il mio computer' will get you laughed at! The word topo has multiple figurative meanings (thief, burglar, bookworm) depending on context and compounds. The feminine topa carries vulgar connotations in certain dialects, so use with caution in formal settings.

exampleSentences.italian: Credimi! Sono sicuro di aver visto un topo in cucina!
exampleSentences.english: Believe me! I'm sure I saw a mouse in the kitchen.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel topo di fogna ci ha rubato tutti i gioielli!
exampleSentences.english: That miserable burglar stole all our jewels!

grammarNotes: Aragosta is a feminine noun (la aragosta). The plural form is aragoste. As a feminine noun, it takes feminine articles (la, una) and feminine adjectives. When used in compound expressions like 'colore aragosta,' it functions as an invariable modifier.
learnerNotes: Note that 'aragosta' derives from Latin 'locusta' (locust), not from the modern Italian word 'locusta' itself—a good example of false cognate territory if you're thinking of insects. The phrase 'colore aragosta' uses the noun as an invariable adjective, a common Italian pattern. Remember the feminine gender: l'aragosta (with elision), una aragosta, le aragoste.

exampleSentences.italian: Adoro mangiare l'aragosta ma è molto costosa.
exampleSentences.english: I love eating lobster but it is very expensive.

exampleSentences.italian: L'aragosta è un crostaceo marino di grandi dimensioni.
exampleSentences.english: The lobster is a large marine crustacean.

exampleSentences.english: Lobster pink is an orange-red shade.

exampleSentences.italian: La polpa di aragosta è considerata un alimento di lusso.
exampleSentences.english: Lobster meat is considered a luxury food item.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form mariti. Derived from Latin maritus (male). Can be used with or without the indefinite article un depending on context. Diminutive maritino is affectionate; marituccio is derogatory.
learnerNotes: Note that Italian frequently omits the article in phrases like 'cerco marito' (I'm looking for a husband) and 'prendere marito' (to get married), which may seem unusual to English speakers. The phrase 'uno straccio di marito' is a colorful idiomatic expression meaning an unsuitable husband, so avoid literal translation. Remember that 'Tra moglie e marito non mettere il dito' is a common saying about not interfering in couples' relationships.

exampleSentences.italian: Vi dichiaro marito e moglie. Ora può baciare la sposa.
exampleSentences.english: I declare you husband and wife. Now you may kiss the bride.

exampleSentences.italian: Cerco marito.
exampleSentences.english: I'm looking for a husband (to marry).

exampleSentences.english: I'm marrying Carlo.

exampleSentences.italian: A causa del suo passato non è mai riuscita a trovare uno straccio di marito.

grammarNotes: Abbraccio is a masculine noun starting with a vowel. The definite article is l'abbraccio (singular) and gli abbracci (plural). The indefinite articles are un abbraccio (singular) and degli abbracci (plural). It derives from the verb abbracciare (to hug) and abbracciarsi (to hug one another), which comes from braccio (arm).
learnerNotes: Abbraccio is commonly used in written correspondence (letters, emails, texts) as a sign-off similar to 'best wishes' in English. It can also close phone conversations. Remember that 'un abbraccio mortale' is an idiom meaning a ruinous bond, not a literal deadly hug. The verb abbracciare (to hug) is regular and useful for daily conversation.

exampleSentences.italian: Si sono date un grande abbraccio.
exampleSentences.english: They gave each other a big hug.

exampleSentences.italian: Ciao Carla, ci sentiamo presto. Un abbraccio!
exampleSentences.english: Bye Carla, speak to you soon. A hug!

grammarNotes: Bruciore is a masculine noun; plural is bruciori. The phrase bruciore di stomaco is composed of bruciore (burning) + di (of) + stomaco (stomach). It agrees in number and gender when used with articles or adjectives: il bruciore, i bruciori.
learnerNotes: Bruciore is widely used beyond digestive issues—it can describe any burning sensation (sore throat, insect bite) or figuratively, emotional pain (shame, defeat). Note that bruciore della vergogna uses the definite article il + bruciore della, not just bruciore di vergogna. Common accompanying verbs are avere (to have) and soffrire di (to suffer from), so familiarize yourself with these collocations.

exampleSentences.english: Acid reflux (reflusso gastrico) is where stomach acid travels up to your throat from your stomach.
