grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural cappelli. Derives from Latin cappellus (from cappa, meaning hood). The diminutive form cappellino is formed by adding the suffix -ino. Gender and number agreement required with articles and adjectives (e.g., un cappello giallo, i cappelli rossi).
learnerNotes: Be careful not to confuse cappello (hat, with double pp) with capello (hair, with single p)—pronunciation clarity is essential. Use berretto instead of cappello when specifically referring to a cap or baseball-style cap. The word extends metaphorically to hat-like objects (mushroom caps, lampshades) and in formal writing means preamble or introduction.

exampleSentences.italian: La mamma indossa un cappello giallo e suo figlio un cappellino rosso.
exampleSentences.english: The mum is wearing a yellow hat and her son a little red hat.

exampleSentences.italian: Mettiti il cappello quando esci. Oggi il sole batte forte.
exampleSentences.english: Wear your hat when you go out. The sun is very strong.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural form 'treni'. The word entered Italian via French 'train' from the verb 'traîner' (to drag). When referring to specific train categories (regionale, intercity, etc.), Italian speakers often omit the word 'treno' entirely, as seen in station announcements.
learnerNotes: Note the key expressions with prepositions: 'in treno' (by train), 'sul treno' (on the train), and 'dal treno' (from the train) are all essential. When describing train status, use 'in orario' (on time), 'in ritardo' (late), or 'in anticipo' (early). The word 'treno' has extended meanings beyond transportation—'un treno di gomme' means a set of tires, so context matters for interpretation.

exampleSentences.italian: Viaggiare in treno può essere veloce quanto prendere un aereo.
exampleSentences.english: Traveling by train can be as fast as taking a plane.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi scusi, quando arriva il treno per Milano? – È in ritardo di 15 minuti. Dovrebbe arrivare alle sei e trentacinque.
exampleSentences.english: Excuse me, when does the train for Milan arrive? – It is 15 minutes late. It should arrive at 6:35.

exampleSentences.italian: Il regionale delle undici e dieci è in arrivo sul binario due.
exampleSentences.english: The 11:10 regional train is arriving at platform 2.

relatedExpressions.meaning: style or way of life (economic sense)
to be late or slow to understand something
to miss out on an opportunity

grammarNotes: Coccola is a feminine noun that typically appears in plural form (le coccole). It takes regular feminine articles: la coccola (singular), le coccole (plural), una coccola (indefinite singular), delle coccole (indefinite plural). The word derives from the verb coccolare and the diminutive term coccolo.
learnerNotes: Coccola predominantly appears in the plural form (le coccole) in everyday Italian, so memorize both singular and plural. The verb coccolare can be positive (to cuddle, to pamper fondly) or negative (to coddle, to spoil excessively), depending on context—pay attention to tone. The reflexive form coccolarsi means either pampering oneself positively or wallowing negatively, so context determines the connotation.

exampleSentences.italian: Ai bambini piccoli piacciono molto le coccole.
exampleSentences.english: Young children really like cuddles.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho voglia di una coccola. Mi vai a prendere un gelato?
exampleSentences.english: I want a treat. Can you go and get me an ice cream?

exampleSentences.italian: Micio è un gatto tranquillo. Ama ricevere le coccole, ma gli piace anche farne!
exampleSentences.english: Micio is a quiet cat. He loves receiving cuddles, but he also likes giving them!

exampleSentences.italian: La sera mi faccio sempre una coccola mangiando un pezzo di cioccolato e guardando un film.
exampleSentences.english: In the evening, I always spoil myself by eating a piece of chocolate and watching a movie.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to spoil oneself/to console oneself (reflexive verb)
to snuggle/to crouch down (reflexive verb with a- prefix)

grammarNotes: Patatine is the plural feminine form. The singular is patatina, a diminutive of patata (potato). The word is feminine: le patatine. When referring to fried potatoes specifically, the adjective fritte (fried, feminine plural) follows: patatine fritte.
learnerNotes: Patatine refers to both potato chips/crisps and French fries in Italian; context or the adjective fritte clarifies which you mean. Avoid confusing patatina with its secondary meanings as a term of endearment or euphemism for children's private parts—use only in appropriate social contexts. Note that pisello (pea) is the male equivalent euphemism.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho ordinato un contorno di patatine fritte al ristorante.
exampleSentences.english: I ordered a side of fries at the restaurant.

exampleSentences.italian: Un sacchetto di patatine costa un euro e cinquanta centesimi.
exampleSentences.english: A bag of chips costs one euro and fifty cents.

relatedExpressions.meaning: term of endearment used by Italian men for wives/girlfriends (literally 'little potato')

grammarNotes: Ridere is an irregular verb derived from Latin. Present tense conjugation: io rido, tu ridi, lui/lei ride, noi ridiamo, voi ridete, loro ridono. The verb can be combined with pronouns to create pronominal forms (ridersi, ridersela, ridersene) with slightly different meanings. It pairs with fare to create expressions like fare una risata (to have a laugh) or far ridere (to make laugh).
learnerNotes: Note that 'far ridere' without an indirect object means 'to be funny' or 'to be ridiculous' (negative sense), while 'far ridere + indirect object pronoun' means 'to make someone laugh.' Italian uses many idiomatic expressions with ridere that reference facial features and body parts—these colorful metaphors are characteristic of Italian and worth memorizing. Be aware that ridere can express both positive (joy) and negative (derision, mocking) emotions depending on context.

grammarNotes: Rimbalzare is an intransitive verb formed from the prefix rin- (intensifier) + balzare (to jump/leap). It can take either essere or avere as its auxiliary verb in the passato prossimo (la palla è rimbalzata or la palla ha rimbalzato). To make it transitive, use far rimbalzare (to make bounce).
learnerNotes: Although rimbalzare is grammatically correct, saltare is commonly used in casual speech, especially when describing people bouncing. Note that rimbalzare has dual auxiliary verb support (essere/avere), which is less common in Italian—both forms are equally acceptable. The figurative sense (news/gossip spreading) is useful for intermediate learners expanding beyond physical meanings.

exampleSentences.italian: La palla è rimbalzata sul pavimento.
exampleSentences.english: The ball bounced off the sidewalk.

exampleSentences.italian: La palla ha rimbalzato.

exampleSentences.italian: Il ragazzo ha fatto rimbalzare la palla contro il muro.
exampleSentences.english: The boy bounced the ball against the wall.

exampleSentences.italian: La notizia è rimbalzata in tutta la città.
exampleSentences.english: The news spread quickly throughout the city.

grammarNotes: Finto is the past participle of fingere (to pretend) used as an adjective. It agrees with the noun in gender and number: finto (masc. sing.), finta (fem. sing.), finti (masc. plur.), finte (fem. plur.). Adjective position matters: after the noun implies insincerity; before the noun implies deception or imposture. As a noun, finto means a phoney or imposter.
learnerNotes: Be careful not to confuse finto with falso: finto describes something artificial or simulated (denti finti), while falso describes something that is opposite of truth or intentionally misleading (notizia falsa). Adjective placement significantly changes meaning—learn both positions. The expression fare il finto tonto is highly idiomatic and worth memorizing as a fixed phrase.

exampleSentences.italian: Preferisco i fiori veri ai fiori finti.
exampleSentences.english: I prefer real flowers to fake flowers.

exampleSentences.italian: Il bambino ha fatto finta di stare male.
exampleSentences.english: The boy pretended to be sick.

exampleSentences.italian: Dai, non fare il finto tonto!
exampleSentences.english: Come on, don't play dumb.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo dipinto di Picasso è un falso.
exampleSentences.english: This Picasso painting is a fake.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural draghi. Derives from Latin draco and Greek drakon. The synonym dragone exists but drago is the standard preferred term in Italian, despite dragone sounding closer to English 'dragon'.
learnerNotes: Avoid the false cognate dragone—while it sounds more like English 'dragon,' drago is the correct standard Italian term. Drago has a figurative meaning when describing someone brilliant or highly skilled at something ('è un drago con i computer'). In rare cases, drago can refer to an aquilone (kite toy), though this usage is uncommon in modern Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: La lotta di San Giorgio contro il drago non è che una leggenda!
exampleSentences.english: St. George's fight with the dragon is nothing but a legend!

exampleSentences.italian: Con i computer è un drago.
exampleSentences.english: He's a whiz at computers.

grammarNotes: Insieme is primarily an adverb meaning 'together.' As a noun (masculine), it refers to a whole, group, or set. When followed by prepositions a or con, it means 'along with' or 'in the company of.' In mathematics, it exclusively translates as 'set' (unlike the synonym assieme). Gender agreement applies only when used as a noun.
learnerNotes: Insieme is more commonly used than its synonym assieme, so prioritize learning this form. Remember that insieme can function as an adverb (most common), a noun (masculine), or work as a preposition when followed by a or con. In mathematical contexts, only insieme translates as 'set'—assieme is not acceptable in this register.

exampleSentences.italian: Stiamo insieme da 10 anni.
exampleSentences.english: We've been together for 10 years.

exampleSentences.italian: Andiamo in vacanza insieme a Gianluca e suo fratello.
exampleSentences.english: We're going on vacation along with Gianluca and his brother.

exampleSentences.english: If you all speak at the same time, I don't understand anything.

grammarNotes: Tigre is a feminine noun (la tigre) with plural tigri. It remains feminine regardless of the animal's biological sex; you specify gender with 'maschio' (male) or 'femmina' (female) when needed. Like other animal nouns, it can be used metaphorically in expressions and idioms.
learnerNotes: Remember that tigre is always feminine in Italian, even when referring to a male tiger (un'tigre maschio, not un tigre maschio). The word is frequently used in idioms and metaphorical expressions relating to fierceness, power, or danger—these are common in Italian political and journalistic discourse. Watch for false cognate confusion with English 'tiger'; the Italian pronunciation and spelling are similar but the grammatical gender requires feminine agreement (la tigre, una tigre femmina).

grammarNotes: Sopravvissuto is a past participle that functions as both noun and adjective. It agrees in gender and number: masculine singular sopravvissuto, feminine singular sopravvissuta, masculine plural sopravvissuti, feminine plural sopravvissute. Derived from the verb sopravvivere (sopra + vivere), it literally means 'lived above/beyond.'
learnerNotes: Sopravvissuto refers only to literal survival of traumatic events, not figurative resilience—don't use it for someone who 'overcomes difficulties.' Use tosto/a (determined) or farcela (to make it) instead. When describing an outdated person, sopravvissuto can mean 'antiquated,' but this is a secondary usage. Remember the synonym superstite is equally valid in both noun and adjective forms.

exampleSentences.italian: Carlo è l'unico sopravvissuto della famiglia.
exampleSentences.english: Carlo is the only survivor of the family.

exampleSentences.italian: i passeggeri sopravvissuti
exampleSentences.english: the surviving passengers

exampleSentences.italian: Non ti preoccupare, ce la farà. Lei è una tosta!
exampleSentences.english: Don't worry, she'll make it. She's a survivor!

relatedExpressions.meaning: close synonym of sopravvissuto; can be noun or adjective

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with regular plural balene. Diminutives balenottero/balenotto refer to whale calves. Related compound nouns include balenottera azzurra (blue whale) and balenottera comune (fin whale). Can be used figuratively to describe an overweight person, typically applied to women.
learnerNotes: Be aware that balena used figuratively to describe an overweight person is considered offensive and should be avoided in polite conversation. The expression 'In culo alla balena' is vulgar slang for wishing good luck—only use with close friends, never with elders. Note that balenottera (fin whale) sounds like a diminutive but historically may have been misinterpreted as one; it's the actual scientific term, not a diminutive form.

exampleSentences.italian: La balena è un grande mammifero marino.
exampleSentences.english: The whale is a large marine mammal.

exampleSentences.italian: Che emozione! Ieri sono riuscito a fotografare una balena che saltava fuori dall'acqua!
exampleSentences.english: What a thrill! Yesterday I managed to photograph a whale jumping out of the water!

relatedExpressions.meaning: in the bum of the whale; vulgar equivalent of 'in bocca al lupo' (good luck expression)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural form assaggi. When combined with the verb fare, it becomes fare l'assaggio (to taste). The diminutive form assaggino (little taste) exists but is less commonly used. Gender agreement applies to adjectives modifying assaggio.
learnerNotes: Use assaggiare (verb) more frequently than fare l'assaggio in everyday speech—both are correct, but assaggiare is more natural. Don't confuse assaggio with degustazione: the latter refers to formal tastings where people evaluate and compare (wine tastings, food tastings), while assaggio is a casual sample. Note that assaggio can also mean 'attempt' or 'test' figuratively, extending beyond food contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Voglio fare l'assaggio di tutti i formaggi in esposizione!
exampleSentences.english: I want to taste all the cheeses on display!

exampleSentences.italian: Assaggia!
exampleSentences.english: Taste it! (imperative)

exampleSentences.italian: Vuoi assaggiare?
exampleSentences.english: Do you want to taste it?

exampleSentences.italian: Questo è solo un assaggio di quello che accadrà.
exampleSentences.english: This is just a taste of what will happen.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to taste (literally: to do a tasting)
to taste (literally: to take a taste)
to attempt a taste / to try
tasting (formal, for structured tastings like wine tastings)

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural 'pance'. Diminutive forms: pancino (boy), pancina (girl). Augmentative: pancione. Related noun pancetta means both 'bacon' and 'belly fat'. The Neapolitan/Sicilian variant 'panza' is also used humorously in Italian.
learnerNotes: Pancia is the colloquial, informal term for belly/tummy. For formal medical contexts, use 'ventre' (abdomen) or 'addome' (abdomen), and 'stomaco' for the stomach organ specifically. The word appears frequently in food-related idioms and expressions about laziness, making it useful for everyday conversational Italian. Note that 'pancetta' has dual meaning: it's both the Italian word for bacon and a humorous term for belly fat.

grammarNotes: Insegnante is a gender-invariant noun that uses articles and adjectives to show gender: un insegnante (male), un'insegnante (female). The plural insegnanti follows the same pattern: gli insegnanti (masculine/mixed), le insegnanti (feminine). When describing profession, Italians use fare l'insegnante (literally 'to do/make the teacher') rather than essere. As an adjective, it appears primarily in fixed expressions: corpo insegnante, personale insegnante.
learnerNotes: Remember to use fare (not essere) when talking about professions: 'Voglio fare l'insegnante' not 'Voglio essere l'insegnante.' Pay attention to article agreement with gender; un'insegnante (feminine) uses the apostrophe before the vowel. Note that more specific terms exist (maestro/maestra for elementary, professore/professoressa for secondary/university) and may be preferred in formal contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Marco è un insegnante di arte mentre Sofia è un'insegnante di fisica.
exampleSentences.english: Marco is an art teacher whereas Sofia is a physics teacher.

exampleSentences.italian: Da grande voglio fare l'insegnante.
exampleSentences.english: I want to be a teacher when I'm older.

exampleSentences.italian: L'insegnante è bravo.
exampleSentences.english: The teacher is good/capable (masculine).

exampleSentences.italian: L'insegnante è brava.
exampleSentences.english: The teacher is good/capable (feminine).

relatedExpressions.meaning: middle school, college, or university teacher

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural supermercati. Derived from the prefix super- (excellent, top quality) + mercato (market). Like most Italian nouns ending in -o, it follows standard masculine plural patterns (-o → -i).
learnerNotes: Supermercato is a direct loanword from English and is universally understood in modern Italian. Remember that in Italian supermarkets, you must weigh produce yourself using electronic scales and attach a price tag before checkout—this is an important cultural difference from some other countries. The measure etto (100g) is standard for deli counter items; tres etti = 300 grams.

exampleSentences.italian: Ora vado al supermercato a fare la spesa.
exampleSentences.english: I'm going to the supermarket now to do the grocery shopping.

exampleSentences.italian: Se vai al supermercato puoi prendere tre etti di prosciutto crudo al bancone dei salumi?
exampleSentences.english: If you go to the supermarket, can you get three hundred grams of raw ham at the deli counter?

relatedExpressions.meaning: to do grocery shopping at the supermarket
superstore (very large self-service store with groceries and general merchandise)

grammarNotes: Sorpresa is a feminine noun with plural sorprese. It derives from the past participle of the verb sorprendere (to surprise). Both singular and plural forms are commonly used in compound expressions with 'a' (festa a sorpresa, visita a sorpresa). The diminutive form sorpresina exists, with plural sorpresine.
learnerNotes: Note that 'sorpresa' is always feminine (una sorpresa, la sorpresa). Two common verbs express 'to surprise someone': prendere/cogliere qualcuno di sorpresa (to take/catch by surprise) and fare una sorpresa a qualcuno (to give a surprise to someone). The adjectives belle (nice) and brutte (unwelcome) must agree with the feminine noun sorpresa.

exampleSentences.italian: La sua decisione mi ha colto di sorpresa.
exampleSentences.english: His decision took me by surprise.

exampleSentences.italian: Abbiamo fatto una bella sorpresa a mia sorella.
exampleSentences.english: We gave my sister a nice surprise.

exampleSentences.italian: Che sorpresa!
exampleSentences.english: What a surprise!

exampleSentences.italian: Che bella sorpresa!
exampleSentences.english: What a nice surprise!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to surprise someone / to give someone a surprise

grammarNotes: Scoiattolo is a masculine noun with regular plural scoiattoli. The diminutive form scoiattolino refers to a small squirrel or young squirrel. The word derives from Greek skiouros, combining skia (shadow) and oura (tail).
learnerNotes: Scoiattolo is used both literally for the animal and figuratively to describe agile, energetic people. Remember the regular plural scoiattoli. Note that Italian uses the singular 'uno scoiattolo' in comparative expressions like 'agile come uno scoiattolo,' similar to English 'as agile as a squirrel.'

exampleSentences.italian: Gli scoiattoli sono tra i mammiferi più diffusi al mondo.
exampleSentences.english: Squirrels are among the most widespread mammals in the world.

exampleSentences.italian: È agile come uno scoiattolo.
exampleSentences.english: He's as agile as a squirrel.

exampleSentences.italian: È veloce come uno scoiattolo.
exampleSentences.english: He's as fast as a squirrel.

exampleSentences.italian: Arrampicarsi come uno scoiattolo.
exampleSentences.english: To climb like a squirrel.

exampleSentences.italian: Quella bambina è proprio agile come uno scoiattolo. Guarda come si arrampica sull'albero!
exampleSentences.english: That little girl really is a squirrel. Look at how she's climbing the tree!

relatedExpressions.meaning: agile as a squirrel (figurative: describing an agile, energetic person)

grammarNotes: Unlike most Italian adjectives, entusiasta does not change its ending (-a) in the singular form regardless of gender (un uomo entusiasta, una donna entusiasta). In the plural, however, it follows regular patterns: masculine -i (entusiasti) and feminine -e (entusiaste). It can also function as a noun meaning 'enthusiast' or 'buff' and is typically followed by the prepositions 'per' or 'di' when not modifying a noun.
learnerNotes: Note that entusiasta is a false cognate in terms of gender agreement—unlike English 'enthusiastic,' the Italian adjective keeps the -a ending for both masculine and singular forms, only changing in the plural. When expressing enthusiasm, use 'essere entusiasta per' for things (risultato, musica) and 'essere entusiasta di' for actions (andare). The noun form (un entusiasta/un'entusiasta) can mean 'enthusiast' or 'buff.'

exampleSentences.italian: un uomo entusiasta
exampleSentences.english: an enthusiastic man

exampleSentences.italian: una donna entusiasta
exampleSentences.english: an enthusiastic woman

exampleSentences.italian: uomini entusiasti
exampleSentences.english: enthusiastic men

exampleSentences.italian: donne entusiaste
exampleSentences.english: enthusiastic women

exampleSentences.italian: essere entusiasta del nuovo progetto
exampleSentences.english: to be enthusiastic about the new project

exampleSentences.italian: essere entusiasta di andare
exampleSentences.english: to be excited to go

exampleSentences.italian: essere entusiasta per il risultato
exampleSentences.english: to be thrilled with the result

exampleSentences.italian: essere entusiasta per la musica rock
exampleSentences.english: to be passionate about rock music

exampleSentences.italian: Il critico è molto entusiasta del nuovo film.
exampleSentences.english: The critic is very enthusiastic about the new film.

exampleSentences.italian: Laura è un'entusiasta della musica classica.
exampleSentences.english: Laura is a classical music buff.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be enthusiastic about / excited for
to be enthusiastic about / excited to

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural spaventi. Often used with specific verbs (fare, mettere, incutere) to express different shades of fright. Can be used hyperbolically with 'da far spavento' to mean 'incredibly' or 'frighteningly' when describing impressions. Frequently appears in exclamations like 'Che spavento!'
learnerNotes: Remember that spavento requires specific prepositions and verbs: use 'dallo spavento' (from fright) after emotional verbs, and 'a qualcuno' when indicating who is scared. The hyperbolic use of 'da far spavento' can mean either extremely positive or extremely negative depending on context—this is not a false cognate but a pragmatic shift. Related verb spaventare means 'to frighten,' while spaventarsi means 'to get scared oneself.'

exampleSentences.italian: La mia mano tremava dallo spavento.
exampleSentences.english: My hand was shaking with fright.

exampleSentences.italian: Che spavento!
exampleSentences.english: What a fright!

exampleSentences.italian: bello da far spavento
exampleSentences.english: incredibly beautiful

exampleSentences.italian: brutto da far spavento
exampleSentences.english: frightfully ugly

exampleSentences.italian: La sua ignoranza fa spavento.
exampleSentences.english: His ignorance is frightening.

to be petrified by the fright
to make you frightened; incredibly (positive) or frighteningly (negative)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural form scheletri. Takes the definite article 'lo' in singular (lo scheletro) and 'gli' in plural (gli scheletri). Indefinite articles are uno/una (uno scheletro) and degli (degli scheletri). The word derives from Greek 'skeletos' meaning 'dried up'.
learnerNotes: Scheletro is commonly used both literally (for bones) and figuratively (for basic structure or outline). The idiom 'avere uno scheletro nell'armadio' is a direct calque from English and is widely understood in Italian. Note that when describing thin people, this expression is colloquial but socially acceptable in neutral contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Durante gli scavi hanno ritrovato uno scheletro.
exampleSentences.english: During the excavations they found a skeleton.

exampleSentences.italian: Il tetto è praticamente completato, lo scheletro della casa pure.
exampleSentences.english: The roof is practically finished, as is the skeleton / framework of the house.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be as skinny as a skeleton
to be reduced to a skeleton
to have skeletons in the closet (to have embarrassing secrets)

grammarNotes: Despite ending in '-a', fantasma is masculine (il fantasma, un fantasma). Its plural is fantasmi (i fantasmi, dei fantasmi). When used as an adjective modifying nouns, it maintains the same form: fantasma for singular nouns and fantasmi for plural nouns, regardless of the noun's gender.
learnerNotes: Fantasma is a false gender cognate—despite ending in '-a', it's masculine, not feminine. This is a Greek loanword shared with English 'phantom'. Remember that when fantasma functions as an adjective (e.g., città fantasma), it doesn't change for feminine nouns; only the number changes in the plural.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è un fantasma che si aggira per la casa tutte le notti.
exampleSentences.english: There is a ghost that roams the house every night.

exampleSentences.italian: Roma è diventata una città fantasma per colpa del virus.
exampleSentences.english: Rome has become a ghost town due to the virus.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a government that acts in hiding and is not officially recognised
a king that is devoid of actual authority and power

relatedExpressions.expression: essere/diventare il fantasma di sé stesso
relatedExpressions.meaning: to be/become a shadow of one's former self
to look like a ghost (pale and gaunt appearance)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural pipistrelli. Takes definite articles il/i and indefinite articles un/dei. Derives from Latin vespertilio (related to vesper, 'evening'), reflecting bats' nocturnal nature. The word also has a secondary meaning: a sleeveless cape or cloak.
learnerNotes: Be careful not to confuse pipistrello with the English word 'pipistrelle,' which refers specifically to a genus of small bats (Pipistrellus). The Italian term is more general. Note that despite their rodent-like appearance, bats are actually more closely related to humans than to mice—a fascinating linguistic trivia point that enriches vocabulary retention. The secondary meaning (sleeveless cape) is archaic but useful to know for reading historical or fashion texts.

exampleSentences.italian: Il pipistrello più grande al mondo è la volpe volante.
exampleSentences.english: The largest bat in the world is the flying fox.

exampleSentences.italian: I pipistrelli passano l'inverno in ibernazione.
exampleSentences.english: Bats spend the winter in hibernation.

exampleSentences.english: the bat
