exampleSentences.italian: La squadra ha concluso il campionato senza successi.
exampleSentences.english: The team finished the championship without any wins.

exampleSentences.italian: la missione ebbe un buon / cattivo successo
exampleSentences.english: the mission had a good / bad outcome

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be a success / to be successful

grammarNotes: Vigliacco is a masculine noun with feminine form vigliacca. Masculine plural: vigliacchi; feminine plural: vigliacche. Articles follow standard patterns (il/i for masc., la/le for fem.). When used as an adjective, it maintains gender and number agreement with the noun it modifies (e.g., un soldato vigliacco, una condotta vigliacca).
learnerNotes: Vigliacco differs from its closest synonym codardo: vigliacco emphasizes someone who flees from danger or exploits the weak, while codardo refers to failing duties due to cowardice. Note the Spanish origin (from bellaco), which is unusual for Italian vocabulary. Distinguish carefully between the noun use (un vigliacco = a coward) and adjective use (un comportamento vigliacco = cowardly behavior).

exampleSentences.italian: Ti sei comportato proprio come un vigliacco.
exampleSentences.english: You acted like a real coward.

exampleSentences.italian: un soldato vigliacco
exampleSentences.english: a cowardly soldier

exampleSentences.italian: comportamento vigliacco
exampleSentences.english: cowardly behaviour

grammarNotes: Ritrovo is a masculine noun. Definite articles: il ritrovo (singular), i ritrovi (plural). Indefinite articles: un ritrovo (singular), dei ritrovi (plural). It derives from the verbs ritrovare and ritrovarsi, combining the prefix ri- (again) with trovare (to find/meet).
learnerNotes: Ritrovo specifically refers to a place where people regularly gather socially or for shared interests, so it's more specific than the generic English 'place.' Remember that 'fare ritrovo' uses the verb fare to mean 'to meet/gather,' which is a common Italian construction pattern. The word is neutral in register and commonly used in everyday conversation.

exampleSentences.italian: Un tempo quel bar era il ritrovo preferito dei giovani.
exampleSentences.english: That cafe was once the favourite haunt of youngsters.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to have a meeting / to meet up (literally: to do a meeting)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun. Definite article: lo strofinaccio (singular), gli strofinacci (plural). Indefinite article: uno strofinaccio (singular), degli strofinacci (plural). Composed of the verb strofinare (to rub) and the pejorative suffix -accio, which denotes something bad or unattractive.
learnerNotes: Strofinaccio has a pejorative connotation built into its etymology; the -accio suffix signals something worn-out or undesirable. Beyond literal household cloths, it's used figuratively to describe people treated poorly or things in bad condition. Note the many regional synonyms in Italy—straccio and cencio are the most universally understood alternatives.

exampleSentences.italian: Passami lo strofinaccio così posso asciugare i piatti.
exampleSentences.english: Hand me the dish towel so I can dry the dishes.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mio capo mi tratta come uno strofinaccio.
exampleSentences.english: My boss treats me like a doormat.

grammarNotes: Perla is a feminine noun with regular plural perle. It derives from Latin perna (leg), named for the leg-of-mutton shape of mollusk shells. The word is used literally for actual pearls and figuratively to describe anything precious, beautiful, or gem-like in quality.
learnerNotes: Remember that perla is feminine (la perla, una perla), so adjectives and articles must agree. The word has rich figurative uses in Italian—it can mean gem, treasure, jewel, or even a blunder/mistake depending on context, so pay attention to surrounding context. Teeth (denti) are often poetically called perle if white and shiny, similar to English 'pearly whites.'

exampleSentences.italian: Il valore di una perla non si distingue solo dal colore, ma anche dalla forma e dal lustro.
exampleSentences.english: The value of a pearl is not only distinguished by the colour, but also by the shape and lustre.

exampleSentences.italian: La figlia di Gianluca è veramente una perla.
exampleSentences.english: Gianluca's daughter is a real gem.

exampleSentences.italian: Bellagio è la perla del Lago di Como.
exampleSentences.english: Bellagio is the jewel of Lake Como.

exampleSentences.italian: Ad un certo punto, nel bel mezzo del suo discorso, ha infilato una perla che ha fatto scoppiare a ridere tutto l'auditorium.
exampleSentences.english: At a certain point in the middle of his speech, he made a blunder that made all the auditorium burst out laughing.

grammarNotes: Senno is a masculine noun (il senno) meaning judgment/wisdom/sense. Poi is an adverb meaning then/later/after. Together they form a fixed expression typically used with the preposition 'col' (con + il) or 'con' to mean 'in hindsight.' The expression is invariable and does not conjugate.
learnerNotes: This is an idiomatic expression best learned as a fixed phrase rather than translating word-by-word. The proverb 'Del senno di poi (ne) son piene le fosse' appears in Manzoni's I Promessi Sposi and is well-known in Italian culture. Use 'col senno di poi' or 'con senno di poi' to introduce retrospective commentary on past events; it often implies mild criticism of decisions made without present knowledge.

exampleSentences.italian: Col senno di poi, saremmo potuti rimanere un giorno in più.
exampleSentences.english: In hindsight / In retrospect, we could have stayed one extra day.

exampleSentences.italian: Del senno di poi (ne) son piene le fosse.
exampleSentences.english: Literally: The pits are full of hindsight.

exampleSentences.italian: È facile parlare col senno di poi.
exampleSentences.english: Literally: It's easy to talk in hindsight.

relatedExpressions.expression: Del senno di poi (ne) son piene le fosse
relatedExpressions.meaning: A famous Italian proverb equivalent to 'Hindsight is 20/20'; it suggests that criticizing past decisions with present knowledge is easy but pointless

grammarNotes: Masculine noun taking articles lo/gli (singular/plural). Plural is spiccioli. When used as an adjective, it agrees in gender with the noun: un euro spicciolo (masculine), moneta spicciola (feminine). Derives from the verb spicciolare (to pick off, to change currency).
learnerNotes: Spicciolo has two distinct meanings: (1) loose change/coins (most common), and (2) simple/banal/common (as an adjective or when describing people). Don't confuse these senses. The informal abbreviation spicci is heavily Roman; avoid using it outside that context unless you're confident in the local register. Remember that the plural spiccioli is often used even when referring to a single transaction of small change.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural capolavori. Composed of capo (head/extremity) + lavoro (work). Agreement follows standard masculine patterns: il capolavoro, i capolavori. Used as a predicate nominative or direct object without article shift.
learnerNotes: Capolavoro has three distinct uses: genuine admiration for great art/literature, extension to any excellent work in various fields, and ironic usage for poor quality or mistakes. The ironic sense is context-dependent; tone and context markers (like exclamation points or negative adjectives) signal the intended meaning. Note that 'un bel capolavoro' in negative contexts is sarcastic—it means you've made a mistake or created a disaster.

exampleSentences.english: The Mona Lisa, Leonardo da Vinci's masterpiece

grammarNotes: Intrippare is a transitive verb meaning 'to obsess' (the obsession is the subject), while intripparsi is its pronominal form meaning 'to become obsessed' (the obsessed person is the subject). Both conjugate regularly following standard -are verb patterns. The pronominal form requires the reflexive pronoun (mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si) before the verb.
learnerNotes: Intrippare is distinctly slang, used primarily among young people; avoid in formal contexts. The term derives from 'trip' (drug-related slang) and 'trippa' (humorous for belly), so it carries informal, youthful connotations. Understand the difference between transitive intrippare ('the series obsesses me') and reflexive intripparsi ('I obsess over the series')—both are grammatically correct but used in different sentence structures.

exampleSentences.english: I gobbled down an entire cake!

grammarNotes: Figlio is a masculine noun; the feminine equivalent is figlia. The plural figli refers to sons (all male) or mixed groups of children (sons and daughters). It agrees in gender and number with the person it describes. Figliolo is an affectionate variant.
learnerNotes: Remember that figli is used for both 'sons' (all male) and 'children' (mixed gender) — context determines meaning. Figlio also functions as a term of endearment from older speakers to younger males and can mean 'fellow' or 'chap' informally. Be cautious with vulgar variants of figlio di buona donna as they are offensive insults.

exampleSentences.italian: Nonostante io abbia sette figlie e un figlio, voglio bene a tutti i miei figli allo stesso modo.
exampleSentences.english: Although I have seven daughters and one son, I love all my children equally.

exampleSentences.italian: Beh figlio mio, la vita è piena di ostacoli, ma non ti devi arrendere!

exampleSentences.english: I love him like a son.

exampleSentences.english: The teacher treats us as if we were his children.

exampleSentences.italian: Ha passato tre mesi in carcere ed era pure innocente, povero figlio!

exampleSentences.italian: Vuole fare un figlio prima di compiere quarant'anni.

grammarNotes: Vita is a feminine noun with plural vite. It shares the Latin root with English 'vital' and 'vitamin'. The word maintains consistent gender and number agreement with modifiers and articles throughout all its semantic uses.
learnerNotes: Vita is a high-frequency word with multiple semantic layers: biological life, individual existence, lifespan, way of living, and metaphorical vitality. Be careful with the expression 'la vita' meaning 'cost of living' rather than 'life' itself—context is crucial. Many common verbs and phrases pair specifically with vita (perdere, godersi, salvare), so learning these collocations will significantly improve your fluency.

grammarNotes: Gennaio is a masculine noun (il gennaio) and, like all Italian month names, is not capitalized unless at the beginning of a sentence—unlike English. It is invariable and always takes the masculine article (il, dello, nel, etc.) when used with definite articles or prepositions.
learnerNotes: Remember that Italian month names are never capitalized (gennaio, febbraio, etc.), even at the beginning of a sentence—this is a key difference from English. When expressing dates in Italian, use the cardinal number preceded by 'il' (il diciannove di gennaio = the 19th of January), not an ordinal as commonly seen in English. Note that gennaio derives from Janus, the Roman god of beginnings and doors, which may help with memory retention.

exampleSentences.italian: Gennaio è il primo mese dell'anno.
exampleSentences.english: January is the first month of the year.

exampleSentences.italian: Gennaio ha trentun giorni.
exampleSentences.english: January has 31 days.

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi è il diciannove di gennaio.
exampleSentences.english: Today is January 19th.

exampleSentences.italian: Caspita! Siamo già oltre la metà del mese!
exampleSentences.english: Wow! We're already over halfway through the month!

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural soprammobili. Composed of sopra (on top of) + mobile (furniture), with doubled 'm' due to syntactic gemination (raddoppiamento fonosintattico), a phonological rule in Italian. Gender agreement applies to articles and adjectives: il soprammobile, un soprammobile, dei soprammobili.
learnerNotes: While primarily literal (a decorative object on furniture), soprammobile has a figurative usage meaning to feel excluded, ignored, or useless—though this is not in most dictionaries and requires poetic context. The doubled 'm' is essential to spelling and pronunciation; forgetting it changes the word's structure. Note that La Repubblica also reports a figurative meaning of 'a person who is nice but lacks intelligence,' though this is rarely used.

exampleSentences.italian: Hanno una casa piena di soprammobili. Spolverarla dev'essere un incubo!
exampleSentences.english: They have a house full of knick-knacks. It must be a nightmare to dust!

exampleSentences.italian: La ragazza è andata via. Era stufa di sentirsi un soprammobile.
exampleSentences.english: The girl left. She was tired of feeling useless.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural forms valige or valigie. Commonly paired with verbs like fare, disfare, aprire, chiudere, and mettere. The figurative expression 'fare valigia' means to pack up or leave (willingly or unwillingly). Can also denote specialized bags (computer bag, projector bag) beyond typical suitcases.
learnerNotes: Note the two accepted plurals: valige (more common, follows Latin pattern) or valigie (follows regular Italian -a to -e pattern). Valigia is feminine, so use la valigia/le valige. Be careful not to confuse valigia (large suitcase) with valigetta (small briefcase) or ventiquattrore (24-hour briefcase)—context matters for professional vs. leisure travel. The figurative 'fare valigia' can mean leaving a job or relationship, not just packing for vacation.

exampleSentences.italian: Chiudi la valigia e caricala in macchina per favore.
exampleSentences.english: Close the suitcase and put it in the car please.

exampleSentences.italian: Può tenere la ventiquattrore con sé signore, ma quella valigia deve andare nella stiva.
exampleSentences.english: You can keep the briefcase with you, sir, but that suitcase needs to go in the cargo hold.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to pack a suitcase; to pack up/leave (figurative)
postal suitcase (historical: bag for mail transport)
bag shop; bag factory; assortment of bags

grammarNotes: Abbastanza derives from a (to) + bastanza (from bastare = to suffice) and exhibits syntactic gemination with a doubled 'b'. It functions as both an adverb meaning 'enough' and as a moderator of adjectives/adverbs meaning 'quite/fairly/rather'. When following a verb or modifying a noun, it typically means 'enough'; when preceding adjectives or adverbs, it indicates 'a moderately high degree'. Context determines the best translation.
learnerNotes: Abbastanza is highly versatile and context-dependent: follow a verb or modify a noun to mean 'enough', but precede adjectives/adverbs to mean 'quite/fairly/rather'. When meaning 'enough', it often pairs with da or per followed by an infinitive or noun phrase. Pay attention to word order—Italian word order (especially whether abbastanza comes before or after the modified word) can shift between 'enough' and 'quite' interpretations.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai mangiato abbastanza?
exampleSentences.english: Have you eaten enough?

exampleSentences.italian: Non abbiamo abbastanza tempo.
exampleSentences.english: We don't have enough time.

exampleSentences.italian: Il tempo mi sembra abbastanza buono per fare una passeggiata.
exampleSentences.english: The weather seems good enough to go on a walk.

exampleSentences.italian: Non è forte abbastanza da ammettere la verità.
exampleSentences.english: He's not strong enough to admit the truth.

exampleSentences.italian: Ne ho abbastanza di lei e delle sue lamentele!
exampleSentences.english: I've had enough of her and her complaints!

exampleSentences.english: fairly quickly

exampleSentences.english: quite slowly

exampleSentences.english: quite well

exampleSentences.italian: abbastanza caro
exampleSentences.english: fairly expensive

exampleSentences.italian: abbastanza intelligente
exampleSentences.english: pretty intelligent

exampleSentences.italian: abbastanza interessante
exampleSentences.english: quite interesting

exampleSentences.italian: abbastanza stupido

exampleSentences.english: Is the coffee strong enough?

exampleSentences.english: Yes, the coffee is strong enough.

exampleSentences.italian: Il caffè è abbastanza forte da svegliarmi.
exampleSentences.english: The coffee is strong enough to wake me up.

exampleSentences.italian: Il caffè è abbastanza forte per i miei gusti.
exampleSentences.english: The coffee is strong enough for my tastes.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to have enough of (someone/something undesirable); to reach one's limit

grammarNotes: Volentieri is an invariable adverb that expresses willingness or enthusiasm. It can function as an affirmative response to invitations or requests, similar to English 'I'd love to' or 'certainly.' The word derives from Latin voluntarie through French volontiers and remains unchanged regardless of gender, number, or context.
learnerNotes: Volentieri is extremely versatile and native-like usage requires understanding both its adverbial function (modifying actions) and its role as an affirmative response. Note that 'spesso e volentieri' is an idiomatic expression where volentieri reinforces frequency rather than willingness, so it can apply to both positive and negative contexts. The opposite malvolentieri/poco volentieri should be memorized as fixed expressions rather than decomposed.

exampleSentences.italian: Tornerei a Venezia molto volentieri.
exampleSentences.english: I would very willingly go back to Venice.

exampleSentences.italian: Ci vediamo spesso e volentieri con i nostri vicini di casa.
exampleSentences.english: We see our neighbours very often.

exampleSentences.italian: Su questa strada le auto vanno troppo forte. Capitano spesso e volentieri incidenti.
exampleSentences.english: Cars go too fast on this road. Accidents happen very often.

exampleSentences.italian: Vieni con noi stasera? – Volentieri!
exampleSentences.english: Will you come with us tonight? – I'd love to!

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi vado in ufficio malvolentieri.
exampleSentences.english: Today I'm reluctant to go into the office.

grammarNotes: Oggi is an invariable adverb derived from Latin hŏdie (contraction of hoc die, meaning 'on this day'). It does not change form based on gender, number, or any grammatical agreement. It can function as a temporal marker for the current day or, in broader contexts, as a reference to the present era or modern times.
learnerNotes: Oggi is frequently used with emphatic forms (oggi stesso, quest'oggi, proprio oggi) to stress immediacy or surprise. Note the distinction between oggi referring to the current 24-hour period versus its use in expressions like 'i bambini di oggi' (children of today/modern children) and 'al giorno d'oggi' (nowadays), where it denotes the present era. Be careful not to confuse 'entro oggi' (by end of day) with 'fino a oggi' (until now/to date); the former is future-oriented while the latter is retrospective.

exampleSentences.italian: Ieri mi hai detto che l'incontro si sarebbe tenuto oggi, ma in realtà ho scoperto che si svolge domani!
exampleSentences.english: Yesterday you told me the meeting would be held today but I found out it's actually taking place tomorrow!

exampleSentences.italian: Mi informerò oggi stesso.
exampleSentences.english: I will find out today.

exampleSentences.italian: Quest'oggi andrò a trovarlo.
exampleSentences.english: I will go and see him today.

exampleSentences.italian: Proprio oggi dovevi venire?
exampleSentences.english: Did you have to come today?

exampleSentences.italian: Riesci a finire il testo entro oggi?
exampleSentences.english: Can you finish the text by the end of the day?

exampleSentences.italian: È vero che i bambini di oggi sono più viziati di quelli di ieri?
exampleSentences.english: Is it true that the children of today are more spoiled than they used to be?

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi più che mai sono convinto di aver fatto la scelta giusta.
exampleSentences.english: Now more than ever I'm convinced that I made the right choice.

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi pomeriggio andrò al negozio.
exampleSentences.english: I will go to the store this afternoon.

relatedExpressions.meaning: by the end of the day

relatedExpressions.expression: Meglio un uovo oggi che una gallina domani

grammarNotes: Fiamma is a feminine noun (la fiamma). Its plural is fiamme (le fiamme). It derives from Latin flamma, the same root as English 'flame.' The word is commonly used both literally (physical flames) and metaphorically (passion, romantic interest, or bright red colours).
learnerNotes: Remember fiamma is feminine (la fiamma, le fiamme). Beyond physical flames, the word extends to metaphorical uses: 'old flame' (romantic partner from the past), passion, and the colour flame-red. Context determines meaning—'Vedi le fiamme?' could mean either literal flames or be figurative depending on the situation.

exampleSentences.italian: la fiamma di una candela
exampleSentences.english: the flame of a candle

exampleSentences.italian: la fiamma di una lucerna
exampleSentences.english: the flame of a lamp

exampleSentences.italian: la fiamma di un fiammifero
exampleSentences.english: the flame of a match

exampleSentences.italian: la fiamma del fornello
exampleSentences.english: the flame of the burner

exampleSentences.italian: La fiamma della candela oscilla va nel vento.
exampleSentences.english: The flame of the candle danced in the wind.

exampleSentences.italian: La casa è stata distrutta dalle fiamme.
exampleSentences.english: The house was destroyed by the fire.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho ritrovato una vecchia fiamma su Facebook.
exampleSentences.english: I found an old flame on Facebook.

relatedExpressions.meaning: backfiring of an engine; rekindling of romantic feelings

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural form grandini. Derived from Latin. Can be used literally for frozen rain pellets or metaphorically for any violent shower of objects (bullets, arrows, insults). The related verb grandinare can take either avere or essere as auxiliary.
learnerNotes: Grandine is primarily a weather term but has important metaphorical uses—think of it as 'shower' or 'torrent' when describing rapid violent delivery of non-weather objects. Note that the verb grandinare is unusual in accepting both avere and essere, so exposure to both forms is important. The expression c'è passata la grandine is colloquial and playful, useful for conversational Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: cade la grandine
exampleSentences.english: the hail falls

exampleSentences.italian: È caduta tanta di quella grandine da rovinare il tetto della nostra macchina!
exampleSentences.english: So much hail has fallen that it ruined the roof of our car!

exampleSentences.italian: grandine di proiettili
exampleSentences.english: hail of bullets

exampleSentences.italian: grandine di frecce
exampleSentences.english: hail of arrows

exampleSentences.italian: grandine di sassi
exampleSentences.english: hail of stones

exampleSentences.italian: grandine di insulti
exampleSentences.english: hail/shower of insults

exampleSentences.italian: Davanti al Palagiustizia è stato travolto da una grandine di insulti!
exampleSentences.english: In front of the courthouse, he was bombarded by a shower of insults!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to hail (verb); takes avere or essere as auxiliary
something was destroyed violently and quickly, or friends ate/drank something very quickly

grammarNotes: Attonito is a four-form adjective: attonito (masculine singular), attonita (feminine singular), attoniti (masculine plural), attonite (feminine plural). It agrees with the noun it modifies in gender and number. Commonly used with the copular verbs essere, rimanere, or restare followed by the prepositions per or da to express 'be/remain/stay astonished by.'
learnerNotes: Attonito is a literary or formal word; in everyday conversation, stupito, sorpreso, or allibito are more common. Remember that the Latin origin tonare (thunder) helps explain the semantic link between thunder's shock and astonishment. Pay attention to gender agreement when describing feminine nouns (attonita, attonite).

exampleSentences.italian: Non appena egli posò gli occhi sulla principessa, rimase attonito dalla sua bellezza.
exampleSentences.english: As soon as he set eyes on the princess, he was stunned by her beauty.

grammarNotes: Trasandato is a four-form adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: trasandato (m.sg.), trasandata (f.sg.), trasandati (m.pl.), trasandate (f.pl.). It derives from the past participle of the obsolete verb trasandare, formed with the prefix trans- (across/beyond) plus andare (to go). It functions as a standard descriptive adjective in predicate or attributive position.
learnerNotes: Trasandato is most commonly heard when describing someone's disheveled appearance or a neglected physical space, making it practical for everyday observation. Don't confuse it with sporco (dirty) or trascurato (neglected); trasandato emphasizes the combined sense of poor condition and lack of care. Remember to apply full four-form agreement like any other adjective ending in -ato.

exampleSentences.italian: Che uomo trasandato!
exampleSentences.english: What a scruffy man!

exampleSentences.italian: Ha le scarpe bucate e la maglietta tutta macchiata.
exampleSentences.english: His shoes have holes in them and his shirt is covered in stains.

exampleSentences.italian: Una casa trasandata
exampleSentences.english: A run-down house

exampleSentences.italian: Un lavoro trasandato
exampleSentences.english: A sloppy job

exampleSentences.italian: Io non sopporto più di vivere in questa casa trasandata!
exampleSentences.english: I can't stand living in this run-down house anymore!

englishTranslation: to the point of bursting / to the breaking point / uncontrollably
grammarNotes: A crepapelle is an idiomatic adverbial phrase composed of the preposition 'a' + the noun 'crepapelle' (from crepare 'to crack/burst' + pelle 'skin'). It functions as an adverb modifying verbs and doesn't decline. The phrase typically appears in the structure '[verb] a crepapelle' and is most commonly used with ridere (to laugh). It conveys intensity and excess in the action being performed.
learnerNotes: This expression is highly idiomatic with no direct English equivalent; memorizing common verb + a crepapelle combinations is essential for recognition and production. While ridere a crepapelle dominates in spoken Italian, the other verb combinations appear mainly in literature and written language. Be aware that a crepapelle carries an intensity marker—it indicates going to an extreme or breaking point, not merely performing the action casually.

exampleSentences.italian: Ridere a crepapelle
exampleSentences.english: To split one's sides with laughter / To burst out laughing

exampleSentences.italian: Far ridere (qualcuno) a crepapelle
exampleSentences.english: To crack (someone) up / To have (someone) in fits

exampleSentences.italian: La prima parte del film mi ha fatto ridere a crepapelle, la seconda mi ha strappato le lacrime!
exampleSentences.english: The first part of the film cracked me up, the second part left me in tears!

exampleSentences.italian: Mangiare a crepapelle
exampleSentences.english: To eat until you burst

exampleSentences.italian: Riempirsi a crepapelle
exampleSentences.english: To stuff one's face

exampleSentences.italian: Bere a crepapelle
exampleSentences.english: To drink oneself under the table

exampleSentences.italian: Sghignazzare a crepapelle
exampleSentences.english: To laugh scornfully and uncontrollably

relatedExpressions.meaning: to laugh uncontrollably / to split one's sides with laughter

grammarNotes: Gente is a feminine collective noun that always takes a singular verb, even though it refers to multiple people. The plural form le genti exists but is rare, used mainly in literature or historical contexts. Unlike English 'people,' you cannot use gente with numbers (e.g., quattro persone, not quattro gente).
learnerNotes: Remember that gente always requires singular verbs (la gente è, not sono), which differs from English. Don't confuse gente with persone: use persone when specifying a quantity (tre persone) or when you need the plural form. The adjective placement in Italian can vary (brava gente or gente brava are both correct), but bella gente often appears before the noun for emphasis.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è tanta gente per strada.
exampleSentences.english: There are lots of people on the street.

exampleSentences.italian: Ci sono tante persone per strada.
exampleSentences.english: There are lots of people on the street.

exampleSentences.italian: La gente è felice.
exampleSentences.english: The people are happy. (literally: the people is happy)

exampleSentences.italian: Dovresti iscriverti a quel club sportivo. Mi dicono che è frequentato da gente per bene.
exampleSentences.english: You should join that sports club. They say that respectable people go there.

exampleSentences.italian: Come il frigo è vuoto? Stai scherzando vero?! Abbiamo gente a cena stasera!
exampleSentences.english: What do you mean the fridge is empty? Are you joking?! We're having guests over for dinner tonight!

exampleSentences.italian: Ciao, gente!
exampleSentences.english: Bye, folks!

exampleSentences.italian: Ci vediamo, gente!
exampleSentences.english: See you, guys!

exampleSentences.italian: Ciao bella gente!
exampleSentences.english: Hello beautiful people!

exampleSentences.italian: Le genti dell'antica Roma
exampleSentences.english: The people of ancient Rome

grammarNotes: Intramontabile is an invariable adjective in terms of gender—both singular and plural forms use the same e/i ending regardless of whether the noun is masculine or feminine. The plural form is intramontabili. It follows standard Italian adjective placement rules and can precede or follow the noun it modifies.
learnerNotes: Intramontabile is a sophisticated, literary adjective frequently used in cultural contexts (music, film, art). The prefix in- + tramontare (to set) creates an elegant negation: something that 'never sets' or 'never fades.' Note the humorous usage shown in the final example, where it can mean someone has been around so long they seem ageless—a playful rather than literal application.

exampleSentences.english: timeless song

exampleSentences.english: Yesterday by the Beatles is a timeless song.

exampleSentences.italian: È proprio intramontabile quella cantante!
exampleSentences.english: That singer really is ageless!

negation prefix; creates the opposite meaning of tramontare

grammarNotes: Amato is the past participle of amare (to love) used as an adjective. It agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: amato (m. sg.), amata (f. sg.), amati (m. pl.), amate (f. pl.). The adjective can appear before or after the noun without significant meaning change. The superlative form amatissimo/a/i/e means 'much loved.'
learnerNotes: While amato is a straightforward past participle-turned-adjective, remember that as a term of endearment it is fairly antiquated and rarely used in modern Italian—amata especially sounds literary or romantic rather than contemporary. The adjective agreement is crucial: always match the ending to the noun's gender and number. Amato can also function as a proper surname (especially D'Amato), which is common in Italy.

grammarNotes: Farina is a feminine noun (la farina). The plural form is farine. It derives from Latin and is used both literally to describe ground grains and figuratively in idioms. When used with adjectives or articles, gender agreement is required (e.g., la farina bianca, le farine diverse).
learnerNotes: Farina is a straightforward feminine noun essential for cooking vocabulary. Be aware of the many compound expressions (farina di grano, farina di ceci, etc.) that specify flour types—these are very common in Italian recipes. The numerous idioms built from farina reflect its cultural importance in Italian cuisine and daily life; focus on the most frequent ones like 'non è farina del tuo sacco' when conversing.

exampleSentences.italian: Invece della farina bianca, ho usato la farina di ceci per fare i pancake.
exampleSentences.english: Instead of white flour, I used chickpea flour to make pancakes.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with regular plural mascherine. It is the diminutive form of maschera (mask). Gender agreement applies when using adjectives: una mascherina riutilizzabile, le mascherine chirurgiche. The word can also refer to a colored patch on an animal's face or costume elements.
learnerNotes: Mascherina is the diminutive of maschera, so it literally means 'little mask'—useful for understanding Italian diminutive suffixes (-ina). Be aware that this word has multiple meanings: air-filtering masks, Carnival masks, sleep masks, and animal face markings. The figurative phrase 'Ti conosco mascherina!' is commonly used in social contexts when someone is being deceptive or disguised.

exampleSentences.italian: È obbligatorio indossare la mascherina quando si entra in un negozio.
exampleSentences.english: It is mandatory to wear a mask when entering a shop.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural peperoni. Agrees with adjectives in gender and number (e.g., peperone rosso, peperoni verdi). Can refer to both the fruit and the plant that bears it. Etymology traces to Latin piper (the spice), though it now denotes the vegetable.
learnerNotes: Be careful not to confuse peperone (bell pepper) with pepperoni (the pizza topping), which is called salame piccante in Italian. Ordering a pizza ai peperoni will give you a pizza with bell pepper slices, not the spicy salami topping. Note that green peppers are unripe versions of red, yellow, or orange peppers and have a more pungent, acidic taste; this distinction matters in cooking.

exampleSentences.italian: Se vai al mercato, puoi prendere dei peperoni?

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural tegole. Derives from Latin tegula (from tegere, 'to cover'). The figurative meaning 'blow' or 'shock' is metaphorical, imagining a tile hitting one's head. Not to be confused with the masculine Tuscan variant tegolo, which refers to a specific type of tile called coppo.
learnerNotes: The figurative meaning 'blow' or 'shock' is idiomatic and frequently used in spoken Italian—learning this extends your vocabulary beyond the literal. Be careful not to confuse tegola (roof tiles) with piastrellare (to tile with bathroom/kitchen tiles called piastrelle). The masculine variant tegolo exists in Tuscan dialect but refers to a specific coppo tile type and should be avoided in standard Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Un tetto di tegole è un tetto coperto di piastrelle.
exampleSentences.english: A tiled roof is a roof covered with tiles.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono cadute delle tegole dal tetto per colpa della tempesta.
exampleSentences.english: Some tiles fell off the roof because of the storm.

exampleSentences.italian: Perdere il lavoro è stata una vera e propria tegola in testa per lui e la sua famiglia.
exampleSentences.english: Losing his job was a real blow for him and his family.

exampleSentences.italian: Che tegola ragazzi, perdere la gara in quel modo!
exampleSentences.english: Man, what a blow to lose the race like that.

exampleSentences.italian: Il pilota sarà furibondo!
exampleSentences.english: The driver must be furious!

grammarNotes: Nottambulo functions as both noun and adjective with four-form gender/number agreement: nottambulo (m. sing.), nottambula (f. sing.), nottambuli (m./mixed pl.), nottambule (f. pl.). When used as an adjective, the ending changes to match the noun it modifies. The term is derived from Latin nox (night) + ambulare (to walk), following the pattern of funambulo (tightrope walker).
learnerNotes: Nottambulo is a literary/less common term compared to tiratardi or the English loanword 'night owl' used colloquially in Italian. Be careful not to confuse it with sonnambulo (sleepwalker)—nottambulo refers to someone awake and active at night, while sonnambulo refers to someone who walks while sleeping. Remember that the four-form agreement pattern (nottambulo/nottambula/nottambuli/nottambule) is essential when using it as an adjective modifying nouns.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho un fratello nottambulo e una sorella sonnambula.
exampleSentences.english: I have a brother who is a night owl and a sister who sleepwalks.

grammarNotes: Pesca is feminine (la pesca, plural le pesche) when referring to the fruit. The masculine form pesco refers to the peach tree. Pesca is also a homonym meaning 'fishing' with identical spelling and pronunciation but different meaning. Gender agreement affects articles and adjectives: una pesca morbida (a soft peach).
learnerNotes: Watch out: pesca has two completely different meanings (the fruit vs. fishing) with identical spelling—context is essential. The feminine form pesca becomes masculine pesco for the tree; remember this gender shift. In Tuscan dialect, pesca figuratively means 'bruise,' so be aware of regional variation. Color pesca is commonly used in fashion and descriptions of skin tone.

exampleSentences.english: to eat a peach

grammarNotes: Rotto is the past participle of rompere (to break) used as an adjective. It agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: rotto (m.sg.), rotta (f.sg.), rotti (m.pl.), rotte (f.pl.). Beyond literal damage, it has figurative meanings including interrupted speech, accustomedness to something, and extreme fatigue.
learnerNotes: Rotto is extremely common and appears in both literal and figurative contexts, so prioritize learning its varied uses. Note that the plural form rotti can also mean 'negligible quantity' when used with money (seicento e rotti = six hundred and change). The idiom per il rotto della cuffia is particularly tricky since it originates from medieval chain mail terminology and doesn't translate literally—memorize it as a fixed expression.

exampleSentences.italian: un braccio rotto
exampleSentences.english: a broken arm (masculine singular)

grammarNotes: Mucca is a feminine noun (la mucca) with plural form mucche. It agrees with feminine articles and adjectives. The verb mungere (to milk) is regular and takes mucca as its direct object (mungere una mucca).
learnerNotes: Prefer mucca or mucca da latte in everyday conversation; vacca is considered vulgar slang when used toward women and should be avoided in polite speech, even though it's technically correct for describing adult breeding cows. Note that bovina (feminine of bovino/bovine) is a more technical term used to describe cattle of any kind. Don't confuse mungere (to milk) with muggire (to moo).

exampleSentences.italian: Molti allevatori continuano a mungere le loro mucche a mano.
exampleSentences.english: Many farmers continue to milk their cows by hand.

exampleSentences.italian: Tu sai qual'è la differenza fra la mucca e la vacca?
exampleSentences.english: Do you know the difference between "mucca" and "vacca"?

relatedExpressions.meaning: cow (specifically adult female that has given birth; considered vulgar slang when applied to women)
cow (any kind, regardless of age or reproductive status)

grammarNotes: As an adjective, cervellotico agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Masculine singular: cervellotico; masculine plural: cervellotici; feminine singular: cervellotica; feminine plural: cervellotiche. It follows standard adjective agreement patterns in Italian and can be used predicatively (Si è comportato in modo cervellotico) or attributively (un uomo cervellotico).
learnerNotes: Cervellotico is derived from a blend of cervello (brain) and zotico (crude/uncouth), making it a relatively informal, expressive term suited for describing both people and ideas. As an Advanced-level word, it's less commonly used in everyday conversation than simpler synonyms like strano or bizzarro. Be careful with gender agreement, especially in written Italian, as the feminine forms (cervellotica/cervellotiche) are frequently used when discussing hypotheses, ideas, or women.

exampleSentences.english: a bizarre tale

grammarNotes: Volpe is a feminine noun (la volpe). Regular plural formation: volpi. Derived from Latin vulpes. Combines with suffixes to form diminutives (volpacchiotto = fox cub) and augmentatives (volpone = wily person), which preserve the feminine gender in standard usage.
learnerNotes: Volpe is commonly used in Italian idioms and expressions that associate foxes with cunning and intelligence, much like in English. Note that 'mangiare pane e volpe' is used exclusively in sarcastic or ironic contexts to imply stupidity—the opposite of its literal meaning—so context is essential. The diminutive volpacchiotto and augmentative volpone are useful for describing fox cubs and sly individuals respectively.

exampleSentences.italian: I cuccioli di volpe stanno giocando fuori dalla tana.
exampleSentences.english: The fox cubs are playing outside the lair.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho rubato 300 euro e l'ho detto a tutti i miei amici. – Ma che cosa mangi la mattina? Pane e volpe?
exampleSentences.english: I stole €300 and told all my friends. – What, are you stupid or something? (Literally: What do you eat in the morning? Bread and fox?)

to be as sly as a fox
to smarten up / become astute (used sarcastically to mean the opposite)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural balzi. Derives from the verb balzare (to bounce). Can be used literally to describe physical movement of elastic objects, or figuratively to denote sudden changes or increases. The feminine homophone balza (cliff, ledge, flounce) should not be confused with this word.
learnerNotes: Balzo has both literal (physical bouncing) and figurative (sudden change/increase) uses; context determines meaning. Do not confuse the masculine balzo with the feminine balza (cliff/ledge), which sounds similar but has completely different meanings. The idiomatic expressions with 'palla al balzo' are useful for speaking about seizing opportunities in everyday Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Con un grande balzo, il lupo si lanciò verso Cappuccetto Rosso.
exampleSentences.english: With a great leap, the wolf lunged toward Little Red Riding Hood.

exampleSentences.italian: un balzo in avanti per la società
exampleSentences.english: a leap forward / a stride forward for the society

exampleSentences.english: Tomorrow a jump in temperature is expected.

grammarNotes: Al di là is an adverbial phrase composed of al (a + il) + di + là. It functions as both an adverb and a preposition. When used as a preposition, it requires 'di' before the noun (al di là di). The modern form al di là (di) is preferred over the traditional di là da in contemporary Italian.
learnerNotes: Do not confuse the adverbial phrase 'al di là' (two words) with the noun 'aldilà' (one word), which refers specifically to the afterlife. When used as a preposition before a noun, always include 'di' (al di là di). Beyond its literal spatial meaning, al di là is frequently used in formal writing to mean 'aside from,' 'setting aside,' or 'regardless of'—contexts where English speakers might use transitional phrases like 'be that as it may' or 'in any case.'

exampleSentences.italian: Al di là c'era il deserto, immenso e dominato da dune enormi.
exampleSentences.english: Beyond lay the desert, immense and dominated by enormous dunes.

exampleSentences.italian: Al di là del fiume, c'è una casetta.
exampleSentences.english: On the other side of the river, there is a small house.

exampleSentences.italian: Di là dal fiume, c'è una casetta.
exampleSentences.english: On the other side of the river, there is a small house.

exampleSentences.italian: Al di là di queste controversie, è chiaro che abbiamo bisogno di maggiori informazioni.
exampleSentences.english: These controversies aside, it is clear that we need more information.

exampleSentences.italian: Il bello di questo lavoro, al di là del fatto che mi permette di lavorare da casa, è che è molto soddisfacente.
exampleSentences.english: The beauty of this job, beyond the fact that it allows me to work from home, is that it is very satisfying.

exampleSentences.italian: La notizia, al di là della sua veridicità o meno, ha danneggiato la sua immagine.
exampleSentences.english: The news, regardless of whether it is true or not, has damaged his reputation.

exampleSentences.italian: Tu credi nell'aldilà?
exampleSentences.english: Do you believe in the afterlife?

relatedExpressions.meaning: on the other side of (traditional, less common form)
the afterlife / the hereafter (written as one word, noun)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural rottami. Derives from rotto (past participle of rompere) plus the suffix -ame, which forms collective nouns often with derogatory connotations. In the sense of 'fragments' or 'scrap metal', it appears predominantly in plural form (rottami metallici).
learnerNotes: Rottame has both literal meanings (broken machines, scrap metal) and figurative meanings (a person in poor physical or mental condition). It carries a mildly derogatory or self-deprecating tone, especially when applied to people—use it humorously rather than as a serious insult. The verb rottamare appears in political jargon to describe sidelining old party members, so it's useful for reading Italian news.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa macchina è un rottame oramai: devo cambiarla.
exampleSentences.english: This car is a wreck. It's time to get a new one.

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi mi sento proprio un rottame.
exampleSentences.english: Today I feel like an absolute wreck.

exampleSentences.italian: Hanno rottamato tutti i vecchi membri del partito.
exampleSentences.english: They got rid of all the old members of the party.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to scrap, to demolish (also used figuratively for marginalizing a person)
the collection and redistribution of scrap metal

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form allarmi. Derives from the military expression All'arme! (To arms!). Used both literally for warning devices and figuratively for anxiety or apprehension. Does not refer to alarm clocks, which use sveglia instead.
learnerNotes: Don't confuse allarme (alarm/alert) with sveglia (alarm clock). Allarme is used both literally for security/warning devices and figuratively for feelings of anxiety or apprehension. The phrase campanello d'allarme literally means 'alarm bell' but is commonly used figuratively to mean 'warning sign' in everyday Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: L'allarme della mia automobile fa le bizze. Scatta ogni volta che apro la portiera.
exampleSentences.english: My car alarm is acting weird. It goes off every time I open the door.

exampleSentences.italian: I gravi fatti della settimana scorsa costituiscono un campanello d'allarme che non può essere ignorato.
exampleSentences.english: The serious events of last week are a warning sign that cannot be ignored.

exampleSentences.italian: Si è messo in allarme quando si è reso conto che i figli non erano ancora tornati a casa.
exampleSentences.english: He was alarmed when he realised that his children had not yet returned home.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to turn on / off the alarm
offence of misleading authorities about a non-existent disaster

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural ruzzoloni. Often used in the phrase 'fare un ruzzolone' (to take a tumble). Can be modified by adjectives like 'brutto' (bad) or 'gran' (great) to emphasize severity. The adverbial form 'a ruzzoloni' or 'ruzzoloni' is commonly used to describe the manner of falling.
learnerNotes: Ruzzolone is onomatopoetic—it sounds like the action it describes, making it memorable. Beyond literal falls, use it figuratively for powerful people who suddenly lose authority. Note the distinction between the noun ruzzolone and the adverbial phrase 'a ruzzoloni'; the latter emphasizes the manner of descent rather than the fall itself.

exampleSentences.italian: Ha fatto un brutto ruzzolone giù da una scalinata.
exampleSentences.english: He took a nasty tumble down a staircase.

exampleSentences.italian: È venuto giù dalle scale a ruzzoloni.
exampleSentences.english: He slipped down the stairs, tumbling as he went.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to take a tumble / to have a hard fall
thick wooden disc used in an obsolete game

grammarNotes: Sfida is a feminine noun with regular plural sfide. It agrees with feminine articles and adjectives (la sfida, una sfida, le sfide). The related verb sfidare is regular and conjugates normally across tenses. When used with preposition di, it forms the adverbial phrase 'di sfida' meaning 'defiantly.'
learnerNotes: Sfida is commonly paired with specific verbs: use 'affrontare' or 'sostenere' for facing challenges, 'lanciare' for issuing them, and 'accettare/raccogliere' for accepting them. In sports contexts, sfida often translates as 'match' or 'competition' rather than the literal 'challenge.' The phrase 'di sfida' is particularly useful for describing attitudes or gestures conveying defiance.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono pronto per affrontare questa nuova sfida, cascasse il mondo!
exampleSentences.english: I'm ready to face this new challenge, no matter what happens!

exampleSentences.italian: La sfida tra la Juventus e la Roma è in programma questa sera alle venti e trenta.
exampleSentences.english: The match between Juventus and Roma is scheduled tonight at 8.30 p.m.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel giocatore mi ha fatto un gesto di sfida.
exampleSentences.english: That player gave me a gesture of defiance.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to issue a challenge / to challenge

grammarNotes: A malapena is an adverbial phrase composed of the preposition 'a' and the noun 'malapena' (from malo/a meaning 'bad' and pena meaning 'pain/suffering'). The preposition 'a' is mandatory and cannot be omitted. The phrase functions as an adverb modifying verbs and often conveys a sense of difficulty or hardship.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'a malapena' always requires the preposition 'a' — you cannot say 'malapena' alone. The phrase often implies hardship or struggle, so it's frequently used with verbs describing difficult actions (riuscire, vedere, sentire). Note that synonyms like 'a stento' and 'a fatica' are interchangeable in most contexts but may vary slightly in tone or frequency of use.

exampleSentences.italian: Il paziente con la bronchite riesce a malapena a respirare.
exampleSentences.english: The patient with bronchitis is hardly able to breathe.

exampleSentences.italian: Senza gli occhiali, vedo a malapena la scritta sul cartello.
exampleSentences.english: Without my glasses, I can barely see the writing on the sign.

englishTranslation: to undo / to untie / to unpack / to dismantle / to unwrap
grammarNotes: Disfare is formed from the prefix dis- (un-) + fare (to do/make). It has two accepted conjugation patterns: one follows fare's irregular conjugation (io disfaccio), while the newer colloquial form follows regular patterns (io disfo). Both versions are grammatically correct. The reflexive form disfarsi means 'to get rid of' (transitive) or 'to rot/melt/come undone' (intransitive pronominal).
learnerNotes: Disfare is widely used in everyday Italian, but be aware it has two acceptable conjugations—ask natives which they prefer for formal writing. The reflexive disfarsi has different meanings depending on context: transitive (get rid of things/people) versus intransitive pronominal (rot, melt, come undone). Remember that soddisfare follows the same dual conjugation pattern, making these exceptions worth noting.

grammarNotes: Bebè is a masculine noun that is invariable (does not change in plural: i bebè). It is borrowed from French bébé, which itself comes from English baby. Unlike bambino/bambina (which can refer to children up to adolescence) or neonato/neonata (specifically newborn), bebè specifically denotes an infant or very young baby.
learnerNotes: Unlike English, bebè in Italian is used exclusively for actual infants and cannot be used as a term of endearment for lovers or spouses. Be aware that bambino/bambina is much broader and can refer to children from infancy through adolescence, so use bebè when you specifically mean a baby or very young infant. The word is invariable in plural (i bebè, not i bebès).

exampleSentences.italian: Quali giochi dovrei scegliere per un bebè di sei mesi?
exampleSentences.english: Which toys should I choose for a 6-month-old baby?

exampleSentences.italian: Hai già fatto domanda per il bonus bebè?
exampleSentences.english: Did you already ask for child benefits?

grammarNotes: As an adjective, viola is invariable—it maintains the same form across gender and number. As a noun denoting the colour, it is always masculine (il viola) despite ending in -a. When referring to the plant genus or the musical instrument, viola is feminine with plural viole.
learnerNotes: Be careful not to confuse viola (purple) with porpora (dark red) or violetto (violet)—these are distinct colours in Italian despite potential confusion in English. Remember that when viola functions as a colour adjective, it never changes form regardless of the noun's gender or number. Note that viola as a noun (the colour) is masculine, but viola as a plant or instrument is feminine.

exampleSentences.english: a purple dress (masculine, singular)

exampleSentences.english: I know someone who always wears purple.

grammarNotes: Scatola is a feminine noun (la scatola); plural is scatole. Diminutives include scatolino (masculine) and scatolina (feminine) for small boxes, and scatolone for large boxes. The word can refer either to the container itself or to its contents.
learnerNotes: Scatola has several colloquial/vulgar idiomatic uses involving the plural scatole (boxes) as a euphemism for testicles—expressions like 'mi stai rompendo le scatole' (you're bothering me) are very common in everyday Italian but should be used cautiously in formal contexts. Note that 'scatola' can mean both the container and its contents, so 'una scatola di biscotti' can mean either 'a box of cookies' or 'a box containing cookies.' The expression 'a scatola chiusa' literally means 'with a closed box' and refers to buying blind, often with trust in quality or brand.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho usato una scatola di cartone per spedire le mie cose in Italia.
exampleSentences.english: I used a cardboard box to ship my belongings to Italy.

exampleSentences.italian: Si è mangiato una scatola di biscotti.
exampleSentences.english: He ate a box of cookies.

exampleSentences.italian: Il ricco mercante d'arte ha acquistato un raro ritratto a scatola chiusa.
exampleSentences.english: The wealthy art dealer purchased a rare portrait sight unseen.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi stai rompendo le scatole!

grammarNotes: Viavai is a masculine noun with an invariant plural form (viavai). It is a compound word formed from via (road/street) + vai (second person singular of andare). Always written as one word, never separated. In mechanical contexts, it describes reciprocating motion.
learnerNotes: Viavai is commonly used to describe busy human or vehicular movement, especially in public spaces. The word's spelling is a frequent error point — learners often write it as two words (via vai), which is incorrect. In mechanical/engineering contexts, viavai specifically denotes reciprocating motion (up-and-down or back-and-forth), so pay attention to context for accurate interpretation.

exampleSentences.italian: Nella piazza c'era un gran viavai di persone.
exampleSentences.english: In the square there was a great coming and going of people.

relatedExpressions.meaning: coming(s) and going(s) — a less common synonym composed of andare (to go) + venire (to come)

grammarNotes: Lavorare is a regular first-conjugation (-are) verb. It can function as both intransitive (non-reflective work) and transitive (working on/with something). Common prepositions include per (for), a/su (on), in/presso (at), and da/come (as). It can also be a synonym for funzionare when describing machines or body parts.
learnerNotes: Lavorare is a core verb, but remember it has multiple uses: literal work, machine operation (funzionare), and business activity. Pay attention to prepositions—lavorare per, a/su, in/presso, and da/come all express different work relationships. Watch for the transitive uses (lavorare la terra, lavorare il pane) which are less common but important in rural contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei lavorare solo quattro giorni a settimana.
exampleSentences.english: I would like to work just four days a week.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa macchina lavora ventiquattro ore su ventiquattro, sette giorni su sette.
exampleSentences.english: This machine operates twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è un solo bar in questo paesino e lavora molto.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural form baracche. Shares etymological origin with English 'barracks' from Catalan barraca. The word extends beyond literal meaning to figurative uses describing unstable institutions, businesses in difficulty, or objects in poor condition.
learnerNotes: Baracca is primarily used in figurative contexts in modern Italian—describing unstable businesses, families in financial difficulty, or broken objects—rather than literal huts. The idioms 'mandare avanti la baracca' and 'piantare baracca e burattini' are particularly useful colloquial expressions. Note that 'baraccone' (large fair tent) carries different connotations and should not be confused with the singular form when discussing fairgrounds.

exampleSentences.italian: Il cane è stato ritrovato all'interno di una baracca.
exampleSentences.english: The dog was found inside a shack.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono io che mando avanti la baracca, non il capo!
exampleSentences.english: I'm the one who keeps the business going, not the boss!

exampleSentences.italian: Dopo il licenziamento, Laura ha piantato baracca e burattini e se n'è andata a vivere a Parigi!
exampleSentences.english: After being laid off, Laura left everything behind and went to live in Paris.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo aspirapolvere è una vera baracca. Quando ti deciderai a cambiarlo?
exampleSentences.english: This vacuum cleaner is a real piece of junk. When will you decide to change it?

englishTranslation: because / given that / since / seeing as how
grammarNotes: Siccome is a causal conjunction composed of sì (yes) + come (how). It takes the indicative mood, not the subjunctive, because it expresses certainty. Crucially, it cannot be followed by che (that)—this is a common error for learners accustomed to perché che constructions.
learnerNotes: Siccome sounds more sophisticated than perché and is preferred in formal and written Italian. Remember: use indicative, never subjunctive, and never add che after siccome—these are the two most common mistakes. Learn the synonyms dato che, visto che, and poiché to vary your causal expressions naturally in speech.

exampleSentences.italian: Siccome piove, oggi non usciamo.
exampleSentences.english: Since it's raining, we aren't going out today.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form vaccini. Can also function as an adjective meaning 'of the cow' (e.g., latte vaccino = cow's milk, carne vaccina = beef). Derived from Latin vacca (cow) and vaccinus (of a cow). When used as an adjective, it agrees with the gender and number of the noun it modifies.
learnerNotes: The word vaccino has an interesting etymological connection to cows (vacca), stemming from Edward Jenner's 1796 discovery that cowpox immunity prevented smallpox. As an adjective, it commonly appears in food contexts (latte vaccino, carne vaccina), so familiarize yourself with these collocations. The figurative use of 'essere vaccinato' to mean 'experienced/grown-up' is idiomatic and useful for understanding colloquial Italian discourse.

exampleSentences.italian: I miei genitori hanno fatto il vaccino la settimana scorsa.
exampleSentences.english: My parents got the vaccine last week.

exampleSentences.italian: Ormai è adulto e vaccinato. Deve trovare la sua strada.
exampleSentences.english: He's a big boy now. He must find his own path.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to get vaccinated (reflexive); figuratively: to be hardened against something
to be a grown-up who can make one's own choices (often ironic)

grammarNotes: Vincitore is masculine singular; plural is vincitori. The feminine forms are vincitrice (singular) and vincitrici (plural). When used as an adjective meaning 'winning' or 'victorious', it agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. It can be substituted with the adjectives vincente or vittorioso.
learnerNotes: Remember that vincitore has both noun and adjective uses—as a noun it means 'winner', but as an adjective it means 'winning' or 'victorious' and must agree with the noun. The feminine forms vincitrice/vincitrici are essential to know, as Italian distinguishes gender consistently. Note the related term premiato/premiata which is sometimes used interchangeably when referring to award recipients.

exampleSentences.italian: Il vincitore del torneo ha donato tutto il premio in denaro a un'organizzazione di beneficenza.
exampleSentences.english: The winner of the tournament donated all the prize money to charity.

exampleSentences.english: the winning player

exampleSentences.italian: la squadra vincitrice
exampleSentences.english: the winning team

exampleSentences.italian: i cavalli vincitori
exampleSentences.english: the winning horses

exampleSentences.italian: le carte vincitrici
exampleSentences.english: the winning cards

grammarNotes: As an adjective, dolce is invariable for gender but changes form for plural (dolce → dolci). It agrees with the noun it modifies regardless of gender (un lampone dolce, una torta dolce). As a masculine noun, it means dessert or sweetness; when referring to sweetness/taste, it is preceded by the definite article il (il dolce).
learnerNotes: Remember that dolce is invariable for gender as an adjective—use the same form regardless of whether the noun is masculine or feminine, only the plural changes. The noun dolce (dessert) is very commonly used in everyday speech; many Italians prefer it to the English loanword 'dessert.' Watch for figurative uses: dolce extends beyond taste to describe pleasant sensations, mild conditions, and even gentle personality traits.

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi piace il caffè che fa Maurizio. È troppo dolce.
exampleSentences.english: I don't like the coffee Maurizio makes. It's too sweet.

grammarNotes: Saggezza is a feminine noun with plural form saggezze. It derives from the adjective saggio (wise) and traces back to Latin sapere (to know). The expression 'con saggezza' (with wisdom) is commonly paired with verbs like parlare, agire, gestire, and vivere.
learnerNotes: Saggezza is best learned as a set phrase: use 'con saggezza' with action verbs rather than standalone. Note that 'denti del giudizio' (literally 'judgement teeth') is the more common term for wisdom teeth in Italian medical language. Common synonyms like buonsenso (common sense), ragionevolezza (reasonableness), and giudizio (judgement) are useful to avoid repetition but carry slightly different nuances.

exampleSentences.italian: Il nuovo capo è molto giovane ma parla con saggezza.
exampleSentences.english: The new boss is very young but he speaks with wisdom.

exampleSentences.italian: La saggezza degli anziani
exampleSentences.english: The wisdom of the elderly

exampleSentences.italian: La saggezza dei proverbi

relatedExpressions.meaning: with wisdom (commonly used with parlare, agire, gestire, vivere)
very wise (declaring someone as possessing great wisdom)

grammarNotes: Camminare is a regular first-conjugation (-are) verb conjugated in the present tense as: io cammino, tu cammini, lui/lei cammina, noi camminiamo, voi camminate, loro camminano. In literary Italian, it can function as a transitive verb taking a direct object. It can also function as a masculine noun meaning 'walk' or 'gait'.
learnerNotes: Italians rarely use camminare alone when discussing 'going for a walk'—instead use fare una passeggiata (casual) or fare una camminata (strenuous). The imperative 'Cammina!' can mean 'Walk!' but preceded by 'ma' becomes an expression of disbelief ('Oh, come on!'). Note that camminare can also mean 'to work' (for mechanical objects) or 'to move forward' (for projects), acting as a synonym for funzionare or andare avanti.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piace camminare per le vie di Torino.
exampleSentences.english: I like walking the streets of Turin.

exampleSentences.italian: Roberta è una spia, te lo giuro! – Ma cammina, dai…
exampleSentences.english: Roberta is a spy, I'm telling you! – Oh, give me a break…

exampleSentences.italian: Il suo camminare avanti e indietro davanti alla casa ha insospettito i poliziotti.
exampleSentences.english: The fact that he was walking back and forth in front of the house made the policemen suspicious.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono mesi che il mio orologio da polso non cammina più. Ormai uso solo il telefono per leggere l'ora.
exampleSentences.english: It's been months since my wristwatch stopped working. These days I only use my cellphone to tell the time.

grammarNotes: Gettonato agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Masculine singular: gettonato; feminine singular: gettonata; masculine plural: gettonati; feminine plural: gettonate. It derives from the verb gettonare (to play on a jukebox), which comes from gettone (token/coin).
learnerNotes: Gettonato is historically tied to Italian pop music culture and jukeboxes, but today it's used colloquially for anything popular—people, places, songs, or ideas. Note that while derived from music terminology, it has broadened significantly in modern usage. This word exemplifies how Italian slang often retains etymological connections to outdated technology (gettoni/coin tokens) even as meanings evolve.

exampleSentences.italian: un cantante gettonato
exampleSentences.english: a popular singer

exampleSentences.italian: una canzone gettonata
exampleSentences.english: a popular song

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form pianoforti. The term is composed of piano (soft) and forte (loud), derived from the original Italian name gravicembalo col piano e forte given by Bartolomeo Cristofori in the early 1700s. In modern Italian, the short form 'piano' is more commonly used as a synonym for pianoforte.
learnerNotes: While pianoforte is the formal, original Italian term, the shortened form 'piano' is more commonly used in modern Italian speech and writing. The word literally means 'soft-loud' (piano + forte), reflecting the instrument's revolutionary ability to produce varying volumes. Note the related term fortepiano (loud-soft) refers specifically to historical pianos from the instrument's invention through the early 19th century.

exampleSentences.italian: Quando ero un ragazzino, suonavo molto bene il pianoforte.
exampleSentences.english: When I was a boy, I used to play the piano very well.

relatedExpressions.meaning: piano dating from early 1700s to early 19th century

grammarNotes: As an adjective, lunatico agrees with the noun it modifies: lunatico (masc. sing.), lunatica (fem. sing.), lunatici (masc. plur.), lunatiche (fem. plur.). When used as a noun, it refers to a moody person and retains the same gender/number agreement patterns.
learnerNotes: Note that lunatico shares etymology with English 'lunatic' but carries a milder meaning in Italian—it describes moodiness rather than insanity. When used as a noun (quel lunatico), it's often informal and can convey both affection and frustration. Remember to apply correct gender/number agreement when using it as an adjective with different nouns.

exampleSentences.italian: Mio fratello è lunatico.
exampleSentences.english: My brother is moody.

exampleSentences.italian: Vivere con lui non è facile.
exampleSentences.english: It's not easy living with him.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel lunatico di mio fratello mi ha fatto impazzire oggi!
exampleSentences.english: That moody brother of mine drove me crazy today!

englishTranslation: toasty / toasted sandwich / grilled cheese sandwich
grammarNotes: Toast is a masculine noun borrowed from English and is invariable in Italian, meaning it does not change in the plural form (il toast, i toast). It is pronounced with a long 'o' sound (/tōst/) rather than the English /toʊst/. In Italian, toast typically refers to a savoury toasted sandwich with fillings like cheese and ham, not a single slice of toasted bread.
learnerNotes: Be careful: in Italian, 'toast' almost always refers to a savoury toasted sandwich, not a single slice of toasted bread like in English. For a single slice, use 'una fetta di pane tostato' or 'pane abbrustolito' instead. The word was borrowed from English, which itself came from Old French, so pronunciation differs from English despite identical spelling.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho mangiato un toast al bar prima di tornare al lavoro.
exampleSentences.english: I ate a toasty at the café before heading back to work.

exampleSentences.italian: Vuoi una fetta di pane tostato? C'è ancora un po' di marmellata in frigo.
exampleSentences.english: Do you want a slice of toast? There is a bit of jam left in the fridge.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a slice of toasted bread (for single slices)
little crust; toasted bread slice from a baguette, ciabatta, or sourdough

englishTranslation: maybe / perhaps / it's possible / may / might
grammarNotes: Può darsi is composed of può (3rd person singular of potere, 'to be able') and darsi (reflexive form of dare, 'to give'). When used in statements, it must be followed by che + subjunctive verb (present, past, imperfect, past perfect, future, or conditional). When used as a response to a question or statement, it stands alone without che. The word anche can be inserted between può and darsi for emphasis.
learnerNotes: Può darsi is more sophisticated than forse or magari and is essential for sounding fluent. Always remember the subjunctive requirement when followed by che—this is a common learner mistake. The expression is very common as a standalone response, so practice using it this way to build naturalism.

exampleSentences.italian: Può darsi che Anna sia in ritardo.
exampleSentences.english: Maybe / Perhaps / It's possible Anna is late.

exampleSentences.italian: Forse Anna è in ritardo.
exampleSentences.english: Anna may / might be late.

exampleSentences.italian: Magari Anna è in ritardo.
exampleSentences.english: Anna may / might be late.

exampleSentences.italian: Verranno alla festa domani? – Può darsi.
exampleSentences.english: Are they coming to the party tomorrow? – Perhaps.

exampleSentences.italian: Forse non verranno alla festa. – Può darsi.
exampleSentences.english: Maybe they won't come to the party. – It's possible.

exampleSentences.italian: Può anche darsi che tutto si risolverà per il meglio.
exampleSentences.english: It is quite possible / It may well be that everything will turn out for the best.

exampleSentences.italian: Potrebbe essere che Anna sia in ritardo.
exampleSentences.english: It could be that Anna is late.

exampleSentences.italian: Potrebbe essere che Federico non abbia tempo.
exampleSentences.english: It is possible that Federico won't have time.

relatedExpressions.meaning: it could be / it is possible (also requires che + subjunctive)
it may well be / it is quite possible (emphatic version)

grammarNotes: As an adjective, pignolo agrees with the noun it modifies: pignolo (masc. sing.), pignola (fem. sing.), pignoli (masc. plur.), pignole (fem. plur.). It can also function as a noun meaning 'fussy person' or 'nitpicker,' maintaining the same gender/number agreement patterns.
learnerNotes: Pignolo is commonly used in the expression 'fare il pignolo' to describe someone being overly fussy or pedantic in the moment. The word's etymology from 'pigna' (pine cone) is interesting but not essential for usage. Note that pignolo can be used as both an adjective and a noun—context determines the function, but the meaning remains consistent.

exampleSentences.italian: Fossi in te accorcerei il video ancora di qualche secondo.
exampleSentences.english: If I were you I would shorten the video by a few extra seconds.

exampleSentences.italian: Dai, non fare il pignolo adesso!
exampleSentences.english: Come on, don't be fussy now!

exampleSentences.italian: Va bene così com'è!
exampleSentences.english: It's fine as it is!

relatedExpressions.expression: fare il pignolo / fare la pignola

to search for a hair in an egg (to split hairs)

grammarNotes: Musica is a feminine noun (la musica). The plural form is musiche. It derives from Greek mousikē (tekhnē). The word is used both literally for composed/performed sounds and figuratively for any pleasing or unpleasing sound.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'suonare' (to play an instrument) is the correct verb for playing music, not 'giocare'. While musica can refer to literal music, it also extends figuratively to any pleasing sound (la musica delle onde = the music of the waves) or even unpleasant sounds in colloquial speech. The diminutive musichetta refers to light or trivial music, particularly the annoying hold music you hear on the phone.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piace ascoltare la musica mentre faccio le pulizie di casa.
exampleSentences.english: I like listening to music while cleaning the house.

exampleSentences.italian: Stasera c'è musica in piazza. Vuoi uscire con noi?
exampleSentences.english: Tonight there is a concert in the square. Do you want to go out with us?

exampleSentences.italian: La musica dei cani continuò fino alle tre di notte.
exampleSentences.english: The sound of the barking dogs continued until 3 a.m.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural spazzolini. Literally means 'little brush' (diminutive of spazza). The feminine form spazzolina exists but refers only to generic small brushes, never toothbrushes. Full form spazzolino da denti is commonly used, though context often allows the shortened form.
learnerNotes: In everyday Italian, people usually say just spazzolino without da denti when the context is clear—avoid adding unnecessary words. Remember that the feminine spazzolina never means toothbrush; it only refers to a small brush, so gender matters here. This word is a good example of Italian diminutives (suffixes like -ino/-ina) that create smaller or affectionate versions of nouns.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho bisogno di comprare un nuovo spazzolino da denti.
exampleSentences.english: I need to buy a new toothbrush.

englishTranslation: out of phase / out of sorts / disoriented / bewildered
grammarNotes: Sfasato is a masculine singular adjective derived from the verb sfasare (to dephase). It agrees with the noun it modifies: sfasata (feminine singular), sfasati (masculine plural), and sfasate (feminine plural). The word has both technical usage in electrical/mechanical contexts and figurative usage to describe a person's mental state.
learnerNotes: Sfasato primarily describes a person who is confused or fatigued, making it useful for everyday conversation despite its technical origins. Be careful not to confuse it with stonato (out of tune/out of sorts), though they can be synonymous in some contexts. The word is especially common when discussing jet lag, fatigue after travel, or general disorientation.

exampleSentences.italian: Il bambino era totalmente sfasato nonostante avesse fatto una lunga nanna.
exampleSentences.english: The baby was completely out of sorts even though he'd had a long nap.

exampleSentences.italian: Abbiamo appena finito il trasloco, finalmente! Che sudata! Mi sento un po' sfasato adesso.
exampleSentences.english: We just finished the move, finally! What an effort! I feel a bit disoriented now.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be out of sorts / disoriented
out of sync with time zones

grammarNotes: Torta is a feminine noun with regular plural torte. It is a generic term for round baked sweets made from flour, sugar, butter, and eggs. The word can denote either sweet cakes or savoury pies depending on context. Diminutive forms tortina and tortino exist with more specific meanings.
learnerNotes: Torta is commonly used for both sweet cakes and savoury pies—context determines the meaning. When referring to savoury versions, look for the qualifier 'salata'. The figurative uses (pie chart, spoils/loot, slapstick gag) are important for advanced comprehension but less critical for A2-B1 learners; focus first on food applications and the idiomatic 'ciliegina sulla torta'.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho mangiato tre fette di torta e adesso ho mal di pancia.
exampleSentences.english: I ate three slices of cake and now I have a stomach ache.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho preparato tre torte salate per la festa di domani: una con le zucchine, una con patate e salsiccia, e una con formaggio e pancetta.
exampleSentences.english: I've made three savoury pies for tomorrow's party: one with zucchini, one with potatoes and sausages, and one with cheese and bacon.

exampleSentences.italian: Mia mamma ha preparato un tortino di carciofi davvero squisito.
exampleSentences.english: My mum made a delicious artichoke pie.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho avuto una giornata terribile. La ciliegina sulla torta è stato tornare a casa e scoprire di aver perso le chiavi.
exampleSentences.english: I had a terrible day. The cherry on top was that I came home and discovered I'd lost the keys.

to divide the cake (share illicit earnings)
cherry on the cake / icing on the cake (detail that completes something positive)

grammarNotes: As an adjective, balordo agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: balordo (m. sing.), balorda (f. sing.), balordi (m. pl.), balorde (f. pl.). It can also function as a noun meaning 'fool' or 'idiot'. The word is rarely found in textbooks but is common in casual native speaker conversation.
learnerNotes: Balordo is a colloquial adjective rarely taught in formal textbooks but frequently used in native conversation—useful for B1+ learners aiming for authentic speech. It can describe people, actions, ideas, weather, or deals, and occasionally functions as a noun meaning 'fool' or 'idiot'. Note that in slang, it can also refer to a thug or delinquent, so context matters for register appropriateness.

exampleSentences.english: a harebrained idea

exampleSentences.italian: Non c'è niente di peggio che fare discorsi balordi con persone balorde.
exampleSentences.english: There is nothing worse than talking about silly things with foolish people.

exampleSentences.italian: sentirsi balordo
