grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural form giovinezze. Derives from the adjective giovane (young). Does not refer to a young person (un giovane), but rather the state or period of being young. Can be used figuratively to describe youthful character or qualities, and metaphorically for things in early stages of development.
learnerNotes: Giovinezza specifically refers to the period or state of being young, NOT a young person—use un giovane or giovani for people. The common synonym gioventù can refer both to the period of youth and to young people collectively (always with definite article: la gioventù). Note that Juventus, the famous soccer club, derives its name from Latin iuventus meaning gioventù.

exampleSentences.italian: La giovinezza è fugace!
exampleSentences.english: Youth is fleeting!

exampleSentences.italian: nella mia giovinezza
exampleSentences.english: in my youth

exampleSentences.italian: durante la mia giovinezza
exampleSentences.english: in my youth

exampleSentences.italian: negli anni della mia giovinezza

exampleSentences.italian: per tutta la mia giovinezza
exampleSentences.english: throughout my youth

exampleSentences.italian: In gioventù non avevamo i cellulari.
exampleSentences.english: In our youth we didn't have cellphones.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a humorous expression for the renewal of youthful enthusiasm and energy in an older person

grammarNotes: Despite ending in '-a', pianeta is masculine (un pianeta, i pianeti), likely due to its archaic form pianeto. The feminine form pianeta exists but has different meanings: chasuble (vestment) or horoscope card. Regular plural formation: pianeta → pianeti.
learnerNotes: Remember that pianeta is masculine (un pianeta, not una), which defies the typical '-a' ending rule—this is a crucial exception to memorize. When discussing planets by name, use proper nouns: Mercurio, Venere, Terra, Marte, Giove, Saturno, Urano, Nettuno. In modern Italian, pianeta is used metaphorically like 'mondo' to describe entire domains (pianeta calcio = soccer world), which is more common in journalistic contexts than everyday speech.

exampleSentences.italian: un piccolo pianeta
exampleSentences.english: a small planet

exampleSentences.italian: dei piccoli pianeti
exampleSentences.english: small planets

exampleSentences.italian: il pianeta rotondo
exampleSentences.english: the round planet

exampleSentences.italian: i pianeti rotondi
exampleSentences.english: the round planets

exampleSentences.italian: La Terra è il terzo pianeta più vicino al sole.
exampleSentences.english: Earth is the third closest planet to the sun.

exampleSentences.italian: Il rover Perseverance è atterrato su Marte il 18 Febbraio 2021.
exampleSentences.english: The rover Perseverance landed on Mars on February 18th 2021.

exampleSentences.italian: Caspita, questa squadra è di un altro pianeta! Sarà un'impresa sconfiggerla.
exampleSentences.english: Wow, this team is out of this world. It's going to be a challenge to beat them.

relatedExpressions.meaning: rocky planets closest to the sun
planets with orbits external to Earth's (Mars to Neptune)
Mercury and Venus, with orbits internal to Earth's
to be from another planet / to be out of this world (exceptional quality)

grammarNotes: Perfino is composed of the prefix per- and the preposition fino (up to/as far as). It is used to emphasize something surprising or extreme. The alternative form persino is completely interchangeable with perfino and equally common.
learnerNotes: Perfino and persino are completely interchangeable—use whichever feels more natural. When choosing between perfino, addirittura, and anche, remember that addirittura has a stronger emphasis while anche is milder. Perfino works well in both emphatic statements and comparative constructions to highlight something surprising or extreme.

exampleSentences.italian: Mio figlio ha vissuto ovunque. Ha perfino trascorso un anno in Antartide!
exampleSentences.english: My son has lived all over the place. He even spent a year in the Antarctic!

exampleSentences.italian: Non lo credevo possibile, ma c'è gente che di calcio ne sa perfino meno di me!
exampleSentences.english: I didn't think it was possible, but there are people who know even less about soccer than me!

exampleSentences.italian: Mio figlio ha vissuto ovunque. Ha addirittura trascorso un anno in Antartide.
exampleSentences.english: My son has lived all over the place. He even spent a year in the Antarctic.

exampleSentences.italian: Mio figlio ha vissuto ovunque. Ha anche trascorso un anno in Antartide.
exampleSentences.english: My son has lived all over the place. He also spent a year in the Antarctic.

exampleSentences.italian: Non lo credevo possibile ma c'è gente che di calcio ne sa addirittura meno di me!
exampleSentences.english: I didn't think it was possible but there are people who know even less about soccer than me!

exampleSentences.italian: Non lo credevo possibile ma c'è gente che di calcio ne sa anche meno di me!
exampleSentences.english: I didn't think it was possible but there are people who know even less about soccer than me!

exampleSentences.italian: Mi viene la pelle d'oca perfino a pensarci.
exampleSentences.english: I get goosebumps just thinking about it.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi viene la pelle d'oca anche solo a pensarci.
exampleSentences.english: I get goosebumps even just thinking about it.

relatedExpressions.meaning: even (alternative form of perfino, completely interchangeable)

grammarNotes: Pesce d'aprile is a compound noun phrase where 'pesce' (fish, masculine) is modified by the prepositional phrase 'd'aprile' (of April). The literal meaning is 'April's fish,' though it functions as a fixed expression for the holiday. No gender agreement needed as it functions as a proper noun for the celebration.
learnerNotes: Pesce d'aprile is primarily used as a proper noun to refer to the April Fools' celebration itself, not as a countable noun. The tradition of attaching a paper fish (pesciolino di carta) to someone's back is the characteristic Italian version of April Fools' pranks. Be aware that this holiday is celebrated differently across Italian-speaking regions, though the core tradition remains consistent.

exampleSentences.italian: Buon pesce d'aprile!
exampleSentences.english: Happy April Fools' Day!

exampleSentences.italian: Ma cos'è, uno scherzo!? Ah già, oggi è il primo aprile!
exampleSentences.english: What's this, a joke? Oh right, today is April 1st!

exampleSentences.italian: Ci sei cascato / cascata!
exampleSentences.english: You fell for it!

relatedExpressions.meaning: a paper fish (the traditional prank object)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun derived from Latin 'terrae motus' (movement of the earth). Takes regular masculine articles: il terremoto (singular), i terremoti (plural); un terremoto (indefinite singular), dei terremoti (indefinite plural). The related verb terremotare (to destroy like an earthquake) produces the past participle terremotato/a.
learnerNotes: Terremoto has a figurative meaning beyond the geological sense: it can describe a very lively, disruptive person (especially children) or a sudden, disruptive change in business/politics. Note that vibrare (to vibrate) and words like magnitudo and scala Richter are technical terms you may encounter in news contexts. The verb terremotare and adjective terremotato/a are less common but useful for advanced discussions of disaster impact.

exampleSentences.italian: Il terremoto ha causato uno tsunami con onde alte sei metri.
exampleSentences.english: The earthquake caused a tsunami with waves that were six meters high.

exampleSentences.italian: La nipote di Giada è un vero terremoto. È impossibile tenerla sotto controllo!
exampleSentences.english: Giada's granddaughter is a real terror. It's impossible to keep her under control!

exampleSentences.italian: Le sue dimissioni inaspettate hanno causato un terremoto all'interno del partito.
exampleSentences.english: His unexpected resignation was like a shock inside the party.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to destroy or devastate like an earthquake
hit by an earthquake (place) or earthquake victim (person)

grammarNotes: Verità is a feminine noun ending in an accented à, which means its plural form remains identical (una verità / due verità). It derives from Latin veritas and is related to English words like verity and verify. The word commonly pairs with specific verbs such as dire, sapere, scoprire, and nascondere.
learnerNotes: Remember that verità is always feminine (la verità), even though it ends in -à. The plural remains the same as the singular, which is common for Italian nouns ending in accented vowels. Pay attention to verb collocations: Italians typically use dire, sapere, scoprire, and nascondere with verità rather than other verbs.

exampleSentences.italian: I ragazzini non dicono sempre la verità ai genitori.
exampleSentences.english: Kids don't always tell their parents the truth.

exampleSentences.italian: Pensavo fosse un film ma in verità si tratta di una serie televisiva composta da dieci episodi.
exampleSentences.english: I thought it was a film but in truth it is a series divided into ten episodes.

relatedExpressions.expression: essere la voce / la bocca della verità
La verità viene sempre a galla

englishTranslation: smash / crash / uproar / racket / loud noise
grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural fracassi. Derived from the verb fracassare (to smash). When used figuratively to mean 'uproar' or 'protest,' it frequently appears in the expressions fare fracasso or fare gran/molto fracasso. In informal speech, fracasso (di) functions as a colloquial synonym for molto (a lot/many).
learnerNotes: Fracasso has multiple meanings depending on context: literally it describes a loud crash or smash, but figuratively it means 'uproar' or 'public scandal.' The informal use as a synonym for molto (fracasso di gente = lots of people) is colloquial and best learned through exposure to native speech. Remember that fare fracasso is a common idiom meaning 'to cause a stir' or 'to create an uproar.'

exampleSentences.italian: Il vaso si è rotto con gran fracasso.
exampleSentences.english: The vase broke with a loud smash.

exampleSentences.italian: I bambini stanno facendo troppo fracasso nel cortile.
exampleSentences.english: The children are making too much of a racket in the courtyard.

exampleSentences.italian: La notizia del suo arresto ha fatto molto fracasso.
exampleSentences.english: The news of his arrest caused a great uproar.

exampleSentences.italian: C'era un fracasso di gente alla festa di Beatrice.
exampleSentences.english: There were lots of people at Beatrice's party.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to cause an uproar / to make a scene
to cause much of an uproar
a lot of / many (informal synonym for molto)

grammarNotes: Mandorla is feminine (la mandorla) with plural mandorle. Do not confuse with the masculine mandorlo (almond tree). When describing items made with almonds, use either 'di mandorle' or 'alla mandorla'; for almond flavor, use 'al sapore di mandorle'.
learnerNotes: Remember that mandorla can mean almond-shaped when used as an adjective (e.g., occhi a mandorla). The word has religious/artistic significance as it also refers to the almond-shaped aureola in Christian iconography. Be careful not to confuse mandorla (the fruit/flavor) with mandorlo (the tree itself).

exampleSentences.italian: Ho preparato dei biscotti alle mandorle e una torta soffice con ciliegie, al sapore di mandorle.
exampleSentences.english: I've made almond cookies and a soft almond-flavoured cake with cherries.

exampleSentences.italian: La modella ha gli occhi a mandorla più belli che io abbia mai visto.
exampleSentences.english: The model has the most beautiful almond eyes I've ever seen.

relatedExpressions.meaning: almond-flavored liqueur or almond biscuit; diminutive of amaro (bitter)

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural form passeggiate. Derives from the verb passeggiare (to walk, stroll, amble). When referring to taking someone on a walk, use the construction portare (qualcuno/il cane) a fare una passeggiata. The word can function both as a concrete noun (a physical walk/path) and metaphorically (something easy to accomplish).
learnerNotes: Passeggiata is a feminine noun; always use la passeggiata in singular and le passeggiate in plural. The phrase fare una passeggiata is idiomatic—use this rather than literal translations. Note that passeggiata can mean 'something easy to accomplish' metaphorically, similar to English 'a walk in the park'—this is a useful cultural parallel for remembering the expression.

exampleSentences.italian: Perché non andiamo a fare una passeggiata nel parco?
exampleSentences.english: Why don't we go on a walk in the park?

exampleSentences.italian: La passeggiata a mare si estende per circa due chilometri.
exampleSentences.english: The seaside promenade is about two kilometres long.

exampleSentences.italian: Superare quell'esame è stato davvero una passeggiata.
exampleSentences.english: Passing that exam was a real cakewalk.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to go for / to take a walk
to go for / to take a walk

relatedExpressions.expression: portare (qualcuno / il cane) a fare una passeggiata
relatedExpressions.meaning: to take someone / a dog on a walk

relatedExpressions.expression: andare a fare due / quattro passi

to go on a walk (for fun or without any real aim)
to go on a (strenuous) walk (to get in shape)
to go for a walk / stroll

relatedExpressions.meaning: to go for a walk (quick and fun with stops along the way, often in the city)

grammarNotes: Uffa is an onomatopoeic interjection used to express frustration, annoyance, or exasperation. It mimics the sound of sighing or huffing. It can be abbreviated to uff or the less common form uffi. As an interjection, it is invariable and does not conjugate or decline.
learnerNotes: Uffa is very informal but not vulgar, making it appropriate for children and casual conversation. It's a mild expression of frustration compared to stronger idioms like Che palle! or Che pizza!. Use it when you want to convey irritation or exasperation in an authentic, natural way without being offensive.

exampleSentences.italian: Uffa, papà! Mario non mi fa giocare con la palla!
exampleSentences.english: Ugh, dad! Mario isn't letting me play with the ball!

exampleSentences.italian: Uffa, ma che caldo! Non ce la faccio più!
exampleSentences.english: Geez, it's so hot! I can't take it anymore!

relatedExpressions.meaning: What balls! (idiom meaning: What a pain!)
What a pizza! (idiom meaning: What a pain!)
Less common variant form of uffa

englishTranslation: out of tune / tone-deaf / clashing / mismatched / out of sorts
grammarNotes: Stonato is an adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: stonato (m.s.), stonata (f.s.), stonati (m.p.), stonate (f.p.). It derives from the verb stonare (to sing/play out of tune). The adjective can be used both literally (music-related) and figuratively (visual harmony, mental state).
learnerNotes: Remember that stonato has multiple meanings depending on context: it refers to musical intonation literally, but figuratively describes anything that clashes visually or mentally (e.g., mismatched clothing, feeling confused). Don't confuse standard Italian stonato with the Italian-American dialect word 'stunad,' which can also mean 'stupid' or 'crazy'—the standard term never carries this connotation. Pay attention to gender/number agreement when using this adjective.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel cantante è stonato come una campana. Come ha fatto ad avere così tanto successo?
exampleSentences.english: That singer is completely tone-deaf. How did he get to be so successful?

exampleSentences.italian: La mia chitarra è un po' stonata. Me la puoi accordare per favore?
exampleSentences.english: My guitar is a little bit out of tune. Can you tune it for me please?

exampleSentences.italian: Quel cappello rosso stona proprio con il tuo vestito.
exampleSentences.english: That red hat really clashes with your outfit.

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi mi sento proprio stonato! Ricordami di non viaggiare mai più in aereo per venti ore di fila…
exampleSentences.english: I feel so out of it today! Remind me to never travel twenty hours by plane ever again…

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be completely tone-deaf (literally: to be out of tune like a bell)
to hit a wrong note / to make a mistake

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form sottobicchieri. Composed of sotto (under/underneath) + bicchiere (drinking glass). Like most Italian nouns ending in -e, it follows regular masculine plural patterns (-e to -i).
learnerNotes: Sottobicchiere is a compound word that follows a logical formation pattern (sotto + bicchiere), making it easier to remember. Note the distinction between sottobicchieri (coasters for drinks), tappetino da tavola (placemats under plates), and tappetino da banco (bar runners)—each serves a specific purpose in Italian homes and establishments. The material vocabulary provided is useful for describing the composition of coasters.

exampleSentences.italian: Usate i sottobicchieri per favore.
exampleSentences.english: Use the coasters please.

exampleSentences.italian: Non voglio vedere macchie sul tavolo!
exampleSentences.english: I don't want to see stains on the table!

relatedExpressions.meaning: bar runner / spill mat (found on bar or pub counters)
table mat / placemat (mat placed under a plate)

grammarNotes: As an adjective, furbo agrees with the noun it modifies: furbo (masc. sing.), furba (fem. sing.), furbi (masc. plur.), furbe (fem. plur.). When used as a noun, it means 'a cunning person' and retains the same four forms. Augmentative forms furbone and furbacchione add a humorous tone.
learnerNotes: Furbo is primarily positive when describing intelligence and quick-wittedness, but becomes negative when implying deception or manipulative behavior—context matters. The phrase 'fare il furbo' often carries a warning or reproach. Note that farsi furbo is reflexive and appears in the command form fatti furbo; this is a common way to urge someone to be smarter or more careful.

exampleSentences.italian: Stasera vado in discoteca… – Ma fatti furbo! Domani hai l'esame!
exampleSentences.english: I'm going to the disco tonight… – Oh come on, smarten up! You have your exam tomorrow!

exampleSentences.italian: Un piano furbo
exampleSentences.english: A cunning plan

exampleSentences.italian: Non fare il furbo con l'insegnante, hai capito?
exampleSentences.english: Don't get clever with the teacher, understand?

relatedExpressions.meaning: to smarten up / wise up; to make oneself clever
to be tricky / get clever (with someone)
a person of extremely subtle cunning (lit: a cunning person cooked thrice)
an out-and-out cunning person; someone very skilled/experienced at something detrimental

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural form guarigioni. When expressing recovery from a specific illness, use the preposition 'da' (guarigione da + noun). Related to the verb guarire (to recover/heal). Can be modified with adjectives like perfetta, completa, lenta, miracolosa to express different types of recovery.
learnerNotes: Guarigione is commonly used in health contexts and 'get well soon' messages. Remember to use 'da' when specifying what someone is recovering from (guarigione dal cancro). Don't confuse guarigione (the noun, recovery) with guarire (the verb, to recover)—both are frequently used in medical conversations.

exampleSentences.italian: una perfetta guarigione
exampleSentences.english: a perfect recovery

exampleSentences.italian: una completa guarigione
exampleSentences.english: a complete recovery

exampleSentences.italian: una guarigione facile / difficile
exampleSentences.english: an easy / difficult recovery

exampleSentences.italian: una pronta guarigione
exampleSentences.english: a speedy recovery
