exampleSentences.english: a slow recovery

exampleSentences.italian: una guarigione miracolosa
exampleSentences.english: a miraculous recovery

exampleSentences.italian: una completa guarigione dal cancro
exampleSentences.english: a full recovery from cancer

exampleSentences.italian: Buona guarigione!
exampleSentences.english: Get well soon!

exampleSentences.italian: Guarisci presto!
exampleSentences.english: Get well soon!

exampleSentences.italian: Ti auguro una pronta guarigione!
exampleSentences.english: I wish you a speedy recovery! (informal)

exampleSentences.italian: Le auguro una pronta guarigione!
exampleSentences.english: I wish you a speedy recovery! (formal)

exampleSentences.italian: Tanti anni fa, quel medico fece molte guarigioni miracolose.
exampleSentences.english: Years ago, that doctor performed many miraculous cures.

relatedExpressions.meaning: I wish you a speedy recovery!

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural alberi. Gender agreement required with articles and adjectives (il/un albero, gli/degli alberi). Augmentative form alberone (big tree), diminutive forms alberello (sapling) and alberetto (small tree) follow standard Italian diminutive/augmentative patterns.
learnerNotes: Albero has multiple meanings depending on context: the primary sense is 'tree' (botanical), but it also means 'mast' (nautical) or 'shaft' (mechanical). The diminutive/augmentative forms (alberetto, alberello, alberone) follow standard patterns but are not equally common in speech. Note the idiomatic use in 'albero genealogico' where the tree metaphor is naturally extended to family structure.

exampleSentences.italian: L'Etiopia ha annunciato di aver piantato più di 350 milioni di alberi in meno di un giorno.
exampleSentences.english: Ethiopia announced it has planted more than 350 million trees in less than a day.

exampleSentences.italian: Clara sta facendo un albero genealogico per scoprire le sue radici.
exampleSentences.english: Clara is preparing a family tree to discover her roots.

relatedExpressions.expression: Guardare l'albero e perdere di vista la foresta
relatedExpressions.meaning: to be unable to see the woods/forest for the trees; to be too involved in a situation to understand it clearly
to be fooled or the victim of a scam, often due to one's own naivety

englishTranslation: pain in the neck / nuisance / pest
grammarNotes: This noun is invariable—it does not change form in the feminine or plural. Gender and number are indicated by the preceding article (un/una for singular, dei/delle for plural). The word is composed of the verb rompere (to break) + the plural noun scatole (boxes), literally 'box-breaker.'
learnerNotes: Rompiscatole is a polite, family-safe way to describe an annoying person. Be aware that numerous vulgar variants exist (rompipalle, rompicoglioni, etc.) that are common in informal Italian but should be avoided in formal settings or around elders. Use the article preceding the noun to determine whether you're referring to a man (un), woman (una), or group (dei/delle), as the noun itself never changes form.

exampleSentences.italian: È un rompiscatole.
exampleSentences.english: He is a pain in the neck.

exampleSentences.italian: È una rompiscatole.
exampleSentences.english: She is a pain in the neck.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono dei rompiscatole.
exampleSentences.english: They are a pain in the neck. (group of men or mixed group)

exampleSentences.italian: Sono delle rompiscatole.
exampleSentences.english: They are a pain in the neck. (group of women)

exampleSentences.italian: Il mio collega è un gran rompiscatole. Non lo sopporto più!
exampleSentences.english: My colleague is a big pain in the neck. I can't stand him anymore.

exampleSentences.italian: Che rompipalle che è il nonno! Oh, scusa nonna, non ti ho sentita entrare. Volevo dire: che gentile che è il nonno!
exampleSentences.english: What a pain in the butt Grandpa is! Oops, sorry Grandma, I didn't hear you come in. I wanted to say: how nice Grandpa is!

relatedExpressions.meaning: vulgar alternative; scassare (to smash) + maroni (euphemism for testicles)

englishTranslation: in fact / as a matter of fact / indeed
grammarNotes: Infatti is an invariable adverb and conjunction used to confirm, prove, or justify a previous statement. It can function as a standalone response to express agreement, or be used ironically to suggest the opposite of what was promised. When used alone, the rest of the sentence is often implied.
learnerNotes: Infatti is extremely useful for connecting ideas logically and for responding naturally in conversation. Pay attention to context: it can be sincere (confirming a statement) or ironic (contradicting what was expected). When used alone as a response, it replaces longer agreement phrases and is very common in spoken Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi piace il caffè: infatti non lo bevo mai.
exampleSentences.english: I don't like coffee: in fact I never drink it.

exampleSentences.italian: Ha promesso di aiutarmi a traslocare, e infatti non si è fatto vivo!
exampleSentences.english: He promised to help me move but of course he didn't show up!

exampleSentences.italian: Ha promesso di aiutarmi a traslocare, e infatti…!
exampleSentences.english: He promised to help me move but…!

exampleSentences.italian: Dovevano passare a prenderci alle sette… – Infatti! Ma dove cavolo sono?
exampleSentences.english: They were supposed to pick us up at seven… – Exactly! Where on earth are they?

exampleSentences.italian: Mi sono veramente divertito l'altra sera! – Infatti! Dobbiamo uscire più sovente!
exampleSentences.english: I had so much fun the other night! – Yeah, I know! We have to go out more often!

grammarNotes: Olio is a masculine noun (il olio); plural is oli. The preposition di becomes d' before vowels, so olio d'oliva is also correct. In Italy, olio alone typically refers to olio di oliva by default. The phrase consists of three words but functions as a single lexical unit in everyday speech.
learnerNotes: Remember that in Italian, olio alone typically means olive oil unless otherwise specified—Italian speakers assume the context. The phrase illustrates the useful preposition di (of), which is essential for forming possessive and descriptive phrases. Be aware that olio can also refer to other oils generically, but olio di oliva is by far the most common in Italian cuisine and conversation.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piace aggiungere un po' di olio piccante sulla pizza!
exampleSentences.english: I like adding a bit of spicy olive oil to my pizza!

exampleSentences.italian: Olio di oliva è usato per condire piatti e antipasti.
exampleSentences.english: Olive oil is used to season dishes and appetisers.

exampleSentences.italian: L'olio d'oliva viene usato come condimento per l'insalata.
exampleSentences.english: Olive oil is used as a dressing for salads.

exampleSentences.italian: Pane e olio è una specialità italiana.
exampleSentences.english: Bread and olive oil is an Italian specialty.

exampleSentences.italian: L'olio extra vergine di oliva è il grado più alto.
exampleSentences.english: Extra virgin olive oil is the highest grade.

relatedExpressions.meaning: olive oil (with apostrophe contraction before vowel)

englishTranslation: maybe / perhaps / if only / even if
grammarNotes: Magari is a versatile adverb with multiple uses. When expressing desire or hypothesis, it typically introduces clauses with the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., 'magari potessimo'). It can function as a standalone one-word response, with meaning determined by intonation and context. As a substitute for 'anche se', it requires the imperfect subjunctive form.
learnerNotes: Magari is a high-frequency word with multiple distinct uses; context and intonation are crucial to understanding meaning. Be cautious with the sarcastic one-word response usage—the same word can mean 'of course!' or 'you think?' depending on tone. When expressing wishes or hypotheticals, always pair magari with the imperfect subjunctive rather than the conditional or indicative moods.

exampleSentences.italian: Magari possiamo incontrarci per un caffè domani.
exampleSentences.english: Perhaps we can meet up for a coffee tomorrow.

exampleSentences.italian: Magari Maria non sa nemmeno che cosa sia Facebook!
exampleSentences.english: Maybe Maria doesn't even know what Facebook is!

exampleSentences.italian: Magari potessimo andare all'estero quest'anno… È tutta colpa di quel maledetto virus!
exampleSentences.english: If only we could go abroad this year… It's all the fault of that damned virus!

exampleSentences.italian: Quanto sarebbe bello poter andare all'estero quest'anno… – Eh, magari!
exampleSentences.english: Wouldn't it be nice if we could go abroad this year… – Yeah, if only!

exampleSentences.italian: Vuoi venire con noi al cinema? – Magari!
exampleSentences.english: Do you want to come to the cinema with us? – Of course!

exampleSentences.italian: Vuoi venire al cinema con noi? – Magari.
exampleSentences.english: Do you want to come to the cinema with us? – Yeah, maybe.

exampleSentences.italian: Forse dovrei chiamare mia mamma per dirle che non vengo a casa stasera. – Eh, magari!
exampleSentences.english: Perhaps I should call my mom to tell her I won't be home tonight. – You think?

exampleSentences.italian: Imparerò l'italiano, magari ci mettessi vent'anni!
exampleSentences.english: I will learn Italian, even if it takes me twenty years!

exampleSentences.italian: Grazia, magari, potrebbe decidere di licenziarsi e mettersi in proprio.
exampleSentences.english: Grazia might even decide to resign and branch out on her own.

relatedExpressions.meaning: Yeah, if only! / You think? (sarcastic response)
expressing strong desire for something unattainable

englishTranslation: to depopulate / to be a success / to be a hit / to draw the crowds
grammarNotes: Spopolare is a regular -are verb formed with the prefix s- (denoting removal or reversal) + popolare. It conjugates as a standard first-conjugation verb. The figurative meaning (to be a hit/success) is often used in the third-person singular or plural to describe trends, people, or media that attract attention.
learnerNotes: The figurative sense (success/popularity) is much more common in modern Italian than the literal depopulation meaning. Pay attention to context: when used with people or trends as the subject, it means 'to be hugely popular'; when used with an action or force, it means 'to empty/depopulate.' This word is best learned through its colloquial usage describing viral trends and popular figures.

exampleSentences.italian: L'epidemia ha spopolato il paese.
exampleSentences.english: The epidemic depopulated the country.

exampleSentences.italian: Ogni estate il caldo torrido spopola la città.
exampleSentences.english: Every summer the scorching heat empties the city.

exampleSentences.italian: Negli ultimi anni è tornata a spopolare tra i giovani un'antica moda: la barba!
exampleSentences.english: In recent years an ancient trend is once again all the rage among young people: the beard!

exampleSentences.italian: Quella ragazza spopola su Instagram: ha già più di centomila follower!
exampleSentences.english: That girl is a huge hit on Instagram: she already has more than 100,000 followers!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be all the rage among young people
to be a huge hit on social media

grammarNotes: Accidenti is the plural form of accidente (mishap/sudden illness) used as an interjection. It expresses multiple emotions including wonder, anger, and annoyance. When followed by the preposition 'a', it is used to curse people or situations mildly. The singular form accidente can also function as a noun meaning 'nothing/anything' in negative contexts or describe an annoying/lively person.
learnerNotes: Accidenti is one of the mildest Italian interjections and is not considered vulgar, making it safe for most contexts. It can express both positive emotions (Wow!) and negative ones (Darn!) depending on context—pay attention to tone. The euphemistic variants (Accipicchia, Accidempoli, Acciderba) tone it down even further and are useful if you want to sound particularly polite or humorous.

exampleSentences.italian: Accidenti, che bella canzone!
exampleSentences.english: Wow, what a beautiful song!

exampleSentences.italian: Accidenti, mi sono scordato di avere un appuntamento oggi! Chissà se riesco ancora ad arrivare in tempo?!
exampleSentences.english: Darn, I forgot I have a meeting today! I wonder if I can still get there in time?!

exampleSentences.italian: Accidenti a lui e alla sua testardaggine!
exampleSentences.english: Darn him and his stubbornness!

exampleSentences.italian: Con tutta questa nebbia, non vedo un accidente!
exampleSentences.english: With all this fog, I can't see a darn thing!

exampleSentences.italian: Copriti bene quando esci, altrimenti ti prenderai un accidente!
exampleSentences.english: Cover yourself well when you get out, otherwise you'll catch your death of cold!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to curse somebody / to send an illness to someone
to catch a sickness / to get sick / to catch one's death

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural bicchieri. Can denote both the container and its contents. When followed by 'di' + drink, it means 'a glass of [drink]'; when followed by 'da' + drink, it describes the glass type (e.g., wine glass). The apocopic form bicchier is commonly used before 'di'. Related forms: bicchierino (small glass), bicchierata (drinking party/glassful/blow with a glass).
learnerNotes: Remember the crucial distinction: 'bicchiere di vino' = a glass of wine (describing contents), while 'bicchiere da vino' = a wine glass (describing purpose). When bicchiere stands alone in contexts like 'andiamo a bere un bicchiere', it typically implies an alcoholic drink, especially wine. The apocopic form 'bicchier' is very common in spoken Italian and before 'di', so familiarize yourself with both forms.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho fatto cadere il bicchiere e si è frantumato in mille pezzi.
exampleSentences.english: I dropped the glass and it shattered into 1000 pieces.

exampleSentences.italian: un bicchiere d'acqua
exampleSentences.english: a glass of water

exampleSentences.italian: un bicchiere di succo
exampleSentences.english: a glass of juice

exampleSentences.italian: un bicchiere di vino
exampleSentences.english: a glass of wine

exampleSentences.italian: un bicchiere di birra
exampleSentences.english: a glass of beer

exampleSentences.italian: un bicchiere da vino
exampleSentences.english: a wine glass

exampleSentences.italian: Andiamo a bere un bicchiere stasera! Pago io!
exampleSentences.english: Let's go have a drink tonight! It's on me!

exampleSentences.italian: un bicchier d'acqua
exampleSentences.english: a glass of water

relatedExpressions.meaning: to drink one too many, to get drunk
to be a piece of cake, to be very easy

relatedExpressions.expression: una tempesta in un bicchier d'acqua
relatedExpressions.meaning: a storm in a glass of water; a great racket or quarrel for nothing

relatedExpressions.expression: perdersi / affogarsi in un bicchier d'acqua
relatedExpressions.meaning: to get confused or worried when faced with minimal difficulties
the final toast, the last glass (a reference to the final drink before heading home on horseback)

grammarNotes: Quindi functions primarily as a conjunction expressing cause-and-effect or logical conclusions. It can appear at the beginning of a sentence or at the end to imply a thought. In archaic usage, it functions as an adverb meaning 'then' or 'next.' The word derives from late Latin 'eccum inde' (from here), though this locative meaning is now obsolete.
learnerNotes: Quindi is one of the most common conjunctions in Italian and should be mastered early. Remember it can appear at sentence start or end; when at the end with trailing ellipsis (…), it implies an unstated conclusion. Don't confuse it with 'allora' (then, which often implies temporal sequence) or 'dunque' (therefore, which emphasizes logical deduction)—while similar, they have subtle contextual differences.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono in ritardo per il colloquio, quindi prendo la metro invece di andare a piedi.
exampleSentences.english: I'm late for the interview, so I'll take the underground instead of walking.

exampleSentences.italian: Quindi, tutto sommato, direi che la serata non è andata poi così male.
exampleSentences.english: So, all in all, I'd say the evening didn't go that bad.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piacerebbe andare con loro ma ho un sacco di lavoro da finire, quindi…
exampleSentences.english: I'd like to go with them but I have a lot of work to finish, so…

exampleSentences.italian: Non dovremmo essere qui. Rischiamo di farci beccare… – E quindi?
exampleSentences.english: We shouldn't be here. We might get caught… – So what?

exampleSentences.italian: Proseguite per altri due isolati e poi voltate a sinistra, quindi camminate per ancora cinque minuti circa, finché non vi ritrovate davanti alla stazione.
exampleSentences.english: Carry on for two more blocks and then turn left, next walk for about five minutes until you find yourselves in front of the station.

relatedExpressions.meaning: So what? / And so…? (sarcastic response indicating something is unimportant)

grammarNotes: Affezionato is the past participle of affezionare (to grow fond). It agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: affezionato (m.s.), affezionata (f.s.), affezionati (m.p.), affezionate (f.p.). When expressing fondness or attachment, it takes the preposition 'a' (affezionato a qualcosa/qualcuno). The superlative form affezionatissimo/a is very common.
learnerNotes: Remember that affezionato requires the preposition 'a' when expressing attachment to someone or something (affezionato a qualcosa), unlike English which uses 'of' or 'to'. When describing a person or animal directly (without a preposition), it means 'affectionate' or 'loving' rather than 'fond.' In commercial contexts, affezionato clients are 'loyal' or 'faithful' customers, which is a useful distinction for Italian business communication.

exampleSentences.italian: Tutta la famiglia è molto affezionata al nostro cane Achille.
exampleSentences.english: The entire family is very fond of our dog Achilles.

exampleSentences.italian: un gatto affezionato
exampleSentences.english: an affectionate cat

exampleSentences.italian: una nipote affezionata
exampleSentences.english: a loving granddaughter

exampleSentences.italian: Bisogna trattare molto bene i clienti più affezionati.
exampleSentences.english: The most loyal customers must be treated very well.

exampleSentences.italian: il tuo affezionato figlio
exampleSentences.english: your loving son

exampleSentences.italian: la tua affezionata figlia
exampleSentences.english: your loving daughter

relatedExpressions.meaning: to grow fond of / to become attached to

grammarNotes: Sempre is an invariable adverb derived from Latin 'semper'. It can function as a temporal adverb (always, continuously), concessive adverb (still, yet), or appear in comparative constructions (sempre più = more and more). When used with 'che' (sempre che), it takes on a conditional meaning (provided that, as long as).
learnerNotes: Sempre has multiple meanings depending on context: 'always' for habitual or continuous actions, and 'still' when expressing continuity despite change or contrast. Watch for the 'sempre che' construction which means 'provided that' and is interchangeable with purché or ammesso che. In comparative phrases like sempre più/meno, sempre acts as an intensifier rather than a temporal marker.

exampleSentences.italian: Giorgio pensa sempre al lavoro.
exampleSentences.english: Giorgio is always thinking about work.

exampleSentences.italian: A cena Giorgio mangia sempre la pasta.
exampleSentences.english: Giorgio always eats pasta for supper.

exampleSentences.italian: Giorgio ti amerà (per) sempre.
exampleSentences.english: Giorgio will always love you.

exampleSentences.italian: Abiti sempre a Torino?
exampleSentences.english: Do you still live in Turin?

exampleSentences.italian: È inaffidabile, lo so, ma è (pur) sempre tuo fratello.
exampleSentences.english: He's unreliable, I know, but he's still your brother.

exampleSentences.italian: Ogni giorno sei sempre più alto!
exampleSentences.english: You are getting taller and taller every day!

exampleSentences.italian: Traslocheremo a settembre, sempre che i lavori finiscano in tempo.
exampleSentences.english: We'll move in September, provided that they finish the job on time.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai ragione, come sempre!
exampleSentences.english: You're right, as always!

exampleSentences.italian: Tifo per la Juve da sempre.
exampleSentences.english: I've supported Juventus all my life.

exampleSentences.italian: Da sempre l'uomo è affascinato dai misteri dell'universo.
exampleSentences.english: Since the dawn of time, mankind has been fascinated by the mysteries of the universe.

exampleSentences.italian: Mauro è rimasto quello di sempre.
exampleSentences.english: Mauro is the same as ever.

exampleSentences.italian: È il miglior giocatore di tennis di sempre.
exampleSentences.english: He is the best tennis player of all time.

relatedExpressions.meaning: always, since the dawn of time, for all one's life
as ever, usual, of all time

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural sbadigli. Because it begins with s + consonant, it takes the articles lo/gli (not il/i) and uno/degli (not un/dei). The augmentative form sbadiglione (a big yawn) uses the -one suffix to intensify the meaning.
learnerNotes: Remember that sbadiglio is masculine and always takes lo/gli articles because of the s + consonant rule—this is a common s + consonant exception to learn. The verb sbadigliare (to yawn) is distinct from the noun; use fare uno sbadiglio as an alternative construction. The contagious nature of yawning is expressed with contagioso/contagiosi (adjective), useful for discussing social phenomena.

exampleSentences.italian: lo sbadiglio
exampleSentences.english: the yawn

exampleSentences.italian: gli sbadigli
exampleSentences.english: the yawns

exampleSentences.italian: uno sbadiglio
exampleSentences.english: a yawn

exampleSentences.italian: degli sbadigli
exampleSentences.english: (some) yawns

exampleSentences.italian: Tratteneva a stento uno sbadiglio mentre ascoltava il discorso.
exampleSentences.english: He barely held back a yawn as he listened to the speech.

exampleSentences.italian: Quanti sbadigli che fai! – Scusa, non ho chiuso occhio tutta la notte.
exampleSentences.english: You're yawning a lot! – Sorry, I didn't sleep all night.

exampleSentences.italian: Il tizio davanti a me si è lasciato scappare uno sbadiglio e, poco dopo, ho cominciato a sbadigliare anch'io!
exampleSentences.english: The guy in front of me let a yawn escape and, soon after, I started to yawn as well!

grammarNotes: Pazzesco is a variable adjective that agrees with the noun it modifies in gender and number: pazzesca (feminine singular), pazzeschi (masculine plural), pazzesche (feminine plural). It derives from pazzo (crazy) but extends meaning beyond person-focused descriptions to encompass exaggerated or incredible qualities of things, states, or situations.
learnerNotes: Pazzesco differs from pazzo in that it describes exaggerated, intense, or incredible qualities of things rather than just describing a person's mental state. Use pazzesco colloquially to express amazement or surprise about situations (e.g., weather, hunger, lateness). Don't confuse it with pazzo, which typically describes insane or irrational behavior in people.

exampleSentences.italian: un uomo pazzo
exampleSentences.english: a crazy man

exampleSentences.italian: un'idea pazza
exampleSentences.english: a crazy idea

exampleSentences.italian: un piano pazzesco
exampleSentences.english: a crazy plan

exampleSentences.italian: fare un freddo pazzesco
exampleSentences.english: to be terribly cold

exampleSentences.italian: fare un caldo pazzesco
exampleSentences.english: to be terribly hot

exampleSentences.italian: avere una fame pazzesca
exampleSentences.english: to be terribly hungry

exampleSentences.italian: avere una sete pazzesca
exampleSentences.english: to be terribly thirsty

exampleSentences.italian: fare una fatica pazzesca
exampleSentences.english: to work really hard / to make a big effort

exampleSentences.italian: È arrivato alla festa con un ritardo pazzesco!
exampleSentences.english: He arrived at the party incredibly late!

exampleSentences.italian: un concerto pazzesco
exampleSentences.english: an amazing concert

exampleSentences.italian: Il nuovo brano di Elisa è pazzesco! Potrei ascoltarlo tutto il giorno senza mai stufarmi!
exampleSentences.english: The new song by Elisa is amazing! I could listen to it all day and never get tired of it!

exampleSentences.italian: Ma è pazzesco! Il pilota ha finito il gran premio su tre ruote!
exampleSentences.english: That's crazy! The driver finished the grand prix on three wheels!

relatedExpressions.meaning: It's crazy! / It's ridiculous! / That's amazing!

englishTranslation: however / yet / but / nonetheless / still / despite
grammarNotes: Tuttavia is a formal conjunction composed of tutta (feminine of tutto, meaning everything) and via (path/way). It connects two contrasting or contradictory statements. Modern Italian allows tuttavia to introduce a sentence, despite traditional rules against starting sentences with conjunctions. It can be intensified with pur tuttavia or the single form purtuttavia.
learnerNotes: Tuttavia is predominantly written rather than spoken Italian, so prioritize it for reading comprehension and formal writing. Don't confuse it with però or ma (both mean 'but' but are far more common in conversation). Remember that in old Italian, tuttavia meant 'still' or 'continuously' — if you encounter this meaning in classical texts, context will clarify the archaic usage.

exampleSentences.italian: Non ha studiato la materia, tuttavia ha deciso di sostenere l'esame.
exampleSentences.english: He did not study the subject, yet he decided to take the exam.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai combinato un bel casino, tuttavia sono disposto a darti un'altra possibilità.
exampleSentences.english: You really messed up. However I'm willing to give you another chance.

exampleSentences.italian: Pisa è nota nel mondo per la Piazza dei Miracoli. Tuttavia ci sono tante altre cose interessanti da vedere…
exampleSentences.english: Pisa is famous for Piazza dei Miracoli. However, there are so many other interesting things to see…

exampleSentences.italian: Non lavorava mai, pur tuttavia fu promosso a capoufficio.
exampleSentences.english: He never worked, yet he was promoted to office manager.

exampleSentences.italian: Quantè bella giovinezza che si fugge tuttavia!
exampleSentences.english: How lovely is youth Which continually slips away

relatedExpressions.meaning: yet, however (intensified form with pur as reinforcer)
yet, however (alternative single-word form, rarely used)
every time that (archaic expression, synonymous with ogni volta che)

grammarNotes: Calvo is a regular adjective that agrees in gender and number: calvo (masc. sing.), calva (fem. sing.), calvi (masc. plur.), calve (fem. plur.). It derives from Latin calvus. When used as a noun, it means 'bald-headed person' or 'baldy' and retains the same gender agreement rules. The expressions essere calvo (to be bald) and diventare calvo (to go/become bald) use different auxiliaries to distinguish state from change.
learnerNotes: Calvo and pelato are both used for 'bald,' but pelato has a broader meaning extending to any hairless body part, while calvo is more specific to baldness of the head. Use essere calvo for the state of being bald, but diventare calvo to express the process of becoming bald—this distinction between stative and dynamic verbs is crucial in Italian. Note that stempiatura (receding hairline) is a common related term you'll encounter in contexts about hair loss.

exampleSentences.italian: Sarò calvo fra qualche anno. Ho già una stempiatura, non vedi?
exampleSentences.english: I'll be bald in a few years. I already have a receding hairline, don't you see?

exampleSentences.italian: Calvo can refer specifically to the head (testa calva = bald head) or to the person who is bald (un uomo calvo = a bald man).
exampleSentences.english: Calvo can refer specifically to the head (bald head) or to the person who is bald (a bald man).

exampleSentences.italian: Da giovane mio padre era un capellone, ma ora è completamente calvo.
exampleSentences.english: My father had lots of hair when he was young, but now he's completely bald.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho la testa tutta pelata adesso. Vabbè, almeno risparmierò i soldi del parrucchiere.
exampleSentences.english: My head is completely bald now. Oh well, at least I won't have to spend money at the hairdresser's.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be balding / to lose one's hair
bald (synonym for calvo, broader meaning including hairless body parts)
person with lots of hair (opposite of calvo)

englishTranslation: corruption/illegal profit scheme / eat up, eat up
grammarNotes: Mangia is the third-person singular present indicative or second-person singular imperative form of mangiare (to eat). When doubled as 'mangia mangia,' it functions as a noun phrase describing systemic corruption. The variant 'magna magna' derives from magnare, the Roman dialect version of mangiare, and carries the same idiomatic meaning.
learnerNotes: While 'mangia mangia' can literally mean 'eat up, eat up!' as an imperative, its idiomatic meaning refers specifically to systemic corruption, bribery, and illegal profit-taking—a critical concept in understanding Italian political discourse. This expression is primarily used in colloquial and journalistic contexts, not formal speech. The regional variant 'magna magna' from Roman dialect is less common but carries identical meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: Lui mangia la colazione.
exampleSentences.english: He eats breakfast.

exampleSentences.italian: Lei mangia la cena.
exampleSentences.english: She eats dinner. / You (formal) eat dinner.

exampleSentences.italian: Il cane mangia la pappa.
exampleSentences.english: The dog eats the food.

exampleSentences.italian: Dai su, mangia la pasta adesso! Altrimenti si raffredda!
exampleSentences.english: Come on, eat the pasta now. Otherwise it will get cold!

exampleSentences.italian: Quel ciclista è un mangiachilometri. È capace di pedalare per lunghissimi tratti senza fermarsi.
exampleSentences.english: That cyclist is unstoppable. He is capable of riding for very long stretches without stopping.

exampleSentences.italian: È inutile partecipare a quella gara d'appalto. Hanno già deciso chi vincerà. È tutto un magna magna!
exampleSentences.english: It's useless to participate in that tender procedure. They've already decided who will win. It's a scam!

exampleSentences.italian: All'interno del governo c'era un mangia mangia generale.
exampleSentences.english: Within the government, corruption was rampant.

relatedExpressions.meaning: someone well-paid but not earning their money, or something that makes you spend a lot of money
someone strongly opposed to the clergy
a person who appears grouchy but is actually kind and sensitive
someone who enjoys long-distance running/cycling/driving, or a vehicle used for long distances

grammarNotes: Scavezzacollo is an invariable noun, meaning it does not change its final -o to -a when referring to females. In the plural, it becomes scavezzacolli for both sexes. It is composed of scavezzare (to break) + collo (neck), literally meaning 'neck-breaker'.
learnerNotes: Remember that scavezzacollo does not follow typical gender agreement rules—use 'la scavezzacollo' for a female without changing the ending. The adverbial phrase 'a scavezzacollo' shifts meaning entirely to describe speed rather than a person, so context is crucial. This is colloquial vocabulary best used when describing reckless or adventurous people informally.

exampleSentences.italian: Quella scavezzacollo di mia sorella va a fare paracadutismo domani.
exampleSentences.english: My daredevil of a sister is going skydiving tomorrow.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural form tatuaggi. Derives from French tatouage and English tattoo. Used with the article un/il (e.g., un tatuaggio, il mio tatuaggio) and agrees with possessive adjectives in gender and number.
learnerNotes: Note the distinction between farsi un tatuaggio and farsi fare un tatuaggio: the latter emphasizes that someone else performs the tattoo, though both are understood similarly in practice. The reflexive construction farsi + infinitive is key here (farsi tatuare = to get tattooed). Tatuaggio permanenti means permanent tattoos, while tatuaggio all'hennè offers a non-permanent alternative.

exampleSentences.italian: Domani mi faccio fare il mio primo tatuaggio. Ho un po' paura!
exampleSentences.english: Tomorrow I'm getting my first tattoo done. I'm a bit scared!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to get a tattoo done (by someone else)

grammarNotes: Speciale remains unchanged in the feminine form (la persona speciale), but becomes speciali in the plural (persone speciali, cose speciali). It derives from Latin specialis, related to species meaning 'appearance.' The word agrees in gender with the noun it modifies, though the singular form works for both masculine and feminine.
learnerNotes: Note that speciale can be used ironically to imply someone is strange or bizarre, not just literally exceptional. As a noun, lo speciale refers to a TV report, newspaper article, or short film about a current topic or person. The English word 'special' has also entered Italian directly in media contexts, so you may hear both speciale and special used interchangeably in broadcasting.

exampleSentences.italian: Maria è una persona davvero speciale.
exampleSentences.english: Maria is a truly special person.

exampleSentences.italian: Pensa sempre agli altri.
exampleSentences.english: She always thinks of other people.

exampleSentences.italian: Un autobus speciale
exampleSentences.english: A special bus

exampleSentences.italian: Una trasmissione speciale
exampleSentences.english: A special broadcast

exampleSentences.italian: Giorgio ha memorizzato ogni singola parola del libro 'Il Signore degli Anelli'. Come ti ho detto, è un tipo 'speciale'!
exampleSentences.english: Giorgio has memorised every single word of The Lord of the Rings. As I told you, he's a 'special' guy!

exampleSentences.italian: Stasera in televisione trasmettono lo speciale su Lady Diana.
exampleSentences.english: Tonight on television they are broadcasting the Lady Diana special.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural form 'pelli'. Comes from Latin 'pellis'. Can refer to human/animal skin, fruit/vegetable peel, leather material, or figuratively to a person's life. Often used in idiomatic expressions where it represents life or existence.
learnerNotes: While 'pelle' and 'cuoio' both mean leather, 'cuoio' refers to thicker, more resistant leather used in manufacturing, whereas 'pelle' is more general. For fruit/vegetable peel, 'buccia' is more commonly used than 'pelle'. Be aware that 'pelle' has extensive figurative usage related to life and risk—mastering these idioms significantly improves colloquial comprehension.

exampleSentences.italian: Biancaneve aveva le labbra rosse come una rosa, i capelli neri come l'ebano e la pelle bianca come la neve.
exampleSentences.english: Snow White had lips as red as a rose, hair as black as ebony, and skin as white as snow.

exampleSentences.italian: Non indossare la giacca di pelle sotto la pioggia! Così la rovini!
exampleSentences.english: Don't wear your leather jacket in the rain! You'll ruin it!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to do someone in, to take someone's life
to put someone's life at risk
to be beside oneself, to be very excited

relatedExpressions.expression: Vendere la pelle dell'orso prima di averlo ucciso
relatedExpressions.meaning: to count one's chickens before they hatch

relatedExpressions.expression: Avere i nervi a fior di pelle
relatedExpressions.meaning: to be on edge, to be high-strung

grammarNotes: Allucinante is an invariable adjective that does not change form for gender or number, remaining the same for both masculine and feminine subjects. The plural form is allucinanti. It functions as a descriptive adjective and can be placed before or after the noun it modifies.
learnerNotes: Allucinante has shifted from its literal meaning (hallucinatory) to become hyperbolic slang among young Italians, used to intensify both positive and negative descriptions—be aware of context to determine if it means 'shocking/horrifying' versus 'amazing/incredible.' The word's invariable nature is unusual compared to most Italian adjectives, so memorize this exception. Note that it derives from the verb allucinare but is almost exclusively used as an adjective in contemporary Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho assistito ad una scena allucinante!
exampleSentences.english: I witnessed a shocking scene!

exampleSentences.italian: Se te la racconto, non ci crederai!
exampleSentences.english: If I tell you about it, you won't believe it!

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi fa un caldo allucinante e ovviamente l'aria condizionata non funziona!
exampleSentences.english: It's incredibly hot today and obviously the air conditioning isn't working!

exampleSentences.italian: uno spettacolo allucinante
exampleSentences.english: a shocking sight

exampleSentences.italian: una cosa allucinante
exampleSentences.english: a shocking thing

englishTranslation: attic / loft / space inside the roof
grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form sottotetti. Composed of sotto (under) + tetto (roof). Generally not naturally lit or ventilated due to lack of windows, making it unsuitable for residential use without modification. Can be transformed into a mansarda (feminine) by adding windows, insulation, and utilities.
learnerNotes: Do not confuse soffitta (attic, feminine) with soffitto (ceiling, masculine)—they sound similar but have completely different meanings. Sottotetto is the technical/architectural term, while soffitta and solaio are more colloquial synonyms. Remember that attico means penthouse, not attic—a crucial distinction for describing Italian real estate!

exampleSentences.italian: Voglio trasformare il sottotetto di casa in un vano abitabile.
exampleSentences.english: I want to turn the attic of the house into a habitable space.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho messo il lampadario in soffitta.
exampleSentences.english: I've put the chandelier in the attic.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho appeso il lampadario al soffitto.
exampleSentences.english: I've hung the chandelier from the ceiling.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei tanto andare a vivere in un attico, ma i prezzi sono esagerati!
exampleSentences.english: I would really like to go and live in a penthouse, but the prices are excessive!

relatedExpressions.meaning: attic (feminine synonym of sottotetto; storage or living space under the roof)
attic (another synonym; space directly under the roof for storage or living)
habitable attic/loft (transformed sottotetto with windows, insulation, and utilities)
penthouse (luxury apartment, NOT a simple attic)

grammarNotes: Permaloso is a masculine singular adjective that agrees with the noun it modifies. Feminine singular: permalosa; masculine plural: permalosi; feminine plural: permalose. It can also function as a noun meaning 'touchy/oversensitive person.' The diminutive form permalosetto means 'somewhat sensitive.'
learnerNotes: Permaloso is commonly used as an adjective to describe people who are easily hurt or offended, even over small matters. Remember to adjust the ending based on gender and number agreement with the noun. The related verb impermalosirsi ('to take offence') is useful for describing the action of becoming offended.

exampleSentences.italian: Mica posso dirgli la verità: è troppo permaloso!
exampleSentences.english: There's no way I can tell him the truth: he's too sensitive!

exampleSentences.italian: Non fare la permalosa! Ti ho detto che mi dispiace!
exampleSentences.english: Don't be so sensitive! I said I'm sorry!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to take offence / to become offended

grammarNotes: Pistacchio is a masculine noun. The plural is formed by dropping the final 'o' to get 'pistacchi'. The word can also refer to the pistachio tree itself, and is used figuratively to describe a soft green colour reminiscent of the pistachio seed.
learnerNotes: English speakers often mispronounce this word by making the 'ch' sound like 'sh' and by not holding the double 'cc' consonant. In Italian, 'ch' is always a hard 'k' sound, and the double 'cc' requires a brief pause. The Italian pronunciation is three syllables (pis-tak-kio) rather than four as in English.

exampleSentences.italian: Adoro il gelato al pistacchio!
exampleSentences.english: I love pistachio ice cream!

exampleSentences.italian: Che buoni che sono questi pistacchi!
exampleSentences.english: These pistachios are so good!

exampleSentences.italian: Cosa ne pensi di questo cappello verde pistacchio?
exampleSentences.english: What do you think of this pistachio-coloured hat?

grammarNotes: Anziano agrees in gender and number: anziano (m. sing.), anziana (f. sing.), anziani (m. pl.), anziane (f. pl.). When used as a noun, it means 'elderly person' or 'senior citizen,' with anziani/anziane referring to 'the elderly' collectively. It can be used in comparative constructions (più anziano di = older than) and superlative forms (il/la più anziano/a = the oldest).
learnerNotes: Anziano is more polite and respectful than vecchio when referring to a person's age; using vecchio can sound impertinent. Remember that anziano only applies to people and senior status, not to objects or things (use vecchio for those). In Italian sociology, anyone over 65 is officially considered anziano, and colloquially, university students attending for over two years are also called anziani.

exampleSentences.italian: Il signore anziano sta camminando lentamente verso la piazza.
exampleSentences.english: The old gentleman is walking slowly towards the square.

exampleSentences.italian: (io) sono anziano / anziana
exampleSentences.english: I am old

exampleSentences.italian: (tu) sei anziano / anziana
exampleSentences.english: you are old (informal)

exampleSentences.italian: (lui) è anziano
exampleSentences.english: he is old

exampleSentences.italian: (lei) è anziana
exampleSentences.english: she is old

exampleSentences.italian: (Lei) è anziano / anziana
exampleSentences.english: you are old (formal)

exampleSentences.italian: (noi) siamo anziani / anziane
exampleSentences.english: we are old

exampleSentences.italian: (voi) siete anziani / anziane
exampleSentences.english: you are old (plural)

exampleSentences.italian: (loro) sono anziani / anziane
exampleSentences.english: they are old

exampleSentences.italian: Mario è più anziano di Maria.
exampleSentences.english: Mario is older than Maria.

exampleSentences.italian: Mario è il più anziano dei tre fratelli.
exampleSentences.english: Mario is the oldest of the three siblings.

exampleSentences.italian: Dobbiamo fidarci degli anziani perché hanno più esperienza di noi.
exampleSentences.english: We have to trust the elderly because they have more experience than us.

relatedExpressions.meaning: an old friend (long-established friendship, not necessarily about age)
the council of elders / elderly council
senior student (university student who has attended for more than two years)

grammarNotes: Evviva is a variation of the interjection Viva! preceded by the conjunction e (and). When followed by a noun, it takes the form 'Evviva + noun' meaning 'long live' or 'hurray for.' It can also function as an invariable masculine noun meaning 'cheer' or 'shout,' used in both singular and plural forms without gender or number agreement.
learnerNotes: Evviva is commonly used in celebratory contexts but can also be used ironically or sarcastically when criticizing someone's behavior. Be aware that the ironic usage reverses the literal meaning—'Evviva la modestia!' directed at a braggart is sarcastic. When functioning as a noun (evviva), it remains invariable (never changes form) despite being masculine, making it easier to use.

exampleSentences.italian: Evviva, abbiamo raggiunto quota mille iscritti su YouTube!
exampleSentences.english: Hurray, we've reached 1000 subscribers on YouTube!

exampleSentences.italian: Evviva gli sposi!
exampleSentences.english: Long live the newlyweds!

exampleSentences.italian: Evviva la modestia!
exampleSentences.english: So much for modesty!

exampleSentences.italian: Il pubblico accolse il giocatore con evviva entusiastici.
exampleSentences.english: The audience greeted the player with enthusiastic cheers.

relatedExpressions.meaning: Long live! / Hurray! (the base interjection without e)

grammarNotes: Tempo is a masculine noun, so the adjective libero agrees in gender and ends with -o. The phrase can be used as a standalone noun in sentences (e.g., 'Passo il tempo libero a...'). Related singular/plural forms maintain masculine agreement.
learnerNotes: Tempo libero is the standard everyday phrase for 'free time,' but Italian offers several alternatives depending on context: ritagli di tempo emphasizes limited, fragmented time; momenti di svago adds a sense of leisure or relaxation. The verb ritagliare (to cut out) is commonly paired with tempo to express 'finding time for' someone or something. Pay attention to whether you need the singular (ritaglio) or plural (ritagli) form when using these expressions.

exampleSentences.italian: Passo il tempo libero a suonare il pianoforte.
exampleSentences.english: I spend my free time playing the piano.

exampleSentences.italian: Leggo solo nei ritagli di tempo, di solito alla sera dopo che i bambini sono andati a dormire.
exampleSentences.english: I only read in my spare time, usually in the evening after the kids have gone to sleep.

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi ho trovato un ritaglio di tempo per scriverti.
exampleSentences.english: Today I had a spare moment to write to you.

exampleSentences.italian: Non ho un momento libero oggi.
exampleSentences.english: I don't have a spare moment today.

exampleSentences.italian: Se hai un attimo (di tempo), te lo vado a prendere.
exampleSentences.english: If you have a moment, I'll go fetch it for you.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai un minuto?
exampleSentences.english: Do you have a minute?

exampleSentences.italian: Vedo se riesco a ritagliarmi un'oretta, così andiamo a mangiare qualcosa.
exampleSentences.english: I'll see if I can find an hour to spare, so that we can go eat something together.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to cut out / dedicate some spare time

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural minestre. Derives from Latin minestrare (to administer). Can be modified by adjectives like calda (warm) or asciutta (dry). Related diminutive minestrina and augmentative minestrone are also feminine and masculine respectively.
learnerNotes: Minestra is a generic term for watery soups with pasta, rice, legumes, and vegetables. Don't confuse it with zuppa, which traditionally contains broth, vegetables, and bread but never pasta, rice, or legumes. Beyond its literal meaning, minestra is used figuratively to describe boring, repetitive situations, while minestrone describes confusing mixtures—useful for advanced expression.

exampleSentences.italian: A mia mamma piace mangiare una buona minestra calda nelle fredde serate invernali.
exampleSentences.english: My mum likes to eat a good warm soup on cold winter evenings.

exampleSentences.italian: Da piccolo mi ricordo il minestrone genovese che preparava la nonna.
exampleSentences.english: I remember the Genoese minestrone soup grandma made when I was little.

exampleSentences.italian: È sempre la solita minestra.
exampleSentences.english: It's the same old thing.

exampleSentences.italian: Quella pagina web è un minestrone di notizie poco interessanti.
exampleSentences.english: That web page is a hodgepodge of not very interesting news.

exampleSentences.italian: In quel ristorante fanno una zuppa di pesce squisita!
exampleSentences.english: In that restaurant they make a delicious fish soup.

relatedExpressions.meaning: dry minestra; historically referred to first courses like risotto, ravioli, or lasagna rather than soup
little soup; a light soup given to children and sick people
big soup; a thick soup with rice or pasta and various vegetables; also used figuratively for a confusing mix of elements
heated soup; same old, same old

englishTranslation: cappuccino (a hot drink of coffee and frothed milk)
grammarNotes: Cappuccino is a masculine noun (il cappuccino). To form the plural, replace the final -o with -i to create cappuccini. The word contains two double consonants (pp and cc) that must be pronounced distinctly with a brief pause and prolonged sound. Pronunciation: /kapːu'tːʃino/.
learnerNotes: A critical cultural rule: never order cappuccino or any milk-based coffee after noon in Italy, especially after meals, as Italians believe dairy after eating disrupts digestion. English speakers often mispronounce the double consonants (pp and cc)—remember to pause slightly and hold these sounds longer than single consonants. The word derives from the Capuchin friars of the Franciscan order (16th century Italy), named for the color similarity between the drink and their brown robes.

exampleSentences.italian: Il cappuccino è una bevanda molto amata in Italia.
exampleSentences.english: The cappuccino is a very popular drink in Italy.

relatedExpressions.meaning: Capuchin monkeys (literally 'cappuccino monkeys' in Italian, named for the resemblance of their fur to the Capuchin friars' robes)
hood (the long, pointed hood worn by Capuchin friars; the etymological source of cappuccino)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural barlumi. Derives from lume (light) + prefix bar- (similar to pejorative bis-). When used literally with sunlight, it typically appears in plural form. Commonly used in figurative expressions to describe something barely perceptible or fleeting.
learnerNotes: Barlume is a more literary and romantic word for dim or faint light; everyday alternatives include lume, luce, or bagliore. It's particularly common in figurative expressions describing abstract concepts (hope, intelligence, honesty) that appear faintly or minimally. Note that the plural barlumi is standard when describing multiple rays or glimmers, especially with natural light.

exampleSentences.italian: Nella stanza buia intravedevo un piccolo barlume di luce provenire dall'esterno.
exampleSentences.english: In the dark room, I saw a glimmer of light coming from outside.

exampleSentences.italian: Gli ultimi barlumi del sole si spegnevano lentamente dietro la montagna.
exampleSentences.english: The last rays of sunlight slowly faded behind the mountain.

englishTranslation: regardless of / apart from / aside from / irrespective of
grammarNotes: This prepositional expression uses the preposition 'da' to introduce the element being excluded or disregarded. It derives from the verb 'prescindere' (to exclude), which is rarely used outside this expression. The expression can be modified with gerund form 'prescindendo da' (meaning identical) or informally as 'a prescindere' without 'da' in colloquial speech.
learnerNotes: Avoid using 'a prescindere' without 'da' in formal writing or academic contexts—this colloquial usage is considered improper. Note that 'prescindere' itself is almost never used outside the set expressions shown here, so focus on memorizing 'a prescindere da' as a fixed formula. Pay attention to the contraction of 'da + il/lo/la' to 'dal/dallo/dalla' when forming examples.

exampleSentences.italian: A prescindere dal voto che hai ottenuto, il tuo impegno è stato esemplare.
exampleSentences.english: Regardless of the grade you got, your dedication has been exemplary.

exampleSentences.italian: A prescindere dallo stress e dalla fatica, il mio lavoro continua a piacermi.
exampleSentences.english: All the stress and pressure aside, I still enjoy my job.

exampleSentences.italian: A prescindere dal fatto che non me lo posso permettere, questo abito non mi sta per niente bene.
exampleSentences.english: Apart from the fact that I can't afford it, this suit doesn't fit me at all.

exampleSentences.italian: Prescindendo da come andranno a finire le cose, possiamo dire di aver fatto del nostro meglio.
exampleSentences.english: Regardless of how things end, we can say that we did our best.

exampleSentences.italian: Hanno criticato la mia decisione, ma continuerò a prescindere (da ciò che pensano).
exampleSentences.english: They criticised my decision, but I will continue regardless (of what they think).

relatedExpressions.meaning: regardless (colloquial, without specifying what is excluded)
regardless of the fact that (colloquial abbreviation of 'a prescindere dal fatto che')

grammarNotes: Gnocchi is the plural form of gnocco (singular). It is a masculine noun in Italian. The word is typically used in the plural form when referring to the dish. Double consonants in Italian (cc) are pronounced with a longer, held sound than single consonants.
learnerNotes: The pronunciation of 'gn' in Italian (represented as ɲ) is distinctly different from English and requires practice—think of the 'ny' sound in 'canyon.' English speakers typically mispronounce gnocchi as 'naw-kee' or 'noh-kee,' but the correct Italian pronunciation is /ˈɲɔk.ki/. Note that gnocchetti, despite sounding like 'small gnocchi,' are actually a type of pasta, not dumplings—a common point of confusion.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piacciono gli gnocchi al pomodoro.
exampleSentences.english: I like gnocchi with tomato sauce.

exampleSentences.italian: Quando vado in Sardegna, la prima cosa che faccio è mangiarmi un bel piatto di malloreddus, anche conosciuti come gnocchetti sardi.
exampleSentences.english: When I go to Sardinia, the first thing I do is eat a good plate of malloreddus, also known as the little Sardinian gnocchi.

exampleSentences.italian: Ridi, ridi che la mamma ha preparato gli gnocchi!
exampleSentences.english: Laugh, laugh because mum made gnocchi!

relatedExpressions.meaning: singular form; also means knot, lump, idiot, or (in slang) hot guy
feminine form of the slang meaning hot girl
diminutive form; small pasta shells (not dumplings), also called malloreddus or gnocchetti sardi
Piedmont specialty with cheese, butter and sage
Campania variation with tomato sauce, mozzarella and basil
made with semolina flour, disc-shaped, prepared with butter, pecorino and parmesan

grammarNotes: Fattoria is a feminine noun with regular plural fattorie. It derives from fattore (farm manager). The phrase 'lavorare in una fattoria' expresses working on a farm. Gender agreement applies to articles and adjectives modifying it (e.g., la fattoria biologica).
learnerNotes: Don't confuse fattoria with 'factory' despite phonetic similarity—this is a classic false cognate. Use allevamento when specifically referring to animal breeding operations (e.g., allevamento di pecore = sheep farm). Azienda agricola is more commercially oriented than fattoria, which simply produces animals and crops.

exampleSentences.italian: Da piccolo sono cresciuto nella fattoria di famiglia.
exampleSentences.english: As a child, I grew up on the family farm.

exampleSentences.italian: Ero circondato da animali di ogni tipo.
exampleSentences.english: I was surrounded by all kinds of animals.

relatedExpressions.meaning: farmhouse where residents work the land but do not own it
square-yard farm at the centre of cultivated land
group of farmhouses in open countryside
animal breeding/farming (used instead of fattoria for livestock)

grammarNotes: Pazienza is a feminine noun with plural pazienze. It derives from Latin patientia (suffering). The word is commonly used with verbs like avere, perdere, portare, and mostrare to express different aspects of patience. Imperative forms (abbi, abbia, abbiate) are frequently used as polite expressions or apologies rather than literal commands.
learnerNotes: Pazienza is highly versatile: beyond its literal meaning, abbi/abbia/abbiate pazienza functions as a polite apology (like saying 'Sorry') and as a complaint similar to 'Oh come on!' Pay attention to register—use the informal abbi with friends and the formal abbia with strangers or authority figures. Related words like impaziente (impatient) and paziente (patient person/medical patient) are useful for B1-level expression.

exampleSentences.italian: Sto per perdere la pazienza!
exampleSentences.english: I'm running out of patience!

exampleSentences.italian: Capita a tutti di attraversare momenti difficili. Abbi pazienza e si sistemerà tutto, vedrai!
exampleSentences.english: We all go through difficult times. Be patient and everything will be fine, you'll see!

exampleSentences.italian: Abbi pazienza, ma oggi non posso accompagnarti.
exampleSentences.english: I'm sorry, but I can't go with you today.

exampleSentences.italian: Abbi pazienza, come faccio a fare tutto in un giorno?
exampleSentences.english: Oh come on, how can I do everything in one day?

exampleSentences.italian: Purtroppo la gita non è andata come speravo. Pazienza!
exampleSentences.english: Unfortunately, the trip didn't pan out the way I had hoped. Oh well!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be patient, to have patience
to prepare oneself to be very patient (to arm oneself with patience)
be patient (command); also used as a polite apology
patience of a Carthusian monk (exceptional patience)
a puzzle or game requiring patience and concentration

englishTranslation: to not give a damn / to not care
grammarNotes: Pronominal verb ending in -sene (combination of si and ne pronouns). The se is the pronoun si transformed before another pronoun; ne is a pronominal particle meaning 'of it/about it'. Conjugates regularly in present tense with the pronouns attached (me ne, te ne, se ne, ce ne, ve ne, se ne). Less common variant infischiarsi exists without ne.
learnerNotes: This colloquial verb is less vulgar than fregarsene but still informal—use it only in casual contexts. The pronominal particle ne can seem confusing, but remember it always attaches to the pronoun before the verb stem (me ne, te ne, se ne, etc.). Note that fischiare means 'to whistle,' but infischiare doesn't exist as a standalone verb, only as the pronominal infischiarsene.

exampleSentences.italian: Chi decide di infischiarsene del distanziamento sociale è un irresponsabile.
exampleSentences.english: Anyone who decides to not care about social distancing is irresponsible.

exampleSentences.italian: (io) me ne infischio
exampleSentences.english: I don't care

exampleSentences.italian: (tu) te ne infischi
exampleSentences.english: You (informal) don't care

exampleSentences.italian: (lui) se ne infischia
exampleSentences.english: He doesn't care

exampleSentences.italian: (lei) se ne infischia
exampleSentences.english: She doesn't care

exampleSentences.italian: (Noi) ce ne infischiamo
exampleSentences.english: We don't care

exampleSentences.italian: (Voi) ve ne infischiate
exampleSentences.english: You (plural) don't care

exampleSentences.italian: (Loro) se ne infischiano
exampleSentences.english: They don't care

exampleSentences.italian: Ma il mio bambino e il suo papà se ne infischiavano, e sorridevano e poi cantavano.
exampleSentences.english: But my boy and his dad didn't give a hoot, and they smiled and then sang.

exampleSentences.italian: Ma il mio bambino e il suo papà se ne infischiavano, di quella trappola che è la città.
exampleSentences.english: But my baby and his dad didn't give a hoot about that trap that is the city.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to not give a damn (more widely known, slightly more vulgar synonym)
variant form of infischiarsene without ne (less common)
French pronominal verb with same meaning; Italian verb is modeled on this

grammarNotes: Focaccia is feminine (la focaccia) with plural form focacce. It is a countable noun that can take articles and adjectives agreeing in feminine form. Regional varieties add descriptive adjectives: focaccia genovese, focaccia barese, focaccia romana, etc.
learnerNotes: Focaccia is a feminine noun (la focaccia), so remember to use feminine articles and adjectives. The pronunciation differs subtly from English: clearly pronounce each vowel (fo-KA-cha) and hold the double 'cc' longer than a single consonant. Note that focaccia can refer both to savory flatbread and regional sweet desserts, so context determines meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: Focaccia è un tipo di pane italiano piatto.
exampleSentences.english: Focaccia is a type of Italian flatbread.

exampleSentences.italian: Preferisci la focaccia o la pizza?
exampleSentences.english: Do you prefer focaccia or pizza?

exampleSentences.italian: La focaccia genovese è caratterizzata dai buchi sulla superficie.
exampleSentences.english: Genoese focaccia is characterized by holes on its surface.

exampleSentences.italian: In una panetteria italiana troverai vari tipi di focaccia.
exampleSentences.english: In an Italian bakery, you will find various types of focaccia.

exampleSentences.italian: La focaccia veneziana è un dolce speciale, un tipo di panettone.
exampleSentences.english: Venetian focaccia is a special sweet, a type of panettone.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to take revenge / to give tit for tat (lit: to give back bread for focaccia)
filled focaccias (with ham, cheese, or vegetables)
Genoese focaccia (from Liguria, with characteristic holes)

grammarNotes: Trifoglio is a masculine noun with regular plural form trifogli. The word derives from Latin trifolium, combining tri- (three) + folium (leaf), reflecting the plant's typical three-leaf structure. Gender agreement applies when using descriptive adjectives (e.g., un trifoglio rosso).
learnerNotes: Trifoglio is commonly encountered in Italian culture, especially through the Alfa Romeo quadrifoglio symbol. The related term quadrifoglio (four-leaf clover) is more culturally significant in Italy than in English-speaking countries. Note that trefoil in English is an alternative name for clover, not a false cognate—both derive from the same Latin root tri- (three) + folium (leaf).

exampleSentences.italian: Non è un quadrifoglio purtroppo, è solo un trifoglio!
exampleSentences.english: It's not a four-leaf clover unfortunately, it's just a three-leaf clover!

exampleSentences.italian: Il trifoglio è una pianta molto diffusa.
exampleSentences.english: Clover is a very widespread plant.

grammarNotes: Malato is a regular adjective with four forms: malato (m. sg.), malata (f. sg.), malati (m. pl.), malate (f. pl.). It agrees with the noun it modifies. As a noun, it means 'sick person' or 'patient' and follows standard noun gender rules (un malato, una malata). The related verb ammalarsi (to get sick) uses malato as its past participle in the form ammalato.
learnerNotes: Malato and ammalato are largely interchangeable for describing people, but ammalato (the past participle of ammalarsi) is preferred in many contexts; however, ammalato is rarely used for animals, plants, or abstract concepts. Use malato di + disease name (malato di cancro) or avere + disease name (ha il cancro) interchangeably to express 'suffering from.' Remember that 'to feel sick/unwell' requires sentirsi male or stare male, not simply essere malato.

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi sembra il caso di andare al pronto soccorso se sei solo leggermente malato!
exampleSentences.english: I don't think it's worth going to the ER if you are only mildly ill!

exampleSentences.italian: Giulia è malata di bronchite e Carlo ha il fegato malato.
exampleSentences.english: Giulia is suffering from bronchitis and Carlo has a damaged liver.

exampleSentences.italian: Che brutto momento che stanno attraversando!
exampleSentences.english: What a difficult time they're going through!

exampleSentences.italian: Viviamo in una società malata!
exampleSentences.english: We live in an ailing society!

exampleSentences.italian: Marco ha la bronchite.
exampleSentences.english: Marco has bronchitis.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi fa male la gamba.
exampleSentences.english: My leg hurts.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be half-sick; not feeling well or just a little bit sick
to have heart disease (literal); to be lovesick (figurative)
to be sick with love; to be lovesick
a hypochondriac; an imaginary sick person
a soccer fanatic; a massive soccer fan

grammarNotes: Formed by taking the feminine singular form of the adjective 'lento' (slow) and adding the suffix '-mente' (equivalent to English '-ly'). This is a standard pattern for creating adverbs from adjectives in Italian. The adverb is invariable and does not change form.
learnerNotes: While 'lentamente' is the strict adverb for 'slowly', 'piano' is more commonly used in everyday speech and commands because it's shorter and more practical. Note that 'piano' has multiple meanings depending on context (slowly, softly, quietly), so 'lentamente' is clearer when you specifically mean the speed. The proverb 'Chi va piano, va sano e va lontano' is culturally important and worth memorizing.

exampleSentences.italian: Cammino lentamente perché mi fa male la gamba.
exampleSentences.english: I'm walking slowly because my leg hurts.

exampleSentences.italian: mangiare lentamente
exampleSentences.english: to eat slowly

exampleSentences.italian: camminare lentamente
exampleSentences.english: to walk slowly

exampleSentences.italian: andare lentamente
exampleSentences.english: to go slowly

exampleSentences.italian: Mi raccomando, versa la crema piano piano.
exampleSentences.english: Please, make sure you pour the cream slowly.

exampleSentences.italian: Pian pianino, il nostro negozio si è fatto conoscere in tutta la città.
exampleSentences.english: Little by little, our shop become well-known all across town.

exampleSentences.italian: Parla adagio o non ti capirà nessuno!
exampleSentences.english: Speak slowly or no one will understand you!

exampleSentences.italian: Vai piano!
exampleSentences.english: Go slowly!

relatedExpressions.meaning: slowly; softly; cautiously; quietly; delicately (depending on context; preferred in commands)

relatedExpressions.expression: piano piano / pian piano / pian pianino
Chi va piano, va sano e va lontano
relatedExpressions.meaning: He who goes slowly, goes healthily and goes far (equivalent to 'Slow and steady wins the race')

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural 'tempi'. In weather contexts, 'tempo' is always singular when referring to weather conditions. Derived from Latin 'tempus' meaning time. Gender agreement is important when using adjectives: 'tempo soleggiato' (sunny weather), 'tempo freddo' (cold weather).
learnerNotes: Italians prefer the verb 'fare' (to make/do) for weather descriptions rather than 'essere' (to be): say 'Fa caldo' not 'È caldo' for weather. Note that 'tempo' also means 'time' in Italian—context determines meaning. The word 'clima' (climate) is different from 'tempo' (weather); use 'clima' for long-term patterns and 'tempo' for current conditions.

exampleSentences.italian: Che tempo fa oggi?
exampleSentences.english: How's the weather today?

exampleSentences.italian: Com'è il tempo a Roma?
exampleSentences.english: What's the weather like in Rome?

exampleSentences.italian: Quando finirà questo brutto tempo? Non ce la faccio più!
exampleSentences.english: When will this bad weather end? I can't take it anymore!

exampleSentences.italian: Fa bello.
exampleSentences.english: It's nice.

exampleSentences.italian: Fa caldo.
exampleSentences.english: It's warm.

exampleSentences.italian: Fa caldissimo.
exampleSentences.english: It's hot.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è (il) sole.
exampleSentences.english: It's sunny.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è (il) vento.
exampleSentences.english: It's windy.

exampleSentences.italian: È nuvoloso.
exampleSentences.english: It's cloudy.

exampleSentences.italian: Fa brutto.
