grammarNotes: Calzone is a masculine noun (il calzone). The plural form is calzoni, following the standard masculine -e to -i ending shift. The authentic Italian pronunciation features /ts/ for the 'z' and a pronounced final 'e' (/e/), distinct from Americanized English versions. Gender agreement applies to any adjectives modifying it (e.g., il calzone classico).
learnerNotes: The word calzone derives from calza (sock/stocking) with the augmentative suffix -one, etymologically connected to trouser legs due to the folded shape. Be aware that English speakers commonly mispronounce this word; the correct Italian pronunciation is /kal'tzone/ with a /ts/ sound, not /z/. This is one of many Italian food terms that have been Americanized over time.

exampleSentences.italian: Sto preparando il calzone classico, ripieno di mozzarella, prosciutto cotto e pomodoro.
exampleSentences.english: I'm preparing the classic calzone filled with mozzarella, cooked ham and tomato.

exampleSentences.italian: I ragazzi seduti al tavolo numero cinque hanno ordinato tre calzoni e tre birre.
exampleSentences.english: The guys sitting at table number five have ordered three calzoni and three beers.

relatedExpressions.meaning: Puglian onion pie (traditional rounded shape from the Puglia region)
onion pizza (alternative name for calzone di cipolla)

grammarNotes: Solletico is a masculine noun with plural solletichi. It is commonly used in the expressions 'fare il solletico' (to tickle) and 'soffrire il solletico' (to be ticklish). The related verb solleticare is a synonym for fare il solletico and follows regular -are conjugation patterns.
learnerNotes: Solletico is primarily a noun, so remember to use 'fare il solletico' (to do the tickle) rather than the verb form for everyday conversation. The idiomatic expression 'non fare nemmeno il solletico' is useful for describing something with minimal impact—a colorful alternative to simply saying 'no effect.' Note that solletico can shift from literal (physical tickling) to figurative (excitement, desire, or incitement), so context is important.

exampleSentences.italian: Smettila di farmi il solletico!
exampleSentences.english: Stop tickling me!

exampleSentences.italian: Ma hai visto quanto è grosso? Un pugno dei tuoi non gli farebbe nemmeno il solletico!
exampleSentences.english: Did you see how big he is? If you punched him, it would have no effect on him!

exampleSentences.italian: Il solletico della curiosità
exampleSentences.english: The thrill of curiosity

relatedExpressions.meaning: to tickle (literally: to do the tickle)
to be ticklish (literally: to suffer from the tickle)
to have very little or no effect whatsoever

relatedExpressions.expression: non sentire il solletico di qualcosa
relatedExpressions.meaning: to not feel the desire for something
to tickle (verb; synonym for fare il solletico)

grammarNotes: As an adjective, nero changes to nera (feminine singular), neri (masculine plural), and nere (feminine plural) to agree with the noun. When used as a noun, un nero means 'a black person.' The augmentative form nerissimo intensifies the meaning to 'very black' or 'extremely black.'
learnerNotes: Nero has many figurative meanings, mostly negative: 'lavorare in nero' (illegal work), 'giornata nera' (bad day), 'essere arrabbiato nero' (furious). Note that 'nero' when referring to Black people or culture is still used in Italian, though 'africano' or 'afroamericano' are increasingly preferred in formal contexts. Be aware that Negro/negr- is an outdated/offensive term; use modern alternatives.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piace il tuo vestito nero. Dove l'hai comprato?
exampleSentences.english: I like your black dress. Where did you buy it?

exampleSentences.italian: Mio papà prende sempre una tazza di caffè nero al mattino.
exampleSentences.english: My dad always has a cup of black coffee in the morning.

exampleSentences.italian: Hanno mandato una squadra speciale per recuperare la scatola nera dell'aereo precipitato nella giungla.
exampleSentences.english: They sent a special team to recover the flight recorder of the plane that crashed in the jungle.

exampleSentences.italian: Tante persone lavorano in nero per non pagare le tasse.
exampleSentences.english: Many people work illegally to avoid paying taxes.

exampleSentences.italian: È stata una giornata nera per l'azienda. Il direttore è arrabbiato nero.
exampleSentences.english: It was a very bad day for the company. The director is furious.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to work illegally / to work under the table

englishTranslation: ciabatta bread / slipper / power strip / worn-out person or thing
grammarNotes: Feminine noun with regular plural form 'ciabatte'. In Italian, it derives from the word for 'slipper' due to the bread's flat, oblong shape. The word has multiple meanings depending on context: primarily a type of bread, but also used colloquially for a power strip/adapter or to describe something worn-out.
learnerNotes: The pronunciation difference between English and Italian lies in the double 'tt' (geminata): hold the consonant briefly before releasing, creating a short pause. Don't be confused by the multiple meanings—context determines whether ciabatta refers to bread, a slipper, or slang for something worn-out. The word entered English from Italian relatively recently (post-1982), so it's an excellent example of food terminology crossing languages.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho comprato tre ciabatte dal panettiere questa mattina.
exampleSentences.english: I bought three ciabatta loaves at the bakery this morning.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a classic Italian bread made from wheat, flour, water, salt, yeast and olive oil

englishTranslation: given that / since / seeing that / considering that / because / in view of the fact that
grammarNotes: Visto che is a causal conjunction that introduces a subordinate clause expressing the reason for the main clause. The verb in the visto che clause must be in the indicative mood, not the subjunctive. When used as a standalone adjective before a noun (without che), visto agrees in gender and number with that noun (visto, visti, vista, viste).
learnerNotes: Remember that visto che always takes the indicative mood, not subjunctive—this is critical for accuracy. When visto appears before a noun without che, treat it as an adjective and match gender/number (e.g., vista la difficoltà, visti i risultati). The colloquial visto e considerato che is more emphatic but conveys the same meaning as visto che alone.

exampleSentences.italian: Visto che era stanco, l'ho messo a dormire subito dopo cena.
exampleSentences.english: Since he was tired, I put him to sleep right after supper.

exampleSentences.italian: Visto il risultato…
exampleSentences.english: Given the result…

exampleSentences.italian: Visti i prezzi…
exampleSentences.english: Given the prices…

exampleSentences.italian: Vista la fatica…
exampleSentences.english: Given the effort…

exampleSentences.italian: Viste le difficoltà…
exampleSentences.english: Given the difficulties…

exampleSentences.italian: Sono abbastanza soddisfatto del risultato viste le difficoltà che abbiamo incontrato.
exampleSentences.english: I am quite satisfied with the result given the difficulties we encountered.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form crepacuori. Composed of crepare (colloquial verb meaning 'to die') + cuore (heart). Typically used with verbs like morire di or soffrire di to express the emotional or metaphorical impact of heartbreak.
learnerNotes: Crepacuore is colloquial and poetic; more common expressions for 'brokenhearted' include avere il cuore spezzato or essere affranto. The word combines crepare (informal for 'to die') with cuore, creating a vivid emotional image. Use morire di or soffrire di as the typical verbs pairing with crepacuore.

exampleSentences.italian: morire di crepacuore
exampleSentences.english: to die of a broken heart

exampleSentences.italian: soffrire di crepacuore
exampleSentences.english: to suffer from a broken heart

exampleSentences.italian: Dopo meno di un mese dalla scomparsa del marito, la vedova morì di crepacuore.
exampleSentences.english: Less than a month after her husband's passing, the widow died of a broken heart.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi si spezza il cuore a vederlo ridotto così.
exampleSentences.english: It breaks my heart to see him like that.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to have a broken heart (lit. to have a fragmented heart)
to have a broken heart (lit. to have a shattered heart)
to have a broken heart (lit. to have a heart in pieces)

grammarNotes: Pera is a feminine noun with plural pere. It derives from Latin pirum. Should not be confused with pero (masculine), which refers to the pear tree itself. Standard gender agreement applies with articles and adjectives.
learnerNotes: Pera is a high-frequency food vocabulary word. Be careful not to confuse pera (the fruit) with pero (the tree)—this is a common mistake for learners. Several idioms use pera metaphorically (weakness, foolishness, heroin use), so context is essential for understanding meaning; farsi una pera in particular is vulgar slang and should be avoided in formal settings.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piace raccogliere le pere dall'albero insieme ai miei fratelli.
exampleSentences.english: I like to pick pears from the tree with my brothers.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to fall asleep suddenly from fatigue; to fall head over heels in love; to be easily fooled
to be weak, feeble, lacking energy
to inject oneself with heroin (allusion to fist shape holding syringe)

relatedExpressions.expression: lasciar le pere in guardia all'orso
relatedExpressions.meaning: to naively trust an unreliable person

grammarNotes: Masculine noun dormiglione (plural dormiglioni) and feminine dormigliona (plural dormiglione). Forms derived from the verb dormire + suffix -one, which attaches to verbs to create agent nouns meaning 'one who often does X' or 'one characterized by X'. Agrees with gender of the person being described.
learnerNotes: Dormiglione is typically colloquial and affectionate rather than insulting. Remember that the -one suffix is productive in Italian for creating agent nouns from verbs. Be careful with gender agreement: use dormiglione for males and dormigliona for females, adjusting plurals accordingly (dormiglioni / dormiglione).

exampleSentences.italian: Svegliati, dormiglione! Abbiamo un sacco di cose da fare oggi.
exampleSentences.english: Wake up, sleepyhead! We have a lot of things to do today.

exampleSentences.italian: Io sono assai mattiniero, mentre lei è una gran dormigliona.
exampleSentences.english: I am a real early bird, while she is a late riser.

relatedExpressions.meaning: early riser / early bird (opposite of dormiglione)
big eater (similar -one suffix formation from mangiare)

grammarNotes: Incorreggibile has the same ending for both masculine and feminine in the singular form. In the plural, it becomes incorreggibili for both genders. While primarily an adjective, it can be used as a noun (l'incorreggibile = the incorrigible one), as in the Battisti song. It's invariable in singular across gender but changes only in plural.
learnerNotes: Incorreggibile is a cognate with English 'incorrigible,' making it relatively intuitive for English speakers. Note that while it can humorously describe a flirtatious person, it's also used seriously to describe systematic defects (smoking habits, poorly written work) that resist improvement. Be aware of register: it's colloquial when describing people playfully but more formal when discussing defects or character flaws.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei ancora tu L'incorreggibile
exampleSentences.english: It's still you, the incorrigible one

exampleSentences.italian: Chi fuma poche sigarette corre meno rischi rispetto ad un fumatore incorreggibile.
exampleSentences.english: Those who smoke only a few cigarettes run less risk than an incorrigible smoker.

exampleSentences.italian: Addirittura tre ragazze ti hanno dato il loro numero di telefono stasera? Ma sei un cascamorto incorreggibile!
exampleSentences.english: Three girls gave you their phone number tonight? You really are an incorrigible flirt!

exampleSentences.italian: Questo compito di matematica contiene veramente troppi errori. È praticamente incorreggibile.
exampleSentences.english: This maths assignment really does contain too many errors. It's practically impossible to correct.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural bottiglie. Derives from Spanish botilla rather than Latin. The diminutive form bottiglietta is used for small bottles (perfume, ink). Related adjective imbottigliato means 'bottled' or 'stuck in traffic.'
learnerNotes: Note the distinction between 'bottiglia da vino' (focusing on the bottle as a vessel) and 'bottiglia di vino' (focusing on the wine inside). Be aware that imbottigliato has dual meanings: 'bottled' and 'stuck in traffic,' so context is essential. The diminutive bottiglietta is worth learning for small bottles like perfume or medicine.

exampleSentences.italian: Puoi aprirmi questa bottiglia per favore? Non ci riesco.
exampleSentences.english: Can you open this bottle for me please? I can't do it.

exampleSentences.italian: Si è bevuto tutte le bottiglie di vino che erano rimaste giù in cantina!
exampleSentences.english: He drank all the bottles of wine that were left down in the cellar!

relatedExpressions.meaning: fake precious stones; low quality optics

grammarNotes: Water is a masculine noun (il water, un water). As a loanword from English 'water closet,' its plural form remains identical to the singular (i water, dei water). In Italian, the 'w' is pronounced like 'v' (vàter), similar to German 'wasser.'
learnerNotes: Although 'water' is a recognized loanword in Italian, it's not the most formal choice; 'gabinetto' or 'bagno' are safer for polite contexts. Note that 'water' sounds like 'vàter' to Italian ears—the 'w' is always pronounced as 'v'. Be cautious with 'cesso,' which is decidedly vulgar and should be avoided in formal situations.

exampleSentences.italian: il water
exampleSentences.english: the toilet

exampleSentences.italian: un water
exampleSentences.english: a toilet

exampleSentences.italian: i water
exampleSentences.english: the toilets

exampleSentences.italian: dei water
exampleSentences.english: some toilets

exampleSentences.italian: Pulire il water è il lavoretto di casa che odio di più.
exampleSentences.english: Cleaning the toilet bowl is the household chore I hate the most.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi scusi, dove posso trovare il water?
exampleSentences.english: Excuse me, where can I find the toilet?

exampleSentences.italian: Il bagno è in fondo al corridoio, dove c'è la scritta WC.
exampleSentences.english: The bathroom is at the end of the corridor, where the word WC is written.

relatedExpressions.meaning: water closet abbreviation (used on signs, pronounced /vuʧˈi/)

grammarNotes: Impavido is a four-form adjective with gender and number agreement: impavido (masc. sing.), impavida (fem. sing.), impavidi (masc. plur.), impavide (fem. plur.). It derives from Latin impavidus (im- prefix + pavidus 'coward'). The adverb form is impavidamente (fearlessly), or alternatively in modo impavido. When placed directly after a verb, impavido itself can function adverbially.
learnerNotes: Impavido is a literary and formal adjective rarely used in everyday conversation; coraggioso is more common in spoken Italian. Remember that it must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. The distinction between impavidamente and in modo impavido is stylistic; both are correct, but the adverb is more concise.

exampleSentences.italian: Il principe impavido sfidò il drago per liberare la principessa rinchiusa nella torre.
exampleSentences.english: The fearless prince challenged the dragon to free the princess locked up in the tower.

exampleSentences.italian: Il principe affrontò impavido il drago.
exampleSentences.english: The prince fearlessly faced the dragon.

englishTranslation: lookalike / doppelgänger / alter ego / double / twin / spitting image
grammarNotes: Sosia is an invariable noun, meaning the ending does not change for gender or number. It can be used with masculine or feminine articles (il/un sosia, la/una sosia) and plural forms (i/dei sosia, le/delle sosia), though some linguists argue it should remain masculine only. The feminine form is widely recognized in modern dictionaries and common in spoken Italian.
learnerNotes: Although some prescriptive linguists insist sosia should only be masculine, modern Italian usage widely accepts feminine forms (la sosia), and these appear in major dictionaries like Treccani. For learners, using either masculine or feminine is acceptable in contemporary Italian, but be aware of the traditionalist position if reading older texts or formal prescriptive sources. The word stems from Roman theatrical tradition (the god Mercury in Amphitruo) and carries a literary, somewhat elevated tone compared to colloquial synonyms like fotocopia or clone.

exampleSentences.italian: Dante è il sosia del boss mafioso Johnny Stecchino.
exampleSentences.english: Dante is the spitting image of the mob boss Johnny Stecchino.

exampleSentences.italian: Ieri ho visto una donna che ti assomiglia molto. Potrebbe essere la tua sosia!
exampleSentences.english: Yesterday I saw a woman that looks a lot like you. She could be your doppelgänger!

relatedExpressions.meaning: double, spitting image, body double (in cinema)
photocopy (used colloquially and in friendly conversation)
to be identical (literally: to be like two drops of water)

grammarNotes: Numero is a masculine noun; plural is numeri di telefono. The phrase can be shortened to just numero when context is clear. Related formal variants include numero telefonico, numero di contatto telefonico, and recapito telefonico (formal/official contexts).
learnerNotes: In Italian conversation, speakers often shorten 'numero di telefono' to just 'numero' when the context is clear—ask 'Fisso o cellulare?' if unsure which type of number is being discussed. The formal register variant 'recapito telefonico' is used in official documents and formal requests; note that 'recapito' alone means 'address' or 'delivery address.' Remember Italy's country code +39 must include the leading 0 from area codes when dialing from abroad (a rule change from pre-1998).

exampleSentences.italian: Mi dai il tuo numero di cellulare?
exampleSentences.english: Can you give me your mobile number?

exampleSentences.italian: Volentieri. Te lo scrivo su questo pezzo di carta.
exampleSentences.english: Certainly. I'll write it on this piece of paper.

exampleSentences.italian: Fisso o cellulare?
exampleSentences.english: Landline or mobile?

exampleSentences.italian: Mi serve anche un suo recapito telefonico.
exampleSentences.english: I also need your phone number.

exampleSentences.italian: Va bene il cellulare?
exampleSentences.english: Is my mobile ok?

exampleSentences.italian: Sì, ma se ha il fisso, scriva anche quello per favore.
exampleSentences.english: Yes, but if you have a landline, write it down too, please.

exampleSentences.italian: Ah, ho dimenticato di mettere +39 davanti al numero di telefono!
exampleSentences.english: Ah, I forgot to put +39 in front of the phone number!

exampleSentences.italian: Ecco perché non riuscivo a collegarmi.
exampleSentences.english: That's why I couldn't get through.

relatedExpressions.meaning: mobile phone number (starts with 3, usually 10 digits)

grammarNotes: As an adjective, rosso agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: rosso (masc. sing.), rossa (fem. sing.), rossi (masc. plur.), rosse (fem. plur.). The feminine form rossa should not be confused with rosa (pink), where the single 's' is pronounced like 'z'. When used as a noun, rosso can refer to a red-haired person (masc.) or abstract concepts like communism.
learnerNotes: Beware of confusing rossa (red, feminine) with rosa (pink)—they sound similar but have different meanings and pronunciations. Rosso has rich figurative uses: it can indicate danger (red light), communism (armata rossa), or debt (essere in rosso). Native speakers also use rosso alone to mean 'red wine' or 'red light,' so context is crucial for understanding.

exampleSentences.italian: un cappello rosso
exampleSentences.english: a red hat

exampleSentences.italian: una gonna rossa
exampleSentences.english: a red skirt

exampleSentences.italian: cappelli rossi
exampleSentences.english: red hats

exampleSentences.italian: gonne rosse
exampleSentences.english: red skirts

exampleSentences.italian: Le regalò una rosa rossa per San Valentino.
exampleSentences.english: He gave her a red rose for Valentine's Day.

exampleSentences.italian: Nel quartiere a luci rosse, un signore, alla guida di una Testarossa, è passato con il rosso dopo aver bevuto troppi bicchieri di rosso.
exampleSentences.english: In the red-light district, a gentleman, driving a Ferrari Testarossa, jumped a red light after drinking too much red wine.

exampleSentences.italian: Non appena la vide, divenne rosso come un papavero.
exampleSentences.english: As soon as he saw her, he went as red as a poppy.

relatedExpressions.meaning: pizza or pasta with tomato sauce
to be in the red, to be in debt
as red as a bell pepper

grammarNotes: Invariable noun that maintains the same form regardless of gender or number. Uses standard articles: un/l' (singular), degli/gli (plural masculine), un'/l' (singular feminine), delle/le (plural feminine). Formed from the verb attaccare (to attack) + briga (quarrel), literally 'quarrel-attacher.'
learnerNotes: This word is frequently used in informal contexts, especially when discussing online behavior or argumentative personalities. Remember it's invariable—don't add feminine or plural endings. The related verb 'attaccare briga' is a common collocation meaning 'to pick a fight,' so learning them together is useful.

exampleSentences.italian: Sembra gentile quando lo incontri di persona, ma sui forum in rete è un attaccabrighe.
exampleSentences.english: He seems nice when you meet him in person, but he always picks fights on online forums.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to pick a fight / to start an argument
less common variant where 'tt' and 'cc' are reversed (from accattare, meaning to plead or appeal for)
belligerent (from litigare, to argue or fight)
someone who gets involved in physical fights (from rissa, scuffle or brawl)

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural 'docce'. The verb 'fare la doccia' (to have a shower) can be used with or without the reflexive pronoun 'si' — 'farsi la doccia' emphasizes that you are performing the action on yourself. Both forms are grammatically correct with subtle differences in emphasis.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'doccia' is always feminine—use 'la doccia' not 'il doccia'. The reflexive form 'farsi la doccia' is very common in natural speech and worth learning as a fixed phrase. Be aware that 'doccia fredda' is an idiomatic expression meaning disappointment, not literally about water temperature.

exampleSentences.italian: Faccio sempre la doccia al mattino, non appena mi sveglio.
exampleSentences.english: I always have a shower in the morning, as soon as I wake up.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi faccio sempre la doccia al mattino, non appena mi sveglio.
exampleSentences.english: I always have a shower in the morning, as soon as I wake up. (lit. I have myself a shower in the morning, as soon as I wake up.)

exampleSentences.italian: La sua partenza improvvisa è stata una doccia fredda per tutti noi.
exampleSentences.english: His departure was a kick in the teeth for us all.

relatedExpressions.expression: fare la doccia / farsi la doccia

relatedExpressions.meaning: hot and cold water shower; rapid succession of good and bad events

grammarNotes: Purché introduces a conditional clause and requires the subjunctive mood in the dependent verb. It combines the archaic word pure ('only') with che ('that'). The conjunction can also appear in elliptical constructions without a complete verb, and occasionally in exclamations with meanings like 'Let's hope...!' or 'If only...!'
learnerNotes: Remember that the verb following purché must be in the subjunctive mood—this is non-negotiable and a common mistake for learners. Purché is more formal/literary than synonyms like basta che or sempre che, so context matters for register. In exclamatory uses, purché shifts meaning significantly ('Let's hope...'), so pay attention to context and punctuation.

exampleSentences.italian: Ti lascio venire con noi purché tu non mi metta in imbarazzo!
exampleSentences.english: I'll let you hang out with us as long as you don't embarrass me!

exampleSentences.italian: Potete giocare dentro purché non facciate troppo rumore.
exampleSentences.english: You can play inside as long as you don't make too much noise.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono ammessi anche i cani, purché tenuti al guinzaglio.
exampleSentences.english: Dogs are also allowed, provided that they are on a leash.

exampleSentences.italian: Purché sia vero!
exampleSentences.english: Let's hope it's true! If only it were true!

exampleSentences.italian: Nel bene o nel male, purché se ne parli.
exampleSentences.english: In the good or in the evil, as long as it is talked about.

exampleSentences.italian: Parlarne bene o parlarne male non importa, purché se ne parli.
exampleSentences.english: It doesn't matter if it is talked about positively or negatively, as long as it is talked about.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with regular plural pappe. The diminutive form pappetta is commonly used. Related verb pappare is regular (-are conjugation) with two distinct meanings: to devour food or to pocket/make off with money/valuables.
learnerNotes: Pappa has a dual register: it refers to actual soft food (baby food, overcooked pasta) but when addressing children, it becomes a general term for any meal regardless of texture, similar to "din-dins" in English. The verb pappare has two unrelated meanings—one for eating and one for illicit acquisition of money—so context is crucial. This is a colloquial, affectionate word rarely used in formal settings.

exampleSentences.italian: Vuoi che mangi questa pappa? Ma neanche morto! Mangiala tu!
exampleSentences.english: You want me to eat this mush? No way! You eat it!

exampleSentences.italian: Bambini, venite a tavola: la pappa è pronta!
exampleSentences.english: Kids, come to the table: breakfast / lunch / dinner is ready!

exampleSentences.italian: Ho dimenticato il risotto sui fornelli ed è diventato una pappetta immangiabile.
exampleSentences.english: I forgot the risotto on the stove and it became an inedible mushy mess.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to want to be spoon-fed / to find everything already done for you
to be perfectly matched, well-suited, best friends
to wolf down / to devour / to gobble up (food); to make off with / to pocket (money, inheritance)

grammarNotes: Calamaro is a masculine noun; the plural form is calamari. Grammatically, calamari functions as a mass noun in English when referring to the food dish. The word shares etymology with calamaio (inkwell), both deriving from the squid's black ink.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'calamari' is the plural form you'll typically see on Italian menus as the food dish. The colloquial use of 'calamari agli occhi' (bags under the eyes) is a vivid idiom—useful for describing tiredness. Be aware that totano is a dialectal/regional alternative, more common in certain parts of Italy, while calamaro remains the standard term.

exampleSentences.italian: Il calamaro si nutre principalmente nelle ore notturne.
exampleSentences.english: The squid eats primarily at night.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei tutto pallido e hai i calamari agli occhi! Stai male? – Un po', non ho chiuso occhio tutta la notte.
exampleSentences.english: You're all pale and you have bags under your eyes! Are you unwell? – A little, I didn't sleep all night.

relatedExpressions.meaning: bags under the eyes (colloquial; literally 'squids at the eyes')
European flying squid (alternative term, often translated as squid)

englishTranslation: to wander / to hang around / to loiter
grammarNotes: Gironzolare is a regular -are verb, making it straightforward to conjugate in all tenses. It derives from girare (to turn/to spin/to travel around). When expressing the sense of pursuing or hanging around a person, it is followed by the preposition intorno (a), meaning 'around.'
learnerNotes: Gironzolare has multiple contextual meanings: aimless wandering, loitering with suspicion, or pursuing someone romantically. Pay attention to context and whether intorno (a) is used to determine the intended meaning. Note that while gironzolare is neutral/colloquial, synonyms like bighellonare (from bighellone, 'loafer') carry slightly more negative connotations of wasting time.

exampleSentences.italian: È da più di tre ore che gironzola per le vie della città.
exampleSentences.english: She's been wandering the city streets for more than three hours.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai visto quel tipo strano che gironzola nell'atrio?
exampleSentences.english: Have you seen that weird guy hanging around in the foyer?

exampleSentences.italian: Ci sono sempre un sacco di ragazzi che gironzolano intorno a Laura.
exampleSentences.english: There are always a lot of boys hanging around Laura.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to hang around someone (with romantic or suspicious intent)
to waste time wandering around aimlessly
to wander around idly or aimlessly
to go around, to go for a stroll, to travel around

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural coperte. Derives from the past participle coperto of the verb coprire (to cover). Gender and number must agree with modifiers and articles. The diminutive copertina refers specifically to book covers and slip covers.
learnerNotes: Coperta has multiple meanings depending on context: primarily 'blanket' for bedding, but also 'deck' on a ship and 'cover' for books—the diminutive copertina is preferred for book covers. The common expression 'sotto le coperte' (under the covers) idiomatically means 'in bed.' Watch out: pile (fleece) is a loanword from English pronounced /pˈail/, not to be confused with pila (battery).

exampleSentences.italian: Amore, mi passi la coperta di lana?
exampleSentences.english: Can you pass me the wool blanket, my love?

exampleSentences.italian: Quale coperta di lana?
exampleSentences.english: Which wool blanket?

exampleSentences.italian: Quella lì sul divano, dietro di te.
exampleSentences.english: The one there on the sofa, behind you.

exampleSentences.italian: Non è lana, è pile.
exampleSentences.english: It's not wool, it's fleece!

exampleSentences.italian: Eh vabbè! Sempre una coperta è!
exampleSentences.english: Oh whatever! It's still a blanket!

exampleSentences.italian: Rimanere sotto le coperte
exampleSentences.english: to stay in bed (lit. to stay under the covers)

exampleSentences.italian: Mi metto sotto le coperte perché ho freddo ai piedi!
exampleSentences.english: I'm going to get under the covers because my feet are cold!

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piace molto la copertina di questo libro. Quasi quasi lo compro.
exampleSentences.english: I really like the cover of this book. I'm half-tempted to buy it.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to snuggle down under the covers

grammarNotes: Fruscio is a masculine noun (il fruscio). The plural form is fruscii, with a double 'i' at the end—an uncommon plural pattern in Italian. The word is onomatopoeic, created to imitate the sound it describes. The related verb frusciare means 'to rustle' or 'to swish.'
learnerNotes: Fruscio is an evocative but advanced vocabulary word—most useful for descriptive writing or audio terminology. Remember the unusual plural fruscii with double 'i'. In audio/music contexts, fruscio di fondo specifically refers to background noise, hiss, or the crackle of old recordings; this technical usage differs from the poetic sense of rustling leaves or water.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piace ascoltare il fruscio delle foglie mosse dal vento.
exampleSentences.english: I like listening to the rustle of the leaves blowing in the wind.

grammarNotes: As an adjective, fantastico agrees with gender and number: fantastico (masc. sing.), fantastica (fem. sing.), fantastici (masc. plur.), fantastiche (fem. plur.). The -o ending is used for masculine nouns and -a for feminine nouns. As a masculine singular noun, it means 'fantasy' or 'fantastic thing' in literary contexts.
learnerNotes: Fantastico is a true cognate with English 'fantastic,' making it easy to remember. Note that it functions as both an adjective (with gender/number agreement) and as a standalone exclamation or noun, so context determines its usage. Be careful not to confuse the adjective meaning 'wonderful' with its noun usage meaning 'fantasy' or 'something imaginary'—the latter is more literary and less common in everyday speech.

exampleSentences.italian: Non è fantastico questo locale?!
exampleSentences.english: Isn't this place fantastic?!

exampleSentences.italian: Vengo qui ogni fine settimana!
exampleSentences.english: I come here every weekend!

exampleSentences.italian: Vieni anche tu alla festa? Fantastico!
exampleSentences.english: You're coming to the party too? Fantastic!

exampleSentences.italian: Un racconto fantastico
exampleSentences.english: A fictional story

exampleSentences.italian: Una creatura fantastica
exampleSentences.english: An imaginary creature

exampleSentences.italian: Un'idea fantastica
exampleSentences.english: A far-fetched idea

exampleSentences.italian: Sto scrivendo una tesi sul fantastico nella letteratura moderna.
exampleSentences.english: I'm writing a thesis about fantasy in modern literature.

grammarNotes: Ciliegia is feminine (la ciliegia). The plural is ciliegie (modern standard) or ciliege (historical variant). The corresponding noun for cherry tree is ciliegio (masculine), formed by replacing the final -a with -o. The diminutive form ciliegina means 'little cherry' and refers specifically to glazed cherries used in desserts.
learnerNotes: Note that ciliegia can also function as an adjective meaning 'cherry-red in colour.' The idiomatic expression 'Una ciliegia tira l'altra' references the botanical fact that cherries grow in pairs attached by stems, making it easy to pick two at once—a clever memory aid. Be aware that 'amico ciliegia' is informal and playful, referencing the maggot (fruit fly larva) often found inside cherries.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho raccolto una manciata di ciliegie dal ciliegio in giardino.
exampleSentences.english: I picked a handful of cherries from the cherry tree in the garden.

exampleSentences.italian: Le bugie sono come le ciliegie: una tira l'altra.
exampleSentences.english: Once you start telling lies, you can't stop. (In the same way you can't stop eating cherries once you start.)

relatedExpressions.meaning: the cherry on top (the finishing touch to something already excellent)
One cherry pulls another / Cherries are addictive / Once I start eating cherries, I can't stop
cherry friend (a playful term for someone who is astute or cunning without naming them explicitly)

grammarNotes: Snello is a four-form adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: snello (masc. sing.), snella (fem. sing.), snelli (masc. plur.), snelle (fem. plur.). The ending changes systematically based on the subject's gender and plurality. This pattern follows standard Italian adjective agreement rules.
learnerNotes: Snello differs from its near-synonym magro in connotation: snello is complimentary and suggests an attractive, healthy slenderness, while magro can imply being too thin or scrawny. Beyond describing people's bodies, snello extends to describe things that are streamlined, functional, or free of unnecessary complexity. Interestingly, it derives from Germanic roots (German 'schnell' = fast) rather than Latin, reflecting historical language contact.

exampleSentences.italian: fisico snello
exampleSentences.english: slender physique (masculine, singular)

exampleSentences.italian: gamba snella
exampleSentences.english: slender leg (feminine, singular)

exampleSentences.italian: fisici snelli
exampleSentences.english: slender physiques (masculine, plural)

exampleSentences.italian: gambe snelle
exampleSentences.english: slender legs (feminine, plural)

exampleSentences.italian: Dopo aver seguito una dieta ferrea, Luigi è di nuovo snello.
exampleSentences.english: After following a strict diet, Luigi is once again slim.

exampleSentences.italian: stile snello
exampleSentences.english: simple style

exampleSentences.italian: processo snello
exampleSentences.english: simplified process

exampleSentences.italian: traffico snello
exampleSentences.english: free-moving traffic

exampleSentences.italian: prosa snella
exampleSentences.english: plain prose

exampleSentences.italian: architettura snella
exampleSentences.english: plain architecture

relatedExpressions.meaning: thin / skinny (often neutral or negative connotation)

grammarNotes: Paghetta is a feminine noun with plural form paghette. It is the diminutive form of paga (salary/pay/wages), formed by adding the diminutive suffix -etta. Like all Italian nouns, it requires gender agreement with articles and adjectives.
learnerNotes: Paghetta is commonly used in Italian families to refer to a regular allowance given to children, often as a reward for chores or as a way to teach money management. The diminutive form -etta makes it sound affectionate and is typical for small amounts of money given to children. Note that while mancetta exists as a synonym, paghetta is far more common in everyday Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: I miei genitori mi danno la paghetta ogni settimana.
exampleSentences.english: My parents give me pocket money every week.

relatedExpressions.meaning: salary, pay, wages (the base word from which paghetta is derived)
tip, gratuity (a far less common synonym for paghetta; diminutive of mancia)

grammarNotes: Bambola is a feminine noun with plural bambole. It derives from the obsolete term bambo (child/foolish), similar to bambino. The diminutive bambolotto refers to a male doll or affectionately to a chubby baby of either sex.
learnerNotes: Bambola has multiple meanings: the primary sense is a toy doll, but it also carries a colloquial (and sometimes derogatory) meaning for an attractive young woman. In sports contexts, it refers to performance collapse or mental fatigue. Be careful not to confuse bambola with bambolotto (male doll or chubby baby), and remember that using bambola for a woman can be offensive depending on context.

exampleSentences.italian: La bambina passa tutto il suo tempo a giocare con le bambole.
exampleSentences.english: The little girl spends all her time playing with dolls.

exampleSentences.italian: giocare con le bambole
exampleSentences.english: to play with dolls

exampleSentences.italian: vestire / svestire una bambola
exampleSentences.english: to dress / undress a doll

exampleSentences.italian: collezionare bambole
exampleSentences.english: to collect dolls

exampleSentences.italian: Che bambola!
exampleSentences.english: What a babe!

exampleSentences.italian: Invece di rimanere lì seduto a pettinare le bambole, perché non vieni a darmi una mano?
exampleSentences.english: Instead of sitting there twiddling your thumbs, why don't you come and give me a hand?

relatedExpressions.meaning: male doll; affectionate term for a chubby baby
to no longer be able to cope or focus due to fatigue or overexertion (sports jargon)
a performance crisis; to be in a state of stupor (sports jargon)
to waste time; to do something utterly pointless

grammarNotes: Despite its -a ending, artista is both masculine and feminine. Plurals are artisti (male/mixed) and artiste (female only). Gender is determined by the indefinite article: un artista (male) vs un'artista (female). Both use the definite article l'.
learnerNotes: Artista is a common false cognate for gender agreement: it looks feminine but applies equally to men and women—use the indefinite article to signal gender. Beyond visual artists, artista broadly covers entertainers, performers, and actors. It can also describe someone skilled in any field (computer whiz, financial wizard) or who appreciates beauty and has an artistic temperament.

exampleSentences.italian: Mauro sta studiando gli artisti del Rinascimento.
exampleSentences.english: Mauro is studying the artists of the Renaissance.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho sempre voluto essere un artista di teatro.
exampleSentences.english: I've always wanted to be a stage performer.

exampleSentences.italian: un artista del computer
exampleSentences.english: a computer whiz

exampleSentences.italian: un artista della finanza
exampleSentences.english: a financial whiz

exampleSentences.italian: Paola ha un'anima d'artista.
exampleSentences.english: Paola has the soul of an artist.

grammarNotes: Bruciapelo is masculine and invariable (does not change form). The expression a bruciapelo consists of the preposition 'a' + bruciapelo. It is derived from the verb bruciare (to burn) + pelo (hair), literally meaning to burn hair at close range. The word can also appear without 'a' in technical textile contexts.
learnerNotes: A bruciapelo has two distinct uses: the literal meaning relates to shooting at very close range, but the figurative sense (catching someone off guard with a sudden question or statement) is much more common in modern Italian. Be aware that this expression is not about shooting guns in most everyday contexts—it's typically used figuratively in conversation and news media to mean 'abruptly' or 'without warning.'

exampleSentences.italian: Il criminale gli sparò a bruciapelo, uccidendolo.
exampleSentences.english: The criminal shot him point-blank, killing him.

exampleSentences.italian: La mia ragazza mi chiese a bruciapelo se ero ancora felice con lei.
exampleSentences.english: My girlfriend asked me point-blank if I was still happy with her.

exampleSentences.italian: Il presidente è abituato a ricevere domande fatte a bruciapelo.
exampleSentences.english: The president is used to receiving pointed questions.

relatedExpressions.meaning: Technical term: a machine that burns the down/nap of cotton fabric (macchina bruciapelo)

grammarNotes: Eccellente is invariable in the singular form for both masculine and feminine nouns (un lavoro eccellente, un'idea eccellente). In the plural, it becomes eccellenti with an -i ending (lavori eccellenti). The adjective can be placed either before or after the noun it modifies without significant change in meaning.
learnerNotes: Eccellente is a cognate with English 'excellent,' making it easy to remember. While buono and squisito are more commonly used for food quality, eccellente works perfectly well in formal contexts. Note that in journalism and archaic Italian, eccellente can refer to VIPs or people of high status, not just the quality of objects—a usage that extends beyond the typical 'excellent' meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: un lavoro eccellente
exampleSentences.english: an excellent job

exampleSentences.italian: un giocatore eccellente
exampleSentences.english: an excellent player

exampleSentences.italian: un pittore eccellente
exampleSentences.english: an excellent painter

exampleSentences.italian: uno scrittore eccellente
exampleSentences.english: an excellent writer

exampleSentences.italian: una prestazione eccellente
exampleSentences.english: an excellent performance

exampleSentences.italian: un'idea eccellente
exampleSentences.english: an excellent idea

exampleSentences.italian: un risultato eccellente
exampleSentences.english: an excellent result

exampleSentences.italian: un eccellente scrittore
exampleSentences.english: an excellent writer

exampleSentences.italian: Il rapporto qualità-prezzo è davvero eccellente.
exampleSentences.english: It is truly excellent value for money.

exampleSentences.italian: C'erano molti personaggi eccellenti all'inaugurazione della nuova stazione.
exampleSentences.english: There were many VIPs at the opening of the new station.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a VIP or person of considerable fame

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural form 'tate'. Tata is onomatopoeic, mimicking baby talk similar to 'nanna' (nap/sleep) and 'pappa' (baby food). The word typically denotes a professional full-time childcare worker rather than an occasional teenage babysitter. When referring to occasional babysitters, Italian speakers often use the English loanword 'babysitter' pronounced with an Italian accent.
learnerNotes: Tata specifically refers to a professional childcare worker, not a teenager who occasionally babysits—for the latter, Italians use the English word 'babysitter'. The word is onomatopoeic, which makes it memorable and authentic to baby-directed speech. Be careful not to confuse tata with its near-synonym bambinaia, which emphasizes salaried, custodial responsibility.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho fatto la tata a tempo pieno presso una famiglia benestante di Torino.
exampleSentences.english: I worked as a full-time nanny for a wealthy family from Turin.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a woman who sells her milk to another mother, or takes care of a baby in place of the mother
a salaried woman responsible for the care and custody of young children in a family
a salaried woman who takes care of the house and gives children an education (governess)

englishTranslation: relentless / obstinate / diehard / passionate / dogged / fierce / stubborn / tenacious
grammarNotes: Accanito is an adjective derived from 'cane' (dog). It agrees with the noun it modifies: masculine singular accanito, feminine singular accanita, masculine plural accaniti, feminine plural accanite. The word can carry positive connotations (passionate, tenacious) or negative ones (obstinate, violent) depending on context.
learnerNotes: Accanito is tricky because it carries dual connotations—use context carefully to understand whether it's complimentary (passionate fan) or critical (stubborn person). The related verb accanirsi and noun accanimento expand its usage; note that accanimento especially emphasizes the intensity or fury of an action. Remember the etymological link to 'cane' (dog) to help memorize the 'unrelenting grip' metaphor underlying the word.

exampleSentences.italian: Mario è un tifoso accanito della Juve.
exampleSentences.english: Mario is a diehard Juve fan.

exampleSentences.italian: Mio zio è un fumatore accanito.
exampleSentences.english: My uncle is a relentless smoker.

exampleSentences.italian: Il circuito di Le Mans è stato teatro di una lotta accanita tra i due piloti.
exampleSentences.english: Le Mans' racetrack was the scene of a fierce battle between the two drivers.

exampleSentences.italian: Il governo corrotto si è accanito contro il popolo.
exampleSentences.english: The corrupt government persecuted the people.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to pick on (someone) / to throw oneself into (something) / to rage (against something)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form menefreghismi. Derived from the expression 'me ne frego' + suffix '-ismo' (-ism). The related adjective/noun menefreghista describes a person with this attitude and can also function as an adjective. Both forms are invariable in gender but menefreghista can take plural -i/-e depending on context.
learnerNotes: Menefreghismo is a distinctly Italian concept without a direct English equivalent, making it useful for expressing complex attitudes about indifference. The word is somewhat informal and colloquial, so use it carefully in formal contexts. Note the related verb fregarsene in all its conjugations—it's colloquial but widely understood and useful for expressing 'not caring' in everyday speech.

exampleSentences.italian: Non è un ragazzo cattivo, ma il suo menefreghismo lo rende antipatico a tutti.
exampleSentences.english: He's not a bad guy, but his couldn't-care-less-attitude makes him appear unpleasant to everybody.

exampleSentences.italian: In ufficio fa sempre il menefreghista. Prima o poi lo licenzieranno.
exampleSentences.english: He always has an uncaring attitude at the office. Sooner or later they'll fire him.

relatedExpressions.meaning: I don't care / I don't give a damn
to not care, to care less (intransitive pronominal verb)
a person who doesn't care; uncaring (noun or adjective)

grammarNotes: Emozionato is an adjective that agrees in gender and number with the subject. Masculine singular: emozionato; feminine singular: emozionata; masculine plural: emozionati; feminine plural: emozionate. The word derives from the verbs emozionare (to move/to touch) and emozionarsi (to be moved/to be touched).
learnerNotes: Remember that emozionato can express both positive emotions (excitement, being moved) and negative ones (nervousness, being worked up)—context determines the meaning. Always check the gender and number of the noun it modifies to use the correct adjective ending. The related verb emozionarsi is reflexive; use it when expressing that someone is moved or touched by something (e.g., Mi sono emozionato = I was moved).

exampleSentences.italian: Luigi è molto emozionato per la partita di stasera.
exampleSentences.english: Luigi is very excited about tonight's game.

exampleSentences.italian: L'attrice era visibilmente emozionata durante la premiazione.
exampleSentences.english: The actress was visibly moved during the award ceremony.

exampleSentences.italian: È talmente emozionato per l'esame di domani che non riesce a stare fermo.
exampleSentences.english: He's so worked up about tomorrow's exam that he can't stay still.

exampleSentences.italian: un uomo emozionato
exampleSentences.english: an excited / moved / nervous man

exampleSentences.italian: una persona emozionata
exampleSentences.english: an excited / moved / nervous person

exampleSentences.italian: dei candidati emozionati
exampleSentences.english: excited / moved / nervous candidates

exampleSentences.italian: delle ragazze emozionate
exampleSentences.english: excited / moved / nervous girls

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be moved / to be touched

grammarNotes: As an adjective, matto agrees with gender and number: -o (masculine singular), -a (feminine singular), -i (masculine plural), -e (feminine plural). It can also function as a noun meaning 'lunatic' or 'crazy person'. Commonly used with essere (to be), andare (to go), and diventare (to become).
learnerNotes: Matto is more colloquial than its synonyms pazzo (mad) and folle (insane). In colloquial speech, when matto modifies a noun (e.g., 'una voglia matta'), it means 'intense' or 'insatiable' rather than literally 'crazy'. Note that scacco matto (checkmate) is a common fixed expression in chess terminology—scacchi (plural) refers to the game of chess itself.

exampleSentences.english: crazy cats (masculine, plural)

exampleSentences.english: crazy people (feminine, plural)

exampleSentences.italian: È diventato matto dopo aver scontato dieci anni di carcere.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei matto?
exampleSentences.english: Are you crazy?

exampleSentences.italian: Fossi matto!
exampleSentences.english: What do you think I am, crazy? (If I were crazy!)

exampleSentences.italian: Ho una voglia matta di andare in vacanza!
exampleSentences.english: I'm dying to go on vacation! (I have an intense desire to go on vacation!)

exampleSentences.english: (This traffic) is enough to make you go mad!

to be stark raving mad (literally: to be crazy enough to be tied up)
to be unpredictable (literally: to be crazy like a horse; used in a kind or playful way)

relatedExpressions.expression: Essere come il matto dei tarocchi
relatedExpressions.meaning: to be everywhere and always appreciated (literally: to be like the fool of the tarot cards)

grammarNotes: Ghianda is a feminine noun requiring feminine articles and adjectives. The definite article is 'la' (singular) and 'le' (plural); the indefinite article is 'una' (singular) and 'delle' (plural, partitive). Regular plural formation: ghianda → ghiande.
learnerNotes: Remember that ghianda is feminine, so you must use 'la' and 'una' in the singular form. The plural 'ghiande' is regular and commonly appears in nature or ecology contexts. The related word 'ghiandaia' (jay) cleverly derives from ghianda, making it a useful mnemonic for remembering both terms.

exampleSentences.italian: Tutti sanno che gli scoiattoli adorano le ghiande.
exampleSentences.english: Everyone knows that squirrels love acorns.

relatedExpressions.meaning: oak tree (the tree that produces acorns)
cupule (the cup-like hat of an acorn)

grammarNotes: Acciuga is feminine (l'acciuga, un'acciuga). The plural form is acciughe (le acciughe, delle acciughe). Like many Italian nouns ending in -a, it follows regular feminine singular/plural patterns. The definite article contracts to l' before the singular form due to the vowel.
learnerNotes: The plural acciughe is much more common in everyday use than the singular. Note the figurative use: calling someone 'un'acciuga' (an anchovy) means they are very thin—a common, affectionate nickname in Italian. The idiom 'stare pigiati come acciughe' uses the colloquial verb pigiare (to press/push) and is useful for describing crowded spaces.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei una pizza con le acciughe e una birra rossa.
exampleSentences.english: I would like a pizza with anchovies and a red beer.

exampleSentences.italian: Sara è diventata magra come un'acciuga da quando ha cominciato a correre tutti i giorni.
exampleSentences.english: Sara has become as thin as a rake ever since she started running every day.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be packed like sardines (literally: to be pressed like anchovies)

grammarNotes: Chiave is a feminine noun. Singular: la chiave; Plural: le chiavi. The word has multiple figurative meanings (solution, means of access, strategic point). In compound nouns like 'parole chiave' (keywords), the second noun doesn't agree in number with the first.
learnerNotes: Italian has no single verb meaning 'to lock'—use 'chiudere a chiave' instead. Note the vulgar slang verb 'chiavare' derived from chiave; avoid it unless you know the context well. Be careful with compound nouns like 'parole chiave' where the second word stays singular despite being semantically plural.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho perso le chiavi di casa! Forse le ho lasciate in ufficio. Vado a controllare, sempre che io riesca a trovare le chiavi della macchina!
exampleSentences.english: I've lost my house keys. Maybe I left them at the office. I'll go and check, that is if I can find the car keys!

exampleSentences.italian: Non riesco ad infilare la chiave nella serratura. Mi sa che mi hanno dato quella sbagliata.
exampleSentences.english: I can't insert the key into the hole. I think they gave me the wrong one.

exampleSentences.italian: Esprimere i propri sentimenti è spesso la chiave per risolvere i problemi coniugali.
exampleSentences.english: Expressing one's feelings is often the solution to solving marital issues.

exampleSentences.italian: Singapore fu la chiave per le attività commerciali della Compagnia Britannica delle Indie Orientali.
exampleSentences.english: Singapore was the key for the trade activities of the British East India Company.

exampleSentences.italian: Non trovo più la mia chiavetta USB. Dentro ci sono le chiavi di accesso di tutto l'ufficio. Sono nei guai!
exampleSentences.english: I can't find my USB stick. Inside there are all the office's passwords. I'm in trouble!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to lock (literally: to close with a key)
to put under lock and key; to keep safe or hidden; to lock someone up

relatedExpressions.expression: avere le chiavi del cuore di qualcuno
relatedExpressions.meaning: to be able to influence someone (lit. to have the keys to someone's heart)

grammarNotes: Voglia is a feminine noun with plural form voglie. It typically appears in the construction avere voglia di (to have a desire/craving for), which expresses an impulsive or dispositional desire rather than a command. Use volere for emphatic commands instead. The conditional form avrei voglia di softens the intensity of desire.
learnerNotes: Distinguish avere voglia di from volere: the former expresses impulsive desire or disposition (I feel like...), while volere is for statements of will or commands. Note that voglia has an unexpected secondary meaning—birthmark—stemming from folklore about pregnant women's unsatisfied cravings. The plural voglie can mean tantrums in children or sexual desire depending on context.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho voglia di un gelato al cioccolato
exampleSentences.english: I have a craving for chocolate ice cream

exampleSentences.italian: Non ho voglia di studiare adesso
exampleSentences.english: I don't feel like studying now

exampleSentences.italian: Ho voglia di fare una passeggiata nel bosco
exampleSentences.english: I am longing for a walk in the woods

exampleSentences.english: I have a craving for pizza tonight. Should we go out for dinner?

exampleSentences.italian: Avrei voglia di un gelato al cioccolato
exampleSentences.english: I would like a chocolate ice cream / I feel like a chocolate ice cream

exampleSentences.italian: Avrei voglia di fare una passeggiata
exampleSentences.english: I would like to go for a walk / I feel like going for a walk

exampleSentences.italian: Hai voglia a parlare per due ore, tanto nessuno ti dà retta
exampleSentences.english: You can talk for hours if you want, but no one will listen to you

exampleSentences.italian: Mio figlio ha una voglia di fragola sulla nuca
exampleSentences.english: My son has a strawberry birthmark on the back of his neck

relatedExpressions.meaning: to have a real desire for something

relatedExpressions.expression: avere una voglia matta di fare qualcosa

restare con la voglia in corpo

I have a desire for you (sexual context)

grammarNotes: In quanto is a conjunctive phrase used to introduce a reason or role. It can be followed directly by a noun (profession/role) where it means 'as', or used as a conjunction meaning 'since/because'. The variant 'in quanto che' (with che) carries the same meaning but is less common. Word order remains flexible depending on context.
learnerNotes: When 'in quanto' is followed by a profession or role noun, it must be translated as 'as' (not 'since/because'). Avoid confusing this phrase with 'quanto' alone, which means 'how much/how many'. The che variant is grammatically correct but stylistically less frequent in modern Italian—stick with the simpler form unless you encounter it in reading.

exampleSentences.italian: Non lo chiamo più in quanto non risponde mai al telefono.
exampleSentences.english: I don't call him anymore as he never answers the phone.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono stanco morto in quanto che mio figlio mi ha tenuto sveglio tutta la notte.
exampleSentences.english: I'm exhausted because my son kept me up all night.

exampleSentences.italian: Ti parlo in quanto medico e in quanto amico: non prendere quella medicina!
exampleSentences.english: I'm speaking to you as a doctor and as a friend: don't take that medicine!

relatedExpressions.meaning: as a doctor (expressing role or capacity)
as an expert (expressing role or capacity)
since / because (variant form with che, less common)

grammarNotes: Sedia is a feminine noun derived from the Latin verb sedere (to sit). The plural form is sedie. It follows regular feminine noun patterns: la sedia (singular), le sedie (plural). Note that diminutives seggiolino and seggiolone are used specifically for child seats, not the standard sedia.
learnerNotes: Remember that sedia is feminine (la sedia), not masculine. Use seggiolino/seggiolone for children's car seats and high chairs, not sedia. In formal contexts, prefer accomodarsi or prendere posto over sedersi when inviting someone to sit; save sedersi for casual situations or commands (Siediti!).

exampleSentences.italian: Il sedile e lo schienale di questa sedia sono molto comodi, però i braccioli sono un po' piccoli.
exampleSentences.english: The seat and the back of this chair are very comfortable, but the arms are a bit small.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi scusi signore, se si può accomodare gentilmente, lo spettacolo sta per iniziare. Grazie!
exampleSentences.english: Excuse me sir, if you could kindly take a seat, the show is about to start. Thank you!

exampleSentences.italian: Mi scusi signore, se può prendere posto gentilmente, lo spettacolo sta per iniziare. Grazie!
exampleSentences.english: Excuse me sir, if you could kindly take a seat, the show is about to start. Thank you!

exampleSentences.italian: Ciao Gianni! Entra pure! Prendi una sedia lì nell'angolo e siediti con noi. Vuoi una birra?
exampleSentences.english: Hi Gianni! Come in! Take a chair from the corner there and sit with us. Do you want a beer?

exampleSentences.italian: Siediti!
exampleSentences.english: Sit down!

exampleSentences.italian: Si sieda!
exampleSentences.english: Sit down! (formal)

relatedExpressions.meaning: to play for the chairs (act in front of a small number of spectators; to talk in vain)
to warm the chair (occupy a job role without doing anything)
to be seated on two chairs (maneuver between two different people or situations to make the most of both)
to sit down, to get comfortable

englishTranslation: outline / silhouette / shape / template / cut-out / target
grammarNotes: Sagoma is a feminine noun. The singular is 'la sagoma' and the plural is 'le sagome'. It agrees with feminine articles and adjectives. The word has multiple semantic fields: architectural/aesthetic shapes, physical templates/cut-outs, shooting targets, and colloquially, an amusing or unusual person.
learnerNotes: Sagoma has four distinct uses: architectural silhouettes, physical templates for copying, shooting targets, and colloquial reference to an amusing person. The colloquial 'character' meaning is informal and affectionate—be cautious using it without established rapport. Don't confuse sagoma with 'forma' (shape/form)—sagoma emphasizes the visual outline or a physical reproduction for practical purposes.

exampleSentences.italian: Riesco a vedere la sagoma di una nave in lontananza.
exampleSentences.english: I can see the outline of a ship off in the distance.

exampleSentences.italian: La leggera curvatura dello schienale addolcisce la sagoma della sedia.
exampleSentences.english: The slight curvature of the back softens the shape of the chair.

exampleSentences.italian: Hanno messo una sagoma di cartone di Babbo Natale all'entrata del centro commerciale.
exampleSentences.english: They put a cardboard cutout of Santa Claus at the mall entrance.

exampleSentences.italian: La forma di ogni pezzo è definita imbastendo la stoffa su una sagoma di carta.
exampleSentences.english: The shape of each piece is defined by tacking the fabric to a paper template.

exampleSentences.italian: L'agente ha mirato con precisione, colpendo la sagoma al centro.
exampleSentences.english: The agent aimed with precision, hitting the target at the centre.

exampleSentences.italian: Tua figlia è davvero una sagoma. Mi fa sempre ridere con le sue barzellette!
exampleSentences.english: Your daughter is a real card. She always makes me laugh with her jokes!

relatedExpressions.meaning: a cardboard cutout or silhouette figure
the architectural profile or outline of a building
to be an amusing or unusual character (colloquial)

grammarNotes: Marciapiede is a masculine noun derived from the verb marciare (to walk) and piedi (feet). The singular form is 'il marciapiede' and the plural is 'i marciapiedi'. It follows regular masculine noun patterns with articles un/il in singular and dei/i in plural.
learnerNotes: Note that marciapiede has two distinct uses: the common one for sidewalks/pavements, and a specialized railway term meaning 'platform.' In train stations, use marciapiede generically or binario when mentioning a specific platform number. Be aware the verb 'battere' with marciapiede carries a strong connotation related to illegal street solicitation, so avoid this collocation in neutral contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: camminare lungo il marciapiede
exampleSentences.english: to walk along the sidewalk

exampleSentences.italian: stare sul marciapiede
exampleSentences.english: to stay on the sidewalk

exampleSentences.italian: salire sul marciapiede
exampleSentences.english: to step onto the sidewalk

exampleSentences.italian: scendere dal marciapiede
exampleSentences.english: to step off the sidewalk

exampleSentences.italian: costeggiare il marciapiede
exampleSentences.english: to run along the sidewalk

exampleSentences.italian: I pedoni devono camminare sul marciapiede, mentre le biciclette devono circolare sulla pista ciclabile (laddove presente) o sulla parte destra della carreggiata.
exampleSentences.english: Pedestrians must walk on the sidewalk, while bikes must circulate on the cycle path (where present) or on the right side of the freeway.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to walk the streets (reference to prostitutes soliciting clients)
platform (alternative to binario when not specifying platform number)

grammarNotes: Mobile is a masculine noun in the furniture sense: il mobile (singular), i mobili (plural). The plural mobili generally refers to furniture as a whole, though the singular is also used in contexts like 'la fiera del mobile' (furniture show). As an adjective, mobile means 'movable or not fixed' and agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies.
learnerNotes: Beware: English speakers often say 'telefono mobile' but Italians use 'telefono cellulare' or simply 'cellulare' for mobile phones instead. The word mobile as a noun (furniture) is masculine and commonly used in plural form (i mobili). As an adjective, mobile means 'movable/not fixed' and is distinct from the English noun sense—use context carefully to determine which meaning applies.

exampleSentences.italian: Non devi per forza comprare dei mobili nuovi.
exampleSentences.english: You don't have to buy new furniture.

exampleSentences.italian: Puoi trovare un sacco di roba di seconda mano in ottime condizioni.
exampleSentences.english: You can find a lot of stuff second-hand in excellent condition.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho confrontato le varie offerte di telefonia mobile ma sono indeciso su quale scegliere.
exampleSentences.english: I've compared the various offers of mobile phone operators, but I'm undecided about which one to choose.

exampleSentences.italian: La gamba di questo tavolo è un po' mobile.
exampleSentences.english: The leg of this table is a bit wobbly.

exampleSentences.italian: Se mi dai un cacciavite, provo a sistemarla.
exampleSentences.english: If you give me a screwdriver, I can try to fix it.

exampleSentences.italian: Il capo della mobile è arrivato, capitano.
exampleSentences.english: The head of the flying squad has arrived, captain.

relatedExpressions.meaning: The woman is fickle (famous Rigoletto aria)

grammarNotes: Rana is a feminine noun (la rana, una rana). Its plural is rane (le rane, delle rane). It derives from Latin and maintains the same spelling. The word can be used figuratively to denote a short, ugly person, though ranocchio is preferred in fairy tales and as an affectionate term for children.
learnerNotes: Remember that rana is feminine (la rana), while the alternative ranocchio is masculine (il ranocchio). The word rana has multiple contexts: literal (the animal), figurative (insulting), and specialized (breaststroke swimming style). Note that in English 'frog' and 'toad' are different, but in Italian toad is rospo (masculine), a completely different word.

exampleSentences.italian: La rana saltò nello stagno gracidando.
exampleSentences.english: The frog jumped into the pond with a croak.

exampleSentences.italian: Dopo aver imparato lo stile cagnolino, ho provato a nuotare a rana.
exampleSentences.english: After learning the dog-paddle, I tried doing the breaststroke.

relatedExpressions.meaning: frog (masculine; used in fairy tales and affectionately with children)

relatedExpressions.expression: Avere le gambe come una rana
relatedExpressions.meaning: to have legs that stick out to the side
to be full of pride, arrogance

relatedExpressions.expression: Fare come la rana con il bue

grammarNotes: Asciugacapelli is a masculine noun composed of the verb asciugare (to dry) and capelli (hair). It is invariable, meaning the plural form is identical to the singular form (l'asciugacapelli / gli asciugacapelli). Like all masculine nouns, it uses the articles un/il in singular and degli/gli in plural.
learnerNotes: While asciugacapelli is the formal/standard term, the colloquial fon is very commonly used in everyday Italian, especially in northern regions. Be aware that fon is sometimes misspelled as 'phon' but both refer to the same appliance. The invariable plural form (same singular and plural) is a key feature—don't add an 'i' at the end for plurals.

exampleSentences.italian: L'asciugacapelli ha cominciato a emanare uno strano odore di bruciato.
exampleSentences.english: The hairdryer has started to give off a strange burning smell.

exampleSentences.italian: Non trovo più il fon. L'hai visto da qualche parte?
exampleSentences.english: I can't find the hairdryer. Have you seen it anywhere?

relatedExpressions.meaning: hairdryer (colloquial alternative term, derived from German Föhn)

grammarNotes: Pappagallo is a masculine noun. The plural is pappagalli. It follows regular -o/-i masculine declension patterns: un pappagallo (singular), dei pappagalli (plural). The article changes accordingly: il pappagallo (definite singular), i pappagalli (definite plural).
learnerNotes: The expressions 'ripetere a pappagallo' and 'fare il pappagallo' are idiomatic and refer to mindlessly repeating someone's words, like a parrot mimicking speech. 'Spappagallare' uses the intensive s- prefix combined with pappagallo to intensify the meaning. Be aware that in casual speech, Italians would say 'Ma che bel pappagallo' rather than 'Ma che bello pappagallo' (the song uses bello for rhythmic purposes).

exampleSentences.italian: Ieri ho visitato uno zoo e ho visto tanti pappagalli colorati.
exampleSentences.english: Yesterday I visited a zoo and saw a lot of colourful parrots.

exampleSentences.italian: Smettila di fare il pappagallo!
exampleSentences.english: Stop repeating everything!

exampleSentences.italian: Ma che bello pappagallo Tutto verde l'occhio giallo
exampleSentences.english: What a beautiful parrot, all green with a yellow eye

grammarNotes: Cellulare is a masculine noun. Singular forms: un cellulare, il cellulare. Plural forms: dei cellulari, i cellulari. It derives from Latin cellularis, from cellula meaning 'little chamber.' The word has secondary meanings as a noun (prison/police van) and as an adjective (cellular, relating to biology).
learnerNotes: While cellulare is the standard Italian term, smartphone is commonly used for modern devices (pronounced with Italian accent, 'zm' instead of 'sm'). The colloquial telefonino is equally widespread in everyday speech. Note the idiomatic expression fare uno squillo—a cultural practice of missed calls used for signaling without actual conversation.

exampleSentences.italian: Uffa, la pagina non si sta caricando! Eppure ho tre tacche sul cellulare!
exampleSentences.english: Darn, the page isn't loading! Yet I've got three bars on my cell phone!

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi ricordo dove ho lasciato il telefonino!
exampleSentences.english: I can't remember where I left my cell phone!

exampleSentences.italian: Ti faccio uno squillo quando arrivo!
exampleSentences.english: I'll give you a ring (implied: but don't pick up) when I get there!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to call someone and let the phone ring once or twice then hang up

grammarNotes: Tardi is an invariable adverb used to describe when something happens. It pairs with verbs like arrivare, tornare, svegliarsi, and alzarsi. The related adjective tardo agrees with gender and number (-o, -a, -i, -e). Tardi should not be used with essere to mean 'to be late to an event'; use essere in ritardo instead.
learnerNotes: Critical distinction: use tardi to say 'it's late' (È tardi) or to describe when an action occurs (arrivare tardi). Use essere in ritardo to say a person is late to a specific event (Sono in ritardo). Both tardi and in ritardo can work with certain verbs like arrivare, but only in ritardo works with essere + personal pronoun for appointment lateness. The adjective tardo means both 'late' (part of period: tardo pomeriggio) and 'slow' (characteristics); context determines meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: Non è un po' tardi per andare in banca?
exampleSentences.english: Isn't it a bit too late to go to the bank?

exampleSentences.italian: Ieri sera abbiamo fatto tardi perché ci divertivamo un sacco.
exampleSentences.english: We were up late last night because we were having so much fun.

exampleSentences.italian: Si sta facendo tardi. Dovremmo tornare a casa prima che la mamma cominci a preoccuparsi!
exampleSentences.english: It's getting late. We should get home before mom starts worrying!

exampleSentences.italian: Ora devo scappare ma ci vediamo più tardi a casa di Luca! – Ok, a più tardi!
exampleSentences.english: I have to run now, but I'll see you later at Luca's house! – Ok, see you later!

exampleSentences.italian: Il nuovo caporeparto è un po' tardo nel prendere delle decisioni.
exampleSentences.english: The new supervisor is a little slow in making decisions.

exampleSentences.italian: È tardi. Devo tornare a casa.
exampleSentences.english: It's late. I need to go home.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono in ritardo. Devo tornare a casa.
exampleSentences.english: I'm late. I have to go home.

exampleSentences.italian: Il treno è in ritardo di cinque minuti.
exampleSentences.english: The train is 5 minutes late.

exampleSentences.italian: Papà arriverà tardi.
exampleSentences.english: Dad will arrive late.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be late (referring to time of day)
to stay up late / to be late

grammarNotes: Tazza is a feminine noun with plural tazze. The diminutive form tazzina refers to a small coffee cup, while tazzone/tazzona or tazza grande denote a large mug. Use the preposition di to describe contents (una tazza di caffè = a cup of coffee) and da to describe the cup's purpose (una tazza da caffè = a coffee cup).
learnerNotes: Pay close attention to the distinction between di and da: una tazza di caffè means the cup contains coffee, while una tazza da caffè is a cup designed for serving coffee. The word tazza derives from Arabic (ṭasa), not Latin like most Italian words, making it a useful vocabulary item. Tazza can also colloquially refer to a toilet bowl alongside the English loanword 'water.'
