exampleSentences.english: the cup (singular)

exampleSentences.italian: una tazza
exampleSentences.english: a cup

exampleSentences.italian: le tazze
exampleSentences.english: the cups (plural)

exampleSentences.italian: La tazza di porcellana mi è scivolata di mano e si è frantumata in mille pezzi.
exampleSentences.english: The china cup slipped out of my hand and smashed into a thousand pieces.

exampleSentences.italian: una tazza di tè
exampleSentences.english: a cup of tea

exampleSentences.italian: una tazza di caffè
exampleSentences.english: a cup of coffee

exampleSentences.italian: una tazza di cioccolata calda
exampleSentences.english: a cup of hot chocolate

exampleSentences.italian: una tazza di brodo
exampleSentences.english: a cup of broth

exampleSentences.italian: una tazza da tè
exampleSentences.english: a teacup

exampleSentences.italian: Non c'è niente di meglio che bere una tazza di caffè di prima mattina.
exampleSentences.english: There is nothing better than having a cup of coffee in the early morning.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa ricetta richiede due tazze di yogurt.
exampleSentences.english: This recipe calls for two cups of yogurt.

englishTranslation: to give up / to give in / to throw in the towel
grammarNotes: Demordere is a compound verb formed from mordere (to bite) + the prefix de- (indicating removal or separation). It is typically used with the negation non in the expression 'Non demordere!' (Don't give up!). The verb can be conjugated like regular -ere verbs, though it is most commonly encountered in infinitive form or imperative mood.
learnerNotes: This verb is almost always used with the negation 'non' (Non demordere!), making it primarily an exhortation not to give up rather than a straightforward statement of surrender. When used positively without 'non,' it means the subject has actually given up or stopped trying. The literal etymology ('to release the bite') helps solidify the metaphorical meaning of abandoning effort or determination.

exampleSentences.italian: Non demordere!
exampleSentences.english: Don't give up!

exampleSentences.italian: Dai, non demordere! Sono sicuro che riuscirai a portare a termine il tuo progetto!
exampleSentences.english: Come on, don't give up! I'm sure you'll manage to complete your project!

exampleSentences.italian: Dopo vari tentativi, i ladri hanno deciso di demordere.
exampleSentences.english: After various attempts, the thieves decided to give up.

grammarNotes: Cintura is a feminine noun (la cintura). The plural form is cinture (le cinture). It derives from Latin cinctura and the verb cingere (to wrap, tie, enclose). The word is used both literally for belts and figuratively for zones or areas surrounding a place.
learnerNotes: Remember that cintura is feminine (la cintura, not il cintura), which affects article and adjective agreement. The word has both literal meaning (clothing item) and figurative uses (zones, lines, waistline), so context matters. The phrasal verb 'stringere la cintura' is idiomatic and means 'to economize' or 'to tighten one's belt' financially, not just physically.

exampleSentences.italian: Guarda, non riesco più ad allacciare la cintura. Mi sa che è ora di perdere qualche chilo…
exampleSentences.english: Look, I can no longer fasten my belt. I think it's time to lose a few pounds…

exampleSentences.italian: Trovo che questi pantaloni siano troppo stretti alle gambe e troppo larghi alla cintura!
exampleSentences.english: I find that these pants are too tight at the legs and too baggy at the waist!

exampleSentences.italian: Le sabbie mobili gli arrivavano fino alla cintura.
exampleSentences.english: The quicksand came right up to his waist.

englishTranslation: crick in the neck / stiff neck
grammarNotes: Torcicollo is a masculine noun composed of torcere (to twist) + collo (neck). Singular forms: un torcicollo, il torcicollo. Plural forms: dei torcicolli, i torcicolli. It is commonly used with the verbs avere (to have) or venire (to come/to get) to express having or acquiring a stiff neck.
learnerNotes: Torcicollo combines two simple words (torcere + collo) but is always used as a single noun rather than two separate words. Remember to use the article (il/un) and conjugate avere or venire appropriately when expressing possession of this condition. In zoology, this word also refers to the wryneck bird, so context determines whether you're discussing a medical condition or wildlife.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho il torcicollo da tre giorni.
exampleSentences.english: I've had a crick in my neck for three days.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi è venuto il torcicollo tre giorni fa.
exampleSentences.english: I got a crick in my neck three days ago.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to have a crick in the neck
to get/develop a crick in the neck

englishTranslation: to curl up / to wind oneself up like a ball of yarn
grammarNotes: Raggomitolarsi is a regular reflexive -are verb conjugated with reflexive pronouns (mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si). Remove the reflexive pronoun to get the transitive form raggomitolare (to wind something up into a ball). Being regular, it follows standard -are conjugation patterns with no irregular forms.
learnerNotes: Remember that raggomitolarsi is reflexive, so it always requires a reflexive pronoun (mi, ti, si, etc.). The transitive form raggomitolare (without the -si) is used when the action is performed on an object rather than on oneself—compare 'si raggomitolò' (he curled up) with 'raggomitolò la lana' (he wound up the wool). The synonym rannicchiarsi conveys the same meaning and is equally useful in everyday Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Il gatto si raggomitolò accanto alla stufa.
exampleSentences.english: The cat curled up beside the stove.

exampleSentences.italian: (io) mi raggomitolo
exampleSentences.english: I curl up

exampleSentences.italian: (tu) ti raggomitoli
exampleSentences.english: You curl up (informal)

exampleSentences.english: He curls up

exampleSentences.english: She curls up

exampleSentences.italian: (Lei) si raggomitola
exampleSentences.english: You curl up (formal)

exampleSentences.italian: (noi) ci raggomitoliamo
exampleSentences.english: We curl up

exampleSentences.italian: (voi) vi raggomitolate
exampleSentences.english: You curl up (plural)

exampleSentences.italian: (loro) si raggomitolano
exampleSentences.english: They curl up

exampleSentences.italian: Raggomitolare la lana è un lavoro lungo e faticoso.
exampleSentences.english: Winding up wool into a ball is a long and tiring job.

to wind (something) up into a ball (transitive form)
ball of wool or yarn (noun from which the verb derives)

grammarNotes: Tacchino is a masculine noun ending in -o with regular plural tacchini. The feminine forms tacchina (singular) and tacchine (plural) exist for female turkeys. It follows standard Italian gender and number agreement patterns with articles and adjectives.
learnerNotes: Note the distinction between the masculine (tacchino/tacchini) and feminine (tacchina/tacchine) forms—both are commonly used. The word refers both to the living bird and the meat itself, similar to English. The common Italian onomatopoeia for turkey sounds is 'glu glu' or 'glo glo' (from gloglottare), not the 'tac tac' that the word's origin might suggest.

exampleSentences.italian: il tacchino
exampleSentences.english: the turkey (masculine singular)

exampleSentences.italian: un tacchino

exampleSentences.italian: la tacchina
exampleSentences.english: the turkey (feminine singular)

exampleSentences.english: a turkey (feminine singular)

exampleSentences.italian: le tacchine
exampleSentences.english: the turkeys (feminine plural)

exampleSentences.italian: delle tacchine
exampleSentences.english: of the turkeys (feminine plural)

exampleSentences.italian: Mio zio alleva tacchini in campagna.
exampleSentences.english: My uncle raises turkeys in the countryside.

exampleSentences.italian: Preferisci il tacchino arrosto o il tacchino farcito?
exampleSentences.english: Do you prefer roast turkey or stuffed turkey?

relatedExpressions.meaning: to blush a lot / to turn red as a turkey

relatedExpressions.expression: fare la ruota come il tacchino
relatedExpressions.meaning: to strut around in a vain manner / to make the wheel like a turkey
to gobble (the sound a turkey makes)

grammarNotes: Vigneto is a masculine noun. The singular articles are il vigneto / un vigneto, and the plural is i vigneti / dei vigneti. It derives from Latin vinetum, which comes from vinum (wine). The word is technically formal and often describes large industrial vineyards.
learnerNotes: Do not confuse vigneto (vineyard) with vignetta (cartoon/comic strip)—they sound similar but have very different meanings. Note the distinction between vigneto (technical, large industrial vineyard) and vigna (informal, smaller family-owned vineyard). Also distinguish vigneto from vite (individual grapevine) and vita (life).

exampleSentences.italian: Pietro era in pensione, e passava le giornate a coltivare un vigneto in Toscana.
exampleSentences.english: Pietro was retired, and spent his days cultivating a vineyard in Tuscany.

exampleSentences.italian: Dov'è il nonno? – È in vigna a controllare la maturazione delle uve.
exampleSentences.english: Where's grandpa? – He's in the vineyard checking the ripeness of the grapes.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to harvest grapes (from vendemmia, grape harvest)
cartoon or comic strip (easily confused with vigneto)

grammarNotes: Guardaroba is a masculine noun despite its final -a ending, derived from French garde-robe (garder + robe). It is invariable in the plural, meaning the form remains unchanged: un guardaroba / i guardaroba. The article and any adjectives must agree with the masculine gender.
learnerNotes: Watch out: guardaroba is masculine (il guardaroba, not la guardaroba), which surprises many learners because of the final -a. The word has three distinct uses: a piece of furniture, a collection of clothes, or a public coatroom/cloakroom. Use armadio when referring only to the furniture piece itself; guardaroba is broader in scope.

exampleSentences.italian: un guardaroba
exampleSentences.english: a wardrobe

exampleSentences.italian: dei guardaroba
exampleSentences.english: of wardrobes

exampleSentences.italian: il guardaroba
exampleSentences.english: the wardrobe

exampleSentences.italian: i guardaroba
exampleSentences.english: the wardrobes

exampleSentences.italian: Il guardaroba di mio figlio è stracolmo di vestiti che non indosserà mai.
exampleSentences.english: My son's wardrobe is overflowing with clothes he will never wear.

exampleSentences.italian: La signora ha un guardaroba molto fornito.
exampleSentences.english: The lady has an extensive wardrobe.

relatedExpressions.meaning: wardrobe (furniture only); does not refer to the collection of clothes or storage room

grammarNotes: Lucertola is a feminine singular noun. The plural form is lucertole. It follows regular feminine -a/-e declension patterns. Article forms: la lucertola (singular), le lucertole (plural); una lucertola (indefinite singular), delle lucertole (indefinite plural).
learnerNotes: Lucertola comes from the same Latin root (lacertus) as English 'lizard,' making it a cognate. The idioms using lucertola reflect Italian cultural observations—sun-loving behavior and skinniness—so understanding context is key to using them correctly. Note that 'pelle di lucertola' is a commercial/technical term, not metaphorical.

exampleSentences.italian: Sapevi che la lucertola si nutre principalmente di insetti?
exampleSentences.english: Did you know that the lizard feeds mainly on insects?

exampleSentences.italian: Mario sta sempre al sole, come le lucertole!
exampleSentences.english: Mario always stays out in the sun, like the lizards!

relatedExpressions.expression: stare al sole come le lucertole
relatedExpressions.meaning: to stay in the sun like lizards; to spend long periods in the sun for a tan or warmth
to be a lizard; to love staying in the sun
to get by/live on lizards; to be very skinny due to eating little

relatedExpressions.expression: trovare/avere la lucertola a due code
relatedExpressions.meaning: to find/have the two-tailed lizard; to be lucky
lizard skin; commercial name for iguana skin used in leather goods

grammarNotes: Sbaglio is a masculine noun requiring articles lo/uno in singular (lo sbaglio, uno sbaglio) and gli/degli in plural (gli sbagli, degli sbagli) because it begins with s + consonant. It derives from the verb sbagliare (to make a mistake), which combines the prefix s- with abbagliare (to blind/dazzle).
learnerNotes: The synonym errore can replace sbaglio in most contexts, but cannot be used in the tag question expressions (o sbaglio?, Ma sbaglio o…). The phrase commettere uno sbaglio implies a more serious mistake than sbagliare or fare uno sbaglio. Use per sbaglio as a common adverbial phrase meaning 'by accident' when describing unintentional actions.

exampleSentences.italian: Da giovane, commisi uno sbaglio che cambiò per sempre la mia vita.
exampleSentences.english: When I was young, I made a mistake that forever changed my life.

exampleSentences.italian: È stato uno sbaglio venire qui.
exampleSentences.english: It was a mistake to come here.

exampleSentences.italian: Scusami, ho preso per sbaglio le tue chiavi.
exampleSentences.english: Sorry, I took your keys by mistake.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo letto è un po' troppo piccolo, o sbaglio?
exampleSentences.english: This bed is a bit on the small side, isn't it?

exampleSentences.italian: Ma sbaglio, o ci siamo già incontrati da qualche parte?
exampleSentences.english: Am I wrong, or have we met somewhere before?

exampleSentences.italian: Correggimi se sbaglio ma, è il tuo compleanno oggi?
exampleSentences.english: Correct me if I'm wrong but is it your birthday today?

exampleSentences.italian: È stato un errore venire qui.
exampleSentences.english: It was a mistake to come here.

exampleSentences.italian: Il tuo compito è pieno di errori.
exampleSentences.english: Your homework assignment is full of mistakes.

exampleSentences.italian: Scusami, ho preso per errore le tue chiavi.
exampleSentences.english: Sorry, I took your keys by mistake.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to commit an error (more serious than fare uno sbaglio)
a case of mistaken identity (mistake of person)
tag question: isn't it? / am I wrong? / right?
Am I wrong or… (colloquial tag question at sentence start)
Correct me if I'm wrong but… (informal)
Correct me if I'm wrong but… (formal)

grammarNotes: Lago is a masculine noun derived from Latin lacum. The plural form is laghi (not lagos), with an inserted 'h' between 'g' and 'i' to preserve the hard 'g' sound. Article forms: il lago (the lake), un lago (a lake); i laghi (the lakes), dei laghi (some lakes).
learnerNotes: Remember the plural uses 'h' (laghi) to keep the hard 'g' sound—this is a common Italian spelling rule. Lago can also mean a pool or puddle of liquid (water, blood) or a flooded area in a home, so context is important. Many famous Italian lakes use 'Lago di' + place name (e.g., Lago di Como, Lago di Garda).

exampleSentences.italian: il lago
exampleSentences.english: the lake

exampleSentences.italian: un lago
exampleSentences.english: a lake

exampleSentences.italian: i laghi
exampleSentences.english: the lakes

exampleSentences.italian: dei laghi
exampleSentences.english: (some) lakes

exampleSentences.italian: Preferiresti vivere vicino al mare o vicino a un lago?
exampleSentences.english: Would you rather live near the sea or near a lake?

exampleSentences.italian: George Clooney è in vacanza sul lago di Como.
exampleSentences.english: George Clooney is on holiday in Lake Como.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è un lago attorno al gabinetto! Che cos'hai combinato?
exampleSentences.english: There's a puddle of water around the toilet! What did you do?

grammarNotes: Intoppo is a masculine noun with regular plural intoppi. It derives from the verb intoppare (to crash, collide, stumble). The word is used both literally (physical obstacles) and figuratively (abstract difficulties). It commonly appears with prepositions and in set phrases involving verbs like trovare, incontrare, superare, and procedere.
learnerNotes: Intoppo is useful for describing both literal physical obstacles and abstract problems or setbacks in everyday speech and writing. It frequently pairs with specific verbs (trovare, superare, incontrare); learning these collocations will make your usage more natural. The phrase 'senza intoppi' (without obstacles) is particularly common in describing events that went smoothly.

exampleSentences.italian: La porta non si chiude. Ci dev'essere un intoppo.
exampleSentences.english: The door won't close. There must be something blocking it.

exampleSentences.italian: Il matrimonio si è svolto senza intoppi.
exampleSentences.english: The wedding went off without a hitch.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to proceed smoothly (lit. to proceed without obstacles)
to encounter obstacles, to come up against obstacles
to put obstacles in the way, to throw up obstacles

grammarNotes: Specchio is a masculine noun. The plural is formed by removing the final -o to get specchi. It uses the definite articles lo/gli (uno specchio, lo specchio, degli specchi, gli specchi). The word derives from Latin speculum and the verb specere (to look).
learnerNotes: Specchio has both literal and figurative meanings—use guardarsi allo specchio for the simple action, but understand it can also mean self-reflection or acknowledging one's faults. The figurative uses (describing calm water or a reflection of the soul/spirit) are common in everyday Italian, so learn these extensions early. Note the diminutive specchietto (little mirror/compact mirror), which is useful vocabulary for shopping or discussing grooming.

exampleSentences.italian: Gianni è proprio vanitoso. Si guarda allo specchio continuamente!
exampleSentences.english: Gianni is so vain. He constantly looks at himself in the mirror!

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi il mare è uno specchio. Potrebbe essere il giorno perfetto per vedere dei delfini!
exampleSentences.english: Today the sea is mirror calm. It could be the perfect day to see dolphins!

exampleSentences.italian: Dicono che gli occhi siano lo specchio dell'anima.
exampleSentences.english: They say that the eyes are the window to the soul.

exampleSentences.italian: Specchio, servo delle mie brame, chi è la più bella del reame?
exampleSentences.english: Magic mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?

relatedExpressions.meaning: to look at oneself in the mirror (literal); to examine one's flaws or reality (figurative)
to look at oneself in the mirror; to be reflected
to stand in front of the mirror

relatedExpressions.expression: Tenere la casa come uno specchio

relatedExpressions.meaning: to take someone as a model; to imitate someone

grammarNotes: Mago is a masculine noun with feminine equivalent maga. Regular plurals are maghi (masculine) and maghe (feminine). Note that magi exists as an alternative masculine plural but is primarily reserved for biblical usage (i tre re Magi). Gender agreement is required with articles and adjectives.
learnerNotes: Mago has multiple meanings: literal (performer of magic tricks, person with magical powers) and figurative (expert/whiz in a skill). The figurative use with 'di' (mago del computer = computer whiz) is common and useful. The feminine maga can describe charm or enchantment, though this usage is less common. Remember that magi is typically used only for biblical references, not general plurals.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mago Merlino ha svelato il nome del futuro re.
exampleSentences.english: Merlin the Wizard has revealed the name of the future king.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mago ha estratto un coniglio dal cilindro.
exampleSentences.english: The magician pulled a rabbit out of the top hat.

exampleSentences.italian: Il piccolo Leonardo ha solo tre anni, ma è un mago del computer.
exampleSentences.english: Little Leonardo is only three years old, but he is a computer whiz.

exampleSentences.italian: Quella ragazza è una maga!
exampleSentences.english: That girl is an enchantress!

relatedExpressions.meaning: feminine form: magician, sorceress, enchantress, witch
the Three Wise Men / the Biblical Magi

grammarNotes: Natale is a masculine noun (il Natale). It derives from Latin natālis, referencing the birth (nascita) of Christ rather than Christ himself. As an adjective, natale means 'of one's birth' or 'native' and agrees with the noun it modifies (e.g., città natale, paese natale). In literary Italian, the plural natali refers to 'birth' or 'origin'.
learnerNotes: Unlike English 'Christmas,' Natale does not explicitly reference Christ but rather his birth. When used as an adjective (natale), remember it must agree with the noun it modifies and is common in fixed expressions like città natale. Be aware that in formal or literary contexts, natale/natali can mean 'birth' or 'origin,' extending beyond the holiday sense.

exampleSentences.italian: È arrivato il Natale!
exampleSentences.english: Christmas is here!

exampleSentences.italian: Buon Natale!
exampleSentences.english: Merry Christmas!

exampleSentences.italian: Natale con i tuoi, Pasqua con chi vuoi.
exampleSentences.english: Christmas with your family, Easter with whoever you want.

englishTranslation: commuter / to commute / to oscillate / to swing
grammarNotes: Pendolare is a regular -are verb meaning to oscillate or swing. As a noun, it refers to a commuter (il/la pendolare for male/female). The gender is indicated by the article, not the ending. When used as an adjective, it describes commuting workers or students (un lavoratore pendolare, una studentessa pendolare). The plural form is pendolari.
learnerNotes: Pendolare derives from pendolo (pendulum) because commuters swing back and forth like a pendulum. Be careful not to confuse pendolare with penzolare—penzolare is more commonly used for something hanging or suspended from above. Remember that pendolare is gender-neutral as a noun; the gender is shown only by the article (il pendolare vs. la pendolare).

exampleSentences.italian: Dal lunedì al venerdì, pendolo tra Torino e Milano.
exampleSentences.english: From Monday to Friday, I commute between Turin and Milan.

exampleSentences.italian: Marta fa la pendolare tra Milano e Genova per motivi lavorativi.
exampleSentences.english: Marta commutes between Milan and Genoa for work reasons.

exampleSentences.italian: un lavoratore pendolare
exampleSentences.english: a commuting worker

exampleSentences.italian: uno studente pendolare
exampleSentences.english: a commuting student

exampleSentences.italian: moto pendolare
exampleSentences.english: pendular motion

relatedExpressions.meaning: to commute / to be a commuter

grammarNotes: Limone is a masculine noun with plural limoni. It can refer to both the fruit and the lemon tree. The expressions 'al limone' or 'al gusto di limone' are used to indicate lemon flavoring. Lemon peel is 'scorza di limone' and a lemon slice is 'una fetta di limone'.
learnerNotes: Limone is masculine (il limone), which is important for adjective agreement. The word also refers to the lemon tree itself, though 'albero di limone' is more precise. Note that 'al limone' is the standard way to express 'lemon-flavored' in Italian cuisine; memorize this prepositional phrase as it's commonly used in food contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: il limone
exampleSentences.english: the lemon

exampleSentences.italian: un limone
exampleSentences.english: a lemon

exampleSentences.italian: i limoni
exampleSentences.english: the lemons

exampleSentences.italian: dei limoni
exampleSentences.english: (some) lemons

exampleSentences.italian: I limoni crescono sull'albero di limone.
exampleSentences.english: The lemons grow on the lemon tree.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei un gelato al (gusto di) limone per favore.
exampleSentences.english: I'd like a lemon flavoured ice cream, please.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be pale (literally: to be as yellow as a lemon)
to exploit someone (literally: to squeeze someone like a lemon)

grammarNotes: Calabrone is a masculine noun. The singular forms are 'un calabrone' (indefinite) and 'il calabrone' (definite). The plural forms are 'dei calabroni' (indefinite) and 'i calabroni' (definite). Related words include 'api' (bees), 'vespe' (wasps), and 'pungiglione' (stinger).
learnerNotes: Note that 'calabrone' derives from Latin 'crabronem'. The idiomatic expression 'essere nero come un calabrone' has two meanings: literally describing someone with very dark skin, but figuratively meaning someone is in a very bad mood. Be careful not to confuse calabroni with 'api' (bees) or 'vespe' (wasps)—they are distinct insects with different characteristics.

exampleSentences.italian: I've never been on the receiving end of a calabrone sting!
exampleSentences.english: I've never been on the receiving end of a calabrone sting!

exampleSentences.italian: A hornet sting is una puntura di calabrone.
exampleSentences.english: A hornet sting is a hornet sting.

exampleSentences.italian: The phrase to be stung by a hornet translates as essere punto/a da un calabrone.
exampleSentences.english: The phrase to be stung by a hornet translates as to be stung by a hornet.

exampleSentences.italian: Cosa accade quando si viene punti da un calabrone?
exampleSentences.english: What happens when you get stung by a hornet?

exampleSentences.italian: La puntura può provocare uno shock anafilattico nelle persone che sono allergiche al veleno iniettato dall'insetto.
exampleSentences.english: The sting can cause anaphylactic shock in people who are allergic to the venom injected by the insect.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be stung by a hornet
to be as black as a hornet; to have a very dark complexion or to be in a very bad mood
stinger (the part of a hornet that holds the sting)

grammarNotes: Multa is a feminine noun derived from Latin. The plural form is multe. It follows regular feminine noun patterns: la multa (the fine), una multa (a fine), le multe (the fines), delle multe (some fines). The related verb multare means 'to fine' or 'to give a ticket.'
learnerNotes: Multa is the everyday word for traffic fines in Italian, though synonyms like contravvenzione, ammenda, and sanzione also exist with slightly different legal nuances. Note that vigile/vigilino (traffic officer) and controllore (ticket inspector on public transport) are different professions who issue different types of fines. The expression 'multa salata' (literally 'salty fine') means an expensive or hefty fine—a useful colloquialism.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho preso una multa salata perché ho lasciato la macchina in divieto di sosta.
exampleSentences.english: I received an expensive fine because I left my car in the no-parking zone.

exampleSentences.italian: Occhio che su questa strada ci sono un sacco di autovelox. Se superi il limite di velocità, ti beccherai di sicuro una multa!
exampleSentences.english: Be careful as there are a lot of speed cameras on this road. If you go over the speed limit, you will definitely get a fine!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to run a red light (literally: to burn the traffic light)
to fine / to give a ticket
speed detection system that calculates average speed between two locations

grammarNotes: Piantagrane is an invariable noun—its form remains unchanged in both feminine and plural forms. The same word is used for il/la piantagrane (singular) and i/le piantagrane (plural). It combines the verb piantare (to plant) with the noun grana (grain, trouble).
learnerNotes: Piantagrane is a colorful colloquial term best used informally. Remember it's invariable—don't add -a or -e for gender/number agreement. The related idiom piantare una grana (to plant trouble) helps explain the metaphorical origin and offers another way to express similar ideas in conversation.

exampleSentences.italian: Dai, finiscila di fare il piantagrane! Non hai niente di meglio da fare?
exampleSentences.english: Come on, stop being a troublemaker! Don't you have anything better to do?

relatedExpressions.meaning: to stir up trouble (literally: to plant a grain)

grammarNotes: Istruzione is a feminine noun (l'istruzione, un'istruzione). The plural is istruzioni. In singular form, it means education/schooling/training; in plural form, the meaning shifts to instructions/directions/orders. It derives from Latin instructio-onis, from the verb instruere (to instruct).
learnerNotes: Pay attention to the singular/plural meaning shift: istruzione (singular) = education, but istruzioni (plural) = instructions. This is a crucial distinction that changes meaning entirely rather than just creating a plural form. In formal contexts, istruzione can also mean 'inquiry' in legal terminology or 'code instruction' in computing. The feminine gender is important for article and adjective agreement.

exampleSentences.italian: L'istruzione superiore non è un privilegio. È un investimento essenziale per il futuro.
exampleSentences.english: Higher education is not a privilege. It is an essential investment for the future.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo articolo fornisce istruzioni dettagliate su come connettersi a una rete Wi-Fi.
exampleSentences.english: This article provides step-by-step instructions on how to connect to a Wi-Fi network.

grammarNotes: Vestaglia is a feminine noun with plural form vestaglie. The definite article is la/le and the indefinite article is una/delle. It derives from the noun veste (dress, clothing, garment) and uses the suffix -aglia, which typically creates female collective nouns denoting a 'rough' or mass version of the base noun.
learnerNotes: Vestaglia is a lightweight dressing gown typically worn at home, while accappatoio is a thicker bathrobe (often made of terrycloth) meant for after bathing. The -aglia suffix is productive in Italian and carries a pejorative or collective sense—learn it alongside the base word veste to understand word formation. Note: mettere (to put on) + la vestaglia uses the reflexive form si è messa when the subject puts it on themselves.

exampleSentences.italian: Elena si è messa la vestaglia non appena è scesa dal letto.
exampleSentences.english: Elena put on her dressing gown as soon as she got out of bed.

exampleSentences.italian: Che differenza c'è tra una vestaglia e un accappatoio? – La stoffa dell'accappatoio è più assorbente e si asciuga più facilmente.
exampleSentences.english: What's the difference between a dressing gown and a bathrobe? – The fabric of the bathrobe is more absorbent and dries more easily.

relatedExpressions.meaning: bathrobe (a similar but thicker, more absorbent garment)

grammarNotes: Spazzatura is a feminine noun (la spazzatura). The plural form is spazzature, though it is used much less frequently than the singular. It requires feminine article and adjective agreement (e.g., la spazzatura puzzolente). The word derives from the verb spazzare (to sweep), which explains its secondary meaning of sweeping.
learnerNotes: Spazzatura has formal synonyms rifiuti and immondizia that are preferred in official or technical contexts. Pattumiera is a common alternative specifically for the garbage can itself. Note the dual meaning: while primarily meaning garbage/trash, it also means sweeping, deriving from spazzare (to sweep)—context will clarify which sense is intended.

exampleSentences.italian: Bisogna portare fuori la spazzatura. Comincia a esserci un odore poco piacevole in cucina!
exampleSentences.english: We need to take out the trash. There is a rather unpleasant smell in the kitchen.

exampleSentences.italian: Non ne posso più di guardare questa tv spazzatura!
exampleSentences.english: I can't watch this trash TV anymore!

relatedExpressions.meaning: dumpster / large bin with wheels for outdoor rubbish collection

grammarNotes: Broncio is a masculine noun with plural bronci. It can also function as a rare adjective meaning sullen or peevish, typically found in literary contexts. The derived pronominal verb imbronciarsi and adjective imbronciato follow regular patterns.
learnerNotes: Broncio is always used with specific verbs (avere, fare, mettere, tenere) rather than as a standalone verb. The expression 'tenere il broncio a qualcuno' uses the indirect object (a qualcuno) to mean 'to hold a grudge against someone.' The near-synonym muso is more commonly encountered and interchangeable in most contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Tenere il broncio per giorni non farà altro che ingigantire il problema.
exampleSentences.english: Sulking for days will only exacerbate the problem.

exampleSentences.italian: Marco tiene il muso da due giorni perché non l'ho portato a vedere la partita.
exampleSentences.english: Marco has been sulking for two days because I didn't take him to see the game.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to have a sulky expression / to pout
to make a sulky expression / to pout
to put on a sulky expression
to hold a sulky expression / to sulk
to be angry with someone / to hold a grudge
to be angry with someone / to hold a grudge
to sulk / to hold a sulky expression

grammarNotes: Moda is a feminine noun; singular la moda, plural le mode. It entered Italian via French mode. The word is used both literally (clothes/fashion industry) and figuratively (trends, fads). When used as an adjective phrase, it takes the preposition di (di moda) or alla (alla moda).
learnerNotes: While moda describes fashion directly, Italians use elegante or chic to describe a fashionable person's appearance—don't translate 'fashionable person' as 'persona di moda.' Note that Italian has borrowed the English word 'fashion' (pronounced /fɛʃən/) as an alternative adjective meaning trendy or fashionable. Moda also extends to non-clothing trends and fads (una moda passeggera), so context determines whether it refers to clothing fashion or broader trends.

exampleSentences.italian: Le scarpe di pelle sono sempre alla moda / di moda.
exampleSentences.english: Leather shoes are always in fashion.

exampleSentences.italian: Lavoro nella moda.
exampleSentences.english: I work in the fashion industry.

exampleSentences.italian: Dario è sempre molto elegante. Non mi stupisce che lavori nella moda!
exampleSentences.english: Dario is always very fashionable. I'm not surprised that he works in the fashion industry!

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi è di moda mangiare cibi sani.
exampleSentences.english: Nowadays eating healthy food is in fashion.

relatedExpressions.meaning: up-to-date with the latest fashion trends

grammarNotes: Sconfinamento is a masculine noun formed from the verb sconfinare plus the suffix -mento, which creates action nouns. The definite article is lo (singular) and gli (plural). The indefinite articles are uno (singular) and degli (plural). It is a regular noun with standard plural formation: sconfinamento → sconfinamenti.
learnerNotes: Sconfinamento has three distinct semantic domains: literal trespassing on property, border/military violations, and figurative use for exceeding moral or legal boundaries. In economics, sconfinamento bancario is a common banking term worth memorizing. Note that oltrepassare is a more specific alternative for physical trespassing on marked properties (fences, tracks), while sconfinamento is broader in application.

exampleSentences.italian: I dimostranti protestarono davanti al municipio per una settimana. Tre di loro furono arrestati per sconfinamento.
exampleSentences.english: Demonstrators protested outside the town hall for a week. Three of them were arrested for trespassing.

exampleSentences.italian: Lo sconfinamento di truppe militari ha generato un clima di tensione tra i due paesi.
exampleSentences.english: The violation of the border has created a climate of tension between the two countries.

exampleSentences.italian: Trovo che ci sia qualche sconfinamento nel suo libro.
exampleSentences.english: I find that some parts of his book overstepped the mark.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to trespass / to cross over / to exceed limits
to trespass (specifically on properties); used for fences, train tracks, etc.
bank overdraft / exceeding a credit limit on a current account

grammarNotes: Telecomando is a masculine noun formed from the prefix tele- (at or over a long distance) + comando (command). The plural form is telecomandi. It follows regular masculine noun patterns and requires the articles il/un (singular) or i/dei (plural).
learnerNotes: Telecomando is a compound word where tele- is a productive prefix in Italian meaning 'at a distance,' also seen in televisione, telefono, and telescopio. Note that while English speakers often shorten 'remote control' to 'remote,' Italian speakers typically use the full word telecomando. Be careful not to confuse il comando (command/order) with il telecomando (remote control) in context.

exampleSentences.italian: Non trovo più il telecomando della TV.
exampleSentences.english: I can't find the TV remote.

exampleSentences.italian: Guarda sotto al divano!
exampleSentences.english: Check under the sofa!

grammarNotes: Kermesse is an invariable feminine noun, meaning its form remains identical in the plural. The definite article is 'la kermesse' (singular) and 'le kermesse' (plural); the indefinite article is 'una kermesse' (singular) and 'delle kermesse' (plural). Despite being invariable, it still takes feminine article and adjective agreement.
learnerNotes: This borrowed Dutch word is commonly used in Italian for major public events and festivals, notably the famous Sanremo Song Festival. Be aware that while invariable in form, it still requires feminine article and adjective agreement ('la kermesse bella', not 'il kermesse'). In sports contexts, it specifically refers to a type of road cycling race popular in Western Europe.

exampleSentences.italian: La kermesse della canzone italiana inizierà domani sera.
exampleSentences.english: The Italian song festival will start tomorrow evening.

relatedExpressions.meaning: sporting festival or road bicycle race

grammarNotes: Ghirlanda is a feminine noun (la ghirlanda). The plural form is ghirlande (le ghirlande). It follows regular feminine noun patterns in Italian, taking the article la/una in singular and le/delle in plural.
learnerNotes: Ghirlanda is most commonly used in seasonal contexts, particularly around Christmas (ghirlanda natalizia). The related verbs ghirlandare and nouns like ghirlandaio are rarely used in contemporary Italian, so focus on learning the main word and its common compound expressions. Remember that this is a feminine noun—always use 'la' or 'una' in singular and 'le' or 'delle' in plural.

exampleSentences.italian: la ghirlanda
exampleSentences.english: the wreath

exampleSentences.italian: una ghirlanda
exampleSentences.english: a wreath

exampleSentences.italian: le ghirlande
exampleSentences.english: the wreaths

exampleSentences.italian: delle ghirlande
exampleSentences.english: (some) wreaths

exampleSentences.italian: Lucia sta attaccando una ghirlanda fatta a mano sulla porta.
exampleSentences.english: Lucia is putting a handmade wreath on the door.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi insegni a intrecciare una ghirlanda di fiori?
exampleSentences.english: Can you teach me how to weave a flower garland?

relatedExpressions.meaning: a person who makes or sells garlands

grammarNotes: Via Lattea is a two-word feminine noun phrase. 'Via' is a feminine noun (plural: vie) meaning street, way, road, or path. 'Latteo' is an adjective meaning 'from milk' or 'like milk,' which becomes 'lattea' in the feminine form to agree with 'via.' The phrase name derives from Latin 'via lactĕa' and Greek 'galaksías kýklos' (milky circle).
learnerNotes: Via Lattea is a proper noun (astronomical term) and should be capitalized when referring to our galaxy. Remember that 'via' is feminine, so adjectives and articles agree in the feminine form. The etymological connection to Latin and Greek (via lactĕa, galaksías kýklos) shows how Italian inherited this term through Romance language development.

exampleSentences.italian: Cerco una guida su come fotografare la Via Lattea.
exampleSentences.english: I am looking for a guide on how to photograph the Milky Way.

exampleSentences.italian: Non conosciamo il numero esatto, ma sappiamo che nella Via Lattea ci sono più di 100 miliardi di stelle.
exampleSentences.english: We don't know the exact number, but we know that there are more than 100 billion stars in the Milky Way.

relatedExpressions.meaning: street, way, road, path, route, passage
milky, dairy, from milk or like milk

grammarNotes: Sgarbo is a masculine noun with plural sgarbi. It takes the definite article lo and indefinite article uno due to the consonant cluster sg-. The definite plural is gli sgarbi and the partitive plural is degli sgarbi.
learnerNotes: Remember that sgarbo pairs naturally with ricevere (to receive) and fare (to do) in fixed expressions. The word has an intuitive opposite, garbo, formed simply by removing the initial 's'. Be careful not to confuse sgarbo (rudeness) with its related adjective sgarbato (a rude person), which follows standard gender agreement in Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: lo sgarbo
exampleSentences.english: the discourtesy

exampleSentences.italian: uno sgarbo
exampleSentences.english: a discourtesy

exampleSentences.italian: gli sgarbi
exampleSentences.english: the discourtesies

exampleSentences.italian: degli sgarbi
exampleSentences.english: (some) discourtesies

exampleSentences.english: to be treated rudely by someone, to be slighted by someone

exampleSentences.italian: fare uno sgarbo a qualcuno
exampleSentences.english: to treat someone rudely, to slight someone

grammarNotes: Birra is a feminine noun; plural form is birre. Definite articles: la birra (singular), le birre (plural). Indefinite articles: una birra (singular), delle birre (plural). Like all feminine nouns in Italian, it requires feminine adjectives and articles in agreement.
learnerNotes: Note that birra is used both literally (the beverage) and figuratively (meaning energy/endurance) in idiomatic expressions—this figurative sense won't be obvious from context alone. The expression 'farci la birra' is idiomatic and ironic, so don't interpret it literally. Be careful with gendered articles: always use 'una birra' (not 'un birra') and 'la birra' (not 'il birra').

exampleSentences.italian: Posso avere una birra rossa media, per favore?
exampleSentences.english: Can I have a medium amber ale, please?

exampleSentences.italian: Puoi farci la birra con quel rottame!
exampleSentences.english: You can't do anything with that piece of junk. (lit. You can make beer with that piece of junk.)

exampleSentences.italian: Ci facciamoci una birra stasera?
exampleSentences.english: Do you want to grab a beer tonight?

exampleSentences.italian: Certo, anche due!
exampleSentences.english: Sure, why not two!

to go at full speed, full throttle, flat out
to overtake someone in a speed competition
to have lots of energy and endurance

grammarNotes: Feminine noun; plural is ortiche. Takes the definite article l'ortica (singular) and le ortiche (plural), and indefinite article un'ortica (singular) and delle ortiche (plural). Derives from Latin urtica.
learnerNotes: Note that ortica is feminine, so adjectives and articles must agree (l'ortica, un'ortica, le ortiche). The idiom 'gettare/buttare alle ortiche' is commonly used in everyday Italian to mean abandoning something; buttare is more colloquial than gettare. Despite its painful sting, ortica is highly valued in Italian cuisine, particularly in northern Italy.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai mai mangiato il risotto con le ortiche?
exampleSentences.english: Have you ever eaten nettle risotto?

exampleSentences.italian: Ho gettato alle ortiche quattro mesi di studi per dedicarmi alla musica.
exampleSentences.english: I threw away four months of study to dedicate myself to music.

relatedExpressions.meaning: nettles grow here; used to describe an overgrown, abandoned location
to throw to the nettles; to abandon something altogether (a passion, interest, opportunity, or investment)

grammarNotes: Gabbiano is a masculine noun with regular plural gabbiani. It derives from Latin gavia. Use the definite article il/i or indefinite article un/dei depending on context: il gabbiano (the seagull), i gabbiani (the seagulls), un gabbiano (a seagull), dei gabbiani (some seagulls).
learnerNotes: Gabbiano is a common word for coastal or marine contexts; you'll encounter it frequently in beach-related vocabulary. Note the diminutive form gabbianello (little gull) and the augmentative associations with specific species. The verb piombare (to swoop/dive) is often used with gabbiani in typical coastal anecdotes about them stealing food.

exampleSentences.italian: Il gabbiano è piombato all'improvviso e mi ha rubato il gelato!
exampleSentences.english: The seagull swooped down unexpectedly and stole my ice cream!

grammarNotes: Pullman is a masculine noun (il pullman, un pullman). As a foreign loanword in Italian, it does not change in the plural form—the article indicates number (i pullman, dei pullman). Note: sometimes mistakenly spelled with a single 'l' (pulman), which is incorrect.
learnerNotes: While the dictionary definition refers specifically to large intercity coaches, pullman is used more broadly in informal spoken Italian across many regions (especially Turin) to mean any bus, including city buses. Don't confuse pullman with pulmino (minibus/school bus)—pulmino is distinctly smaller. Watch out for the common misspelling 'pulman' with one 'l'; always use two 'l's.

exampleSentences.italian: Prendo il pullman perché sono senza macchina.
exampleSentences.english: I'm taking the coach bus because I don't have a car.

exampleSentences.italian: A che ora passa il pullman? – Alle otto e trentacinque. – Grazie!
exampleSentences.english: What time does the bus arrive? – At 8:35. – Thank you!

exampleSentences.italian: Non posso venire a prenderti domani. Dovrai tornare a casa con il pulmino della scuola.
exampleSentences.english: I can't come to pick you up tomorrow. You'll have to come home on the school bus.

englishTranslation: the blues / down in the dumps / a knot in one's stomach / a lump in one's throat
grammarNotes: Magone is a masculine noun derived from Lombardic origins. The plural is magoni, though the singular form is almost always used in practice. It takes standard masculine articles: il magone (definite singular), un magone (indefinite singular), i magoni (definite plural), dei magoni (partitive plural). The word is typically used with specific verbs like avere, prendere, venire, provare, and salire.
learnerNotes: Magone is a useful colloquial word for expressing emotional sadness or physical sensations of anxiety (tightness in stomach). Note that it has a secondary, unrelated meaning as 'gizzard' (bird's stomach), so context is essential. Do not confuse magone with mago (wizard) despite their similar appearance; they have completely different etymologies and meanings.

exampleSentences.italian: Come mai hai il magone oggi?
exampleSentences.english: Why are you down in the dumps today? Why have you got the blues today?

exampleSentences.italian: Mi viene il magone solo a pensarci.
exampleSentences.english: It gets me down just thinking about it. I get a lump in my throat just thinking about it.

exampleSentences.italian: Provo un magone ogni volta che rivedo i video di mio figlio da neonato.
exampleSentences.english: I get a lump in my throat every time I see videos of my son as a newborn.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to have the blues / to be down in the dumps
to get down / to become depressed
to get someone down / to make someone depressed
to feel a lump in one's throat / sadness

grammarNotes: Cucchiaio is a masculine noun. Definite article: il cucchiaio (singular), i cucchiai (plural). Indefinite article: un cucchiaio (singular), dei cucchiai (plural). The word derives from Latin cochlearium. Related forms include the diminutive cucchiaino (teaspoon) and augmentative cucchiaione (ladle).
learnerNotes: Cucchiaio is very common in everyday Italian, especially when discussing meals and cooking. Note that cucchiaio can mean both 'spoon' (the object) and 'spoonful' (the quantity), depending on context—un cucchiaio di zucchero means 'a spoonful of sugar.' The diminutive cucchiaino is equally important to learn, as it's frequently used for teaspoons and dessert spoons in Italian cuisine.

exampleSentences.italian: Tua figlia riesce già a mangiare con il cucchiaio?
exampleSentences.english: Can your daughter already eat with a spoon?

exampleSentences.italian: un cucchiaio di zucchero
exampleSentences.english: a spoonful of sugar

exampleSentences.italian: La ricetta richiede due cucchiai di zucchero e un cucchiaio di latte.
exampleSentences.english: The recipe calls for two spoonfuls of sugar and one spoonful of milk.

exampleSentences.italian: una cucchiaiata di minestra
exampleSentences.english: a spoonful of soup

relatedExpressions.meaning: soft creamy dessert eaten with a spoon (e.g., pudding, custard)

relatedExpressions.expression: Essere da raccogliere / da raccattare col cucchiaio
relatedExpressions.meaning: to be unable to stand up due to fatigue or being in a bad way

relatedExpressions.expression: Vuotare / Svuotare il mare con il cucchiaio
relatedExpressions.meaning: to work long and hard on something without obtaining relevant results

grammarNotes: Fata is a feminine noun with plural form fate. It follows regular feminine -a/-e declension. Gender agreement is required with articles (la fata, le fate) and adjectives (e.g., la Fata Turchina).
learnerNotes: Remember that fata is feminine, so always use la/una/le with it. The diminutive fatina is also feminine (la fatina). Be careful not to confuse fiabe and favole with fata—while all relate to fairy tales, fiabe and favole are the preferred terms for the story genre itself, whereas fata refers to the magical creature. The expression mani di fata is commonly used figuratively to praise someone's manual dexterity.

exampleSentences.italian: la fata
exampleSentences.english: the fairy

exampleSentences.italian: una fata
exampleSentences.english: a fairy

exampleSentences.english: the fairies

exampleSentences.english: The fairy turned the pumpkin into a carriage.

exampleSentences.italian: Come sei brava a ricamare. Hai delle mani di fata!
exampleSentences.english: You're so good at embroidery. You have nimble fingers!

fairy hands; skilled hands at sewing/embroidery

grammarNotes: Schietto is a four-form adjective that agrees with the gender and number of the noun it modifies: schietto (masc. sing.), schietta (fem. sing.), schietti (masc. plur.), schiette (fem. plur.). It derives from Gothic slaihts via Tuscan stietto and can function both literally (describing purity or authenticity) and figuratively (describing character or communication).
learnerNotes: Schietto has two main semantic domains: literal (purity/authenticity of substances or languages) and figurative (frankness/sincerity of people and their communication). When describing people or interpersonal qualities, it carries a positive connotation of honesty and directness, not rudeness. Remember to apply correct gender and number agreement—this is essential for proper usage in written and formal contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho provato a leggere una novella scritta in fiorentino schietto ma non ho capito un bel niente!
exampleSentences.english: I tried to read a short story written in pure Florentine but I didn't understand anything!

exampleSentences.english: pure gold

exampleSentences.english: pure Italian (unaffected by dialects or foreign terms)

exampleSentences.english: a straightforward man

grammarNotes: Comportamento is a masculine noun with regular plural comportamenti. It agrees with masculine articles and adjectives (il comportamento, un comportamento, i comportamenti, dei comportamenti). Derived from the verbs comportare (to entail) and comportarsi (to behave/react).
learnerNotes: Comportamento is frequently paired with adjectives to describe specific types of behaviour (buon, cattivo, strano, violento). Remember that comportarsi is the reflexive verb form meaning 'to behave/react,' while comportare means 'to entail'—these are distinct verbs. The word extends beyond human behaviour to describe how substances or systems react physically or chemically, making it useful in scientific contexts.

exampleSentences.english: the behaviour

exampleSentences.italian: un comportamento
exampleSentences.english: a behaviour

exampleSentences.italian: i comportamenti
exampleSentences.english: the behaviours

exampleSentences.english: (some) behaviours

exampleSentences.english: This type of behaviour is normal for a child his age.

exampleSentences.italian: Comportati bene con la nonna, mi raccomando!
exampleSentences.english: Behave yourself with grandma, please!

exampleSentences.italian: Sono state eseguite diverse simulazioni al fine di osservare il comportamento del materiale nello spazio.
exampleSentences.english: Various simulations were performed in order to observe the behaviour of the substance in space.

grammarNotes: Cavatappi is an invariable masculine noun, maintaining the same form in both singular and plural. All nouns ending in -i in the singular are invariable, including analisi, brindisi, and crisi. Use the article il/un for singular and i/dei for plural.
learnerNotes: Cavatappi is composed of cavare (to remove/extract) + tappo (cork/stopper), making it easy to remember. Note that apribottiglie is used specifically for metal caps, while cavatappi works for any bottle stopper. The word tirabusciò is regional and rarely encountered in standard Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei aprire questa bottiglia di vino ma non trovo il cavatappi!
exampleSentences.english: I would like to open this bottle of wine but I can't find the corkscrew!

exampleSentences.italian: Dove hai messo l'apribottiglie? – L'ho perso. Usa i denti!
exampleSentences.english: Where did you put the bottle opener? – I lost it. Use your teeth!

bottle opener (for metal caps); combination of aprire + bottiglie
corkscrew (dialectal, southern Italy); from French tirebouchon

englishTranslation: to rack one's brains / to tire one's brain out
grammarNotes: Scervellarsi is a regular -are pronominal verb requiring the pronominal particles (mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si). It conjugates like standard -are verbs but always includes the reflexive particle. The pronunciation of 'sc' is typically ʃ, though pronouncing the 's' in isolation (sʧ) is also acceptable in this case.
learnerNotes: Remember that scervellarsi is pronominal, so you must always include the reflexive particle—never say 'scervello' alone. The prefix 's-' here denotes loss or absence (absence of brains/composure). Be aware of the rich set of synonyms provided; while scervellarsi is common and neutral, expressions like rompersi la testa are more colloquial.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono giorni che mi scervello per trovare una soluzione!
exampleSentences.english: I've been racking my brains for days to find a solution!

exampleSentences.italian: Marco si sta scervellando sui libri per prepararsi all'esame. È molto provato.
exampleSentences.english: Marco is studying really hard to prepare for the exam. He's very tired.

grammarNotes: Limpido is a four-form adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Masculine singular: limpido; masculine plural: limpidi; feminine singular: limpida; feminine plural: limpide. The adjective can be used both literally (describing physical clarity) and figuratively (describing mental or moral clarity).
learnerNotes: Limpido is a cognate with English 'limpid,' making it relatively easy to remember, though 'limpid' is less common in English than 'clear.' The word functions well in both literal descriptions (weather, water) and figurative contexts (conscience, mind, reasoning), so exposure to both uses is important. Note that related adverb limpidamente and noun limpidezza maintain the same root, facilitating word family recognition.

grammarNotes: Brina is a feminine noun (la brina). The plural form is brine, though it is rarely used in practice. It derives from the Latin pruina and forms several related verb and noun derivatives through common Italian prefixes (brinare, sbrinare, sbrinamento, sbrinatore).
learnerNotes: Brina specifically refers to hoarfrost or the crystalline frost that forms naturally, while gelata emphasizes a sudden cold snap with ice formation. Remember that sbrinare (to defrost) uses the prefix s- to indicate removal, a common pattern in Italian. The plural brine exists grammatically but is almost never used in everyday speech.

exampleSentences.italian: La brina può essere dannosa per la vegetazione.
exampleSentences.english: Frost can be harmful to vegetation.

exampleSentences.italian: Devo sbrinare il frigo.

grammarNotes: Coltello is a masculine noun. The definite article is 'il' (singular) and 'i' (plural); the indefinite article is 'un' (singular) and 'dei' (plural). It derives from Latin cultellus, a diminutive form of culter.
learnerNotes: Coltello has rich figurative and idiomatic usage beyond its literal meaning of 'knife'—many idioms relate to conflict, advantage, or emotional pain. Pay attention to the distinction between 'il coltello' (the knife) and 'un coltello' (a knife) depending on context. The various compound forms (coltello da cucina, coltello da pane) are common in everyday Italian and worth memorizing for practical use.

exampleSentences.italian: Ci vuole molto tempo prima che i bambini imparino ad usare un coltello correttamente.
exampleSentences.english: It takes a long time for children to learn how to use a knife correctly.

grammarNotes: Presentimento is a masculine noun with regular plural forms (presentimenti). It derives from the verb presentire (pre- + sentire). Can be followed by either the conjunction che (allowing future, subjunctive, or conditional verbs) or the preposition di (requiring infinitive form). Gender and number agreement applies in standard ways.
learnerNotes: Although presentimento has a cognate in English (presentiment), it is far more commonly used in Italian everyday speech, where you'll encounter it frequently in phrases like 'avere un brutto presentimento.' Don't confuse it with sensazione (sensation), which lacks the foreboding connotation. Pay attention to the syntax: use che + future/subjunctive/conditional or di + infinitive depending on the structure you choose.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho un brutto presentimento per la gara di domani.
exampleSentences.english: I have a bad feeling about tomorrow's race.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho un buon presentimento per il nuovo album di Eros Ramazotti.
exampleSentences.english: I have a good feeling about Eros Ramazotti's new album.

exampleSentences.italian: Avevo il presentimento che non lo avrei mai più rivisto.

grammarNotes: Spuntino is a masculine noun. The singular forms are lo spuntino / uno spuntino, and the plural forms are gli spuntini / degli spuntini. The expression 'fare uno spuntino' means 'to have a snack.' Etymology is uncertain according to Treccani, though Il Devoto–Oli suggests it derives from spunto.
learnerNotes: Distinguish spuntino (light, anytime snack) from merenda (heavier, afternoon-specific snack around 4-5pm). While English 'snack' is sometimes used in Italian, it's pronounced differently (/znɛk/). Stuzzichini are appetizer-style snacks served with drinks, not to be confused with full spuntini.

exampleSentences.italian: Sto morendo di fame! A pranzo ho fatto solo uno spuntino.
exampleSentences.english: I'm starving! I only had a snack for lunch.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho ancora fame. Quasi quasi mi faccio uno spuntino di mezzanotte!
exampleSentences.english: I'm still hungry. I might just have a midnight snack!

relatedExpressions.meaning: a light and salty snack to whet the appetite before a meal

grammarNotes: As an adjective, freddo changes ending by gender and number: freddo (masc. sing.), fredda (fem. sing.), freddi (masc. plur.), fredde (fem. plur.). As a noun, it is masculine singular (il freddo) and can be pluralized in fixed expressions like i primi freddi. Commonly used with avere freddo (to be cold - personal feeling) and fare freddo (to be cold - weather condition).
learnerNotes: Remember that 'freddo' as an adjective must agree with the noun it modifies in both gender and number. Don't confuse the expressions 'avere freddo' (personal feeling) and 'fare freddo' (describing weather). Note that 'freddo' has figurative meanings beyond temperature: it can mean 'detached/indifferent' or 'level-headed/calm' depending on context.

exampleSentences.italian: le dita fredde
exampleSentences.english: cold fingers

exampleSentences.italian: Domani sarà una giornata molto fredda. La temperatura scenderà sotto lo zero!
exampleSentences.english: Tomorrow will be a very cold day. The temperature will go below zero.

exampleSentences.italian: Una persona fredda raramente mostra le sue emozioni.
exampleSentences.english: A cold person rarely shows his/her emotions.

exampleSentences.italian: Non posso darvi una risposta adesso. Devo ragionare a mente fredda.
exampleSentences.english: I can't give you an answer now. I need to think clearly.

exampleSentences.italian: Ragazzi, calma e sangue freddo! Spiegatemi per bene cosa è successo.
exampleSentences.english: Guys, calm down! Tell me exactly what happened.

exampleSentences.italian: Fa troppo freddo fuori! Ho già abbastanza freddo qui in casa, figurati se esco!
exampleSentences.english: It's too cold outside! I'm cold enough as it is here at home, so there's no way I'm going out!

exampleSentences.italian: Mi viene freddo solo a pensarci!
exampleSentences.english: It gives me the shivers just thinking about it!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to reason with a clear mind; to think clearly without emotional influence
in cold blood; without feeling or mercy
the first cold spells of the season

grammarNotes: Allettante is a regular adjective ending in -e that does not change form when modifying masculine or feminine singular nouns (un prezzo allettante, una proposta allettante). The plural form for both genders is allettanti (prezzi allettanti, proposte allettanti). It derives from the verb allettare (to entice, to attract).
learnerNotes: Allettante is a sophisticated adjective commonly used in business, marketing, and formal contexts to describe offers, proposals, or opportunities. Do not confuse it with the verb allettare; remember that allettante as an adjective does not change in the singular regardless of gender. Note that synonyms like seducente and stuzzicante carry slightly different connotations—use allettante for professional or neutral contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: un prezzo allettante
exampleSentences.english: a tempting price

exampleSentences.italian: una proposta allettante
exampleSentences.english: an attractive proposal

exampleSentences.italian: Il Barcellona sta preparando un'offerta allettante per il difensore juventino.
exampleSentences.english: Barcelona is preparing an attractive offer for the Juventus defender.

exampleSentences.italian: prezzi allettanti
exampleSentences.english: tempting prices

exampleSentences.italian: proposte allettanti
exampleSentences.english: attractive proposals

exampleSentences.italian: Questa mattina c'erano dei prezzi molto allettanti nel centro commerciale.
exampleSentences.english: This morning there were very tempting prices in the shopping centre.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to entice, to attract, to tempt

grammarNotes: Etichetta is a feminine noun beginning with a vowel. Definite articles: l'etichetta (singular), le etichette (plural). Indefinite articles: un'etichetta (singular), delle etichette (plural). The diminutive suffix -etta indicates 'little thing attached,' reflecting its etymology from Old French estiquier meaning 'to attach.'
learnerNotes: The word etichetta has multiple meanings: the literal sense (a physical label on products) and the figurative sense (a stereotyping label applied to people). Watch the vowel contraction: use l'etichetta and un'etichetta, not lo/uno. The phrase affibbiare un'etichetta is useful for discussing stereotyping in contemporary discourse.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa bottiglia di vino non ha un'etichetta con il prezzo.
exampleSentences.english: This bottle of wine doesn't have a price tag.

exampleSentences.italian: All'inizio della sua carriera tennistica, i giornalisti avevano affibbiato a Dimitrov l'etichetta di nuovo Federer.
exampleSentences.english: At the beginning of his tennis career, journalists labelled Dimitrov the new Federer.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to put a label on something

grammarNotes: Senso is a masculine noun. The plural is sensi. It takes the definite article il (singular) and i (plural), and the indefinite article un (singular) and dei (plural). The word has multiple distinct meanings in Italian, requiring context to disambiguate.
learnerNotes: Senso is highly polysemous; the meaning depends on context. Don't confuse 'avere senso' (to make sense) with 'fare senso' (a separate expression). The phrase 'In che senso?' is essential everyday Italian for asking clarification. Note that sensi in plural can mean 'consciousness' (e.g., perdere i sensi = lose consciousness), not just 'senses.'

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi a scuola, abbiamo imparato i cinque sensi.
exampleSentences.english: Today at school, we learned about the five senses.

exampleSentences.italian: Un senso di responsabilità.
exampleSentences.english: A sense of responsibility.

exampleSentences.italian: Se sei privo di sensi, sei incosciente.
exampleSentences.english: If you are without your senses, you are unconscious.

exampleSentences.italian: Perdere i sensi significa perdere conoscenza.
exampleSentences.english: To lose one's senses means to lose consciousness.

exampleSentences.italian: In che senso?
exampleSentences.english: What do you mean? / In what sense?

exampleSentences.italian: Trovo che sia una persona ingenua. – In che senso "ingenua"? A me sembra abbastanza astuto invece…
exampleSentences.english: I find him to be a naive person. – What do you mean "naive"? He seems quite astute to me…

exampleSentences.italian: Senza senso.
exampleSentences.english: Senseless / meaningless.

exampleSentences.italian: Un senso di nausea.
exampleSentences.english: A sensation of nausea.

exampleSentences.italian: In un certo senso, siamo soci io e te.
exampleSentences.english: In a way, you and I are partners.

exampleSentences.italian: Occhio! Questa via è a senso unico.
exampleSentences.english: Careful! This is a one-way street.

exampleSentences.italian: Beh, non saprei cosa dirti, nel senso che non so assolutamente nulla di questa faccenda.
exampleSentences.english: Well, I don't know what to tell you, in the sense that I know absolutely nothing about this matter.

exampleSentences.italian: Ha senso.
exampleSentences.english: It makes sense.

exampleSentences.italian: Non ha senso.
exampleSentences.english: It doesn't make sense.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to regain consciousness / to come to one's senses
What do you mean? / In what sense?
in the sense that / meaning that
(expression introduced but not completed in article)

englishTranslation: wisecrack / witticism / facetious joke / wittiness / facetiousness
grammarNotes: Feminine noun (la spiritosaggine) with regular plural (le spiritosaggini). Derived from the adjective spiritoso using the productive suffix -aggine, which attaches to adjectives to form nouns denoting typically negative qualities or character traits. The noun can refer either to witty remarks/jokes or to a person's witty/facetious character depending on context.
learnerNotes: Spiritosaggine typically carries a negative or mildly pejorative connotation when referring to inappropriate or tasteless jokes that fall flat. The -aggine suffix is a useful pattern for building nouns from adjectives, but remember these derived nouns usually denote unflattering qualities. Context determines whether you're describing the jokes themselves or someone's personality trait of being facetious.

exampleSentences.italian: Ne abbiamo abbastanza delle tue spiritosaggini!
exampleSentences.english: We've had enough of your wisecracks!

exampleSentences.italian: La sua spiritosaggine dà fastidio a tutti.
exampleSentences.english: His facetiousness gets on everyone's nerves.

grammarNotes: Forchetta is a feminine noun requiring the articles la (singular) and le (plural). It is the diminutive form of forca (pitchfork), derived from Latin furca. The related noun forchettata (a forkful, or the act of stabbing with a fork) is also feminine.
learnerNotes: Remember that forchetta is feminine (la forchetta), which affects article and adjective agreement. The idiom 'essere una buona forchetta' is a humorous way to describe someone who enjoys eating well. Note that forchettata, while primarily meaning a forkful, can also humorously refer to stabbing someone with a fork—useful for understanding context in informal Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: la forchetta
exampleSentences.english: the fork

exampleSentences.english: a fork

exampleSentences.english: the forks

exampleSentences.english: (some) forks

exampleSentences.english: plastic fork

exampleSentences.italian: forchetta da tavola
exampleSentences.english: dinner fork

exampleSentences.english: silver fork

exampleSentences.italian: forchettone
exampleSentences.english: carving fork

exampleSentences.italian: forchetta di acciaio
exampleSentences.english: steel fork

exampleSentences.italian: forchetta da dessert
exampleSentences.english: dessert fork
