grammarNotes: Dicembre is a masculine noun in Italian (il dicembre). Like all month names in Italian, it is not capitalized, unlike English. It is invariable and does not change in plural form. The word derives from Latin 'decem' (ten), as December was originally the tenth month of the Roman calendar.
learnerNotes: Remember that month names in Italian are never capitalized, even at the beginning of a sentence—a key difference from English. The phrase 'a dicembre' (in December) uses the preposition 'a' rather than 'in'. Note that Dicembre has two important Italian celebrations: the Immaculate Conception (8th) and St. Lucia's feast day (13th), which are culturally significant beyond Christmas itself.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei mai stato in Italia a dicembre?
exampleSentences.english: Have you ever been to Italy in December?

exampleSentences.italian: Dicembre è il dodicesimo mese dell'anno.
exampleSentences.english: December is the twelfth month of the year.

exampleSentences.italian: Dicembre consiste di trent'un giorni.
exampleSentences.english: December consists of 31 days.

exampleSentences.italian: A dicembre, gli italiani preparano l'albero di Natale l'8 dicembre.
exampleSentences.english: In December, Italians prepare the Christmas tree on December 8th.

exampleSentences.italian: Dicembre è il mese più magico per visitare l'Italia.
exampleSentences.english: December is the most magical month to visit Italy.

relatedExpressions.meaning: Christmas tree (traditionally put up on December 8th)

grammarNotes: Conto is a masculine noun requiring the articles il/un/i/dei. The phrase combines conto (calculation/count) with alla rovescia (backwards/inside out). The verb form is 'fare il conto alla rovescia' (to do the countdown) or 'contare alla rovescia' (to count backwards). Alla rovescia is an adverbial phrase modifying the action.
learnerNotes: Note that conto has multiple meanings (calculation, restaurant check, sum, importance) depending on context—here it means 'count' or 'calculation.' The phrase alla rovescia literally means 'inside out' or 'backwards,' but in this context specifically means 'backwards/in reverse order.' Alla rovescia is an adverbial phrase, so it doesn't change form regardless of the noun it modifies.

exampleSentences.italian: Stasera faremo il conto alla rovescia per accogliere il nuovo anno.
exampleSentences.english: Tonight we will be counting down to welcome in the new year.

exampleSentences.italian: La gente comincia a contare alla rovescia partendo dal numero dieci.
exampleSentences.english: People are starting to count down from the number ten.

exampleSentences.italian: Dieci, nove, otto, sette, sei, cinque, quattro, tre, due, uno…Buon Anno!
exampleSentences.english: Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one…Happy New Year!

grammarNotes: Mezzanotte is a feminine noun formed by combining mezzo (half/middle) + notte (night). The adjective mezzo becomes mezza to agree with the feminine noun notte, whereas in mezzogiorno (noon) mezzo remains masculine because giorno is masculine. The plural forms are rare but can be either mezzenotti or mezzanotti, taking the articles la/le (definite) or una/delle (indefinite).
learnerNotes: Mezzanotte can refer both to the time (midnight) and to the actual sound of bells chiming at midnight—context determines the meaning. The plural form is extremely rare in everyday Italian, so focus on the singular. Remember that gender agreement with mezzo is crucial: mezza for feminine nouns (mezzanotte), but mezzo for masculine nouns (mezzogiorno).

exampleSentences.italian: Caspita, è già mezzanotte. Dovrei andare a dormire.
exampleSentences.english: Oh my, it's already midnight. I should go to bed.

exampleSentences.italian: La mezzanotte è suonata senza che me ne sia accorto.
exampleSentences.english: Midnight struck without my realising it.

grammarNotes: Edera is a feminine noun beginning with a vowel. It takes the definite article l'edera (singular) and le edere (plural), and the indefinite articles un'edera (singular) and delle edere (plural). As a feminine noun, any modifying adjectives must agree in gender and number.
learnerNotes: Remember that edera is feminine, so articles and adjectives must agree (l'edera rossa = red ivy, not il/un edera). The expression 'attaccarsi come l'edera' can carry a negative connotation when describing a clingy person. Note that 'edera velenosa' (poison ivy) is not a true ivy botanically, but Italians call it by this name regardless.

exampleSentences.italian: In Cina c'è un villaggio abbandonato totalmente ricoperto di edera.
exampleSentences.english: In China there is an abandoned village completely covered with ivy.

exampleSentences.italian: L'edera è una pianta rampicante che cresce sui muri.
exampleSentences.english: Ivy is a climbing plant that grows on walls.

relatedExpressions.meaning: clinging like ivy; suggesting something is tenacious and long-lasting
to stick like ivy; refers to a person who is difficult to get rid of or who grows fond of somebody

grammarNotes: Bolognese is an adjective derived from the city name Bologna. It agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: bolognese (masculine/feminine singular), bolognesi (plural). The pronunciation of 'gn' represents a palatal nasal sound (ɲ) not found in English, and the final 'e' is pronounced as a schwa-like sound, not silent.
learnerNotes: English speakers often mispronounce 'bolognese' by dropping the final 'e' sound entirely (BO-LO-NAIZ). Remember that in Italian, the 'gn' combination is a single palatal nasal sound (similar to the 'ny' in 'canyon'), not pronounced as two separate letters. The word-final 'e' should be pronounced clearly, similar to the vowel sound in English 'bait' or 'sail'.

exampleSentences.italian: Marco è bolognese.
exampleSentences.english: Marco is from Bologna.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo piatto è tipicamente bolognese.
exampleSentences.english: This is a typical Bolognese dish.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai mai mangiato il ragù alla bolognese?
exampleSentences.english: Have you ever eaten ragù alla bolognese?

grammarNotes: Idoneo is a regular adjective with four forms based on gender and number: idoneo (masc. sing.), idonea (fem. sing.), idonei (masc. plur.), idonee (fem. plur.). It typically requires the prepositions 'a' or 'per' before its complement: 'idoneo a' (fit for) or 'idoneo per' (suitable for). The choice between 'a' and 'per' is largely interchangeable, though 'per' is more common in modern usage.
learnerNotes: Idoneo is a formal, somewhat literary adjective commonly used in official or legal contexts (military service, qualifications, formal meetings). While synonyms like 'adatto' are more frequently heard in everyday conversation, idoneo carries a more official tone. Pay attention to preposition choice: 'idoneo a + infinitive/noun' or 'idoneo per + noun' are both correct, with slight preference for 'per' in modern Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: il giorno idoneo
exampleSentences.english: the suitable day

exampleSentences.english: The young man is fit for military service.

exampleSentences.italian: Non è il momento idoneo per parlarne.

grammarNotes: Mistero is a masculine noun derived from Latin mysterium. It takes the definite articles il (singular) and i (plural), and indefinite articles un and (dei) misteri. Like most Italian nouns, it agrees in gender and number with modifying adjectives.
learnerNotes: Mistero refers to unsolved puzzles or difficult-to-understand situations and people. Note that giallo is a separate term specifically for detective/crime fiction, not interchangeable with mistero in all contexts. The word's modern usage has shifted from its Latin roots in religious rites to everyday puzzles and enigmas.

exampleSentences.italian: La scomparsa di Amelia è un vero mistero.
exampleSentences.english: Amelia's disappearance is a real mystery.

exampleSentences.italian: Guarda, mio fratello è un mistero. Sparisce per settimane, non si fa mai sentire e poi, all'improvviso, bussa alla tua porta così, senza preavviso.
exampleSentences.english: Look, my brother is a mystery. He disappears for weeks, he never calls and then, out of the blue, he knocks on your door just like that, without warning.

relatedExpressions.meaning: mystery/detective novel (literally 'yellow,' from the yellow covers of Giallo Mondadori book series)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun (il mare). Regular pluralization: il mare → i mari, un mare → dei mari. Takes standard masculine articles: il (definite singular), un (indefinite singular), i (definite plural), dei (indefinite plural). Often abbreviated to 'Mar' in proper names of seas.
learnerNotes: Mare resembles English 'marine' and derives from Latin, making it easy to remember. Note the distinction between 'mare' (the sea itself) and 'al mare' (the seaside as a destination or concept). Mare is frequently used figuratively to mean 'a lot of' something (un mare di compiti = a sea of homework), so context is important to distinguish literal from figurative usage.

grammarNotes: Sapientone is masculine (plural sapientoni); sapientona is feminine (plural sapientone). The word uses the augmentative suffixes -one and -ona added to the noun sapiente, which literally means 'big knower.' Gender and number agreement is required with articles: il sapientone, i sapientoni, la sapientona, le sapientone.
learnerNotes: Sapientone/a is distinctly colloquial and pejorative—use it to describe someone dismissively. The expression 'fare il sapientone' is more versatile for indirect self-deprecation (e.g., apologizing before giving an opinion). Note that the feminine plural is sapientone (not sapientoni), which differs from typical feminine plurals ending in -e.

grammarNotes: As an adjective, certo agrees with the noun it modifies: certo (masc. sing.), certa (fem. sing.), certi (masc. plur.), certe (fem. plur.). It can also function as a noun meaning 'certainty,' as a pronoun meaning 'certain people,' or as an adverb meaning 'certainly.' The Latin root is certum, from cernĕre (to distinguish).
learnerNotes: Certo is a highly versatile word that functions as adjective, noun, adverb, and pronoun depending on context. The expression 'Ma certo!' is an extremely common colloquial response meaning 'of course!' and is essential for everyday conversation. Be careful not to confuse certo with the adverb certamente (certainly), which is more emphatic and formal—certo used as an adverb is less common but still acceptable.

exampleSentences.english: I'm certain they will come tonight.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun (l'aiuola, le aiuole). Uses definite articles l'/le and indefinite articles un'/delle. The plural aiuole uniquely contains all five Italian vowels (a, e, i, o, u) separated only by the consonant L. Pronunciation is challenging for English speakers due to four adjacent vowel sounds in the singular form.
learnerNotes: Aiuola and its variant aiola are perfect synonyms, but aiuola is considered more literary. Many Italians use aiola in everyday speech due to pronunciation ease. Be aware of the challenging vowel cluster—practice the pronunciation carefully. The compound aiuola spartitraffico is useful for travel/driving contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Non calpestare l'aiuola!
exampleSentences.english: Don't walk on the flowerbed!

exampleSentences.italian: Si dice aiola o aiuola?
exampleSentences.english: Do you say 'aiola' or 'aiuola'?

grammarNotes: Pretendere is a regular -ERE verb conjugated as: io pretendo, tu pretendi, lui/lei pretende, Lei pretende (formal), noi pretendiamo, voi pretendete, loro pretendono. It can be followed by a noun, adverb, or the infinitive (pretendo di + infinitive). It is a classic false cognate with English 'pretend', though some semantic overlap exists in archaic or specialized contexts.
learnerNotes: Pretendere is a notorious false cognate: it does NOT mean 'to pretend' in the sense of feigning or acting. Use it for 'to expect,' 'to demand,' or 'to insist on.' Remember that pretendere can take a direct noun (pretendo rispetto) or require the construction pretendo di + infinitive (pretendo di sapere). The connection to English 'pretend' only applies to archaic meanings related to 'laying claim to' something.

exampleSentences.italian: Non pretendo che tu mi accompagni ogni volta.
exampleSentences.english: I don't expect you to come with me every time.

exampleSentences.italian: Pretendere alla corona.
exampleSentences.english: To pretend / aspire to the throne.

exampleSentences.english: I can't pretend / presume to know what you're going through.

grammarNotes: Allora is a highly flexible word functioning as adverb (meaning 'then' or 'at that time'), conjunction (meaning 'so' or 'in that case'), or adjective (describing something from a particular era, used with definite article l'). As an adjective, it precedes the noun: l'allora presidente. Its meaning shifts based on syntactic context and is fundamental to conversational Italian.
learnerNotes: Allora is one of the most frequently used words in Italian but deceptively complex due to its multiple functions. The key to mastery is recognizing context: as an adverb it marks temporal reference; as a conjunction it signals logical consequence or conversation structure; as an adjective it always appears with the article l' before a noun. In colloquial speech, allora frequently opens sentences to grab attention (like 'right then' in English) and should not always be translated literally—learn it through example sentences rather than trying to match each usage to a single English equivalent.

exampleSentences.italian: Allora non capivo perché Antonio non voleva andarci.
exampleSentences.english: At the time I didn't understand why Antonio didn't want to go.

exampleSentences.italian: Allora si usava salvare tutto su floppy disc.
exampleSentences.english: Back then they used to save everything onto floppy discs.

exampleSentences.italian: Si chiama Yoko Ono, l'allora fidanzata e poi moglie di John Lennon.
exampleSentences.english: She's called Yoko Ono, the then girlfriend and later wife of John Lennon.

exampleSentences.italian: Allora ci vediamo domani!
exampleSentences.english: See you tomorrow then! Well, see you tomorrow!

exampleSentences.italian: Se vuoi venire anche tu, allora preparati.
exampleSentences.english: If you want to come as well, then get ready.

exampleSentences.italian: Le scuole erano chiuse per la neve e allora sono rimasto a casa.
exampleSentences.english: The schools were closed due to snow and so I stayed at home.

exampleSentences.italian: Allora…vorrei cominciare a parlare di un argomento che interessa molti lettori di questo blog.
exampleSentences.english: Now then…I'd like to begin by talking about a topic that interests many of the readers of this blog.

exampleSentences.italian: Antonio non mi tratta bene. – E allora, lascialo!
exampleSentences.english: Antonio doesn't treat me well. – Then leave him!

exampleSentences.italian: Allora? Cosa ti ha detto?
exampleSentences.english: So? What did he say?

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi mi sono lavato i denti. – E allora?
exampleSentences.english: Today I brushed my teeth. – So what?

relatedExpressions.meaning: in that very moment, in that precise moment
from that moment on, since then, ever since
from that time, in those days

grammarNotes: Ciottolo is a masculine noun, the diminutive form of the archaic word ciotto. The plural is ciottoli. It takes the definite articles il/i and indefinite articles un/dei. In Tuscany, it can also mean a terracotta dish.
learnerNotes: Do not confuse ciottolo (pebble) with the similar-sounding ciotola (bowl/dish). Ciottolo refers to smooth, water-rounded stones, while the adjective ciottoloso describes surfaces made of pebbles or cobblestones. Regional variation: in Tuscany, ciottolo can also mean a terracotta dish, so context is important.

exampleSentences.italian: Prese un ciottolo e lo gettò nell'acqua.
exampleSentences.english: He picked up a pebble and threw it in the water.

relatedExpressions.meaning: pebbly; cobblestone (when referring to a road surface)

grammarNotes: Mano is feminine (la mano, le mani) despite ending in -o, because it derives from Latin manus, a fourth-declension feminine noun. This gender is retained across all Romance languages. Articles: definite (la/le), indefinite (una/delle mani).
learnerNotes: Remember that mano is feminine despite the -o ending—this is a notorious exception. Hands appear extensively in Italian idioms, so learning common expressions will significantly improve fluency. Pay attention to the distinction between expressions using 'la mano' (the hand/one's hand) versus 'le mani' (the hands/one's hands), as usage differs from English.

exampleSentences.italian: Man mano che rendiamo il piatto più goloso, le calorie salgono.
exampleSentences.english: The tastier we make the dish, the more the calories increase.

exampleSentences.italian: Non mi dedico alla cucina da un po'. Spero di non aver perso la mano!
exampleSentences.english: I haven't done much cooking in a while. I hope I haven't lost the knack for it!

relatedExpressions.meaning: off the beaten track / out of the way
to get the hang of something
to be out of practice / rusty / to lose the knack for something
to ask for something / to beg
to be close at hand, within reach

relatedExpressions.expression: mettere mano al portafoglio / alla borsa
relatedExpressions.meaning: to pay one's share, chip in
to take control of the situation

relatedExpressions.expression: starsene con le mani in mano
relatedExpressions.meaning: to be idle, to twiddle one's thumbs
to have holes in one's hands / to spend money frivolously

grammarNotes: Masculine noun (il battibecco). Plural forms the -co → -chi (i battibecchi), not -ci. Takes standard masculine articles: il/un (singular), i/dei (plural). When used as a verb, employ either battibeccare or the expression avere un battibecco, typically followed by the preposition con (with).
learnerNotes: Battibecco is a colloquial, colorful word evoking the image of fighting birds (literally from battere 'to hit' + becco 'beak'). It refers specifically to brief, trivial verbal quarrels rather than serious conflicts. Note that both battibeccare (verb) and avere un battibecco (expression) require the preposition con when indicating the person involved.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho avuto un battibecco con un cliente noioso.
exampleSentences.english: I had a quarrel with an annoying customer.

exampleSentences.italian: Perché battibecchi sempre con tua sorella?
exampleSentences.english: Why are you always bickering with your sister?

relatedExpressions.meaning: to have a quarrel / to quarrel
to quarrel / to squabble / to bicker

grammarNotes: Masculine noun taking regular articles: il pasticcio (singular), i pasticci (plural). Indefinite forms: un pasticcio, (dei) pasticci. The word has dual meanings: literally a type of pie or casserole dish, and figuratively any chaotic or disorganized situation.
learnerNotes: Pasticcio is a false cognate with English 'pastiche'—they share etymology but mean entirely different things. Pastiche refers to an artistic medley, while pasticcio means mess or chaos. Use this word in informal, conversational Italian to describe disorganized situations; it's colloquial but not rude. The related verb pasticciare and noun pasticcione/pasticciona are useful for expanding expression around this concept.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa traduzione è un gran pasticcio.
exampleSentences.english: This translation is a real mess.

exampleSentences.italian: Che pasticcio!
exampleSentences.english: What a mess!

exampleSentences.italian: pasticci di carne
exampleSentences.english: meat pies

exampleSentences.italian: pasticci di spinaci
exampleSentences.english: spinach pies

relatedExpressions.meaning: to make a mess, to scribble, to mess around (verb)
mess maker (noun; often used jokingly with children)

grammarNotes: Despite ending in -a, clima is masculine and takes masculine articles: il clima (singular), i climi (plural). The indefinite articles are un clima and (dei) climi. This is an exception to the typical feminine -a ending pattern in Italian.
learnerNotes: Be careful: clima is masculine (il clima), not feminine despite the -a ending. Don't confuse clima (long-term weather patterns) with tempo (short-term weather). Clima can also mean 'atmosphere' or 'mood' figuratively when describing the overall spirit of a place or group (e.g., un clima accogliente = welcoming atmosphere).

exampleSentences.italian: Com'è il clima in Giappone?
exampleSentences.english: What's the climate like in Japan?

exampleSentences.italian: Il clima politico è in fermento. Tra poco ci sono le elezioni.
exampleSentences.english: The political climate is in turmoil. The elections will be held soon.

grammarNotes: Spinoso is a regular adjective with four forms based on gender and number. Masculine singular: spinoso; feminine singular: spinosa; masculine plural: spinosi; feminine plural: spinose. The ending changes to agree with the noun it modifies. Beyond literal meaning (thorny plants), it functions metaphorically to describe abstract concepts like problems or sensitive topics.
learnerNotes: Remember that spinoso works like English 'thorny' in both literal and figurative contexts—you can use it for both plants and sensitive topics. The figurative meanings (difficult, awkward, sticky, touchy) are especially useful for discussing problems or uncomfortable conversations. Be careful to match the adjective ending to the noun's gender and number, as this is a regular four-form adjective.

exampleSentences.italian: il cespuglio spinoso
exampleSentences.english: the prickly bush

exampleSentences.italian: la pianta spinosa
exampleSentences.english: the prickly plant

exampleSentences.italian: i rami spinosi
exampleSentences.english: the prickly branches

exampleSentences.italian: le foglie spinose
exampleSentences.english: the prickly leaves

exampleSentences.italian: Il gambo della rosa è molto spinoso.
exampleSentences.english: The stem of the rose is very thorny.

exampleSentences.italian: È un argomento un po' spinoso. Non ho voglia di parlarne.
exampleSentences.english: It's a bit of a touchy subject. I don't want to talk about it.

relatedExpressions.meaning: porcupine (literally: spiny pig, from porca + spina)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun taking articles il/i (definite) and un/dei (indefinite). Commonly used in plural form brividi. Combines with verbs avere, venire, avvertire, mettere, dare, or far venire to express the sensation of shivers or chills running through the body.
learnerNotes: Brivido typically appears in plural (brividi) in everyday speech. The verb pattern 'mi vengono i brividi' uses an impersonal construction common in Italian—literally 'shivers come to me'—rather than the direct 'I have shivers.' Note that brivido can mean both physical shivers and emotional thrills depending on context; da brivido is particularly useful for describing spine-tingling experiences.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi vengono i brividi quando ho la febbre.
exampleSentences.english: I get the shivers when I have a fever.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo film dell'orrore mi mette i brividi ogni volta che lo guardo!
exampleSentences.english: This horror film sends shivers down my spine every time I watch it!

relatedExpressions.meaning: I get the shivers (lit. the shivers come to me)
to send shivers down one's spine

grammarNotes: Odierno is a four-form adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: odierno (masc. sing.), odierna (fem. sing.), odierni (masc. plur.), odierne (fem. plur.). It derives from Latin hodiernus and is commonly used in advanced contexts like news articles and academic writing. The adjective always precedes or follows the noun it describes.
learnerNotes: Odierno is primarily used in formal, written contexts such as news, academia, and official documents—you'll rarely hear it in everyday conversation where italians prefer 'di oggi' or 'di questi giorni'. Pay attention to gender and number agreement, as mistakes are common. Note that odierno emphasizes modernity or currency rather than simply 'today,' so context matters when choosing between odierno and other time-related descriptors.

exampleSentences.italian: La lezione odierna è posticipata fino a nuovo avviso.
exampleSentences.english: Today's lesson is postponed until further notice.

exampleSentences.italian: le tecnologie odierne
exampleSentences.english: modern technology

exampleSentences.italian: la situazione odierna
exampleSentences.english: the current situation

exampleSentences.italian: gli appuntamenti odierni
exampleSentences.english: today's appointments

exampleSentences.italian: l'odierno bollettino meteorologico
exampleSentences.english: today's weather report

relatedExpressions.meaning: nowadays / these days (alternative expression for modern times)

englishTranslation: despite / in spite of / although / even though / however
grammarNotes: Nonostante has three main functions: (1) as a preposition meaning 'despite/in spite of,' it precedes a noun and remains invariable; (2) as a conjunction, it's followed by 'che' (often omitted) and a subjunctive verb; (3) as an adverb meaning 'however,' it combines with 'ciò' in various forms (ciò nonostante, ciònonostante). The archaic two-word spelling 'non ostante' shows agreement with plural nouns, but this is rare in modern Italian.
learnerNotes: Nonostante is more formal and common in written Italian than speech. When using it as a conjunction, the subjunctive verb is required after 'che,' even though native speakers often omit 'che' itself. Be aware that 'ciò nonostante' (with ciò) means 'however' and connects independent clauses, while simple 'nonostante' as a preposition connects to a noun phrase—don't confuse these distinct uses.

exampleSentences.italian: Marco è uscito, nonostante la neve.
exampleSentences.english: Marco went out in spite of the snow.

exampleSentences.italian: Nonostante tutto, le vuole ancora bene.
exampleSentences.english: Despite everything, he still loves her.

exampleSentences.italian: Nonostante (che) si fosse allenato duramente, non riuscì a vincere la gara.
exampleSentences.english: Even though he trained hard, he didn't manage to win the race.

exampleSentences.italian: Nonostante (che) sia tardi, non vado a dormire.
exampleSentences.english: Although it's late, I'm not going to sleep.

exampleSentences.italian: Ha perso tutti i suoi soldi – ciò nonostante non vuole l'aiuto della sua famiglia.
exampleSentences.english: He lost all his money – however he refuses his family's help.

relatedExpressions.meaning: although / even though (conjunction form with che)

grammarNotes: Orecchio is masculine singular, derived from Latin auriculam. It has two plurals: orecchi (masculine, referring to ears individually) and orecchie (feminine, referring to a pair of ears or ears as one entity). The feminine singular form orecchia exists but rarely indicates the organ; instead it denotes ear-like protruding objects. Gender and number agreement is essential when using articles and adjectives with these forms.
learnerNotes: Pay careful attention to the plural forms: use orecchi for individual ears (e.g., five pig ears) but orecchie for a person's pair of ears as a single unit (e.g., red ears from cold). The feminine singular orecchia is rarely used literally to mean the organ itself; it typically refers to ear-shaped objects like folded page corners. Orecchio appears in numerous idiomatic expressions in Italian, and these figurative uses of orecchi are far more common than literal ones.

exampleSentences.italian: L'orecchio è l'organo del corpo umano preposto alla funzione uditiva.
exampleSentences.english: The ear is the organ of the human body responsible for auditory function.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi sono fatto il piercing all'orecchio destro.
exampleSentences.english: I got my right ear pierced.

exampleSentences.italian: Ha comprato cinque orecchi di maiale da dare al suo cane.
exampleSentences.english: He bought five pig ears to give to his dog.

exampleSentences.italian: Il bimbo aveva le orecchie rosse per il freddo.
exampleSentences.english: The boy had red ears due to the cold.

exampleSentences.italian: Fare l'orecchia alla pagina significa piegare l'angolo di una pagina.
exampleSentences.english: To fold down the corner of a page (making an ear-like shape) serves as a bookmark.

relatedExpressions.expression: Anche i muri hanno le orecchie

relatedExpressions.meaning: to have a good ear for music
to have a sharp sense of hearing

relatedExpressions.expression: Mettere una pulce nell'orecchio di qualcuno
relatedExpressions.meaning: to put a bug in someone's ear

grammarNotes: Masculine noun starting with a vowel, taking the definite article l' (singular) and gli (plural). The indefinite articles are un (singular) and degli (plural). It derives from Latin aequinoctium (aequus + nox noctis). Regular plural formation: equinozio → equinozi.
learnerNotes: This is a scientific/astronomical term, so it's formal and specialized. While it appears to be a cognate with English 'equinox,' remember it's pronounced with Italian phonetics: eh-kwee-NOH-tsyoh. The dates mentioned (March 19-21 and September 21-24) are useful context for understanding why the article emphasizes variability.

exampleSentences.italian: L'equinozio non cade sempre nello stesso giorno.
exampleSentences.english: The equinox doesn't always fall on the same day.

relatedExpressions.meaning: leap years (cause variation in equinox dates)

grammarNotes: Squillo is a masculine noun beginning with sq-, so it requires the special definite article lo (singular) and gli (plural), with corresponding indefinite articles uno and degli. The plural form is squilli. Gender agreement is required with adjectives and articles modifying this word.
learnerNotes: The expression 'fare uno squillo' is distinctly Italian and reflects cellphone culture from the early 2000s when calls were expensive; while still understood, it's less common with modern unlimited plans. Remember that squillo derives from the verb squillare (to ring), which may help with retention. The word applies to ringing sounds from phones, doorbells, and trumpets—notice the context determines the exact English equivalent.

exampleSentences.italian: lo squillo
exampleSentences.english: the ring

exampleSentences.italian: gli squilli
exampleSentences.english: the rings

exampleSentences.italian: uno squillo
exampleSentences.english: a ring

exampleSentences.italian: degli squilli
exampleSentences.english: some rings

exampleSentences.italian: Ti faccio uno squillo quando arrivo!
exampleSentences.english: I'll give you a ring (and then hang up) when I arrive!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to give someone a missed call; to let the phone ring once or twice without expecting them to pick up, historically used to avoid telephone charges

grammarNotes: Ricetta is a feminine noun taking the articles la (singular), le (plural), una (indefinite singular), and (delle) ricette (indefinite plural). It follows regular feminine noun patterns and agrees with feminine adjectives and pronouns. The word has two primary meanings—culinary recipe and medical prescription—but context typically disambiguates usage.
learnerNotes: Ricetta is a false cognate with English 'recipe'—while it does mean recipe in culinary contexts, it equally means prescription in medical contexts, so always check context. Remember the feminine gender (la ricetta, una ricetta). The figurative sense meaning 'solution' or 'remedy' is productive in modern Italian, especially in journalism; expand your mental associations beyond food and medicine.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho seguito la ricetta alla lettera.
exampleSentences.english: I followed the recipe to the letter.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono andato a ritirare la ricetta in farmacia.
exampleSentences.english: I went to pick up the prescription at the pharmacy.

exampleSentences.italian: una ricetta contro la noia
exampleSentences.english: a remedy against boredom

exampleSentences.italian: ricetta scaccia crisi
exampleSentences.english: a solution for fighting economic downturn

grammarNotes: Masculine noun starting with a vowel, taking the article l' in singular. Plural is gli aeroplani. Derives from Latin aer (air) and planus (plane) via French aéroplane. In everyday usage, Italians prefer the abbreviated form aereo rather than the full aeroplano.
learnerNotes: While aeroplano is the formal/correct term, most native speakers use aereo in everyday conversation—learn both forms to understand spoken Italian. Many Italians mistakenly pronounce/spell it as *aereoplano, thinking aereo derives from aeroplano, but it's actually the reverse. Note that verbs related to flying typically pair with aereo rather than the full form aeroplano.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo aeroplano è molto grande!
exampleSentences.english: This airplane is really big!

exampleSentences.italian: l'aeroplano
exampleSentences.english: the airplane

exampleSentences.italian: gli aeroplani
exampleSentences.english: the airplanes

exampleSentences.italian: un aeroplano
exampleSentences.english: an airplane

exampleSentences.italian: Sbrighiamoci, non vogliamo perdere l'aereo!
exampleSentences.english: Let's hurry up, we don't want to miss the plane!

relatedExpressions.meaning: airplane (common everyday form); also used in attacco aereo (air attack) and posta aerea (air mail)
colloquial variant with inverted letters 'e' and 'r'

grammarNotes: Biberon is an invariable masculine noun, meaning its form remains unchanged in both singular and plural. Use the article il/un for singular and i/dei for plural. It follows regular masculine noun patterns with articles and adjectives.
learnerNotes: Biberon is a French loanword (from Latin bibere, 'to drink') and is invariable—never add an -i or -e in plural. The idiom 'avere ancora bisogno del biberon' is useful for describing immaturity in casual Italian. Note the synonym poppatoio is less common but more literary/formal.

exampleSentences.italian: il biberon
exampleSentences.english: the baby bottle

exampleSentences.italian: i biberon
exampleSentences.english: the baby bottles

exampleSentences.italian: un biberon
exampleSentences.english: a baby bottle

exampleSentences.italian: dei biberon
exampleSentences.english: (some) baby bottles

exampleSentences.italian: Il bambino preferisce il seno al biberon.
exampleSentences.english: The baby prefers the breast to the bottle.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to still need one's baby bottle (idiom describing someone immature, naive, or inexperienced)
synonym for baby bottle; derived from poppare (to drink mother's milk)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun beginning with a consonant. Singular articles: il modo (definite), un modo (indefinite). Plural articles: i modi (definite), dei modi (indefinite). Derives from Latin modus ('measure'). Commonly used in prepositional phrases and idiomatic expressions.
learnerNotes: Modo is extremely versatile and appears in countless set expressions—focus on learning the most common prepositional phrases like 'in modo da' and 'in modo che' as fixed chunks. Note that 'modi' (plural) can specifically refer to manners or behaviour, often with a negative connotation (e.g., 'brutti modi'). Be aware that modo can mean 'opportunity' or 'possibility' in contexts like 'dare modo di' rather than just the literal 'way'.

exampleSentences.italian: Perché si comporta in quel modo?
exampleSentences.english: Why is he behaving in that way?

exampleSentences.italian: Devi fare in modo che la tua voce venga ascoltata.
exampleSentences.english: You have to make sure your voice is heard.

exampleSentences.italian: Che modi sgarbati! Comportati bene per favore!
exampleSentences.english: What bad manners you have! Behave yourself please!

exampleSentences.italian: Gli darò modo di pensarci.
exampleSentences.english: I'll give him the opportunity / possibility to think about it.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è modo e modo di dire le cose.
exampleSentences.english: There's a right way and a wrong way to say things.

exampleSentences.italian: Sempre a modo mio
exampleSentences.english: Always my way

So as to / In such a way to
In such a way as to
Not at all / In no way
To give somebody a way to do something
According to the rules or conventions of expected behaviour
There's a right way and a wrong way

grammarNotes: Conchiglia is a feminine noun taking the definite article 'la' (singular) and 'le' (plural). The plural form is conchiglie. It follows regular feminine noun patterns: una conchiglia (a shell), le conchiglie (the shells). The word derives from Latin conchylium and Greek konkhýlion, both meaning something concave.
learnerNotes: Do not use conchiglia for egg shells or nut shells—use guscio instead. Conchiglia refers specifically to shells from living marine creatures. In its plural form, conchiglie is a common pasta shape (similar to English 'shells' or 'conchiglioni' for larger versions).

exampleSentences.italian: Ho trovato una bellissima conchiglia sulla spiaggia.
exampleSentences.english: I found a beautiful shell on the beach.

exampleSentences.italian: Il nostro portachiavi è a forma di conchiglia.
exampleSentences.english: Our keychain is shaped like a shell.

relatedExpressions.meaning: protective cup for groin (used in sports)

grammarNotes: Libreria is a feminine noun taking the articles la (singular), le (plural), una (indefinite singular), and delle (indefinite plural). It is a false cognate with English 'library,' which translates to biblioteca in Italian. The word has multiple meanings: primarily a bookshop/bookstore, secondarily a piece of furniture (bookcase) or room for storing books.
learnerNotes: Beware of the false cognate: libreria ≠ library. Always remember that a public library in Italian is called una biblioteca, not una libreria. The word libreria can refer to a physical bookshop, a piece of furniture, or abstractly to a collection of books—context determines the precise meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: Vado in libreria a comprare un libro.
exampleSentences.english: I'm going to the bookstore to buy a book.

exampleSentences.italian: Mettiamo tutti i libri nella libreria.
exampleSentences.english: Let's put all the books in the bookcase.

exampleSentences.italian: Giorgio ha una libreria enorme.
exampleSentences.english: Giorgio has an enormous library / collection of books.

relatedExpressions.meaning: Marciana Library (formerly known as la Libreria Pubblica di San Marco)

grammarNotes: Nanna is a feminine noun (la nanna, le nanne). It is a phonosymbolic term, meaning the word's sound evokes its meaning. While primarily used with children, it can be used playfully with adults. It commonly appears with four specific verbs: fare la nanna, andare a nanna, mettere a nanna, and mandare a nanna.
learnerNotes: Nanna is distinctly childish and cute—avoid using it in formal contexts. The phrase mandare a nanna has two meanings: literally 'to put to bed' and figuratively 'to discard/retire' (like an old computer). While dormire and sonno are more standard, nanna is widely used in everyday speech with children and is worth recognizing.

exampleSentences.italian: È ora di fare la nanna.
exampleSentences.english: It's time to sleep.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho mandato a nanna il mio vecchio computer.
exampleSentences.english: I put my old computer out to pasture.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to sleep / to go to sleep / to go to bed / to have a sleep
to go to sleep / to go to bed
to send to bed / to put out to pasture (figurative)

grammarNotes: Moquette is an invariable feminine noun, meaning its form does not change in the plural. The article and any modifiers change (la/le, una/delle), but the noun itself remains moquette in both singular and plural forms.
learnerNotes: Moquette is a French loanword commonly used in Italian for fitted carpeting. Note that wall-to-wall carpets are relatively uncommon in Italian homes compared to the UK and North America—Italians typically prefer parquet floors with area rugs (tappeti) instead. Be aware that invariable nouns are a small but important category in Italian; always check the article or context to determine singular vs. plural.

exampleSentences.italian: la moquette
exampleSentences.english: the carpet

exampleSentences.italian: le moquette
exampleSentences.english: the carpets

exampleSentences.italian: una moquette
exampleSentences.english: a carpet

exampleSentences.italian: delle moquette
exampleSentences.english: (some) carpets

exampleSentences.italian: Il 98% delle case inglesi ha la moquette, mentre in Italia la percentuale è del 2%.
exampleSentences.english: 98% of British homes have carpet, while in Italy the percentage is 2%.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun starting with a vowel. Definite article: l'unghia (singular), le unghie (plural). Indefinite article: un'unghia (singular), delle unghie (plural). Derives from Latin ungula via Tuscan ugna.
learnerNotes: Remember that unghia is feminine (l'unghia, un'unghia) and loses the 'n' before vowels in the indefinite article. Use le unghie delle mani vs. dei piedi to specify hands vs. feet. Many reflexive verbs pair with unghie (tagliarsi, limarsi, dipingersi), so practise these common collocations for nail care vocabulary.

exampleSentences.italian: L'unghia del dito indice cresce più velocemente di quella del mignolo.
exampleSentences.english: The nail of the index finger grows faster than that of the little finger.

exampleSentences.italian: Dobbiamo tagliare le unghie al gatto! Guarda come ha conciato il divano!
exampleSentences.english: We have to cut the cat's claws! Look at what he did to the couch!

exampleSentences.italian: Il mio gatto mi ha dato un'unghiata in faccia!
exampleSentences.english: My cat scratched my face!

exampleSentences.italian: Aggiungi ancora un'unghia di zucchero e sarà perfetto.
exampleSentences.english: Just add a little bit more sugar and it will be perfect.

relatedExpressions.expression: farsi le unghie / farsi fare le unghie
relatedExpressions.meaning: to do one's nails / to get one's nails done

relatedExpressions.expression: dipingersi le unghie / farsi dipingere le unghie
relatedExpressions.meaning: to paint one's nails / to get one's nails painted
a scratch made by a fingernail

relatedExpressions.expression: Difendersi con le unghie e con i denti
Cadere / finire tra le unghie di (qualcuno)
relatedExpressions.meaning: To fall into the clutches of (someone)

grammarNotes: Aiuto is a masculine noun taking articles l'aiuto (singular), un aiuto (singular indefinite), gli aiuti (plural), and degli aiuti (plural indefinite). It is also the first-person singular present conjugation of the verb aiutare ('I help'). The gender does not change when referring to a female assistant.
learnerNotes: Note that aiuto functions both as a standalone noun ('help') and as the first-person singular conjugation of aiutare—context determines usage. The plural form aiuti typically refers to material aid (food, clothing, money) rather than abstract help. Aiuto! as an interjection is equivalent to the English emergency call 'Help!'

exampleSentences.italian: (io) Aiuto mio fratello a fare i compiti.
exampleSentences.english: I help my brother do his homework.

exampleSentences.italian: Posso chiedere il tuo aiuto con questo rompicapo?
exampleSentences.english: Can I ask for your help with this dilemma?

exampleSentences.italian: Non so che cosa avremmo fatto senza il vostro aiuto.
exampleSentences.english: I don't know what we would have done without your support.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei stato di grande aiuto!
exampleSentences.english: You've been a big help!

exampleSentences.italian: Aiuto! Mi hanno rubato la borsa!
exampleSentences.english: Help! They stole my bag!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to come to the aid (of someone)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun beginning with 'a' taking the definite article 'l'' and indefinite article 'un'. Plural forms are 'gli abiti' and 'degli abiti'. In formal contexts, abito is preferred over its synonym vestito, which is more colloquial. Abito can also mean 'habit' or 'custom' in a figurative sense.
learnerNotes: Abito and vestito are near-synonyms, but abito is formal/elevated while vestito is casual—use abito for fancy events, formal descriptions, or figurative 'habits/customs.' Remember the masculine article 'l'' before abito (not 'la'). The plural vestiti refers generically to 'clothes,' whereas abiti specifically means 'more than one suit/dress.'

exampleSentences.italian: l'abito
exampleSentences.english: the dress / suit / gown

exampleSentences.italian: gli abiti
exampleSentences.english: the dresses / suits / gowns

exampleSentences.italian: un abito
exampleSentences.english: a dress / suit / gown

exampleSentences.italian: degli abiti
exampleSentences.english: (some) dresses / suits / gowns

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piacciono molto gli abiti in questo negozio.
exampleSentences.english: I really like the suits / dresses in this shop.

exampleSentences.italian: È difficile cambiare gli abiti mentali.
exampleSentences.english: It's difficult to change one's mental habits.

relatedExpressions.meaning: the habit doesn't make the monk / you can't judge a book by its cover

grammarNotes: Procione is a masculine noun. It follows regular masculine noun declension patterns: il procione (the raccoon, singular), i procioni (the raccoons, plural), un procione (a raccoon, singular), dei procioni (some raccoons, plural). As a masculine noun, all modifiers and articles must agree in gender.
learnerNotes: Procione is a straightforward masculine noun commonly used in Italian wildlife contexts. Note the alternative name orsetto lavatore ('washing bear') exists but is less common; procione is the modern standard term. Be aware that the word comes from Greek and refers specifically to the North American animal, so it may be less familiar in conversational Italian unless discussing nature or animals.

exampleSentences.italian: I procioni sono attratti dai bidoni della spazzatura.
exampleSentences.english: Raccoons are attracted to trash cans.

exampleSentences.italian: il procione
exampleSentences.english: the raccoon

exampleSentences.italian: i procioni
exampleSentences.english: the raccoons

exampleSentences.italian: un procione
exampleSentences.english: a raccoon

relatedExpressions.meaning: literally 'washing bear'; an alternative Italian name for raccoon, from Linnaeus's Ursus lotor classification
the dexterous front paws (a distinctive feature of raccoons)
the black facial mask (distinctive marking of raccoons)

relatedExpressions.expression: gli anelli chiari e scuri alternati della coda
relatedExpressions.meaning: the alternating light and dark rings of the tail (raccoon's ringed tail)

englishTranslation: disarray / mess / confusion / upside-down / shambles / topsy-turvy
grammarNotes: Masculine noun with plural form soqquadri. Notably one of only two Italian words with consecutive Q letters (along with the near-obsolete biqquadro/beqquadro). Can be used predicatively after nouns with the preposition 'a' (e.g., una stanza a soqquadro), or as the object of common verbs like mettere.
learnerNotes: Soqquadro is rarely used outside the fixed expression 'mettere a soqquadro,' so focus on learning this collocation rather than the word in isolation. The etymological origin (sotto quadro, 'under square') relates to builders' terminology but is not essential to know for usage. This is a relatively advanced, less-common word—prioritize more frequent synonyms like disordine or confusione for everyday conversation.

exampleSentences.italian: I ladri hanno messo a soqquadro la casa.
exampleSentences.english: The thieves turned the house upside down.

exampleSentences.italian: una stanza a soqquadro
exampleSentences.english: a room in disarray

relatedExpressions.meaning: to turn everything upside-down / to make a mess of

grammarNotes: Bocciolo is a masculine noun. The plural is boccioli. It takes the articles il/i (definite) and un/dei (indefinite). The related term boccio also means bud and derives from bocciolo, used in the fixed phrase 'in boccio' (in the process of budding/blooming).
learnerNotes: Bocciolo is a nature-related noun useful for spring vocabulary. Don't confuse it with bottone (button), which can mean bud in certain contexts but primarily means button. Related terms germoglio (sprout) and virgulto (offshoot) are distinct stages of plant growth; bocciolo specifically refers to the unopened flower bud.

exampleSentences.italian: Sotto casa mia c'è un albero pieno di boccioli.
exampleSentences.english: In front of my house there is a tree covered in buds.

exampleSentences.italian: Bisogna proteggere il fiore quando è in boccio.
exampleSentences.english: The flower must be protected when it is blooming.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to bud / to put out buds
in the process of budding or blooming
button (synonym for bud in botanical context)

grammarNotes: Capriola is a feminine noun; plural form is capriole. Uses definite article la (singular) / le (plural) and indefinite article una (singular) / delle (plural). Derives from Latin capreŏla (diminutive of capra, goat), reflecting its etymological connection to animal movement.
learnerNotes: Capriola has multiple contexts: literal (gymnastics, acrobatics, children's play), figurative (sudden policy changes in politics), and specialized (equestrian movements, classical dance). Don't confuse it with salto (jump) or capitombolo (clumsy tumble), though capriola can work as a synonym for both depending on context. The word conjures animal agility from its etymological roots—useful for remembering its playful, dynamic connotation.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi insegni a fare le capriole?
exampleSentences.english: Can you teach me how to do somersaults?

exampleSentences.italian: Sta facendo le capriole dalla gioia.
exampleSentences.english: He's so happy he is jumping.

exampleSentences.italian: Stai attento, o farai una bella capriola giù per le scale!
exampleSentences.english: Be careful, or you'll take a tumble down the stairs!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to do a somersault; (figuratively) to make a complete and sudden change in opinion or policy
an about-turn in politics; a sudden policy reversal

grammarNotes: Ritornello is a masculine noun derived from the verb ritornare (to return) with the diminutive suffix -ello. As a masculine noun, it takes the articles il/i (definite) and un/dei (indefinite). The plural form is ritornelli. The word literally means 'the little thing that returns.'
learnerNotes: Ritornello has a dual meaning: in music it refers to a recurring passage or chorus, but figuratively it can mean any complaint or comment repeated excessively. Be aware that while 'refrain' in English can be a verb (to refrain from), the Italian ritornello is exclusively a noun. The word is common in music theory contexts but less frequent in everyday conversation unless discussing music.

exampleSentences.italian: Il ritornello di questa canzone è molto orecchiabile, non trovi?
exampleSentences.english: The refrain of this song is very catchy, don't you think?

exampleSentences.italian: Smettila con questo ritornello!
exampleSentences.english: Stop going on and on!

relatedExpressions.meaning: a boring refrain / a tedious comment repeated over and over

grammarNotes: Masculine noun taking il/i for definite articles and un/dei for indefinite articles. Plural form is ponti. Derives from Latin pontem. Commonly paired with the verb attraversare (to cross).
learnerNotes: Don't confuse 'Ne è passata di acqua sotto i ponti' (time has passed) with the English 'water under the bridge' (something is no longer important)—use 'acqua passata' for that meaning. The idiom 'fare il ponte' is specifically Italian and refers to extending a weekend by taking a holiday on the connecting workday. Note that ponte can mean both the physical bridge and figuratively a connection or link between things.

exampleSentences.italian: Dobbiamo attraversare il ponte per arrivare al parco.
exampleSentences.english: We need to cross the bridge to get to the park.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho deciso di tagliare i ponti con alcuni dei miei parenti.
exampleSentences.english: I've decided to cut off ties with some of my relatives.

exampleSentences.italian: Siccome giovedì è festa, venerdì faremo il ponte.
exampleSentences.english: Since Thursday is a holiday, we'll take the Friday off and have a long weekend.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to cut off ties with someone
to bridge a gap (between people, countries, or cultures)

relatedExpressions.expression: Ne è passata di acqua sotto i ponti!
relatedExpressions.meaning: A lot of water has gone under the bridges! (indicating a significant passage of time)

grammarNotes: Solstizio is a masculine noun taking the articles il (singular) and i (plural). The indefinite forms are un solstizio (singular) and dei solstizi (plural). The word derives from Latin solstitium, combining sol (sun) and sistere (to stop), reflecting the astronomical phenomenon where the sun appears to pause in its celestial path.
learnerNotes: Solstizio is a cognate with English 'solstice,' making it easy to recognize and remember. Note the compounds solstizio d'inverno (winter) and solstizio d'estate (summer) to specify which solstice is being discussed. This formal, specialized term is commonly used in academic and scientific contexts when discussing seasons and astronomy.

exampleSentences.italian: il solstizio
exampleSentences.english: the solstice

exampleSentences.italian: i solstizi
exampleSentences.english: the solstices

exampleSentences.italian: un solstizio
exampleSentences.english: a solstice

exampleSentences.italian: dei solstizi
exampleSentences.english: (some) solstices

exampleSentences.italian: Il 21 dicembre si verificherà il solstizio d'inverno.
exampleSentences.english: The winter solstice will occur on December 21st.

grammarNotes: Foglia is a feminine noun with plural form foglie. It takes the definite articles la/le and indefinite articles una/delle. Do not confuse with the masculine foglio (sheet/page, plural fogli), which refers to sheets of paper rather than botanical leaves.
learnerNotes: Remember that foglia is feminine (la foglia) while foggio (sheet of paper) is masculine (il foglio)—this is a common source of confusion. The idiom mangiare la foglia references Homer's Odyssey and means to be perceptive or insightful. Tremare come una foglia is a useful colloquial expression for describing nervousness or physical trembling.

exampleSentences.italian: La foglia è mossa dal vento.
exampleSentences.english: The leaf blows in the wind.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho incollato una foglia su un foglio di carta.
exampleSentences.english: I stuck a leaf onto a piece of paper.

exampleSentences.italian: Tremava sempre come una foglia prima di parlare in pubblico.
exampleSentences.english: He always shook like a leaf before speaking in public.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to read between the lines; to understand something not explicitly stated
to shake like a leaf; to tremble

relatedExpressions.expression: non si muove neanche una foglia
relatedExpressions.meaning: not even a leaf moves (there is no wind)

grammarNotes: Pomello is a masculine noun, the diminutive form of pomo (apple). It takes standard masculine articles: il pomello (singular definite), i pomelli (plural definite), un pomello (singular indefinite), dei pomelli (plural indefinite). The word derives from the spherical shape of apples and applies to any rounded knob or bulge.
learnerNotes: Pomello has multiple distinct meanings: doorknob/ornamental knob (most common), gear shift knob, and cheekbone (less common). Distinguish pomello from maniglia (handle): a pomello must be rotated, while a maniglia must be pushed down. The diminutive form -ello suggests a small or rounded object, which helps explain the semantic range from small apples to protruding facial features.

exampleSentences.italian: Sto girando il pomello della porta.
exampleSentences.english: I'm turning the doorknob.

exampleSentences.italian: Lo riconoscerai subito! Ha il naso piuttosto grande e i pomelli sporgenti.
exampleSentences.english: You will recognise him right away! He has a rather large nose and protruding cheekbones.

relatedExpressions.meaning: apple (less common); fruit resembling an apple

grammarNotes: As an adjective, prevenuto agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: masculine singular -o (prevenuto), feminine singular -a (prevenuta), masculine plural -i (prevenuti), feminine plural -e (prevenute). As a noun, it primarily functions in forensic/legal contexts and follows standard masculine noun patterns in singular and plural forms.
learnerNotes: Note that prevenuto has dual meanings: as an adjective meaning 'prejudiced/biased' in modern Italian, and as a noun meaning 'the accused/defendant' in legal/forensic language. The legal noun form is archaic and primarily encountered in historical texts. When used as an adjective with 'contro' (against), it describes bias toward a specific group or person.

exampleSentences.italian: un uomo prevenuto
exampleSentences.english: a prejudiced man

exampleSentences.italian: una donna prevenuta
exampleSentences.english: a prejudiced woman

exampleSentences.italian: degli uomini prevenuti
exampleSentences.english: (some) prejudiced men

exampleSentences.italian: delle donne prevenute
exampleSentences.english: (some) prejudiced women

exampleSentences.italian: Giorgio è prevenuto contro gli stranieri.
exampleSentences.english: Giorgio is prejudiced against foreigners.

exampleSentences.italian: Il prevenuto ha perso il controllo della sua autovettura.
exampleSentences.english: The accused lost control of his car.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to beat someone to something; to prevent; to warn; to cause someone to feel prejudiced

englishTranslation: jumble / rabble / mix / mishmash / hodgepodge / mob
grammarNotes: Feminine noun beginning with a vowel. Articles: l'accozzaglia (singular), le accozzaglie (plural); un'accozzaglia (indefinite singular), delle accozzaglie (indefinite plural). Derived from the verb accozzare (to mix/throw together), which comes from cozzare (to collide/butt heads).
learnerNotes: This word is phonetically expressive—the double 'zz' sound mirrors its meaning of disorder and chaos. Use it when describing messy collections of people or things with a mildly negative or disparaging tone. Remember it's always feminine, so use agreement accordingly (un'accozzaglia strana, le accozzaglie varie).

exampleSentences.italian: un'accozzaglia di idee
exampleSentences.english: a mix of ideas

exampleSentences.italian: un'accozzaglia di cose inutili
exampleSentences.english: a hodgepodge of useless things

exampleSentences.italian: un'accozzaglia di gioventù
exampleSentences.english: a rabble of youths

exampleSentences.italian: C'era un'accozzaglia di giovani davanti al locale.
exampleSentences.english: There was a rabble of youngsters in front of the pub.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to mix together, to throw together

grammarNotes: Feminine noun taking the articles la/le (singular/plural) and una/delle. Parola is a feminine noun, so adjectives and articles must agree in gender. The plural form parole can mean 'words,' 'remarks,' 'speech,' or 'idle chatter' depending on context.
learnerNotes: Parola is a false cognate with English 'parole,' which refers to prisoner release—note that Italian uses 'parola d'ordine' for password in general speech, but 'password' (English) for computer contexts. The plural 'parole' significantly expands meaning beyond just 'words' to include 'remarks,' 'idle chatter,' or 'speech,' so context is crucial. Remember the gender: 'la parola' (feminine), not 'il parola,' and all adjectives must agree in gender.

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi ho imparato una parola nuova.
exampleSentences.english: Today I learned a new word.

exampleSentences.italian: Rimanere senza parole
exampleSentences.english: To be speechless (lit. to remain without words)

exampleSentences.italian: Queste sono solo parole
exampleSentences.english: This is just idle chatter

exampleSentences.italian: Avere l'ultima parola
exampleSentences.english: To have the last word

exampleSentences.italian: Avere la parola pronta
exampleSentences.english: To have a ready answer

exampleSentences.italian: Basta con questi giri di parole, vieni al dunque!
exampleSentences.english: Enough beating around the bush, get to the point!

exampleSentences.italian: La parola è una delle cose più importanti che possiede l'essere umano.
exampleSentences.english: Speech is one of the most important things that human beings possess.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai la mia parola!
exampleSentences.english: You have my word!

exampleSentences.italian: La parola di Dio
exampleSentences.english: The word of God

exampleSentences.italian: Smettila di dire tutte queste parolacce!
exampleSentences.english: Stop saying all those swear words!

relatedExpressions.meaning: beating around the bush / roundabout way of speaking
to have a way with words / the gift of gab
to be as good as one's word
to take someone at their word
to put in a good word

englishTranslation: down / duvet / comforter / down jacket / feather duster / dart
grammarNotes: Masculine noun derived from piuma (feather). Takes regular definite articles il/i piumini and indefinite articles un/dei piumini. The word has expanded semantically over time to encompass multiple objects that contain or resemble down feathers, demonstrating how Italian vocabulary can be polysemous.
learnerNotes: Piumino is a polysemous word with multiple meanings depending on context—duvet, down jacket, feather duster, and dart. Context is crucial to understand which meaning is intended. The related term piumone is now interchangeable with piumino for duvet/down jacket meanings, though piumone can also refer to quilts (trapunti). Pay attention to context clues and surrounding vocabulary to disambiguate.

exampleSentences.italian: il piumino
exampleSentences.english: the down / the duvet (singular)

exampleSentences.italian: i piumini
exampleSentences.english: the downs / the duvets (plural)

exampleSentences.italian: un piumino
exampleSentences.english: a down / a duvet (singular indefinite)

exampleSentences.italian: dei piumini
exampleSentences.english: some downs / some duvets (plural indefinite)

exampleSentences.italian: Fa troppo caldo per il piumino. Bastano le lenzuola.
exampleSentences.english: It's too hot for the duvet. The sheets are enough.

exampleSentences.italian: Prendi il piumino e dai una bella spolverata allo schermo della TV.
exampleSentences.english: Get the feather duster and give the TV screen a good dusting.

relatedExpressions.meaning: duvet / down jacket (synonym that evolved from a trademark; also can mean quilt/trapunto)

englishTranslation: to upset / to mess up / to turn something on its head / to disrupt
grammarNotes: A regular -ARE verb with a straightforward conjugation pattern (io scombussolo, tu scombussoli, lui/lei scombussola, noi scombussoliamo, voi scombussolate, loro scombussolano). The prefix s- at the beginning reverses meaning, similar to English 'un-'. Also exists as the intransitive pronominal form scombussolarsi.
learnerNotes: Scombussolare is a moderately advanced word describing emotional or situational disruption; use it to express being thrown off-balance or having plans derailed. The related adjective scombussolato is commonly used in conversation to express feeling unsettled or shaken. Note the dual etymology from either bussola (compass) or bussolo (box), both evoking imagery of disorder.

exampleSentences.italian: La neve potrebbe scombussolare tutti i nostri piani.
exampleSentences.english: The snow might disrupt all our plans.

exampleSentences.italian: È ancora scombussolato per quel brutto incidente in moto.
exampleSentences.english: He is still shaken because of that bad motorcycle accident.

grammarNotes: Miscela is a feminine noun, so it uses the articles la (singular definite) and le (plural definite), and una (singular indefinite) and delle (plural indefinite). The word derives from Latin miscellus (mixed) via the verb miscere (to mix). Being feminine, any adjectives modifying miscela must agree in gender and number.
learnerNotes: Miscela is commonly used in everyday contexts—from household cleaning to coffee culture—making it practical vocabulary. Remember it's always feminine (la miscela, una miscela), even when the component parts might be masculine. The word can refer to both physical mixtures (liquids, solids, fuel) and abstract blends (colours, emotions, sounds), so don't limit its use to chemistry contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Usiamo una miscela di aceto e acqua per disinfettare il bagno.
exampleSentences.english: We use a mixture of vinegar and water to sanitise the bathroom.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa miscela è molto aromatica, non trovi?
exampleSentences.english: This coffee blend is very aromatic, don't you think?

exampleSentences.italian: Questo dipinto è caratterizzato dalla sua miscela di colori vivaci.
exampleSentences.english: This painting is characterised by its blend of vibrant colours.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with two plural forms due to Latin neuter origin: feminine plural le sopracciglia (referring to a pair of eyebrows, more common) and masculine plural i sopraccigli (referring to multiple individual eyebrows). The feminine plural -a ending reflects the Latin neuter plural supercilia. The erroneous form le sopracciglie does not exist in standard Italian.
learnerNotes: Always use the feminine plural le sopracciglia when referring to someone's pair of eyebrows, as this is standard usage. The masculine plural i sopraccigli is rarely used and only when discussing multiple individual eyebrows from different people. Avoid the non-standard form le sopracciglie, which some native speakers may use incorrectly but is not considered correct Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Le sopracciglia di Anna sono molto scure e definite.
exampleSentences.english: Anna's eyebrows are very dark and defined.

exampleSentences.italian: I tre ragazzi hanno tutti e tre un piercing ai sopraccigli destri.
exampleSentences.english: The three boys all have a piercing on their right eyebrows.

grammarNotes: Camicia is a feminine noun. The singular definite article is 'la' and plural is 'le'. The plural form is 'camicie' (not 'camice') because feminine nouns ending in -cia without accent take -cie in plural when a vowel precedes the c, and the 'i' helps distinguish it from the masculine noun 'camice' (doctor's coat).
learnerNotes: Distinguish camicia (formal button-down shirt) from maglietta (casual T-shirt) and maglia (heavy-cloth shirt). Note that camicia can extend metaphorically to mean any protective covering or casing in technical contexts. Many Italian idioms use camicia figuratively to express poverty, hard work, or close relationships—these are essential for conversational fluency.

exampleSentences.italian: Non so se indossare una maglietta o una camicia oggi.
exampleSentences.english: I'm not sure whether to wear a T-shirt or a (button down) shirt today.

exampleSentences.italian: Il medico indossa una camicia sotto il camice.
exampleSentences.english: The doctor is wearing a shirt underneath his scrubs.

exampleSentences.italian: Mangio spesso le uova in camicia.
exampleSentences.english: I often eat poached eggs.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be born with a silver spoon in one's mouth

relatedExpressions.expression: Essere culo e camicia con qualcuno
relatedExpressions.meaning: to be as thick as thieves
to lose one's shirt / to put one's shirt on something

englishTranslation: to poke / to pick at / to prod / to tease / to provoke / to stimulate / to excite / to arouse
grammarNotes: Regular -are verb with multiple literal and figurative meanings. The reciprocal form stuzzicarsi means 'to tease one another' and is commonly used with continuous actions. Conjugates regularly: stuzzico, stuzzichi, stuzzica, stuzzichiamo, stuzzicate, stuzzicano. Past participle: stuzzicato.
learnerNotes: Stuzzicare has two main figurative senses: 'to tease/provoke' (using words as metaphorical pokes) and 'to stimulate/excite' (appealing to senses or emotions). The reciprocal stuzzicarsi is very common in everyday speech for playful teasing. Note that while the literal sense involves physical poking, the figurative uses are much more frequent in conversation.

exampleSentences.italian: Il bambino continuava a stuzzicare la sua ferita sul braccio.
exampleSentences.english: The boy continued to pick the wound on his arm.

exampleSentences.italian: Non stuzzicare tuo fratello!
exampleSentences.english: Don't tease your brother!

exampleSentences.italian: Quei due si stuzzicano di continuo.
exampleSentences.english: Those two are constantly teasing each other.

grammarNotes: Stravolto is a regular adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies (stravolto, stravolta, stravolti, stravolte). It derives from the past participle of the verb stravolgere and functions as a descriptive adjective. Often used predicatively with essere ('essere stravolto').
learnerNotes: Stravolto has multiple meanings that can seem contradictory: it can mean 'upset/disturbed' or 'twisted/distorted,' but in everyday Italian conversation, the most common usage is 'exhausted.' Context is crucial to understanding which meaning applies. Don't confuse it with simple tiredness (stanco)—stravolto implies a more dramatic state of exhaustion or emotional upheaval. The verb stravolgere combines travolgere with the intensive prefix s-, making it a good example of Italian prefix usage.

exampleSentences.italian: I Queen hanno stravolto le regole della musica.
exampleSentences.english: Queen turned the rules of music on their head.

exampleSentences.italian: un viso stravolto dal dolore
exampleSentences.english: a face twisted with pain

exampleSentences.italian: essere stravolto dalla notizia
exampleSentences.english: to be upset by the news

exampleSentences.italian: avere gli occhi stravolti
exampleSentences.english: with one's eyes popping out of one's head

exampleSentences.italian: una verità stravolta
exampleSentences.english: a distorted truth

exampleSentences.italian: Sono stravolto…vado a dormire.
exampleSentences.english: I'm exhausted…I'm going to bed.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to turn something on its head; to distort; to upset; to revolutionize

grammarNotes: Borraccia is a feminine noun. The plural form is borracce (not borraccie) because the -cia ending is preceded by a consonant. Definite articles: la borraccia (singular), le borracce (plural). Indefinite articles: una borraccia (singular), delle borracce (plural).
learnerNotes: The word borraccia comes from Spanish borracha (leather jug), showing how Romance languages share vocabulary. Pay attention to the plural spelling rule: -cia preceded by a consonant becomes -ce in plural, while -cia preceded by a vowel becomes -cie (e.g., ciliegia → ciliegie). Italians often use the English loanword 'thermos' interchangeably with borraccia termica when referring to insulated bottles.

exampleSentences.italian: La borraccia è una buona alternativa ecologica alle bottiglie di plastica monouso.
exampleSentences.english: The water bottle is a good ecological alternative to disposable plastic bottles.

relatedExpressions.meaning: thermos (alternative Italian term for insulated water bottle)

grammarNotes: Mangione is a masculine noun formed from the verb mangiare (to eat) + the augmentative suffix -one. It has a feminine form mangiona. The singular masculine and plural feminine forms are identical (il mangione / le mangione). Use definite articles il/i for masculine and la/le for feminine, or indefinite articles un/dei and una/delle respectively.
learnerNotes: Mangione has dual meanings: literally it describes a voracious eater in a playful, non-pejorative way, but figuratively it can mean someone who greedily prioritizes personal gain at others' expense. The diminutive suffix -one is productive in Italian for creating words describing large or exaggerated qualities. Note that the feminine plural form le mangione breaks the typical pattern (should technically be le mangione, not le mangioni) as shown in the article.

exampleSentences.italian: Mio figlio è un gran mangione.
exampleSentences.english: My son is a big eater.

grammarNotes: Penna is a feminine noun. Definite articles: la penna (singular), le penne (plural). Indefinite articles: una penna (singular), delle penne (plural). The word derives from Latin pinna meaning 'bird feather' and historically referred to quills used for writing before modern pens were invented.
learnerNotes: Do not confuse penna (pen/feather) with pena (pain/suffering/penalty), which sounds similar but has very different meanings. Penna is also the Italian word for the cylinder-shaped pasta 'penne,' designed to resemble fountain pen nibs. The word has extended metaphorically to mean 'writer' or 'author,' so expressions like 'una buona penna' refer to writing skill rather than literal pens.

exampleSentences.italian: Non sono più capace di scrivere bene con la penna.
exampleSentences.english: I'm no longer able to write well with a pen.

exampleSentences.english: I'm too used to the keyboard!

exampleSentences.italian: Penso che sia una delle migliori penne del giornalismo italiano.
exampleSentences.english: I think he's one of the best writers in Italian journalism.

To die / suffer a serious injury (literally: To leave / lose one's feathers)

grammarNotes: Basso is a regular adjective derived from Latin bassum with four forms: basso (masc. sing.), bassa (fem. sing.), bassi (masc. pl.), basse (fem. pl.). When used as an adverb, it remains invariable. As a noun, it commonly refers to bass singers/instruments in music or the lower part of something.
learnerNotes: Basso is highly versatile with multiple meanings depending on context—always consider whether it describes physical height/position (low/short), quality/intensity (low), or figurative meaning (vile/humble). Remember that for describing a person's height, use 'di bassa statura' or the comparative 'più basso/a di'. Be aware it also functions as a noun in musical contexts (bass singer, double bass) and for the bottom/lower part of objects.
