grammarNotes: Cannuccia is a feminine noun (la cannuccia). The plural is cannucce (not cannuccie) because the -cia ending is preceded by a consonant. It takes articles: la/le (definite) and una/delle (indefinite). The word is derived from canna (reed/cane) in its diminutive form.
learnerNotes: Pay attention to the plural form: cannucce (not cannuccie). This spelling rule applies to -cia endings preceded by consonants; if preceded by a vowel, use -cie instead (e.g., acacia → acacie). By extension, cannuccia can refer to any long tubular object, such as a pen barrel, so context matters for accurate interpretation.

exampleSentences.italian: Preferisco bere con la cannuccia.
exampleSentences.english: I prefer drinking with a straw.

exampleSentences.italian: Le cannucce di plastica sono dannose per l'ambiente.
exampleSentences.english: Plastic straws are harmful to the environment.

exampleSentences.italian: Una cannuccia può essere usata per bere acqua.
exampleSentences.english: A straw can be used to drink water.

grammarNotes: Giocoso is a regular adjective with gender and number agreement. Masculine singular ends in -o (un bambino giocoso), feminine singular in -a (una bambina giocosa), masculine plural in -i (i bambini giocosi), and feminine plural in -e (le bambine giocose). It derives from Latin iocosus and maintains consistent declension patterns.
learnerNotes: Giocoso extends beyond 'playful' to describe a light-hearted or ironic tone in literary, musical, or artistic contexts—pay attention to context to distinguish between the literal 'playful' sense and the figurative 'whimsical/ironic' sense. The adverb giocosamente is useful for describing actions performed in a playful manner. Note that giocoso shares etymology with gioco (game), so the relationship aids memorization.

exampleSentences.italian: un bambino giocoso
exampleSentences.english: a playful boy / child

exampleSentences.italian: una bambina giocosa
exampleSentences.english: a playful girl

exampleSentences.italian: i bambini giocosi
exampleSentences.english: the playful boys / children

exampleSentences.italian: le bambine giocose
exampleSentences.english: the playful girls

exampleSentences.italian: Il bambino giocoso mi ha fatto uno sguardo birichino.
exampleSentences.english: The playful child gave me a mischievous look.

grammarNotes: Carattere is a masculine noun. Singular: il carattere (definite), un carattere (indefinite). Plural: i caratteri (definite), dei caratteri (indefinite). The diminutive form caratterino exists, referring to someone with a fiery or difficult personality. When referring to a character in fiction, use personaggio instead.
learnerNotes: Be careful not to confuse carattere (personality/character) with personaggio (character in a story). Carattere also means printed letter or symbol, as in computer passwords. The word can extend to mean 'mettle' or 'backbone' when describing someone's resilience, and 'nature' or 'feature' in scientific contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Bruno ha un carattere molto difficile.
exampleSentences.english: Bruno has a very difficult personality/character.

exampleSentences.italian: Certo che tuo figlio ha proprio un bel caratterino!
exampleSentences.english: Your son certainly has quite the temper!

exampleSentences.italian: La password deve essere lunga almeno nove caratteri.
exampleSentences.english: The password needs to be at least 9 characters long.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a man of character (strong and resilient)

grammarNotes: Sovrappensiero is an adverb formed from sovra- (variant of sopra-, meaning 'above/over') + pensiero (thought). The double P results from raddoppiamento (consonant doubling). While soprappensiero is listed as the main form in some dictionaries, sovrappensiero is now preferred in modern usage, likely due to euphonic reasons (three consecutive Ps in soprappensiero are harder to pronounce). As an adverb, it is invariable.
learnerNotes: Sovrappensiero is useful for describing moments of absent-mindedness or distraction. Note that while soprappensiero exists as a variant, sovrappensiero has become the preferred modern form among Italian speakers. This word exemplifies the phonetic phenomenon of lenition in Italian, where the harsh [p] sound becomes the softer [v] sound for easier pronunciation—a helpful pattern to recognize in other Italian words.

exampleSentences.italian: Ero sovrappensiero e ho messo il sale nel caffè invece dello zucchero.
exampleSentences.english: While lost in thought, I added salt to my coffee instead of sugar.

exampleSentences.italian: Ascoltavo il loro discorso sovrappensiero.
exampleSentences.english: I listened to their conversation absent-mindedly.

relatedExpressions.meaning: alternative variant (less common); also means 'lost in thought'
variant prefix of sopra-, more common in modern Italian

grammarNotes: Sogno is a masculine noun taking articles il/i (definite) and un/dei (indefinite). It derives from Latin somnium. The first-person singular present indicative of sognare is also sogno (I dream). Related verb forms include sognare (to dream), sognante (dreamy), and sognatore/sognatrice (dreamer).
learnerNotes: Note that sogno functions both as a noun (dream) and as the first-person singular present of sognare (I dream)—context clarifies which meaning applies. The expression 'un sogno nel cassetto' (literally 'a dream in the drawer') is a charming idiom worth memorising for figurative use. Watch for the preposition da before sogno to signal an adjective-like meaning (dreamlike/marvellous), as in 'una casa da sogno' (a dream house).

exampleSentences.italian: Ieri notte ho fatto un bel sogno.
exampleSentences.english: I had a good dream last night.

exampleSentences.italian: Sogno di volare.
exampleSentences.english: I dream of flying.

exampleSentences.italian: Il mio sogno è di vivere in Italia un giorno.
exampleSentences.english: My dream is to live in Italy one day.

exampleSentences.italian: Lei è la ragazza dei miei sogni.
exampleSentences.english: She is the girl of my dreams.

exampleSentences.italian: Vieni con me alla festa? – Neanche per sogno!
exampleSentences.english: Are you coming with me to the party? – Not a chance!

relatedExpressions.meaning: a lifelong unrealised dream (literally: a dream in the drawer)
to see someone/something in a dream

relatedExpressions.expression: Neanche per sogno! / Nemmeno per sogno!
relatedExpressions.meaning: In your dreams! / Not a chance!
Am I dreaming, or am I awake? (from Verdi's I Vespri Siciliani)

englishTranslation: but rather / on the contrary / but / however
grammarNotes: Bensì is primarily a conjunction composed of bene (good) and sì (yes). It introduces a statement that opposes or contradicts a previous statement, typically following a negation. In archaic Italian, it can function as an adverb meaning 'certainly' or 'absolutely,' but this usage is obsolete in modern Italian.
learnerNotes: Bensì is more formal and literary than its everyday substitutes (ma, invece, piuttosto, anzi), so expect to encounter it primarily in written material like newspapers and journals rather than casual conversation. Always use it after a negation to introduce a contrasting statement. The archaic adverbial usage meaning 'certainly' or 'absolutely' should not be used in modern Italian and is mentioned only for recognition purposes.

exampleSentences.italian: In realtà lui non era affatto un professionista, bensì un dilettante.
exampleSentences.english: He actually wasn't a professional at all, but rather an amateur.

exampleSentences.italian: In realtà non era affatto un professionista, ma un dilettante.
exampleSentences.english: He actually wasn't a professional at all, but an amateur.

exampleSentences.italian: In realtà non era affatto un professionista, ma invece un dilettante.
exampleSentences.english: He actually wasn't a professional at all, but rather an amateur.

exampleSentences.italian: In realtà non era affatto un professionista, ma piuttosto un dilettante.
exampleSentences.english: He actually wasn't a professional at all, but rather an amateur.

exampleSentences.italian: In realtà non era affatto un professionista, anzi era un dilettante.
exampleSentences.english: He actually wasn't a professional at all, in actual fact he was an amateur.

exampleSentences.italian: Molti lo davano per matto, alcuni bensì gli davano retta.
exampleSentences.english: Many thought he was crazy, but some paid attention to him.

exampleSentences.italian: È bensì vero che sono stanco, ma voglio venire ugualmente.
exampleSentences.english: It is absolutely true that I'm tired, but I want to come all the same.

grammarNotes: Eppure is a compound conjunction formed from e (and) + pure (also/even). It is invariable and does not change form. It typically appears at the beginning of a clause to express contradiction or surprise, and can carry a reprimanding tone depending on context.
learnerNotes: Eppure is more sophisticated than ma or però and is particularly useful when you want to emphasize contradiction or surprise. It can stand alone at the start of a sentence or clause for rhetorical effect, especially in reprimanding contexts. Be aware that "Eppur si muove!" is a famous historical reference often alluded to in modern Italian discourse to counter denial of evidence.

exampleSentences.italian: Sapeva di sbagliare, eppure l'ha fatto!
exampleSentences.english: He knew he was making a mistake, and yet he still did it.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono esausto, eppure devo andare al lavoro.
exampleSentences.english: I'm exhausted, but/yet I have to go to work.

exampleSentences.italian: Eppure te l'avevo detto!
exampleSentences.english: But I did tell you so!

exampleSentences.italian: Eppur si muove!
exampleSentences.english: And yet, it moves!

relatedExpressions.meaning: despite that / in spite of that
also / even (on its own as conjunction)

grammarNotes: Masculine invariable noun. Takes the definite articles il (singular) and i (plural), and indefinite articles un (singular) and dei (plural). The word does not change form in the plural, making it an invariable noun—a characteristic of many borrowed words in Italian.
learnerNotes: Bidet is a French loanword (from Old French bider, 'to trot') that has been fully adopted into Italian. It's an invariable masculine noun, meaning its plural form is identical to the singular—common for borrowed words ending in a consonant. In Italy, bidets have been legally mandated in residential bathrooms since 1975, so this is culturally significant vocabulary for anyone discussing Italian homes.

exampleSentences.italian: Non avevo mai visto un bidet prima di visitare l'Italia.
exampleSentences.english: I'd never seen a bidet before visiting Italy.

grammarNotes: Famigerato is a four-form adjective that agrees with the noun it modifies in gender and number. Masculine singular ends in -o (famigerato), feminine singular in -a (famigerata), masculine plural in -i (famigerati), and feminine plural in -e (famigerate). The adjective derives from Latin famigeratus (past participle of famigerare, 'to make famous') and has shifted in meaning from positive 'famous' to negative 'notorious/infamous' over time.
learnerNotes: Famigerato is a literary and formal adjective rarely used in everyday conversation; you'll encounter it in news, historical texts, or academic writing. The semantic shift from positive 'famous' to negative 'notorious' reflects how Latin famigeratus evolved in Italian—be aware that older texts may use it positively. Always remember to adjust the ending based on the noun's gender and number, just like other regular four-form adjectives.

exampleSentences.english: the notorious criminal

exampleSentences.italian: la ladra famigerata
exampleSentences.english: the infamous thief

exampleSentences.italian: i criminali famigerati
exampleSentences.english: the notorious criminals

exampleSentences.italian: le ladre famigerate
exampleSentences.english: the infamous thieves

exampleSentences.italian: Gli agenti di polizia hanno arrestato il famigerato ministro.
exampleSentences.english: The police officers have arrested the infamous minister.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun derived from Latin momentum. Takes definite articles il (singular) and i (plural), and indefinite articles un and dei. Appears in numerous time-related expressions where English often uses 'time' rather than 'moment.' Can refer to a brief instant, an extended period, or an opportunity depending on context.
learnerNotes: Momento is a high-frequency word that extends far beyond literal 'moment' in time. Pay special attention to the idiomatic expressions listed—many Italian speakers use these phrases daily, and they differ significantly from English constructions. Note that 'momento' can mean an extended 'period' (un brutto momento = a rough patch), so context determines whether to translate as 'moment,' 'time,' or 'period.'

exampleSentences.italian: Aspetta un momento, non sono ancora pronto!
exampleSentences.english: Wait a moment, I'm not ready yet!

exampleSentences.italian: Non c'è un momento da perdere!
exampleSentences.english: There is no time to lose!

exampleSentences.italian: Sbrighiamoci, il festeggiato arriverà da un momento all'altro!

exampleSentences.italian: So che stai passando un brutto momento. È un momento difficile per tutti noi.
exampleSentences.english: I know you're going through a bad time. It's a difficult period for all of us.

exampleSentences.italian: Abbiamo passato dei bei momenti insieme, io e te.
exampleSentences.english: We had some good times, you and me.

exampleSentences.italian: Dobbiamo cogliere il momento!
exampleSentences.english: We have to seize the moment/opportunity!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to look forward to / to not be able to wait

grammarNotes: Mese is a masculine noun with plural mesi. It takes the definite article il/i and indefinite article un/dei. Month names (gennaio, febbraio, etc.) are not capitalized in Italian, following the same rule as days of the week. The word appears frequently in temporal expressions and can extend meaning to monthly salary or rent payments.
learnerNotes: Remember that Italian month names are never capitalized, unlike in English—write gennaio, not Gennaio. The expression 'al mese' (per month) is commonly used for recurring payments or frequency; note the preposition al rather than per. Be aware that mese can mean both calendar month and monthly salary/rent amount depending on context, so watch for these extended uses.

englishTranslation: to melt / to sweat excessively / to be moved / to flee
grammarNotes: A regular -ARE verb with multiple uses: transitive (melting objects), intransitive pronominal (squagliarsi), and idiomatic (squagliarsela). In present tense, conjugates as: squaglio, squagli, squaglia, squagliamo, squagliate, squagliano. The reflexive form squagliarsi carries figurative meanings of emotional overwhelm or sweating from heat; squagliarsela means to flee or escape.
learnerNotes: Squagliare is a regional/colloquial alternative to the more standard sciogliere, so context matters for register. The reflexive forms—especially squagliarsela—carry idiomatic meanings far removed from literal melting; squagliarsela in particular is distinctly colloquial and means to flee or escape. Note that squagliare comes from s- + quagliare (to curdle), rooted in Latin coagulare, which explains its formal structure despite being less common than sciogliere.

exampleSentences.italian: Il sole ha squagliato il mio gelato.
exampleSentences.english: The sun melted my ice cream.

exampleSentences.italian: Il gelato si è squagliato al sole.
exampleSentences.english: The ice cream melted in the sun.

exampleSentences.italian: Basta che lei mi guardi in un certo modo e io mi squaglio completamente.
exampleSentences.english: All she has to do is look at me in a certain way and I completely melt.

exampleSentences.italian: Guarda quei ragazzi, hanno bevuto un sacco di birra e adesso se la squagliano senza pagare…
exampleSentences.english: Look at those guys, they drank loads of beer and now they're taking off without paying…

relatedExpressions.meaning: to melt (intransitive, reflexive); to sweat from heat; to be overwhelmed by emotion
to flee, to take off, to run away without paying

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural form 'sere'. Takes definite articles 'la sera' (the evening) and 'le sere' (the evenings), and indefinite articles 'una sera' (an evening) and 'delle sere' (some evenings). Derived from late Latin 'sēra', an ellipsis of 'sēra diēs' meaning 'late part of the day'.
learnerNotes: Unlike English, Italian 'sera' encompasses both 'evening' and 'night', so expressions like 'stasera' (tonight), 'domani sera' (tomorrow night), and 'ieri sera' (last night) are commonly used. The greeting 'Buona sera' is typically used from late afternoon (around 5 pm) onward. When followed by 'da' (e.g., 'abito da sera'), it specifies clothing or items designed for evening wear at formal events.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono partiti che era quasi sera.
exampleSentences.english: They left when it was almost evening.

exampleSentences.italian: Stasera vado in discoteca con gli amici.
exampleSentences.english: I'm going to the disco with my friends tonight.

exampleSentences.italian: Buonasera Maria, come sta?
exampleSentences.english: Good evening, Maria. How are you?

relatedExpressions.expression: rosso di sera bel tempo si spera
relatedExpressions.meaning: red in the evening, hopefully good weather (proverb; English equivalent: red sky at night, sailor's delight)

grammarNotes: Domanda is a feminine noun taking the articles la/le (definite) and una/delle (indefinite). It derives from the verb domandare (to ask). The meaning shifts contextually: in conversation it means 'question,' in formal documents it means 'request/application,' and in economics it means 'demand.' Gender agreement is essential when using modifying adjectives.
learnerNotes: Pay close attention to context: domanda as 'question' is conversational, while domanda as 'application/request' appears in formal administrative settings. The verb pairing changes by context—use 'fare' for asking questions but 'presentare' when submitting formal applications. In economics, domanda always means 'demand' and is a critical term for intermediate learners studying business Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho una domanda da farti.
exampleSentences.english: I have a question for you.

exampleSentences.italian: Secondo te, le scuole riapriranno domani visto che questa bufera di neve sta passando? – Bella domanda!
exampleSentences.english: In your opinion, will the schools re-open tomorrow since this snowstorm is coming to an end? – Good question!

grammarNotes: Ragione is a feminine noun (la ragione). It has multiple semantic fields in Italian: it can denote the human capacity for logical thinking, a motive or cause, or the concept of being correct/right. The expression avere ragione (to be right) is one of the most common uses and requires the auxiliary avere in compound tenses.
learnerNotes: Ragione is a false cognate: while it resembles English 'reason,' the most common expression avere ragione means 'to be right,' not 'to have reason.' Pay attention to the distinction between avere ragione (general correctness) and avere ragione di qualcuno (to get the better of someone). The reflexive expression farsi una ragione di qualcosa is particularly useful for describing emotional resilience in Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono contento che tu abbia ascoltato la voce della ragione.
exampleSentences.english: I'm glad you listened to the voice of reason.

grammarNotes: Nemico is a masculine noun (il nemico, i nemici) with feminine form nemica (la nemica, le nemiche). It agrees in gender and number when used as an adjective. Takes standard Italian articles: definite (il/la/i/le) and indefinite (un/una/dei/delle). Related to English 'nemesis' through shared etymological origin.
learnerNotes: Remember nemico shares roots with English 'nemesis,' making it a cognate worth noting. When used as an adjective (soldati nemici, linee nemiche), it must agree with the noun in gender and number. Be careful not to confuse the masculine/feminine forms; nemica is used only for female enemies or in feminine contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Non vorrei proprio averlo come nemico.
exampleSentences.english: I wouldn't want him as an enemy.

exampleSentences.italian: I soldati feriti sono caduti in mano al nemico.
exampleSentences.english: The injured soldiers fell into enemy hands.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi è diventato nemico dopo la disputa.
exampleSentences.english: He became hostile towards me after the argument.

exampleSentences.italian: L'alcol è nemico del fegato.
exampleSentences.english: Alcohol is bad for the liver.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to give oneself up to the enemy

grammarNotes: Basta functions as an interjection but derives from the verb bastare (to be enough/suffice). When used with 'che' it means 'as long as' or 'provided that'. When followed by an infinitive verb, it translates to 'just' or 'all you need to do'. The verb bastare is regular in the present tense: io basto, tu basti, lui/lei basta, noi bastiamo, voi bastate, loro bastano.
learnerNotes: Basta is extremely common in Italian households and conversational Italian—parents use it frequently with children. Pay attention to context: as an interjection it's direct and emphatic (Stop!), but with 'che' or an infinitive it becomes more conditional or instructional (as long as / just do). Note that 'quanto basta' is a cooking expression meaning 'to taste' or 'as much as needed.'

exampleSentences.italian: Basta urlare! Non riesco a sentire la TV!
exampleSentences.english: Stop yelling! I can't hear the TV!

exampleSentences.italian: Basta! Se continui a fare così, ti mando a letto!
exampleSentences.english: (That's) enough! If you continue to behave like that, I'll send you to bed!

exampleSentences.italian: Aggiungi zucchero quanto basta, ma senza esagerare.
exampleSentences.english: Add just enough sugar, but don't overdo it.

exampleSentences.italian: Basta che tu mi dica la verità.
exampleSentences.english: You just need to tell me the truth.

exampleSentences.italian: Basta che andiamo tutti insieme e sarò felice.

grammarNotes: Arroventato is a regular adjective derived from the verb arroventare (made from rovente + prefix a-). It agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies (arroventato, arroventata, arroventati, arroventate). Beyond its literal meaning of 'red-hot,' it has a figurative sense meaning 'heated' or 'overexcited,' particularly in expressions like 'discussione arroventata' (heated argument).
learnerNotes: Arroventato has both literal (physical heat) and figurative (emotional intensity) uses; context determines which applies. The reflexive verb arroventarsi is common when describing objects becoming hot or people becoming emotionally heated. Note that while arroventa is the third-person singular present tense of the verb, arroventato is strictly the adjective form—don't confuse conjugation with adjectival agreement.

exampleSentences.italian: il ferro arroventato
exampleSentences.english: the red-hot iron

exampleSentences.italian: l'estate arroventata
exampleSentences.english: the scorching summer

exampleSentences.english: a heated argument

grammarNotes: Storia is a feminine noun taking the articles la/le (definite) and una/delle (indefinite). Its primary meaning is 'history' rather than 'story' despite the English cognate. The word is highly polysemous, requiring context to determine which of its seven main meanings applies.
learnerNotes: Be careful with this false cognate: while 'storia' can mean 'story', its primary meaning is 'history'. Context is crucial—'la storia' in academic settings typically means 'history', while in narrative contexts it means 'story'. Note that 'storie' (plural) intensifies meanings like 'lies' or 'fuss', making it colloquial and informal. When referring to romantic relationships or excuses, storia takes on a more conversational tone.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi interessa molto la storia del cinema.
exampleSentences.english: I'm very interested in the history of cinema.

exampleSentences.italian: Ti ho già letto questa storia mille volte!
exampleSentences.english: I've already read you this story a thousand times!

exampleSentences.english: What do you want me to say… it's the story of my life.

exampleSentences.english: My son told me a bunch of lies.

exampleSentences.english: He made up an excuse to not go to school.

exampleSentences.english: My daughter didn't make a fuss in the car.

grammarNotes: Spinta is a feminine noun, taking the articles la/le (definite) and una/delle (indefinite). It derives from the past participle of spingere (to push). The diminutive form spintarella means a light nudge, while spintone means a heavy shove. Spinta agrees in gender with adjectives (e.g., una leggera spinta, una grossa spinta).
learnerNotes: Spinta has multiple meanings: the concrete sense of a physical push (used with ricevere/dare), the figurative sense of motivation or incentive, and the colloquial sense of unfair string-pulling or influence. Pay attention to context to determine which meaning applies. The word is feminine, so remember la spinta and una spinta; common adjectives like leggera (light) and grossa (big) must agree in gender.

exampleSentences.italian: Carlo ha ricevuto una spinta dal bullo ed è caduto per terra.
exampleSentences.english: Carlo was pushed by the bully and fell to the ground.

exampleSentences.italian: Il bullo ha dato una spinta a Carlo, facendolo cadere per terra.
exampleSentences.english: The bully pushed Carlo, causing him to fall on the ground.

exampleSentences.italian: Le parole incoraggianti di Alessia mi hanno dato la spinta che mi serviva per iniziare il nuovo progetto.
exampleSentences.english: Alessia's encouraging words gave me the incentive I needed to start the new project.

exampleSentences.italian: Mario ha fatto carriera a forza di spinte.
exampleSentences.english: Mario climbed the corporate ladder thanks to string-pulling.

to give a push / to push

grammarNotes: Pelliccia is a feminine noun. Singular articles: la pelliccia (definite), una pelliccia (indefinite). Plural articles: le pellicce (definite), delle pellicce (indefinite). Like most Italian nouns ending in -cia, the plural changes the ending to -ce.
learnerNotes: Pelliccia refers both to animal fur on a living creature and to fur used for clothing/coats. Remember the feminine gender and plural form (le pellicce) to ensure correct article and adjective agreement. Note that visone (mink), volpe (fox), and cane-procione (raccoon dog) are common fur-bearing animals mentioned in Italian contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: In inverno, la pelliccia del gatto è più folta per proteggerlo dal freddo.
exampleSentences.english: In the winter, the cat's fur is thicker to protect it from the cold.

exampleSentences.italian: Nella preistoria, le pellicce erano necessarie all'uomo per coprirsi e resistere al freddo.
exampleSentences.english: In prehistoric times, furs were necessary for man to cover himself and withstand the cold.

grammarNotes: Svago is a masculine noun. The definite articles are lo svago (singular) and gli svaghi (plural). The indefinite articles are uno svago and degli svaghi. It derives from the verb svagarsi (to distract oneself / take one's mind off something).
learnerNotes: Svago specifically refers to leisure time or activities for relaxation, distinct from simple 'free time' (tempo libero). The related adjective svagato describes a distracted or absent-minded person, so be careful not to confuse the noun and adjective forms. The plural svaghi is commonly used when referring to multiple entertainment or recreational activities available in a place.

exampleSentences.italian: Voglio prendermi qualche giorno di svago.
exampleSentences.english: I want to take a few days off work to relax.

exampleSentences.italian: Un social dovrebbe essere usato come svago o come strumento istruttivo, non come mezzo per sfogare le proprie frustrazioni.
exampleSentences.english: A social network should be used as a form of recreation or an educational tool, not as a means to vent one's frustrations.

exampleSentences.italian: In questa città ci sono pochi svaghi per i giovani.
exampleSentences.english: There isn't much to do in this city for young people.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to take one's mind off something / to distract or divert oneself
absent-minded / having one's head in the clouds
to take a day off to relax

grammarNotes: As an adjective, secco agrees with the noun: secco (masc. sing.), secca (fem. sing.), secchi (masc. pl.), secche (fem. pl.). It can also function as a noun meaning 'dry land' or 'dryness,' and as an adverb when describing manner of speech or action.
learnerNotes: Remember that secco differs from asciutto: secco means moisture is lacking where it should be present (e.g., dry hair implying unhealthy brittleness), while asciutto simply means not wet. However, both are often interchangeable in common contexts like 'dry throat' or 'dry climate.' Watch for the figurative use of secco meaning 'curt' or 'brusque' in describing someone's tone or manner—it's frequently used and carries a negative connotation.

grammarNotes: Gonfio agrees with the noun it modifies: feminine gonfia, plural gonfi (masculine) or gonfie (feminine). It functions as a standard adjective and can appear before or after the noun. The opposite is formed with the prefix s-: sgonfio (deflated).
learnerNotes: Gonfio can describe physical states (inflated objects, swollen body parts) or emotional states when used with 'di + noun' (gonfio di gioia, gonfio di rabbia). Don't confuse it with 'pieno' (full) — gonfio specifically implies expansion beyond normal size. The idiom 'andare a gonfie vele' is a useful colloquial expression worth memorizing.

exampleSentences.italian: Il pallone è gonfio? Bene, allora giochiamo!
exampleSentences.english: Is the ball inflated? Good, then let's play!

exampleSentences.italian: Ah, mamma mia, come mi sento gonfio. Ho mangiato davvero troppo!
exampleSentences.english: Oh boy, I feel so bloated. I ate way too much!

exampleSentences.italian: Hai il piede gonfio. Ti fa male?
exampleSentences.english: Your foot is swollen. Does it hurt?

exampleSentences.italian: Luigi aveva il cuore gonfio di gioia perché era riuscito a coronare il suo sogno.
exampleSentences.english: Luigi's heart was full of joy because he had achieved his dream.

exampleSentences.italian: Il lavoro sta andando a gonfie vele.
exampleSentences.english: The job is going swimmingly.

exampleSentences.italian: Il palloncino è tutto sgonfio, buttiamolo via.
exampleSentences.english: The balloon is completely deflated, let's throw it away.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to go swimmingly / to go with full sails

grammarNotes: Marmellata is a feminine noun (la marmellata). It is countable and typically used in the singular, though the plural form marmelate exists. It combines with prepositions such as 'di' to specify flavor (marmellata di fragole = strawberry jam).
learnerNotes: In formal EU contexts, marmellata specifically refers to preserves made from citrus fruits (minimum 20% fruit content), while confettura applies to other fruits (minimum 35% content). However, everyday Italian speakers use marmellata loosely for any jam. Be aware that the English 'marmalade' is a false cognate—it specifically means marmellata di arance (orange jam), not all jam. Remember the feminine article: 'la marmellata.'

exampleSentences.italian: Sto spalmando la marmellata su una fetta di pane tostato.
exampleSentences.english: I'm spreading the jam on a piece of toast.

englishTranslation: to walk along / to run along / to skirt / to sail along the coast
grammarNotes: Costeggiare is a regular -are verb conjugated normally in all tenses. In the present tense: io costeggio, tu costeggi, lui/lei/Lei costeggia, noi costeggiamo, voi costeggiate, loro costeggiano. The verb derives from the noun 'costa' (coast) and retains maritime origins while being used more broadly for movement along or around objects.
learnerNotes: Costeggiare originally meant 'to sail along the coast' in nautical contexts but has expanded to mean moving along or around any object rather than through it. Pay attention to its transitive use with both active (people moving) and passive (geographical features being flanked) constructions. The agricultural sense ('to level with a plow') is rarely encountered in modern usage.

exampleSentences.italian: Abbiamo costeggiato l'isola fino ad arrivare al porto principale.
exampleSentences.english: We sailed around the island until we reached the main port.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho costeggiato il muro del giardino finché non ho visto il cancello.
exampleSentences.english: I walked along / skirted the garden wall until I saw the gate.

exampleSentences.italian: La strada costeggiava il fiume.
exampleSentences.english: The road ran alongside the river.

exampleSentences.italian: Il fiume era costeggiato da una strada.
exampleSentences.english: The river was flanked by a road.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun beginning with st-, so it takes the articles lo (singular) and gli (plural). Singular indefinite article is uno. The plural form stenti is more commonly used in fixed expressions describing poverty or hardship. Derived from the verb stentare (to struggle, to find difficult).
learnerNotes: Stento has multiple meanings depending on context: severe hardship/suffering (noun), difficulty/struggle (noun), and barely/hardly (adverbial form a stento). The plural stenti appears more frequently in idiomatic expressions about poverty. Don't confuse a stento (barely) with con stento (with difficulty) — both express difficulty but a stento emphasizes the barely-managed achievement, while con stento emphasizes the effort required.

exampleSentences.italian: Lo hanno salvato da una vita di stenti e sfruttamento.
exampleSentences.english: They saved him from a life of hardship and exploitation.

exampleSentences.italian: Ha finito il compito con molto stento.
exampleSentences.english: He completed the task with great difficulty.

exampleSentences.italian: Dopo l'incidente, Elia si reggeva a stento sulle gambe.
exampleSentences.english: After the accident, Elia could hardly/barely stand up.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to live a life of hardship

grammarNotes: Già is a monosyllabic adverb marked with a grave accent. It typically appears between the auxiliary verb and past participle in passato prossimo (ho già mangiato). Già da + noun/adjective means 'even from/as.' When written as one word (giacché), it functions as a formal conjunction meaning 'since.'
learnerNotes: Già is pronounced as one syllable ('jah'), not two. In passato prossimo, it must go between the auxiliary (ho, hai, ha, etc.) and the past participle—never at the beginning or end. Pay attention to context: già can mean 'already,' 'yet,' 'before,' or 'even' depending on the sentence structure and English translation that feels most natural. In casual speech, già often confirms statements with a neutral or slightly sarcastic tone (Eh, già = 'Yup').

exampleSentences.italian: Ho già mangiato.
exampleSentences.english: I've already eaten.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho già letto questo libro. Ne hai un altro?
exampleSentences.english: I've already read this book. Do you have another one?

exampleSentences.italian: Mi dispiace, ma devo andare. – Di già?
exampleSentences.english: Sorry, but I have to go. – What, already?

exampleSentences.italian: Hai già visto il nuovo film di Scorsese?
exampleSentences.english: Have you seen Scorsese's new film yet?

exampleSentences.italian: Te l'ho già detto mille volte.
exampleSentences.english: I've told you a thousand times before.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono già arrivati i tuoi genitori? – No, sono in ritardo.
exampleSentences.english: Have your parents arrived yet? – No, they're late.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei già stato a Firenze?
exampleSentences.english: Have you been to Florence before?

exampleSentences.italian: Già da bambina, voleva diventare una ballerina.
exampleSentences.english: Even as a little girl, she wanted to be a dancer.

exampleSentences.italian: Già nei tempi antichi, il cioccolato era considerato cibo per privilegiati.
exampleSentences.english: Even in ancient times, chocolate was considered a food for the privileged.

exampleSentences.italian: Giacché non potete venire sabato, abbiamo deciso di spostare l'appuntamento a domenica.
exampleSentences.english: Since you cannot come on Saturday, we have decided to change the date to Sunday.

exampleSentences.italian: Già che ci sei, prendi anche un po' di frutta.
exampleSentences.english: While you're at it, pick up some fruit as well.

exampleSentences.italian: È lui il nuovo allenatore? – Eh, già.
exampleSentences.english: Is he the new coach? – Yup.

exampleSentences.italian: Giorgio Napolitano, già presidente della Repubblica
exampleSentences.english: Giorgio Napolitano, former President of the Republic

grammarNotes: Minuto is a masculine noun taking articles il/i (definite) and un/dei (indefinite). As an adjective meaning 'tiny' or 'minuscule', it agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies (e.g., caratteri minuti, una ragazza minuta). The word derives from late Latin minutum and maintains both temporal and size-related meanings in modern Italian.
learnerNotes: Note the false cognate: English 'minute' (the adjective meaning small) and Italian 'minuto' share the same root and meaning, but Italian minuto functions as both noun and adjective depending on context. When minuto means 'tiny', it must agree with the noun: caratteri minuti (tiny characters), but il minuto (the minute) uses the masculine form. The figurative sense of minuto as 'moment/instant' is common in everyday speech and appears frequently in idiomatic expressions.

exampleSentences.italian: Tra un minuto l'orologio batterà la mezzanotte.
exampleSentences.english: In one minute the clock will strike midnight.

exampleSentences.italian: Mancano dieci minuti alle quattro. Ci prepariamo per uscire?
exampleSentences.english: It's ten minutes to four. Shall we get ready to go out?

exampleSentences.italian: Non c'è un minuto da perdere.
exampleSentences.english: There isn't a minute to lose.

exampleSentences.italian: Aspetta un minuto!
exampleSentences.english: Wait a minute!

exampleSentences.italian: Mio figlio non sta mai fermo un minuto.
exampleSentences.english: My son never sits still for a minute.

exampleSentences.italian: Aspetta due minuti, adesso arrivo!
exampleSentences.english: Wait a second, I'm coming now!

grammarNotes: Cetriolo is a masculine noun. The definite article is il (singular) and i (plural); the indefinite article is un (singular) and dei (plural). It follows regular noun patterns with plural ending -i.
learnerNotes: Note that cetriolo has a figurative insult meaning ('stupid person' or 'moron') that is commonly used in Italian. Be aware that cocomero is an alternative regional term, particularly in Sicily, Veneto, and Friuli, though it also means 'watermelon' in southern Italy. If learning Italian-American slang, jadrool/chadrool derives from the southern dialectal form cidrule.

exampleSentences.italian: Ricordati di prendere un po' di cetrioli quando vai al supermercato.
exampleSentences.english: Remember to buy some cucumbers when you go to the supermarket.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel cetriolo ha rovinato tutto.
exampleSentences.english: That moron ruined everything.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun beginning with sp-, taking the definite article 'lo' and indefinite article 'uno'. The word is invariable, meaning singular and plural forms are identical: lo spaventapasseri (the scarecrow) and gli spaventapasseri (the scarecrows).
learnerNotes: Note that Italian emphasizes the sparrow threat (passero) rather than the crow (corvo) as in English. The word combines spaventare (to scare) + passeri (sparrows), reflecting this cultural difference. Remember that spaventapasseri is invariable, so you don't add -i for plural—the article changes instead (lo/gli, uno/degli).

exampleSentences.italian: I corvi sono troppo intelligenti per lasciarsi spaventare da uno spaventapasseri.
exampleSentences.english: Crows are too intelligent to be scared off by a scarecrow.

exampleSentences.italian: Lo spaventapasseri ha una testa di zucca con sopra un cappello da contadino.
exampleSentences.english: The scarecrow has a pumpkin head with a farmer's hat on top.

exampleSentences.italian: Un vermiglio Priapo sia messo a custodia dell'orto abbondante di frutta, perché con terribile falce cacci lontano gli uccelli.
exampleSentences.english: And in the garden let Priapus stand to frighten birds, his sickle in his hand.

relatedExpressions.meaning: alternative word for scarecrow; also means bogeyman in non-agricultural contexts
puppets, dolls, dummies (alternative term for scarecrows)
to scare (verb from which spaventapasseri is derived)

grammarNotes: Scolapasta is a masculine noun (lo scolapasta) despite ending in -a. It is invariable in the plural, meaning it retains the same form in both singular and plural (gli scolapasta, not scolapaste). The word is a compound formed from the verb scolare (to drain) and the noun pasta.
learnerNotes: Remember that scolapasta is masculine (lo, uno, gli, degli) despite its -a ending—this is an exception to the typical feminine gender pattern. The prefix s- adds an intensive value to the verb colare, so scolare is a strengthened form of colare. Related kitchen utensils like colino, setaccio, and vaglio have distinct uses: colino strains liquids, setaccio separates particles by size, and vaglio is archaic but survives in the idiom passare al vaglio.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho ereditato uno scolapasta da mia mamma.
exampleSentences.english: I inherited a colander from my mom.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi passi il colino? Devo filtrare il succo.
exampleSentences.english: Can you pass me the sieve? I have to strain the juice.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to examine carefully before coming to a conclusion

grammarNotes: As an adjective, folle retains its form for both masculine and feminine singular (l'uomo folle, la donna folle) but becomes folli in the plural (gli uomini folli, le donne folli). It can also function as a noun meaning a disturbed or crazy person. The unrelated noun folla (crowd) shares the same plural form folli but has different etymology.
learnerNotes: Folle is one of three interchangeable terms for 'crazy' in everyday Italian alongside pazzo and matto; all are used similarly with no significant register difference. Be careful not to confuse the adjective folle with the noun folla (crowd), which shares the same plural form but is etymologically unrelated. The automotive expression in folle (in neutral) is a common idiomatic use worth memorizing for intermediate learners.

exampleSentences.italian: l'uomo folle
exampleSentences.english: the crazy man

exampleSentences.italian: la donna folle
exampleSentences.english: the crazy woman

exampleSentences.italian: gli uomini folli
exampleSentences.english: the crazy men

exampleSentences.italian: le donne folli
exampleSentences.english: the crazy women

exampleSentences.italian: La mia vicina di casa era folle. Tutti lo sapevano.
exampleSentences.english: My next-door neighbour was crazy. Everybody knew it.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho sempre pensato che il progetto fosse folle e irrealizzabile.
exampleSentences.english: I always thought the project was crazy and unfeasible.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei stato folle a sfidarlo.
exampleSentences.english: You were crazy to challenge him.

exampleSentences.italian: Aveva una paura folle dei ragni.
exampleSentences.english: He had an uncontrollable fear of spiders.

exampleSentences.italian: Non voglio avere nulla a che fare con quel folle.
exampleSentences.english: I don't want to have anything to do with that nutter.

grammarNotes: Leccapiedi is an invariable noun, meaning its form does not change in singular or plural. It is gender-neutral and can take both masculine articles (il, un, i, dei) and feminine articles (la, una, le, delle) depending on context. The word is composed of leccare (to lick) + piedi (feet), literally meaning 'feet-licker'.
learnerNotes: Leccapiedi is widely used in professional and informal contexts to describe obsequious behavior, but it carries a decidedly negative and insulting tone—use carefully. The word first appeared in the 1700s and remains common today. Remember that as an invariable noun, you cannot pluralize it by changing its ending; instead, vary the article (il leccapiedi vs. i leccapiedi).

exampleSentences.italian: L'ho sempre detto che lui è un leccapiedi.
exampleSentences.english: I've always said that he was a bootlicker.

exampleSentences.italian: Lecchi sempre i piedi al capo.
exampleSentences.english: You're always sucking up to the boss.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to lick someone's feet (to suck up to someone)

grammarNotes: Contento is a four-form adjective that agrees in gender and number with the subject: contento (m. sg.), contenti (m. pl.), contenta (f. sg.), contente (f. pl.). It denotes a subdued or contained form of happiness, often expressing temporary satisfaction rather than profound joy. The word derives from Latin contĕntus, the past participle of continere (to contain).
learnerNotes: Contento and felice both mean 'happy' but carry different nuances: contento refers to temporary, smaller-scale satisfaction (e.g., pleased with results), while felice denotes deeper, more enduring contentment and overall well-being. Beware the false cognate with English 'content' (noun)—contento is an adjective meaning 'happy/satisfied,' not 'what is contained.' Remember to adjust the ending based on the subject's gender and number in all contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono contento di vederti.
exampleSentences.english: I'm glad / happy to see you.

exampleSentences.italian: Aveva un'espressione molto contenta.
exampleSentences.english: She had a very happy expression.

exampleSentences.italian: E va bene, sei più bravo di me. Sei contento adesso?

grammarNotes: Spesso is a versatile adverb that can be positioned flexibly within a sentence—before the verb, after the verb, or at the beginning. It originates from the adjective spesso (thick) and shares identical pronunciation and spelling with this adjective, which can create context-dependent ambiguity. The superlative form spessissimo conveys the meaning of molto spesso (very often).
learnerNotes: Beware of the homonymy: spesso as an adverb means 'often,' but spesso as an adjective means 'thick'—context clarifies which is intended. When using sempre più spesso, remember that molto spesso is the more direct equivalent of the superlative spessissimo. The expression spesso e volentieri sounds positive but can describe negative recurring events, so avoid assuming a positive connotation.

exampleSentences.italian: Spesso indosso dei maglioni spessi.
exampleSentences.english: I often wear thick sweaters.

exampleSentences.italian: Sento spesso i miei genitori.
exampleSentences.english: I'm often in touch with my parents.

exampleSentences.italian: Spesso chi beve rischia di fare un incidente.
exampleSentences.english: Often those who drink risk having an accident.

exampleSentences.italian: Andiamo sempre più spesso in montagna.
exampleSentences.english: We go to the mountains more and more often.

exampleSentences.italian: Quanto spesso vai al cinema?
exampleSentences.english: How often do you go to the cinema?

exampleSentences.italian: Spesso e volentieri avvengono incidenti mortali su quest'autostrada.
exampleSentences.english: Fatal accidents often happen on this highway.

grammarNotes: Colibrì is an invariable masculine noun, meaning its singular and plural forms are identical. It takes the articles il/i (definite) and un/dei (indefinite). The final syllable is stressed (co-li-BRÌ), requiring an accent on the final ì. Like other words with final-syllable stress (libertà, caffè, città), this accent is mandatory in writing.
learnerNotes: Note that colibrì is borrowed from Spanish and entered Italian through that language. The accent mark on the final ì is not optional—it must appear in writing to indicate the stress pattern. Interestingly, Treccani lists an alternative pronunciation with stress on the first syllable (CO-li-bri), but this is less common; the standard stressed pronunciation is co-li-BRÌ.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho visto un colibrì volare vicino alla finestra.
exampleSentences.english: I saw a hummingbird fly by the window.

exampleSentences.italian: il colibrì
exampleSentences.english: the hummingbird

exampleSentences.italian: i colibrì
exampleSentences.english: the hummingbirds

exampleSentences.italian: dei colibrì
exampleSentences.english: (some) hummingbirds

exampleSentences.italian: I colibrì sono gli uccelli più piccoli del mondo.
exampleSentences.english: Hummingbirds are the smallest birds in the world.

grammarNotes: Stasera is a contracted form combining questa (this) with sera (evening), formed by dropping the initial 'que-'. It is invariable and does not change for gender or number. The noun sera itself can denote either evening (late afternoon until bedtime) or night, making stasera context-dependent in translation.
learnerNotes: Stasera is preferred in everyday speech over the longer questa sera for brevity, though both are correct. Note that sera covers the period from late afternoon until bedtime, so stasera can mean either 'this evening' or 'tonight' depending on context—use the one that fits your intended meaning. Avoid confusing stasera with 'sto pomeriggio (this afternoon), which is very informal; say oggi pomeriggio instead.

exampleSentences.italian: Stasera / Questa sera ha piovuto tantissimo!
exampleSentences.english: It rained a lot this evening.

exampleSentences.italian: Penso che tornerò a casa tardi stasera.
exampleSentences.english: I think I'll be coming home late tonight.

exampleSentences.italian: Se non vado in ufficio stasera, dovrò andarci domani.
exampleSentences.english: If I don't go to the office this evening, I'll have to go tomorrow.

exampleSentences.italian: Voglio ballare tutta la sera!
exampleSentences.english: I want to dance all evening!

exampleSentences.italian: Voglio ballare tutta la notte!
exampleSentences.english: I want to dance all night!

grammarNotes: Prezzo is a masculine noun (il prezzo). It derives from Latin pretium. The word can function literally as the cost of an item or figuratively as the cost/consequence of achieving something. Agreement with adjectives follows standard masculine singular patterns (un buon prezzo, il prezzo alto).
learnerNotes: Prezzo is commonly paired with verbs like spuntare, sparare, alzare, and abbassare. Remember the figurative usage: 'il prezzo del successo' (the price of success) refers to metaphorical costs or sacrifices. Don't confuse prezzo (the numerical cost) with costo (the economic expense) or valore (worth/value), though they often overlap in meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: Il venditore mi ha fatto un buon prezzo per questo divano.
exampleSentences.english: The seller gave me a good price for this couch.

exampleSentences.italian: Quanto costa questo libro? Non vedo il prezzo.
exampleSentences.english: How much is this book? I can't see the price.

exampleSentences.italian: Stacchiamo il prezzo prima che veda quanto mi è costato questo orologio!
exampleSentences.english: Let's remove the price tag before she sees how much this watch cost me!

exampleSentences.italian: Mettersi la cintura, per quanto sia scomodo, è un piccolo prezzo da pagare per la sicurezza.
exampleSentences.english: Wearing a seatbelt, as uncomfortable as it is, is a small price to pay for safety.

relatedExpressions.meaning: at/for the price of (literal or figurative)

grammarNotes: Qualcosa is an indefinite pronoun derived from qualche (some) and cosa (thing). It is used in affirmative and interrogative statements; in negative statements, niente (nothing) must be used instead. Qualcosa can be followed by di + masculine adjective (e.g., qualcosa di interessante) or by altro becoming qualcos'altro.
learnerNotes: Remember to use niente (not qualcosa) in negative statements. Qualcosa translates as 'something' in affirmative sentences but as 'anything' in questions. When followed by an adjective, always use di + masculine form (qualcosa di interessante, not qualcosa interessante), as the adjective agrees with the implied masculine noun cosa.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho qualcosa da darti.
exampleSentences.english: I have something to give you.

exampleSentences.italian: Non ho niente da darti.
exampleSentences.english: I have nothing / don't have anything to give you.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai qualcosa da darmi?
exampleSentences.english: Do you have something / anything to give me?

exampleSentences.english: I said something to him.

exampleSentences.italian: Non gli ho detto niente.

exampleSentences.italian: Gli hai detto qualcosa?
exampleSentences.english: Did you say something / anything to him?

exampleSentences.italian: Vuoi fare qualcosa? – No, non voglio fare niente.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è un qualcosa di lui che ti fa sentire molto al sicuro.
exampleSentences.english: There's a certain something about him that makes you feel very safe.

grammarNotes: Signore is a masculine noun with regular article agreement: il signore (the man), i signori (the men), un signore (a man), dei signori (some men). When used before a surname, it becomes signor (without final -e), often abbreviated as sig. The plural signori can also be the plural of signora (lady), distinguished only by the article used. The diminutive form is signorino (young master).
learnerNotes: Remember that signore differs from uomo (man): signore is polite and refined, while uomo is generic and less formal. When addressing someone directly or before a surname, drop the final -e and write signor (e.g., signor Rossi, not signore Rossi). Note that the abbreviation sig. is never capitalized in Italian, unlike Mr. in English—this is a common mistake for learners.

grammarNotes: Mai means 'never/not ever' when paired with the negative adverb non, creating a double negative (which is grammatically correct and common in Italian). In simple tenses, mai follows the conjugated verb; in compound tenses, it sits between the auxiliary verb and past participle. Mai means 'ever' in interrogative sentences and with conditional statements, and can also be used for emphasis in WH-questions.
learnerNotes: Remember that Italian accepts and requires double negatives (non + mai) where English uses only one negative—'Non ho mai' literally means 'I have not ever' but translates as 'I have never.' The position of mai varies: after simple verbs, between auxiliary and past participle in compound tenses, and between modal verbs and infinitives. Watch the distinction between semmai (one word = 'if anything') and se mai (two words = 'if ever,' requires subjunctive).

exampleSentences.italian: Non ho mai visto un canguro.
exampleSentences.english: I have never seen a kangaroo.

exampleSentences.italian: Non è mai uscita con nessuno.
exampleSentences.english: She's never gone out with anyone.

exampleSentences.italian: Non vuole mai tornare a casa.

exampleSentences.italian: Come mai sei arrivato così tardi?

exampleSentences.italian: Portati una giacca, caso mai facesse freddo.

exampleSentences.italian: Mai e poi mai tornerò in quel locale.

exampleSentences.italian: Devi decidere: se vuoi andare, è ora o mai più.

exampleSentences.italian: Matteo è più testardo che mai.

exampleSentences.italian: Semmai direi che è il contrario.

exampleSentences.italian: Se mai dovessi cambiare idea in futuro, fammi sapere!

grammarNotes: Schifo is a masculine noun. The plural forms (gli schifi, degli schifi) are rarely used. It appears most commonly in the expression 'fare schifo' (to be disgusting). When used with indirect object pronouns (mi, ti, gli), it takes on the meaning 'to gross someone out.' The related adjective schifoso and verb schifare carry equivalent meanings.
learnerNotes: Schifo is highly colloquial and frequently used in everyday Italian speech. The expression 'fare schifo' is the most common construction—remember that with indirect object pronouns, it translates as 'to gross someone out' rather than 'to be gross.' The phrase 'da far schifo' is useful for expressing envious admiration (e.g., 'ricco da far schifo' = stinking rich), which is a distinctly Italian idiom without direct English equivalents.

exampleSentences.italian: Il cibo dei fast food fa schifo. Non lo mangio mai.
exampleSentences.english: Fast food is gross. I never eat it.

exampleSentences.italian: Quest'anno la nostra squadra ha fatto proprio schifo.

exampleSentences.italian: Che schifo!
exampleSentences.english: Yuck! / Gross! / Ew! / Nasty!

exampleSentences.italian: Non infilare le dita nel naso! Che schifo!
exampleSentences.english: Don't stick your finger up your nose! Yuck!

exampleSentences.italian: Questo hamburger è uno schifo. La carne sa di cartone!

exampleSentences.italian: È un film che fa schifo! / È un film schifoso!

grammarNotes: Pomeriggio is a masculine noun with plural form pomeriggi. It takes masculine articles: il pomeriggio (the afternoon), un pomeriggio (an afternoon), i pomeriggi (the afternoons), dei pomeriggi (some afternoons). The related adjective pomeridiano describes something occurring in the afternoon.
learnerNotes: While 'buon pomeriggio' exists, Italians rarely use this greeting in practice, preferring to transition directly from 'buongiorno' to 'buonasera'. The adjective 'pomeridiano' is commonly paired with nouns (e.g., sonnellino pomeridiano, riposo pomeridiano) to indicate afternoon activities. Remember pomeriggio is masculine, so use 'il' and 'un', not 'la' or 'una'.

exampleSentences.italian: Ci vediamo questo pomeriggio!
exampleSentences.english: See you this afternoon!

exampleSentences.italian: Mio padre fa sempre un sonnellino pomeridiano.
exampleSentences.english: My father always has an afternoon nap.

exampleSentences.italian: Buon pomeriggio!
exampleSentences.english: Good afternoon!

grammarNotes: Pensare is a regular -are verb conjugated in the present tense as: penso, pensi, pensa, pensiamo, pensate, pensano. It commonly takes the prepositions di (followed by infinitive) or a (meaning 'about/of'). When followed by che and a subordinate clause, the verb typically appears in the subjunctive mood, especially when expressing opinion rather than certainty.
learnerNotes: Note that pensare + che typically requires the subjunctive in the subordinate clause unless the speaker has absolute certainty. The pronominal form pensarci (pensare + ci) is very common in expressions like 'Ci penso io!' and 'non ci penso neanche'. The preposition choice matters: use 'di' before infinitives and 'a' when expressing 'thinking about' a specific person or thing.

exampleSentences.italian: Penso di andare al cinema stasera.
exampleSentences.english: I think I'll go to the cinema tonight.

exampleSentences.italian: Penso di sì.
exampleSentences.english: I think so.

exampleSentences.english: I don't think so.

exampleSentences.english: I'm thinking about / of you.

exampleSentences.english: I think you are correct.

exampleSentences.italian: Penso anch'io che lui è Mario. Riconosco la sua andatura.
exampleSentences.english: I also think it's Mario. I recognise his gait.

exampleSentences.italian: Pensa che bello se tutti mantenessero le loro promesse.
exampleSentences.english: Just think how nice it would be if everyone kept their promises.

exampleSentences.italian: E pensare che l'amavo davvero! Che sciocco che sono stato!
exampleSentences.english: And to think that I actually loved her! I've been such an idiot!

grammarNotes: Carino is the diminutive form of caro (dear) and agrees with gender and number: carino (masc. sing.), carina (fem. sing.), carini (masc. pl.), carine (fem. pl.). It functions as a standard adjective, typically placed before or after the noun it modifies. Can also be used predicatively with essere.
learnerNotes: Carino is highly versatile and commonly used in daily Italian conversation. Remember that the translation shifts depending on context: use 'cute' for children/animals, 'pretty' for girls/aesthetic descriptions, and 'kind/nice' for actions and deeds. The exclamation 'Ma che carino/a!' is extremely common in spoken Italian and worth memorizing as a set phrase.

exampleSentences.english: It was a kind gesture on his part.

grammarNotes: Divertente is the present participle of the verb divertire. As an adjective, it agrees with the noun it modifies: divertente (singular), divertenti (plural). It functions identically for both masculine and feminine nouns in the singular form, changing only in the plural. The verb divertirsi (reflexive form) means 'to have fun' or 'to amuse oneself.'
learnerNotes: Beware: English speakers often confuse 'fun' and 'funny,' but divertente can mean both depending on context—it describes entertaining activities, amusing stories, or people who make you laugh. The related verb divertire means 'to entertain' or 'to amuse,' so remember divertirsi when you want to say 'I had fun' (mi sono divertito/a). Note that while divertente itself is gender-invariant in the singular, the past participle of divertirsi does change: mi sono divertito (m.) / divertita (f.).

grammarNotes: As an adjective, fico/figo agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: fico (masc. sing.), fica (fem. sing.), fichi (masc. plur.), fiche (fem. plur.). The superlative form is created with the suffix -issimo/-issima (e.g., fighissimo). Northern Italian pronunciation is figo instead of fico.
learnerNotes: Do not confuse fico the adjective with fico the noun (fig fruit). Be aware that fico/fica has vulgar connotations—specifically, the feminine form fica can refer to female genitalia, so use carefully in formal contexts. The etymology is uncertain but likely stems from 1970s Roman youth slang, making it a relatively modern colloquialism.

grammarNotes: Cercare is a regular -ARE verb. In the present tense: cerco, cerchi, cerca, cerchiamo, cercate, cercano. When meaning 'to try,' it must be followed by di + infinitive (cercare di fare), not a + infinitive. It cannot be directly followed by a noun in the 'to try' sense.

Don't confuse cercare (to search for) with other 'to try' verbs like provare and tentare; each has distinct usage patterns.
