grammarNotes: Laggiù is a compound adverb formed by combining là (there) and giù (down), with the doubling of the 'g' in giù. It is invariable and does not change form based on gender, number, or any grammatical agreement. The related adverb lassù (up there) follows the same formation pattern but with su (up) instead of giù.
learnerNotes: Laggiù specifically means 'down there' in a literal spatial sense or 'down south' when referring to southern Italy. Do not confuse it with lassù (up there), which is formed with su instead of giù. Remember that the double 'g' in giù is retained in the compound form, making the pronunciation distinct from simpler location words.

exampleSentences.italian: Guarda laggiù, vedo qualcosa che brilla! Andiamo a vedere che cos'è.
exampleSentences.english: Look down there, I can see something shiny! Let's go see what it is.

exampleSentences.italian: Laggiù in Sicilia abitano i miei zii.
exampleSentences.english: My aunt and uncle live down south in Sicily.

exampleSentences.italian: Dove abiti? – In quella casa laggiù.
exampleSentences.english: Where do you live? – In that house over there.

exampleSentences.italian: Lassù su quel ramo c'è un nido di scoiattolo.
exampleSentences.english: There's a squirrel's nest up there on the branch.

exampleSentences.italian: Spero che mia nonna mi veda da lassù.
exampleSentences.english: I hope my grandmother can see me from up there.

grammarNotes: Schiaccianoci is an invariable masculine noun composed of the verb schiacciare (to crush) and the plural noun noci (walnuts). As an invariable noun, it maintains the same form in both singular and plural: lo schiaccianoci / gli schiaccianoci. It follows standard masculine article patterns (lo/gli in definite form, uno/degli in indefinite form).
learnerNotes: Schiaccianoci is a compound word worth memorizing as a unit rather than translating literally. Note that it's invariable—the plural form doesn't change, which is unusual for Italian nouns and makes it easier to use consistently. This word is particularly useful during Christmas season (stagione natalizia) in Italian-speaking households.

exampleSentences.italian: Dove vogliamo mettere lo schiaccianoci quest'anno? Sul davanzale?
exampleSentences.english: Where do we want to put the nutcracker this year? On the windowsill?

exampleSentences.italian: Ho rotto il guscio della noce con la mandibola dello schiaccianoci.
exampleSentences.english: I broke the walnut's shell with the nutcracker's lower jaw.

grammarNotes: Vischio is a masculine noun. It takes the definite article 'il' (singular) and 'i' (plural), and indefinite article 'un' (singular) and 'dei' (plural). Regular masculine noun following standard Italian gender and number agreement patterns.
learnerNotes: Vischio is a masculine noun commonly associated with Christmas traditions and kissing customs. Note that mistletoe is actually parasitic and poisonous, despite its romantic connotations in English-speaking cultures. The expression 'baciarsi sotto al vischio' uses the reflexive form and is typically encountered in festive or romantic contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Si sono baciati sotto al vischio.
exampleSentences.english: They kissed underneath the mistletoe.

exampleSentences.italian: Il vischio è una pianta parassita e velenosa.
exampleSentences.english: Mistletoe is a parasitic and poisonous plant.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun beginning with a vowel, taking l' (singular) and gli (plural) as definite articles. Indefinite articles are un (singular) and degli (plural). Derived from the verb addobbare (to decorate/adorn). The plural form is addobbi.
learnerNotes: Addobbo and decorazione are largely interchangeable for Christmas ornaments, though addobbo is more specific to festive decoration. Note the reflexive form addobbarsi means 'to dress up lavishly' rather than simply 'to decorate'—be careful not to confuse the non-reflexive (transitive) and reflexive (intransitive) uses. The word is common during holiday contexts, making it useful seasonal vocabulary.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho comprato degli addobbi da appendere sull'albero di Natale.
exampleSentences.english: I bought some decorations to hang on the Christmas tree.

exampleSentences.italian: l'addobbo
exampleSentences.english: the decoration / ornament

exampleSentences.italian: gli addobbi
exampleSentences.english: the decorations / ornaments

exampleSentences.italian: un addobbo
exampleSentences.english: a decoration / ornament

exampleSentences.italian: degli addobbi
exampleSentences.english: (some) decorations / ornaments

relatedExpressions.meaning: to decorate, to adorn, to deck out
to adorn oneself, to dress up in a lavish way

grammarNotes: Gioia is a feminine noun taking the articles la (singular) and le (plural). The indefinite articles are una (singular) and delle (plural). As a feminine noun, any adjectives modifying it must agree in gender and number.
learnerNotes: Note that gioia has a secondary meaning: jewel, gem, or precious stone (e.g., coperta di gioie = covered in jewels). The expression 'che gioia' is often used sarcastically in everyday Italian, so context is essential for determining the speaker's true intent. As a term of endearment, 'gioia' and 'gioia mia' are particularly common in family contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Il bambino ha fatto un salto di gioia quando ha ricevuto il suo regalo di Natale.
exampleSentences.english: The boy jumped for joy when he received his Christmas present.

exampleSentences.italian: Il Natale è il momento ideale per festeggiare le gioie della vita.
exampleSentences.english: Christmas is the ideal time to celebrate the joys of life.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei la mia gioia, figlia mia.
exampleSentences.english: You're the light of my life, my daughter.

exampleSentences.italian: Che gioia essere qui!
exampleSentences.english: How nice it is to be here!

exampleSentences.italian: Che gioia, sta piovendo di nuovo!
exampleSentences.english: Oh great, it's raining again!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to live it up / have a wild time

relatedExpressions.expression: essere fuori di sé dalla gioia

relatedExpressions.meaning: how nice / that's great (can be sincere or sarcastic)
never a joy! (expressing perpetual disappointment or frustration)

grammarNotes: Attraversare is a regular -ARE verb conjugating predictably in all tenses. In the first-person plural form (attraversiamo), it can mean either 'we cross' or 'let's cross' depending on context. The verb is commonly used with a preposition indicating the mode of transportation (in macchina, in bicicletta, in aereo, etc.) rather than a separate action verb as in English.
learnerNotes: Unlike English, which uses specific action verbs (walk, swim, bike, fly), Italian uses attraversare with a preposition indicating the means of crossing. Remember that attraversiamo can function as an imperative ('let's cross') in addition to a declarative statement ('we cross'). The figurative meaning ('to experience/go through') is equally important as the literal sense and appears frequently in conversation.

exampleSentences.italian: Devi darmi la mano quando attraversiamo la strada.
exampleSentences.english: You must give me your hand when we cross the street.

exampleSentences.italian: Dai, attraversiamo la strada. Il semaforo è verde!
exampleSentences.english: Come on, let's cross the street. The traffic light is green!

exampleSentences.italian: Se attraversiamo qui, ci mettiamo solo cinque minuti per arrivare a casa.
exampleSentences.english: If we cross here, it will only take five minutes to get home.

exampleSentences.italian: Giorgia sta attraversando un brutto momento. Forse dovremmo andare a trovarla.
exampleSentences.english: Giorgia is going through a bad time. Maybe we should go see her.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to go through a difficult period

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with feminine form cascamorta (rarely used). Plural forms: cascamorti (masculine), cascamorte (feminine). Uses definite articles il/i and indefinite articles un/dei. Derived from the idiom cascare morto (to drop dead), combining cascare (to fall) + morto (dead).
learnerNotes: Cascamorto describes insincere flirting driven by hidden motives rather than genuine affection—it carries a negative connotation unlike neutral terms like corteggiatore. The expression fare il cascamorto is commonly used and means to behave in an overly sentimental, grovelling manner. Note that while the feminine form cascamorta exists grammatically, it is rarely used in practice.

exampleSentences.italian: In ufficio, Mario fa il cascamorto con tutte le sue colleghe.
exampleSentences.english: In the office, Mario hits on all his female colleagues.

exampleSentences.italian: Però ricordati che non devi fare il cascamorto!
exampleSentences.english: But remember, you mustn't do the 'cascamorto'!

exampleSentences.italian: Eh Luisella, io se casco, casco morto dalla fame!
exampleSentences.english: Well Luisella, if I fall, I'll fall dead from hunger.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to flirt with someone in a nauseating way / to hit on someone

grammarNotes: Incantevole is an adjective ending in -e that maintains the same form for both masculine and feminine singular (il luogo incantevole, la persona incantevole). In the plural, the -e changes to -i for both genders (i luoghi incantevoli, le persone incantevoli). It derives from the verb incantare and ultimately from Latin cantare ('to sing').
learnerNotes: Incantevole is a literary and somewhat elevated adjective; in everyday conversation, you may hear synonyms like delizioso (delightful) or favoloso (fabulous) more frequently. Note that incanto has a secondary meaning of 'auction' in commercial contexts, so context is important. This word pairs well with places, experiences, and people, and carries positive emotional connotations.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo posto è davvero incantevole!
exampleSentences.english: This place is truly enchanting!

englishTranslation: to wag one's tail / to kowtow / to grovel
grammarNotes: Scodinzolare is a regular -are verb conjugated like parlare. The verb contains the diminutive 'codinzolo' (from coda, meaning tail), so the object is embedded in the word itself and doesn't require explicit mention. It has both literal (animal tail-wagging) and figurative (human kowtowing/groveling) meanings.
learnerNotes: This word is memorable because the tail (coda) is literally hidden in the verb form itself, eliminating the need to say 'il cane scodinzola la coda.' Be aware of the figurative meaning when used with people—it implies subservience or excessive flattery. The humorous sense of 'wiggling walk' is primarily applied to women and may carry gendered connotations in use.

exampleSentences.italian: Il cane scodinzola perché è tornato il suo padrone.
exampleSentences.english: The dog is wagging its tail because its master came back.

exampleSentences.italian: Tutti scodinzolano dietro al capo.
exampleSentences.english: Everyone kowtows to the boss.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to kowtow to / grovel before someone
to walk with a wiggle (humorous usage)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural. Takes definite articles il/i and indefinite articles un/dei. Derivatives from lavanda (wash/washing). Can be specified as lavandino della cucina (kitchen sink) or lavandino del bagno (bathroom sink).
learnerNotes: Lavandino is a northern Italian word but understood across all regions. Important: in informal speech, lavandino also means a glutton or someone who eats without regard for food quality—a colloquial insult. Be aware of regional synonyms: use lavello for kitchen sink and lavabo for bathroom sink in standard Italian if you want to be precise, though lavandino works for both.

exampleSentences.italian: il lavandino
exampleSentences.english: the sink

exampleSentences.italian: i lavandini
exampleSentences.english: the sinks

exampleSentences.italian: un lavandino
exampleSentences.english: a sink

exampleSentences.italian: dei lavandini
exampleSentences.english: (some) sinks

exampleSentences.italian: Oh no, il lavandino è intasato! Abbiamo uno sturalavandini?
exampleSentences.english: Oh no, the sink is clogged! Do we have a plunger?

exampleSentences.italian: Ehi, ma sei un lavandino!
exampleSentences.english: Hey, you're a glutton! (literally: You're a kitchen sink!)

grammarNotes: Dolciastro is a four-form adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. The masculine singular ends in -o (dolciastro), feminine singular in -a (dolciastra), masculine plural in -i (dolciastri), and feminine plural in -e (dolciastre). This pattern is consistent with regular first-group adjectives in Italian.
learnerNotes: Dolciastro carries a negative connotation unlike its root word dolce; it implies excessive sweetness that is unpleasant or artificial. When used to describe people or mannerisms, it often suggests insincerity or affectation. Remember to always adjust the ending to match the noun's gender and number, as this is crucial for grammatical accuracy in Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: il vino dolciastro
exampleSentences.english: the sickly sweet wine

exampleSentences.italian: la torta dolciastra
exampleSentences.english: the sickly sweet cake

exampleSentences.italian: i vini dolciastri
exampleSentences.english: the sickly sweet wines

exampleSentences.italian: le torte dolciastre
exampleSentences.english: the sickly sweet cakes

exampleSentences.italian: La minestra ha un sapore dolciastro.
exampleSentences.english: The soup has a sickly sweet flavour.

exampleSentences.italian: "Buonasera" disse l'uomo, con una voce dolciastra.
exampleSentences.english: "Good evening," the man said, in a sickly sweet voice.

relatedExpressions.meaning: sickly sweet voice (often used figuratively to indicate insincerity)

grammarNotes: Burro is a masculine noun. Definite articles: il burro (singular), i burri (plural). Indefinite articles: un burro (singular), dei burri (plural). When used attributively with 'al', it means 'made with/containing butter' (e.g., pasta al burro).
learnerNotes: Be careful not to confuse Italian burro (butter) with Spanish burro (donkey) — a classic false cognate between Romance languages. The expression 'avere le mani di burro' is very common and should be memorized as a fixed phrase. Note that 'burro di cacao' refers to both cocoa butter and lip balm in Italian, regardless of actual ingredients.

exampleSentences.italian: Vuoi che spalmi un po' di burro sul pane?
exampleSentences.english: Do you want me to spread some butter on the bread?

exampleSentences.italian: Questa bistecca è un burro!
exampleSentences.english: This steak melts in your mouth!

exampleSentences.italian: Non darlo a Gianni – ha le mani di burro!
exampleSentences.english: Don't give it to Gianni – he has butterfingers!

relatedExpressions.meaning: born lucky (literally: with their bum in butter)

relatedExpressions.expression: dare un po' di burro a qualcuno
relatedExpressions.meaning: to act obsequiously towards someone to obtain something

grammarNotes: Vivere is an irregular second-conjugation verb ending in -ERE. In the present tense: io vivo, tu vivi, lui/lei vive, Lei vive, noi viviamo, voi vivete, loro vivono. When used intransitively, it takes either essere or avere as auxiliary (avere preferred in modern Italian); when transitive, it always requires avere.
learnerNotes: Vivere is highly versatile and extends beyond simple 'to live': it can mean 'to experience', 'to exist for a duration', or characterize a lifestyle. Pay attention to auxiliary verb choice in compound tenses—modern Italian prefers avere for intransitive uses. Note that vivere can also function as a noun meaning 'way of life' (il vivere in Italia).

exampleSentences.italian: Chi vuole vivere per sempre?
exampleSentences.english: Who wants to live forever?

exampleSentences.italian: Ho vissuto in Germania per tanti anni.
exampleSentences.english: I lived in Germany for many years.

exampleSentences.italian: Gandhi ha vissuto per 78 anni.
exampleSentences.english: Gandhi lived for 78 years.

exampleSentences.italian: Vivo in questa casa da 30 anni.
exampleSentences.english: I've lived in this house for 30 years.

exampleSentences.italian: E vissero felici e contenti.
exampleSentences.english: And they all lived happily ever after.

exampleSentences.italian: Ha vissuto dei momenti molto belli durante il suo anno all'estero.
exampleSentences.english: He experienced wonderful moments during his year abroad.

exampleSentences.italian: I miei genitori hanno vissuto a Firenze per tanti anni.
exampleSentences.english: My parents lived in Florence for many years.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho vissuto una vita felice.
exampleSentences.english: I've lived a happy life.

exampleSentences.italian: Vive di pane e pasta.
exampleSentences.english: He lives on bread and pasta.

exampleSentences.italian: Vive di rendita.
exampleSentences.english: He lives on a private income.

exampleSentences.italian: Devo vivere di espedienti.
exampleSentences.english: I have to live by my wits.

exampleSentences.italian: Vivono per i loro figli.
exampleSentences.english: They live for their children.

exampleSentences.italian: Vive da gran signore.
exampleSentences.english: He lives like a lord.

grammarNotes: Gradasso is a masculine noun that takes standard masculine articles (il, un, i, dei). When referring to a female, it requires feminine endings: -a for singular (la gradassa, una gradassa) and -e for plural (le gradasse, delle gradasse). The word originated as a character name from Orlando Inamorato but is now a common dictionary entry.
learnerNotes: Gradasso is a literary-origin word tied to Renaissance epic poetry, making it somewhat elevated for everyday speech, though it appears in modern Italian dictionaries. The expression 'fare il gradasso' is the most practical way to use this word in conversation. Be aware that synonyms like millantatore and smargiasso exist and are more commonly used in contemporary Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Volevi fare il gradasso parlando in inglese, e invece hai fatto una brutta figura.
exampleSentences.english: You wanted to show off by speaking in English, but instead you made a bad impression.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to show off / to brag / to behave like a braggart

grammarNotes: Mezzogiorno is a masculine noun combining mezzo (half) + giorno (day). It takes standard masculine articles: il mezzogiorno (singular), i mezzogiorni (plural), un mezzogiorno (indefinite). When referring to time, it is often used with the preposition 'a' (a mezzogiorno = at noon). It has a secondary meaning referring to geographical direction (south) or regions in Southern Italy.
learnerNotes: Mezzogiorno is commonly used in time expressions where English speakers might say 'twelve' (e.g., suonare mezzogiorno = to strike twelve). The casual abbreviation 'mezza' (half) is frequently used in informal speech to mean 12:30, but context determines whether it refers to noon or midnight. Note the geographical/political sense: il Mezzogiorno refers to Southern Italy with specific historical and economic significance, distinct from the simple directional meaning (south-facing).

exampleSentences.italian: La lezione comincia a mezzogiorno in punto.
exampleSentences.english: The lesson begins at noon on the dot.

exampleSentences.italian: Quando è suonato mezzogiorno, Lucia è uscita per fare una passeggiata.
exampleSentences.english: When the clock struck twelve, Lucia went out for a walk.

exampleSentences.italian: La mia stanza è esposta a mezzogiorno.
exampleSentences.english: My room faces south.

exampleSentences.italian: Ci vediamo alla mezza, ok?
exampleSentences.english: See you at noon / midnight, ok?

exampleSentences.italian: Il nuovo partito politico continua a crescere, soprattutto nel Mezzogiorno d'Italia.
exampleSentences.english: The new political party continues to grow, especially in Southern Italy.

relatedExpressions.meaning: Southern Italy (regions of the former Kingdom of the Two Sicilies)
casual term for 12:30 (either a.m. or p.m., depending on context)

grammarNotes: Premuroso is a four-form adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: premuroso (m.s.), premurosa (f.s.), premurosi (m.p.), premurose (f.p.). It commonly pairs with the prepositions con (with) or verso (towards) to express the direction of care or attention. The word derives from the noun premura (care/attention) and the verb premere (to press/push, figuratively to matter).
learnerNotes: Premuroso is a common descriptive adjective for people and relationships. Remember that it must agree with the subject's gender and number—this is essential for correct usage. The synonyms attento (attentive), carino (nice/kind), affettuoso (affectionate), and riguardoso (respectful/considerate) have slightly different nuances; premuroso emphasizes active, proactive care rather than passive politeness.

exampleSentences.italian: l'uomo premuroso
exampleSentences.english: the caring man

exampleSentences.italian: la donna premurosa
exampleSentences.english: the caring woman

exampleSentences.italian: gli uomini premurosi
exampleSentences.english: the caring men

exampleSentences.italian: le donne premurose
exampleSentences.english: the caring women

exampleSentences.italian: Elena è sempre così premurosa con noi.
exampleSentences.english: Elena is always very thoughtful towards us.

exampleSentences.italian: Sei molto premuroso verso i tuoi amici.
exampleSentences.english: You are very caring towards your friends.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to press/push; to matter/be of importance

grammarNotes: Arzigogolato is a four-form adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Masculine singular ends in -o (arzigogolato), feminine singular in -a (arzigogolata), masculine plural in -i (arzigogolati), and feminine plural in -e (arzigogolate). It is commonly used as a predicate adjective with essere or as an attributive adjective before/after the noun.
learnerNotes: Arzigogolato is a rather literary and somewhat humorous term—the word itself is notoriously tongue-twisting, which fits its meaning perfectly. It's typically used in formal or written contexts to describe unnecessarily complex explanations, speeches, or writing styles. Be careful not to confuse it with similar-sounding adjectives; this word has a specific connotation of being deliberately or unnecessarily complicated rather than simply difficult.

exampleSentences.italian: Il discorso del professore era così arzigogolato che persino gli studenti più attenti fecero fatica a seguirlo.
exampleSentences.english: The professor's speech was so convoluted that even the most attentive students struggled to follow it.

exampleSentences.italian: il discorso arzigogolato
exampleSentences.english: the convoluted speech

exampleSentences.italian: la poesia arzigogolata
exampleSentences.english: the convoluted poem

exampleSentences.italian: i discorsi arzigogolati
exampleSentences.english: the convoluted speeches

exampleSentences.italian: le poesie arzigogolate
exampleSentences.english: the convoluted poems

relatedExpressions.meaning: to elaborate / daydream / go off on a tangent
beating around the bush / a roundabout expression

englishTranslation: in love / enamored / in love with
grammarNotes: Innamorato is an adjective that agrees with the subject's gender and number: masculine singular innamorato, feminine singular innamorata, masculine plural innamorati, feminine plural innamorate. It typically requires the preposition di (of) before its object. It can also function as a noun meaning 'lover' or 'lovebird'.
learnerNotes: Remember that innamorato always requires the preposition di before the object of affection (innamorato di qualcosa/qualcuno). The idioms with pazzo, cotto, and perso are very common in spoken Italian and convey stronger emotion than innamorato alone. Note that innamorato can describe feelings toward objects (places, activities, food), not just people, making it more versatile than English 'in love with'.

exampleSentences.italian: Giulio è innamorato di Chiara.
exampleSentences.english: Giulio is in love with Chiara.

exampleSentences.italian: Mia sorella è innamorata pazza di un ragazzo italiano.
exampleSentences.english: My sister is head-over-heels in love with an Italian boy.

exampleSentences.italian: Io sono innamorato della costiera amalfitana.
exampleSentences.english: I love the Amalfi Coast.

exampleSentences.italian: I due innamorati si sono incontrati al parco.
exampleSentences.english: The two lovebirds met in the park.

relatedExpressions.meaning: madly in love / head-over-heels in love
madly in love / lost in love
to enchant / to make someone fall in love with you

grammarNotes: Masculine noun taking il/un in singular and i/dei in plural. The plural form changes -go to -ghi to preserve the hard G sound: il fango → i fanghi. As a masculine noun, any modifying adjectives must agree in gender and number.
learnerNotes: Remember the plural -go → -ghi change is essential for correct pronunciation and spelling. While fango primarily means mud, it also has figurative meanings related to dishonor or defamation, especially in idiomatic expressions. Use coperto di fango or sporco di fango rather than the adjective fangoso in conversational Italian, as natives prefer these literal expressions for describing muddy objects.

exampleSentences.italian: I bambini saltano nel fango.
exampleSentences.english: The children jump in the mud.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai le scarpe sporche di fango. Toglile prima di entrare in casa!
exampleSentences.english: You have muddy shoes. Take them off before coming inside the house!

exampleSentences.italian: Come osi trascinare il nome di mia madre nel fango?
exampleSentences.english: How dare you drag my mother's name through the mud?

relatedExpressions.meaning: to roll around in the mud
to speak badly about someone / discredit them / mud-sling
to throw someone in the mud / discredit someone

grammarNotes: Birbone functions as both noun and adjective with full gender/number agreement. As a noun, masculine singular is 'birbone', feminine singular is 'birbona', masculine plural is 'birboni', and feminine plural is 'birbone' (identical to masculine singular). When used as an adjective, it agrees with the noun it modifies and can add emphatic intensity to descriptors of temperature, emotion, and hunger.
learnerNotes: Birbone is most commonly encountered as a noun directed at children, functioning similarly to 'birichino' or 'monello'. When used as an adjective for intensification (e.g., 'un freddo birbone'), it adds emphatic emphasis rather than changing the core meaning. Be careful with gender agreement—the feminine plural form 'birbone' is identical to the masculine singular, so context is essential.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi hai giocato un tiro birbone.
exampleSentences.english: You played a dirty trick on me.

exampleSentences.italian: fa freddo > fa un freddo birbone
exampleSentences.english: it is cold > it is terribly cold

exampleSentences.italian: fa caldo > fa un caldo birbone
exampleSentences.english: it is hot > it is terribly hot

exampleSentences.italian: avere paura > avere una paura birbona
exampleSentences.english: to be scared > to be very scared

exampleSentences.italian: avere fame > avere una fame birbona
exampleSentences.english: to be hungry > to be very hungry

exampleSentences.italian: avere sete > avere una sete birbona
exampleSentences.english: to be thirsty > to be very thirsty

exampleSentences.italian: Vieni qui birbone che ti prendo!
exampleSentences.english: Come here, little rascal, I'm going to get you!

relatedExpressions.meaning: a humorous diminutive of birbone, meaning the same thing (little rascal)

grammarNotes: Dissestato is an adjective that agrees with the gender and number of the noun it modifies: dissestato (masc. sing.), dissestata (fem. sing.), dissestati (masc. plur.), dissestate (fem. plur.). It can also function as a noun to describe a financially ruined person, though this usage is rare. The word derives from the verb dissestare (to destabilize, upset, unbalance, or ruin) and noun dissesto (instability, disarray).
learnerNotes: Dissestato is not commonly used in everyday speech; it appears primarily in formal or technical contexts describing damaged infrastructure or financial instability. Remember that when used as a noun (il/la dissestato/a), it refers to a financially ruined person—a rare usage. Pay attention to gender agreement when modifying nouns, as this is essential for correct usage.

exampleSentences.italian: una strada dissestata
exampleSentences.english: an uneven / rutty / bumpy road

exampleSentences.italian: un fondo/manto stradale dissestato
exampleSentences.english: an uneven road surface

exampleSentences.italian: una struttura dissestata
exampleSentences.english: a damaged structure

exampleSentences.italian: un meccanismo dissestato
exampleSentences.english: an unbalanced mechanism

exampleSentences.italian: una casa dissestata
exampleSentences.english: a damaged / unstable house

exampleSentences.italian: Dicono che il marciapiede dissestato di via Milano verrà presto riparato.
exampleSentences.english: They say the bumpy sidewalk in via Milano will soon be repaired.

exampleSentences.italian: Hanno tentato in tutti modi di salvare l'azienda, ma era troppo dissestata.
exampleSentences.english: They tried in every way to save the company, but it was too financially unstable.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to destabilize, upset, unbalance, or ruin

grammarNotes: Anno is a masculine noun meaning 'year,' and bisestile is an adjective that agrees with it in gender and number. The phrase anno bisestile remains unchanged in plural (gli anni bisestili). The term bisestile derives from Latin bissextilis, composed of 'bis' (twice) and 'sextus' (sixth), referring to the doubling of the sixth day before the calends of March in the Roman calendar.
learnerNotes: The term anno bisestile may seem complex due to its Latin etymology, but it's identical to the English 'bissextile year,' making it easier to recognize. Remember that in Italian, leap years add an extra day to February (febbraio), just as in English. The rule for determining leap years in the Gregorian calendar is important: every four years, except centuries (divisible by 100) unless also divisible by 400—2000 was a leap year, but 1900 was not.

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi è il 29 febbraio? – Sì, il 2024 è un anno bisestile.
exampleSentences.english: Is today February 29th? – Yes, 2024 is a leap year.

relatedExpressions.meaning: the month in which the extra day (29th) is added in a leap year
Gregorian calendar, the system in which leap years occur every four years (except for years divisible by 100 but not by 400)

grammarNotes: Meno male is an interjection expressing relief. It can be written as two words or one (menomale), with both forms considered correct by Accademia della Crusca. When followed by 'che' and a declarative sentence, the verb must be in the indicative mood, not the subjunctive. The expression literally means 'less bad.'
learnerNotes: Meno male is highly colloquial and perfect for expressing relief in everyday conversation. Remember that after 'meno male che,' you must use indicative mood (e.g., 'Meno male che ci sei tu!' not 'che si sia tu!'). Don't confuse the exclamation with the literal meaning 'less bad'—context will clarify which meaning applies.

exampleSentences.italian: Domani non dovrebbe piovere. – Meno male!
exampleSentences.english: It shouldn't rain tomorrow. – Phew!

exampleSentences.italian: Menomale che ti senti meno male di ieri.
exampleSentences.english: Thank goodness you don't feel as bad as yesterday.

exampleSentences.italian: Meno male che ci sei tu!
exampleSentences.english: Thank goodness you are here!

relatedExpressions.meaning: thank goodness that (followed by indicative verb)

grammarNotes: Grattacapo is a masculine noun composed of grattare (to scratch) + capo (head), literally meaning 'head-scratcher.' It is regular in formation: il grattacapo (singular), i grattacapi (plural). It takes standard masculine articles: il/un in singular, i/dei in plural.
learnerNotes: Grattacapo is more colorful and colloquial than the standard 'problema,' so it's effective for informal speech and adds native-like fluency. Note the plural form i grattacapi—remember this irregular masculine plural ending (-i). Be careful not to confuse it with other compound words; the literal 'head-scratcher' meaning helps memorization.

exampleSentences.italian: È stato un bel grattacapo per tutti gli architetti coinvolti nella costruzione della casa.
exampleSentences.english: It was a real headache for the architects involved in the construction of the house.

exampleSentences.italian: Il video trapelato ieri ha creato un bel po' di grattacapi a lui e alla sua squadra.
exampleSentences.english: Yesterday's leaked video has caused a lot of headaches for him and his team.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to give someone a headache / cause someone trouble
to get into trouble / a bind
to get into trouble / face problems

grammarNotes: Spietato is an adjective that agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Masculine singular: spietato; feminine singular: spietata; masculine plural: spietati; feminine plural: spietate. The word derives from the noun pietà (pity) with the negating prefix s-, literally meaning 'without pity.'
learnerNotes: Spietato is primarily used in formal or literary contexts to describe harsh judgments, legal decisions, or intense competition. When describing people in legal/judicial roles (judge, prosecutor, dictator), it emphasizes cruelty or mercilessness; when describing competition, it emphasizes aggressive or cutthroat intensity. Pay attention to gender/number agreement—this is essential for accuracy, especially in written Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Solo un giudice spietato può emettere una sentenza del genere.
exampleSentences.english: Only a merciless judge could deliver such a verdict.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è una concorrenza spietata tra le due squadre.
exampleSentences.english: There is fierce competition between the two teams.

relatedExpressions.expression: fare una corte spietata a qualcuno
relatedExpressions.meaning: to court someone relentlessly / to chase after somebody

englishTranslation: like this/that, so, in this manner, as follows, that way
grammarNotes: Così is written with an accented ì, placing stress on the final syllable. It functions as an adverb (indicating manner), conjunction (expressing cause, purpose, or comparison with così...che/così...da patterns), and adjective (modifying nouns, meaning 'such' or 'like this'). When used as an adverb after adjectives/adverbs, it references size or dimension; as a conjunction, it can mean 'therefore' or 'so that'; as an adjective, it agrees contextually with the noun it modifies.
learnerNotes: Così is highly versatile but context-dependent; focus on distinguishing between its adverbial use (manner/degree), conjunctive use (cause/purpose), and adjectival use (quality/description). The pattern così...che/da expresses consequence and is common in Italian writing; listen carefully to native speakers for the natural pronunciation of the accented final ì. Remember that così often begins sentences for emphasis or logical progression, particularly after e (and).

exampleSentences.italian: Il cassetto si apre così.
exampleSentences.english: The drawer opens like this / in this way.

exampleSentences.italian: Per cucinare la pasta bisogna fare così.
exampleSentences.english: You cook the pasta as follows. / This is how you cook the pasta.

exampleSentences.italian: Così finisce il libro.
exampleSentences.english: This / That is how the book ends.

exampleSentences.italian: No, non ho detto così.
exampleSentences.english: No, that's not what I said.

exampleSentences.italian: La pozzanghera era grande così!
exampleSentences.english: The puddle was this big!

exampleSentences.italian: Ti ama così tanto. Sei molto fortunata.
exampleSentences.english: He loves you so much. You're very lucky.

exampleSentences.italian: Sembrava così gentile ed educato. Come ho potuto sbagliarmi così?
exampleSentences.english: He seemed so kind and polite. How could I have been so wrong?

exampleSentences.italian: Monica l'ha salutato e così ho fatto anch'io.
exampleSentences.english: Monica said hello to him and so did I.

exampleSentences.italian: Era così alto che toccava il soffitto con la testa.
exampleSentences.english: He was so tall that his head touched the ceiling.

exampleSentences.english: Why were you stupid enough / so stupid as to risk your life?

exampleSentences.italian: Aveva la tosse, così non è andato a scuola.
exampleSentences.english: He had a cough so he didn't go to school.

exampleSentences.italian: E così? Hai deciso se vuoi unirti a noi?
exampleSentences.english: Well then? Have you decided if you want to join us?

exampleSentences.italian: Mettiti la giacca, così non prendi freddo.
exampleSentences.english: Put on your jacket, that way / so that you won't get cold.

exampleSentences.italian: Maria è così come la immaginavo.
exampleSentences.english: Maria is just as I imagined.

exampleSentences.italian: Le tende possono essere utilizzate nei concerti, così come nei festival.
exampleSentences.english: The tents can be used in concerts, as well as at festivals.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei abitare in una casa così!
exampleSentences.english: I'd like to live in a house like this!

exampleSentences.italian: Hai mai visto un posto così?
exampleSentences.english: Have you ever seen such a place?

relatedExpressions.meaning: What more could you ask for!
That's right. / That's how it is.
If only that were the case!

grammarNotes: Sfacciato is an adjective that agrees with gender and number: -o (masculine singular), -a (feminine singular), -i (masculine plural), -e (feminine plural). The word derives from faccia (face) with the negating prefix s-, meaning 'without face/respect'. When used as a noun, it means an impudent or brazen person and follows standard noun agreement rules.
learnerNotes: Sfacciato describes personality traits or behavior that is disrespectful and arrogant. Beyond people, it can describe objects as 'gaudy' or 'showy' (e.g., bright colors, excessive luxury), so context determines whether it's criticizing manners or aesthetics. The related expressions faccia tosta and faccia di bronzo are common colloquial synonyms emphasizing boldness or nerve; these are useful alternatives to master for natural conversation.

exampleSentences.italian: l'uomo sfacciato
exampleSentences.english: the insolent man

exampleSentences.italian: la donna sfacciata
exampleSentences.english: the insolent woman

exampleSentences.english: the insolent men

exampleSentences.italian: Sei proprio uno sfacciato, Mario!
exampleSentences.english: You are such an impudent person, Mario!

exampleSentences.italian: I suoi capelli sono di un rosso sfacciato.
exampleSentences.english: Her hair is a gaudy shade of red.

grammarNotes: Tonfo is a masculine noun taking the articles il/i (definite) and un/dei (indefinite). The diminutive forms are tonfetto, tonfettino, and tonfino. It is onomatopoeic in origin, derived from Lombardic *tumpf. The verb form is fare un tonfo (to make a thud).
learnerNotes: Tonfo has a dual meaning: literally, the sound of something heavy falling (onomatopoeic), and figuratively, a major failure or flop in entertainment. While 'fiasco' and 'flop' are also used in Italian, tonfo is the native Italian term. Remember it's masculine (il tonfo, un tonfo) and takes standard masculine noun articles.

exampleSentences.italian: Il masso fece un tonfo cadendo nell'acqua.
exampleSentences.english: The boulder fell into the water with a thud.

exampleSentences.italian: La prima del suo nuovo film è stato un tonfo!
exampleSentences.english: The opening night of his new film was a flop!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to make a thud; to flop or fail

grammarNotes: Feminine noun taking the articles la (singular) and le (plural). Indefinite articles are una (singular) and delle (plural). Derived from pozza with a double diminutive suffix (-anghera). Specifically refers to rainwater puddles on the ground, distinguishing it from the more generic pozza.
learnerNotes: Pozzanghera is more specific than its root word pozza—use pozzanghera only for puddles formed by rainwater on the ground. The word already implies dirty/muddy water, but you can add 'di fango' for emphasis. This is a common word in everyday speech, especially when talking about children playing or rainy weather.

exampleSentences.italian: C'è una grossa pozzanghera sulla strada.
exampleSentences.english: There is a big puddle on the street.

exampleSentences.italian: A mio figlio piace saltare su e giù nelle pozzanghere di fango.
exampleSentences.english: My son likes jumping up and down in muddy puddles.

relatedExpressions.meaning: generic puddle or pool of liquid (water, milk, juice, etc.)

grammarNotes: Macchia is a feminine noun (la macchia, le macchie). It takes the articles la/le (definite) and una/delle (indefinite). The word derives from Latin macŭla and has multiple meanings: physical stains/spots, animal fur markings, and vegetation-related meanings. Related verbs include macchiare (to stain) and macchiarsi (to stain oneself).
learnerNotes: Macchia is commonly used with the verbs levare, togliere, or rimuovere when removing stains, and farsi/macchiarsi when accidentally getting stained. The idiomatic expressions a macchia di leopardo and a macchia d'olio are particularly useful for describing scattered distributions and rapid spread. Note that while macchia primarily means 'stain,' it has secondary meanings related to vegetation and hiding, so context is important for comprehension.

exampleSentences.italian: Perché questa macchia non va via?
exampleSentences.english: Why won't this stain come out?

exampleSentences.italian: Ti sei fatto una macchia sulla maglietta. Bisogna levarla subito!
exampleSentences.english: You've got a stain on your shirt. You need to remove it right away!

exampleSentences.italian: Ti sei macchiato la maglietta. Bisogna pulirla subito!
exampleSentences.english: You've stained your shirt. You need to wash it right away!

exampleSentences.italian: Ecco una mappa dei casi, diffusi a macchia di leopardo in tutto il mondo.
exampleSentences.english: Here is a map of the cases, scattered sporadically around the world.

exampleSentences.italian: La notizia si sta diffondendo a macchia d'olio.
exampleSentences.english: The news is spreading like wildfire.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to leave a stain / to stain
to get a stain / get stained
like an oil stain; spreading quickly
a stain on someone's honour; a blemish
to take to the bush / hide out

grammarNotes: Schiera is a feminine noun with regular plural schiere. It takes the definite articles la/le and indefinite articles una/delle. The word originally referred to military formations but has expanded to mean any homogenous group of people or things. The expression 'a schiera' (in formation) and its plural 'a schiere' (in large numbers) are common prepositional uses.
learnerNotes: Schiera originally meant military ranks but now applies to any group, animate or inanimate—think of it as a collective noun like 'flock' or 'swarm.' The expressions 'case a schiera' and 'villette a schiera' refer to residential housing types common in Italy, so recognizing these compounds is useful. Note that 'a schiere' conveys a sense of arriving together in large numbers, not just any group.

exampleSentences.italian: una schiera di soldati
exampleSentences.english: a line or row of soldiers

exampleSentences.italian: schiere nemiche
exampleSentences.english: enemy troops

exampleSentences.italian: Il comandante condurrà la schiera dall'accampamento alla città.
exampleSentences.english: The commander will lead the troops from the camp to the city.

exampleSentences.italian: una schiera di turisti
exampleSentences.english: a flock of tourists

exampleSentences.italian: una schiera di api
exampleSentences.english: a swarm of bees

exampleSentences.italian: una schiera di libri
exampleSentences.english: a hoard of books

exampleSentences.italian: una schiera di ammiratori
exampleSentences.english: a host of admirers

exampleSentences.italian: una schiera di paparazzi
exampleSentences.english: a crowd of paparazzi

exampleSentences.italian: Una schiera di formiche si presentò al nostro picnic!
exampleSentences.english: A host of ants showed up at our picnic!

exampleSentences.italian: I tifosi si presentarono a schiere in piazza.
exampleSentences.english: The supporters arrived in large numbers in the square.

grammarNotes: Marachella is a feminine noun (la marachella, le marachelle). It takes regular feminine articles and pluralizes to -e. In plural, the indefinite article becomes 'delle' (delle marachelle = some tricks). The word originated from Hebrew but has evolved semantically from 'spy' to its modern meaning of mischief or prank.
learnerNotes: Marachella describes a forgivable, playful transgression—not serious wrongdoing. The word has Hebrew origins filtered through Triestine dialect, making it less common in standard Italian but recognizable in colloquial speech. Note the semantic shift from its original meaning: the phrase 'fare la marachella' retains the archaic 'spy' sense, so context is important when interpreting this expression.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono un po' stufo delle tue marachelle!
exampleSentences.english: I'm a bit tired of your tricks!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be a spy (archaic/original meaning); to play a trick

grammarNotes: Tuffo is a masculine noun taking articles il/i (definite) and un/dei (indefinite). It derives from the verb tuffare (to plunge/immerse) and the reflexive tuffarsi (to dive/immerse oneself). Related nouns include tuffatore (male diver), tuffatrice (female diver), and tuffista (diver of either gender).
learnerNotes: Tuffo has both literal meanings (diving into water) and figurative extensions (leaps through time/space, emotional jumps). The phrase 'fare un tuffo' is equally common as the reflexive 'tuffarsi' for expressing the action of diving. Pay attention to context: tuffo in sporting contexts may refer to dives in soccer (diving saves) or aeronautics (nosedives), not just water activities.

exampleSentences.italian: Ha fatto un tuffo in piscina dal trampolino.
exampleSentences.english: He dove into the pool from the diving board.

exampleSentences.italian: Farò un tuffo veloce in mare prima di tornare a casa.
exampleSentences.english: I'll take a quick dip in the sea before heading home.

exampleSentences.italian: Con un tuffo si buttò sul divano.
exampleSentences.english: With a leap he threw himself onto the sofa.

relatedExpressions.expression: buttarsi / gettarsi a tuffo su qualcosa
relatedExpressions.meaning: to try and grab something greedily
to feel one's heart leap / a skipped heartbeat

grammarNotes: Lana is a feminine noun derived from Latin. Definite articles: la lana (singular), le lane (plural). Indefinite articles: una lana (singular), delle lane (plural). The expression 'di lana' describes objects made of wool, while the adjective 'lanoso' describes things made of or resembling wool.
learnerNotes: Lana has both literal (sheep's wool, fabric) and figurative meanings; when used figuratively to describe a person as 'lana' or 'una buona lana,' it carries a negative connotation implying they are untrustworthy or disreputable. The phrase 'della stessa lana' relies on this figurative usage and cannot be translated word-for-word. Note that 'lanoso' is the common adjective for describing woolen items; don't confuse it with 'lanosissimo' (very woolly).

exampleSentences.italian: Ho un maglione di lana che mi dà prurito.
exampleSentences.english: I have a wool sweater that makes me itchy.

exampleSentences.italian: Quando fa freddo, mi piace avvolgermi in questa coperta lanosa.
exampleSentences.english: When it's cold, I like to wrap myself up in this wooly blanket.

exampleSentences.italian: Che lana quel ragazzo. Non mi fido di lui!
exampleSentences.english: That guy's such a scoundrel. I don't trust him!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to come from the same negative background; to share undesirable tendencies

relatedExpressions.expression: essere una questione di lana caprina
relatedExpressions.meaning: to be a futile argument, moot point, or unproductive discussion

grammarNotes: As an adjective, guasto agrees with the noun in gender and number: guasto (m.s.), guasti (m.p.), guasta (f.s.), guaste (f.p.). As a noun, it is masculine with plural guasti. Guasto is the past participle of the verb guastare (to break, to spoil).
learnerNotes: Guasto functions both as an adjective (requiring gender/number agreement) and as a noun (masculine). In figurative contexts, it can mean corrupt or depraved when describing people or situations. Remember that non guasta + infinitive is a common colloquial construction meaning 'won't hurt' or 'wouldn't be bad,' as in 'una vacanza non guasta' (a vacation wouldn't hurt).

exampleSentences.english: The elevator is broken again!

grammarNotes: Nascondere is a regular -ERE verb conjugated in the present tense as: io nascondo, tu nascondi, lui/lei nasconde, noi nascondiamo, voi nascondete, loro nascondono. It is a transitive verb requiring a direct object. The reflexive form nascondersi (to hide oneself) is used when describing hiding from someone or something, or figuratively when something is hidden behind something else.
learnerNotes: Remember that nascondere is transitive and always requires a direct object (e.g., 'nascondere il giocattolo'). Use the reflexive form nascondersi when expressing hiding from someone or something (e.g., 'nascondersi dietro la siepe'). The game 'hide-and-seek' is specifically called nascondino, not just nascondere; knowing this distinction helps in authentic conversation.

exampleSentences.italian: Io nasconderò il giocattolo e tu lo dovrai cercare.
exampleSentences.english: I'll hide the toy and you'll have to find it.

exampleSentences.italian: Dietro il suo sorriso si nasconde tanto dolore.

grammarNotes: As an adjective, piatto agrees with the gender and number of the noun it modifies (piatto/piatta/piatti/piatte). As a noun, piatto is exclusively masculine with plural piatti. The adjective derives from Latin plattum and can describe physical flatness, calm water, geometric angles, or figuratively describe dull/boring things.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'piatto' as a noun (meaning plate/dish) is always masculine (il piatto, i piatti), while the adjective form agrees with the noun it modifies. In restaurant contexts, 'piatto' commonly refers to the food itself, not just the physical plate—context determines meaning. Be aware of the figurative use meaning 'dull/boring,' which requires understanding nuanced registers beyond literal flatness.

grammarNotes: Masculine noun taking the articles il (singular) and i (plural). Indefinite articles are un (singular) and dei (plural). In Italian, the verb used with rubinetto is aprire/chiudere (to open/close) rather than the English 'turn on/off'. Can extend to mean valve when qualified, as in rubinetto del gas (gas valve) or rubinetto dell'acqua (water valve).
learnerNotes: Note that Italians often say 'aprire/chiudere l'acqua' (open/close the water) instead of using rubinetto directly when discussing tap flow. The word derives from French robinet (from robin, an old word for sheep) because early taps were shaped like sheep's heads—an interesting etymological detail. Remember to use aprire/chiudere rather than 'turn on/off' when speaking about taps in Italian.

grammarNotes: Chiamare is a regular -ARE verb conjugated normally in present tense. It takes a direct object pronoun (lo, la, li, le) when meaning 'to call someone.' The reflexive form chiamarsi means 'to call oneself' and is used to express one's name (io mi chiamo). Unlike its synonym telefonare, chiamare requires no preposition with a direct object.
learnerNotes: Remember that chiamare uses direct object pronouns (lo, la, li, le), not indirect pronouns—this differs from telefonare, which requires indirect pronouns and the preposition 'a'. The reflexive form chiamarsi is essential for introductions; it's how Italians naturally express 'my name is' rather than translating word-for-word. Watch out for the common mistake of adding 'a' after chiamare when calling someone (❌ Lui chiama a Giovanni).

exampleSentences.italian: Lui chiama Giovanni.
exampleSentences.english: He calls Giovanni.

exampleSentences.italian: Lui lo chiama.
exampleSentences.english: He calls him.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural form cortecce (not corteccie). Uses definite article la (singular) / le (plural) and indefinite article una / delle. The -cia ending becomes -ce in the plural form, which is a regular pattern for Italian feminine nouns ending in -cia/-cie.
learnerNotes: Corteccia has both literal (tree bark) and anatomical (brain/organ cortex) meanings—context will clarify which is intended. The plural form cortecce is irregular in that -cia becomes -ce rather than -cie, so memorize this pattern. Note the figurative use describing external appearance or personality facades, though this poetic usage is less common in everyday speech.

exampleSentences.italian: Tocca la corteccia dell'albero: è molto ruvida.
exampleSentences.english: Touch the bark of the tree: it's very rough.

exampleSentences.italian: La corteccia cerebrale è considerata la struttura più complessa tra tutti i sistemi viventi.
exampleSentences.english: The cerebral cortex is considered the most complex structure among all living systems.

exampleSentences.italian: Sotto una corteccia di zucchero scoprirai un cuore di cioccolato.
exampleSentences.english: Under a sugary shell, you will discover a chocolatey centre.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun (la scaramanzia). Plural forms are le scaramanzie (definite) and delle scaramanzie (indefinite). The adjective scaramantico/scaramantica describes superstitious people or tendencies and can function as both adjective and noun (superstitious person).
learnerNotes: Scaramanzia is a specifically Italian cultural concept rooted in superstitious practices to ward off bad luck. The expression 'per scaramanzia' is commonly used in everyday speech to excuse avoiding mention of something unlucky. Note that the etymology traces to chiromancy (palm reading), though this connection is not universally accepted.

exampleSentences.italian: Non diciamo nulla per scaramanzia!
exampleSentences.english: Let's not say anything, just to be on the safe side!

exampleSentences.italian: Mia nonna è molto scaramantica: non passa mai sotto una scala.
exampleSentences.english: My grandma is very superstitious: she never walks under a ladder.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to avoid attracting bad luck; for luck, just in case, just to be on the safe side
break a leg (literally: in the mouth of the wolf; opposite-statement superstition)
superstitious person or adjective describing superstitious tendencies

grammarNotes: Fazzoletto is a masculine noun, the diminutive form of the archaic fazzolo. It takes the regular masculine articles: il fazzoletto (singular), i fazzoletti (plural), un fazzoletto (indefinite singular), dei fazzoletti (indefinite plural). Further diminutives like fazzolettino are common in Italian speech.
learnerNotes: Fazzoletto covers both cloth handkerchiefs and disposable tissues with a single word—use fazzoletto di carta or fazzoletto di stoffa to specify which type if context is unclear. The figurative sense of 'a small plot of land' is less common but worth knowing. Note that carta velina (tissue paper in general) is distinct from fazzoletto and refers specifically to thin decorative or wrapping paper.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho usato un fazzoletto di carta per soffiarmi il naso.
exampleSentences.english: I used a tissue to blow my nose.

exampleSentences.italian: Mia nonna indossava sempre un fazzoletto in testa.
exampleSentences.english: My grandma always wore a handkerchief on her head.

exampleSentences.italian: Possiedo solo un fazzoletto di terra.
exampleSentences.english: All I own is a small plot of land.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to tie a knot in one's handkerchief (as a memory aid)

grammarNotes: Noia is a feminine noun taking the articles la/una (singular) and le/delle (plural). It derives from Provençal enoja via Late Latin inodiare. The noun pairs with various verbs to create idiomatic expressions; gender agreement is required with adjectives modifying it.
learnerNotes: Noia is closely related to the verb annoiarsi (to be bored), but the noun is less frequently used by learners. Note the false cognate parallel: English 'annoyance' and Italian 'noia' share etymology through Latin, making them genuinely cognate rather than false cognates. The preposition 'di' is optional in phrases like 'Luca è (di) una noia mortale,' both versions are acceptable.

exampleSentences.italian: Continua a sbadigliare per la noia.
exampleSentences.english: He keeps yawning from boredom.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho avuto delle noie all'aeroporto.
exampleSentences.english: I had some trouble at the airport.

exampleSentences.italian: Smettila di dar noia a tuo fratello!
exampleSentences.english: Stop annoying your brother!

exampleSentences.italian: Che noia questo film!
exampleSentences.english: This film is so boring!

exampleSentences.italian: Luca è una noia mortale.
exampleSentences.english: Luca is a dead bore.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to relieve the boredom (literally 'to kill the boredom')
to relieve the boredom (literally 'to win over boredom')
to have problems with someone / something

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with feminine counterpart sposa (bride). Plural sposi can mean either 'grooms' or 'newlyweds/bride and groom' depending on context. Uses definite article lo (lo sposo) and indefinite article uno (uno sposo). In plural, uses gli sposi and degli sposi. Gender and number agreement required with adjectives and articles.
learnerNotes: While marito is the standard word for 'husband,' sposo also carries this meaning, particularly in formal or ceremonial contexts (wedding vows) and colloquial speech among friends. Note that sposi in plural typically refers to a couple (newlyweds) rather than multiple grooms, so context is essential. The word derives from Latin sponsum, relating to the idea of a promise or engagement in marriage.

exampleSentences.italian: Lo sposo è molto elegante.
exampleSentences.english: The groom is very elegant.

exampleSentences.italian: Facciamo un brindisi agli sposi!
exampleSentences.english: Let's raise our glasses to the newlyweds!

exampleSentences.italian: Vuoi tu, Bianca, prendere come tuo sposo il qui presente Timoteo?
exampleSentences.english: Do you, Bianca, take Timoteo as your (lawfully wedded) husband?

exampleSentences.italian: Allora Enrica, come sta il tuo sposo?
exampleSentences.english: So Enrica, how's your husband?

relatedExpressions.meaning: newlyweds / bride and groom / married couple
Long live the bride and groom!
The Betrothed (famous novel by Alessandro Manzoni)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun that follows regular Italian article patterns. Singular forms: il putiferio (definite), un putiferio (indefinite). Plural forms: i putiferi (definite), dei putiferi (indefinite). Commonly paired with action verbs such as sollevare, far scoppiare, and scatenare.
learnerNotes: Putiferio is a deformation of vituperio and carries a distinctly colloquial, dramatic tone—use it when describing significant upheaval or chaos. Beyond its primary meaning of 'commotion,' it can also mean 'mess' or 'jumble' in figurative contexts. This word is most effective with dynamic verbs that convey action or escalation.

exampleSentences.italian: La nuova proposta di legge potrebbe sollevare un putiferio in parlamento.
exampleSentences.english: The new bill could stir up a commotion in parliament.

exampleSentences.italian: Si scatenerà un putiferio quando scopriranno cos'hai fatto.
exampleSentences.english: All hell will break loose when they find out what you've done.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to kick up a fuss / to stir up a commotion
to set off / unleash a commotion

grammarNotes: Scimmia is a feminine noun (la scimmia, una scimmia). The plural is le scimmie (definite) and delle scimmie (indefinite). As a feminine noun, all adjectives and articles must agree in gender and number. The word derives from Latin simia, ultimately from Greek simós meaning 'snub-nosed.'
learnerNotes: Note that scimmia specifically refers to monkeys with tails, while scimmie antropomorfe (apes) do not have tails. The idiom 'avere la scimmia' is widely used in Italian to describe addiction or obsession and is worth memorizing. Be careful not to confuse scimmia with related words like scimmione (ape/oaf) or the verb scimmiottare (to imitate).

exampleSentences.italian: La scimmia si arrampica sull'albero.
exampleSentences.english: The monkey is climbing the tree.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to do the monkey / little monkey (to mimic or act foolishly)
big monkey; ape; a large, oaf-like person with little intelligence (literal or figurative)
having the characteristics of a monkey or ape

relatedExpressions.expression: Essere agile / arrampicarsi come una scimmia

to be ugly, ungainly, and very hairy; to be very agile; to have an unpleasant character; to imitate someone
to have a monkey on one's back; to have an addiction (alcohol, drugs, shopping, etc.)
to get a monkey, to become addicted
to have a monkey on one's shoulder (variant of avere la scimmia)

grammarNotes: Bagnato is an adjective and past participle of bagnare (to wet). It agrees with gender and number: bagnata (feminine singular), bagnati (masculine plural), bagnate (feminine plural). It can also function as a noun referring to a wet surface or ground.
learnerNotes: Bagnato fradicio is the standard colloquial way to emphasize 'soaking wet' in everyday Italian—use this instead of just bagnato when you want to stress the degree of wetness. Remember that bagnato can function as both an adjective (describing something as wet) and a noun (referring to a wet surface itself), which is less common in English. The related verb bagnare (to wet/water) is regular and frequently used with reflexive form bagnarsi (to get wet).

exampleSentences.italian: I miei capelli sono bagnati.
exampleSentences.english: My hair is wet.

exampleSentences.italian: Attento a non scivolare sul bagnato!
exampleSentences.english: Be careful not to slip on the wet ground!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to act very shy and awkward; to be exhausted or without energy

relatedExpressions.expression: Se non è zuppa, è pan bagnato
relatedExpressions.meaning: It's six of one and half a dozen of the other
rain is good luck on your wedding day

grammarNotes: Occhiata is a feminine noun formed from occhio (eye) + the suffix -ata. Regular plural: occhiate. Singular forms: l'occhiata (the glance), un'occhiata (a glance). The noun follows standard feminine noun agreement patterns with articles and adjectives.
learnerNotes: Occhiata is extremely common in everyday Italian, particularly in the phrase 'dare un'occhiata' (to give a quick look), which you'll hear constantly in shops and casual conversation. Remember that 'dare un occhio' and 'dare un'occhiata' can mean both 'to take a quick look' AND 'to keep an eye on' depending on context—use context clues to determine which meaning applies. The diminutive 'occhiatina' emphasizes the casual, brief nature of the look.

exampleSentences.italian: Posso aiutarLa? – No, grazie, do solo un'occhiata.
exampleSentences.english: Can I help you? – No, thank you, I'm just looking.

exampleSentences.english: to check the mail

exampleSentences.italian: dare un'occhiata al giornale
exampleSentences.english: to have a quick look at the newspaper

exampleSentences.italian: dare un'occhiata / un occhio al cane
exampleSentences.english: to keep an eye on the dog / to look after the dog

exampleSentences.italian: Puoi dare un'occhiata / un occhio ai bambini per 5 minuti?
exampleSentences.english: Can you look after the kids for five minutes?

exampleSentences.italian: un'occhiata d'intesa

exampleSentences.english: a questioning look

grammarNotes: As an adjective, magro agrees with the subject's gender and number: magro (masc. sing.), magra (fem. sing.), magri (masc. pl.), magre (fem. pl.). It derives from Latin macrum. When used as a noun, magro refers to lean meat and magra to a slim woman, maintaining gender agreement.
learnerNotes: Magro is versatile with four distinct meanings (physical thinness, low-fat food, scarcity/meagerness, and meat abstinence), so context is crucial. Note the distinction with snello: magro is neutral/negative ('too thin'), while snello is complimentary ('attractively slender'). In religious contexts, magro relates to Catholic fasting practices and meatless meals, particularly important in Italian culture.

exampleSentences.italian: Penso che Marco sia troppo magro.
exampleSentences.english: I think Marco is too thin.

exampleSentences.italian: Devo comprare un chilo di magro per la ricetta.
exampleSentences.english: I have to buy a kilo of lean meat for the recipe.

exampleSentences.italian: Come faccio a vivere con uno stipendio così magro?
exampleSentences.english: How can I live on such a meager salary?

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi mangiamo di magro.
exampleSentences.english: Today we're not eating meat.

relatedExpressions.meaning: fake slim (a Sicilian dish; someone who appears slim but isn't)
to make a bad impression, to make a gaffe
time of extreme poverty (lit. time of slim cows)
day of abstinence from meat; a bad day (figurative)

grammarNotes: Bizza is a feminine noun taking the articles la/una (singular) and le/delle (plural). The singular form typically pairs with the verb prendere (prendere una bizza), while the plural form frequently combines with fare (fare le bizze). Both definite and indefinite articles must agree with the feminine gender.
learnerNotes: Bizza specifically refers to brief, childish tantrums (unlike the more generic capriccio), making it especially useful for describing children's behavior. Note the strong association: use fare le bizze (plural) for the behavior itself, but prendere una bizza (singular) when someone has a single tantrum episode. The word has colloquial, informal register—appropriate for casual conversation but not formal writing.

exampleSentences.italian: Non sopporto le tue bizze!
exampleSentences.english: I can't stand your tantrums!

exampleSentences.italian: Quando la bambina ha smesso di fare le bizze, si è divertita un mondo.
exampleSentences.english: When the little girl stopped acting up, she had lots of fun.

exampleSentences.italian: Il bimbo piccolo ha preso una bizza ed è diventato viola dal pianto.
exampleSentences.english: The toddler had a tantrum and turned purple from crying.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to act up / to behave like a spoilt child

grammarNotes: Masculine noun taking regular definite and indefinite articles: il sonno (singular), i sonni (plural). Uses the verb avere to express sleepiness in Italian (ho sonno = I am sleepy), unlike English which uses 'to be.' Combines with adjectives like leggero (light sleep) and pesante (heavy sleep) to describe sleep quality.
learnerNotes: Do not confuse sonno (sleep) with sogno (dream)—they sound similar but have entirely different meanings. Remember that Italian uses avere sonno (literally 'to have sleepiness') where English uses 'to be sleepy'—this is a common structure in Italian for describing physical states. Sonno can also mean 'peace' or 'silence with no activity' metaphorically, extending beyond its literal sleep meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: Sto cascando dal sonno e non sono neanche le nove di sera!
exampleSentences.english: I'm asleep on my feet and it's not even 9pm!

exampleSentences.italian: Ho sonno.
exampleSentences.english: I am sleepy.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai sonno?
exampleSentences.english: Are you sleepy?

exampleSentences.italian: Non ho sonno.
exampleSentences.english: I'm not sleepy.

exampleSentences.italian: Che sonno che ho. Continuo a sbadigliare!
exampleSentences.english: I am so sleepy. I can't stop yawning!

exampleSentences.italian: Questa lezione mette sonno.
exampleSentences.english: This lesson is so boring / is putting me to sleep.

exampleSentences.italian: Il villaggio era immerso nel sonno.
exampleSentences.english: The village was sound asleep.

exampleSentences.italian: Mio figlio non fa più il sonnellino pomeridiano.
exampleSentences.english: My son no longer has an afternoon nap.

to struggle to stay awake (literally: to fight with sleep)
to make up for lost sleep / catch up on sleep

grammarNotes: Benessere is a masculine noun. In singular form, it typically uses the definite article il (il benessere = the well-being) and indefinite article un (un benessere = a well-being). The plural forms are i benesseri (the well-beings) and dei benesseri (some well-beings), though plural usage is less common. As a compound word, it combines bene (well/good) + essere (to be/being).
learnerNotes: Benessere has multiple meanings depending on context: physical/mental well-being, and also wealth or affluence. While it primarily means 'well-being,' the broader sense of prosperity is important to recognize. Note that the plural forms (benesseri) are rarely used in practice, as benessere is typically treated as an uncountable noun.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi sono preso a cuore il mio benessere.
exampleSentences.english: I've taken my well-being to heart.

exampleSentences.italian: La sua famiglia vive nel benessere.
exampleSentences.english: His family is well-off.

relatedExpressions.meaning: indicator of well-being (used instead of 'poverty index' in Italian)

grammarNotes: Stivale is a masculine noun. It takes the articles lo (singular) and gli (plural). The plural form is stivali. Diminutive form stivaletto refers to ankle boots or booties. Like all Italian nouns, it agrees with adjectives and articles based on its masculine gender.
learnerNotes: Remember that stivale is masculine, so use lo/gli and masculine adjectives. The plural stivali takes gli as the article. When used with clothing verbs like indossare or mettersi, these are reflexive constructions (mettersi gli stivali = to put boots on oneself). The three idioms at the end are less commonly used but worth knowing for cultural understanding.

exampleSentences.italian: I tuoi stivali sono molto carini. Dove li hai comprati?
exampleSentences.english: Your boots are really nice. Where did you buy them?

exampleSentences.italian: Mettiti gli stivali – sta piovendo!
exampleSentences.english: Put on your boots – it's raining!

relatedExpressions.meaning: good for nothing, worthless, a poor excuse for something (old-fashioned expression)
to annoy someone, get on someone's nerves
the Italian peninsula (due to its boot-like shape)

grammarNotes: Pelo is a masculine noun taking the articles il/un (singular) and i/dei (plural). For hair on a person's head, use capello (single strand) or capelli (whole head of hair) instead. Pelo can refer to individual hairs or an entire animal's coat/fur.
learnerNotes: Remember to use capelli (plural) when talking about the hair on someone's head as a whole, not pelo. The word pelo has several figurative meanings (split second, surface) beyond its literal sense, especially in common idioms like 'per un pelo.' Related verbs include pelare (to peel/skin, or figuratively to rip off), spelare (to lose hair), and depilare (to remove body hair for beauty purposes).

exampleSentences.italian: I peli regolano la temperatura corporea.
exampleSentences.english: Hair regulates body temperature.

exampleSentences.italian: Oh no, ho un capello bianco!
exampleSentences.english: Oh no, I have a white hair!

exampleSentences.italian: Maria ha i capelli castani.
exampleSentences.english: Maria has brown hair.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo gatto ha un pelo molto morbido.
exampleSentences.english: This cat has very soft fur.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho perso l'autobus per un pelo.
exampleSentences.english: I just missed the bus.

relatedExpressions.meaning: almost / nearly / just / just in time
not harm a hair on someone's head

relatedExpressions.expression: Il lupo perde il pelo ma non il vizio
