englishTranslation: meanwhile / in the meantime / yet / but / anyway / for now
grammarNotes: Intanto is composed of the preposition 'in' and the adverb 'tanto' (originally written as two words in older Italian). It is invariable and does not conjugate. Its meaning varies significantly by context: temporal (meanwhile), contrastive (yet/but), or conclusive (anyway). It can be preceded by conjunctions like 'e' (and) or 'ma' (but) to enhance its function.
learnerNotes: Intanto is highly contextual—always consider the surrounding words and punctuation to determine which meaning applies. The expression 'E intanto io pago!' is a very common colloquial complaint structure worth remembering as a set phrase. Avoid 'per intanto' unless absolutely necessary; use 'per ora' instead for 'for now,' as it is more standard and preferred by Italian language authorities.

exampleSentences.italian: Scusa, devo finire una cosa velocemente. Tu intanto comincia ad andare, e ti raggiungo il prima possibile.
exampleSentences.english: Sorry, I have to finish something quickly. In the meantime, you get going, and I'll join you as soon as possible.

exampleSentences.italian: Intanto che la cena cuoce, prepariamo l'aperitivo.
exampleSentences.english: While the dinner is cooking, let's prepare the aperitif.

exampleSentences.italian: Hanno sempre sminuito il suo talento ma intanto lui si è costruito una bella carriera.
exampleSentences.english: They've always belittled his talent, yet he made a nice career for himself.

exampleSentences.italian: E intanto io pago!
exampleSentences.english: And yet I'm paying!

exampleSentences.italian: La qualità delle trasmissioni televisive è sempre peggio. E intanto io pago!
exampleSentences.english: The quality of TV programs is getting worse and worse. Talk about money wasted!

exampleSentences.italian: Intanto questo lavoro è concluso. Domani penseremo al prossimo.
exampleSentences.english: Anyway this job is done. We'll think about the next one tomorrow.

exampleSentences.italian: Dice di essere senza un soldo? Intanto si è appena comprato la macchina nuova.
exampleSentences.english: He's saying he has no money? For one thing, he just bought himself a new car.

exampleSentences.italian: Per intanto mettiti questa maglia. Te ne compro una più adatta nel pomeriggio.
exampleSentences.english: Put on this shirt for now. I'll buy you a more suitable one this afternoon.

relatedExpressions.meaning: and yet / and in the meantime (often used for expressing frustration)
for now (rare usage, not recommended by language authorities)

grammarNotes: Gratificante is invariable for gender but changes form in the plural. Singular forms (both masculine and feminine) use gratificante; plural forms use gratificanti. The adjective typically modifies nouns referring to jobs, activities, or relationships. It derives from the verb gratificare (to reward/to gratify/to compensate financially).
learnerNotes: Gratificante is commonly used in professional and personal contexts to describe jobs, hobbies, or relationships. Remember that while the feminine and masculine forms are identical in singular (un'attività gratificante vs. un lavoro gratificante), the plural distinguishes gender with gratificanti. Don't confuse it with soddisfatto (satisfied), which describes a person's feeling rather than the quality of an experience.

exampleSentences.italian: Finalmente ho trovato un lavoro gratificante che mi rende felice.
exampleSentences.english: I've finally found a rewarding job that makes me happy.

exampleSentences.italian: un lavoro gratificante
exampleSentences.english: a rewarding job (masculine, singular)

exampleSentences.italian: un'attività gratificante
exampleSentences.english: a rewarding activity (feminine, singular)

exampleSentences.italian: dei lavori gratificanti
exampleSentences.english: rewarding jobs (masculine, plural)

exampleSentences.italian: delle attività gratificanti
exampleSentences.english: rewarding activities (feminine, plural)

exampleSentences.italian: Lavorare per quell'azienda è poco gratificante, però almeno mi danno tanti giorni di ferie.
exampleSentences.english: It's not very rewarding working for that company, but at least they give me a lot of days off.

grammarNotes: Calzante is an invariable adjective ending in -e, having only two forms: singular calzante (for both masculine and feminine nouns) and plural calzanti. It agrees in number with the noun it modifies. The word derives from the verb calzare (to put on, to fit) and ultimately from Latin calceare (to put on shoes).
learnerNotes: Calzante has both literal and figurative uses; while it can describe footwear that fits well, it's more commonly used figuratively to mean 'suitable' or 'apt' when describing opinions, decisions, examples, descriptions, and responses. Note that calzante can also function as a noun meaning 'shoehorn,' making it a true dual-use word. The -e ending makes it invariable in gender but variable in number (calzante/calzanti).

exampleSentences.italian: una scarpa calzante
exampleSentences.english: a well-fitting shoe

exampleSentences.italian: delle scarpe calzanti
exampleSentences.english: well-fitting shoes

exampleSentences.italian: uno stivale calzante
exampleSentences.english: a well-fitting boot

exampleSentences.italian: degli stivali calzanti
exampleSentences.english: well-fitting boots

exampleSentences.italian: Queste scarpe sono perfettamente calzanti.
exampleSentences.english: These shoes fit perfectly.

exampleSentences.italian: È un paragone molto calzante.
exampleSentences.english: That's a very fitting comparison.

relatedExpressions.meaning: shoehorn (synonym of calzante when used as a noun)

grammarNotes: Imbranato is a regular adjective with four forms: imbranato (m.s.), imbranata (f.s.), imbranati (m.p.), imbranate (f.p.). It agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. The word can function as a noun (e.g., un imbranato = a clumsy person) and follows standard adjective placement patterns.
learnerNotes: Imbranato is distinctly colloquial, so avoid it in formal contexts. When used as a noun (e.g., è un imbranato), it's somewhat informal and can carry a slightly mocking or affectionate tone. Remember the four-form gender/number agreement pattern common to all Italian adjectives; the feminine noun form uses the apostrophe (un'imbranata) before a vowel.

exampleSentences.italian: Luigi è un tipo imbranato.
exampleSentences.english: Luigi is a clumsy guy.

exampleSentences.italian: Giovanni, invece, è molto sicuro di sé.
exampleSentences.english: Giovanni, on the other hand, is very confident.

exampleSentences.italian: Quella ragazza è proprio un'imbranata!
exampleSentences.english: That girl is a real klutz!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to get confused (uncommon verb derived from imbranato)

grammarNotes: Occhiolino is a masculine noun, the diminutive form of occhio (eye), literally meaning 'small eye.' It takes regular masculine articles: un occhiolino (a wink), l'occhiolino (the wink), degli occhiolini (some winks), gli occhiolini (the winks). The primary usage is in the expression 'fare l'occhiolino' (to wink).
learnerNotes: Occhiolino is the most common and casual way to express 'wink' in Italian. Don't confuse it with battito di ciglia (blink)—a wink is intentional and visible to the recipient, while a blink is involuntary. The expression 'fare l'occhiolino' can also mean 'to look longingly at' when directed at an object rather than a person, so context is important.

exampleSentences.italian: Le ho fatto l'occhiolino per farle capire che stavo dalla sua parte.
exampleSentences.english: I winked at her to let her know I was on her side.

exampleSentences.italian: Lucia sta facendo l'occhiolino alla borsa di Gucci.
exampleSentences.english: Lucia is looking longingly at the Gucci bag.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to wink; to look longingly at (something)
to wink (used when there is clear understanding between interlocutors)
to wink (literally: to squeeze the eye)
wink; rapid eyelid closure (also medical term for defense reflex)
to blink (literally: to beat the eyes)
to blink (literally: to bang the eyelids)

grammarNotes: Russare is a regular -are verb conjugated like parlare in the present tense. The infinitive form can be nominalized by adding the article 'il' (il russare = snoring). It follows standard -are verb patterns with no irregularities or stem changes.
learnerNotes: Russare entered Italian through Lombard, a Northern Italian dialect, reflecting how languages borrow words across regions. The gerund form (il russare) is commonly used to refer to the action of snoring as a noun. Note the distinction between russare (general snoring) and ronfare/ronfamento (loud, heavy snoring), which are more emphatic synonyms.

exampleSentences.italian: (io) russo
exampleSentences.english: I snore

exampleSentences.italian: (tu) russi
exampleSentences.english: you snore (singular, informal)

exampleSentences.italian: (lui) russa
exampleSentences.english: he snores

exampleSentences.italian: (lei) russa
exampleSentences.english: she snores

exampleSentences.italian: (Lei) russa
exampleSentences.english: you snore (singular, formal)

exampleSentences.italian: (noi) russiamo
exampleSentences.english: we snore

exampleSentences.italian: (voi) russate
exampleSentences.english: you snore (plural)

exampleSentences.italian: (loro) russano
exampleSentences.english: they snore

exampleSentences.italian: Smettila di russare! Mi impedisci di dormire.
exampleSentences.english: Stop snoring! You're stopping me from sleeping.

exampleSentences.italian: Il russare di suo marito la costringeva a dormire sul divano.
exampleSentences.english: Her husband's snoring forced her to sleep on the sofa.

grammarNotes: Gattonare is a regular -are verb, conjugated predictably in the present tense. The verb's meaning shifts contextually: with human babies it means 'to crawl,' while with predatory animals it means 'to stalk or crouch.' Its etymology derives from the noun gattoni (on all fours), which itself comes from gatto (cat).
learnerNotes: Gattonare is primarily used for babies crawling or animals stalking; do not use it for human stalking behavior, where perseguitare or fare stalking are correct. The expression gatton gattoni adds emphasis to stealthy movement and is commonly used with predatory animals. Remember the verb's dual meaning depends entirely on the subject—human infants versus animals—to avoid confusion.

exampleSentences.italian: Mia figlia ha cominciato a gattonare molto presto.
exampleSentences.english: My daughter started crawling very early.

exampleSentences.italian: Il leone si avvicinò gatton gattoni verso la sua preda.
exampleSentences.english: The lion crept stealthily toward its prey.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to move forward on all fours
stealthily creeping along the ground to avoid detection

grammarNotes: Aspirapolvere is an invariable masculine noun, meaning it does not change in the plural form. Use the masculine article 'il/l'/un' in singular and 'gli/degli' in plural. It is a compound word formed from the verb aspirare (to suck/inhale) and polvere (dust).
learnerNotes: Remember that aspirapolvere is invariable—don't add 'i' in the plural. The most common phrase is 'passare l'aspirapolvere' (to vacuum), where 'passare' literally means 'to pass.' Note the related but distinct term 'scopa elettrica' (electric broom) and 'battitappeto' (carpet sweeper) for other cleaning appliances.

exampleSentences.italian: Puoi mettere in carica l'aspirapolvere?
exampleSentences.english: Can you charge the vacuum cleaner?

exampleSentences.italian: Bisogna passarlo prima che arrivino gli ospiti.
exampleSentences.english: We have to vacuum before the guests arrive.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to vacuum (literally: to pass the vacuum)
to turn on the vacuum cleaner
to turn off the vacuum cleaner

englishTranslation: on all fours / on one's hands and knees
grammarNotes: Carponi is an invariable adverb used to describe a position or manner of movement. It is commonly paired with verbs of motion (camminare, avanzare, strisciare) and state (stare, essere). An archaic doubled form carpon carponi exists for emphatic effect. Alternative spellings include 'a carponi' with the preposition a.
learnerNotes: Carponi is always paired with a verb to show action or position; it never changes form. The word is probably derived from Latin carpere (to swipe, pilfer), though the etymology is not entirely clear. The colloquial synonym gattoni is equally common and may be more frequently used in everyday speech.

exampleSentences.italian: Per nascondersi dai paparazzi, l'attore ha camminato carponi fra le automobili.
exampleSentences.english: To hide from the paparazzi, the actor crawled on all fours amongst the cars.

exampleSentences.italian: camminare carponi
exampleSentences.english: to walk on all fours, to crawl

exampleSentences.italian: avanzare carponi
exampleSentences.english: to crawl on all fours

exampleSentences.italian: strisciare carponi
exampleSentences.english: to crawl on all fours

exampleSentences.italian: stare carponi
exampleSentences.english: to be on all fours

exampleSentences.italian: essere carponi
exampleSentences.english: to be on all fours

exampleSentences.italian: mettersi carponi
exampleSentences.english: to get down on all fours

relatedExpressions.meaning: on all fours (variant with preposition a)
on all fours (emphatic, archaic doubled form emphasizing prolonged duration or discomfort)
on all fours (synonym derived from gattonare, to crawl)
on four paws (literal: on four paws, especially used for animals)

grammarNotes: Siepe is a feminine noun (la siepe). The plural form is siepi. It derives from Latin saepes. The word can be used literally for hedges and shrubs, and figuratively for groups of people forming a physical barrier.
learnerNotes: Siepe has multiple meanings depending on context: primarily a literal hedge in gardening/landscaping contexts, but figuratively refers to a human barrier or line of people. In horse racing, siepe means a hurdle or fence, though ostacolo and barriera are also common terms. The expression fare siepe is now archaic and rarely encountered in modern Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Abita in una villa circondata da una siepe molto alta.
exampleSentences.english: She lives in a villa surrounded by a tall hedge.

exampleSentences.italian: Una siepe di poliziotti sbarrava la strada ai manifestanti.
exampleSentences.english: A line of policemen blocked the road so that the protesters could not pass.

englishTranslation: no less than / nothing less than / you don't say
grammarNotes: Nientepopodimeno is a compound adverb formed from niente (nothing) + po' po' (a little, little) + (di) meno (less). It is typically followed by the comparative conjunction che (than) when used to mean 'no less than.' The word can function as an emphatic adverb or, less commonly, as an exclamation expressing surprise.
learnerNotes: Nientepopodimeno is primarily used in colloquial, humorous contexts and became popularized by actor Mario Riva's television program in the late 1950s. While charming, it is less commonly used than its synonyms nientemeno or addirittura, making it more of a recognition word for learners. This word is best reserved for understanding Italian media and literature rather than active production at the A2-B1 level.

exampleSentences.italian: Il Signor Rossi ha nientepopodimeno che centodieci anni!
exampleSentences.english: Mr. Rossi is no less than one hundred and ten years old!

exampleSentences.italian: Ho fatto una scommessa e ho vinto un milione di euro! – Nientepopodimeno!
exampleSentences.english: I placed a bet and won a million euros! – You don't say!

englishTranslation: relief from the heat / coolness / relief / comfort
grammarNotes: Refrigerio is a masculine noun. The plural form is refrigeri. It follows regular masculine noun patterns: un refrigerio (singular), i refrigeri (plural); il refrigerio, dei refrigeri. The word is more common in written or literary contexts than in everyday speech.
learnerNotes: Refrigerio is predominantly used in formal, written, or literary contexts rather than everyday conversation. While it can literally mean physical cooling (e.g., from heat or sunburn), it frequently extends metaphorically to psychological comfort or relief from suffering. Be aware that English speakers often use 'relief' or 'coolness' separately, but refrigerio captures both the physical sensation and emotional comfort in a single word.

exampleSentences.italian: Abbiamo apprezzato la vista sul mare e il refrigerio della brezza marina.
exampleSentences.english: We enjoyed the sea view and the refreshing coolness of the marine breeze.

exampleSentences.italian: Finalmente arriva un po' di refrigerio dopo tanti giorni di caldo soffocante.
exampleSentences.english: Finally some relief is coming after many days of sweltering heat.

grammarNotes: Finocchio is a masculine noun with regular pluralization: un finocchio → dei finocchio, il finocchio → i finocchi. It takes standard masculine articles and adjective agreement. The word has multiple meanings: the primary culinary reference to the vegetable, and a vulgar slang term for a homosexual man.
learnerNotes: Be aware that finocchio has a vulgar slang meaning unrelated to the vegetable; context is essential to avoid offense or misunderstanding. The bulbous variety is preferred raw for better flavor, while both types work for cooking. Fennel seeds (semi di finocchio) are commonly used in Italian cuisine and herbal remedies, making this vocabulary useful for both culinary and health-related discussions.

exampleSentences.italian: Before moving to Italy, I was completely unfamiliar with the finocchio.
exampleSentences.english: Before moving to Italy, I was completely unfamiliar with fennel.

exampleSentences.italian: Qual è il modo migliore per tagliare i finocchi?
exampleSentences.english: What is the best way to cut fennel?

exampleSentences.italian: Mi faccio una tisana ai semi di finocchio. Ne vuoi una?
exampleSentences.english: I'm going to make myself a fennel seed herbal tea. Do you want one?

relatedExpressions.meaning: fennel gratin (braised fennel with cheese and breadcrumbs)
wild fennel (diminutive forms, mainly Lazio region)

grammarNotes: Mammone is masculine singular; feminine form is mammona. Plural forms: mammoni (masculine), mammone (feminine plural—note the confusing identical form). The word is formed from mamma (mom) + the augmentative suffix -one (big). When applied to children, it is affectionate; when applied to adults, it becomes distinctly pejorative.
learnerNotes: Mammone carries very different connotations depending on context and age: it's sweet and affectionate for children but becomes insulting when describing adults. Be aware that the feminine plural form mammone is identical to the masculine singular, which can cause confusion. This word is distinctly colloquial Italian and would not be used in formal writing.

exampleSentences.italian: Mio figlio è diventato un mammone.
exampleSentences.english: My son has become a mama's boy.

exampleSentences.italian: Massimo non è un mammone, a differenza di suo fratellino Simone.
exampleSentences.english: Massimo isn't a mama's boy unlike his younger brother Simone.

exampleSentences.italian: Mario è un mammone buono a nulla!
exampleSentences.english: Mario is a good-for-nothing mummy's boy!

relatedExpressions.meaning: a fantasy creature from Italian fairytales used to scare children
mammon (biblical term for material wealth viewed as an evil influence)

grammarNotes: Carciofo is a masculine noun. The plural form is carciofi. It takes the definite article il (singular) / i (plural) and indefinite article un (singular) / dei (plural). The word derives from Arabic kharshuf rather than Latin, making it an exception among Italian vocabulary.
learnerNotes: Note that carciofo has an Arabic origin (kharshuf), not Latin, making it a loanword. The figurative meaning—calling someone 'un carciofo' as an insult—refers to a foolish or dull person, so avoid using it literally in conversational contexts without care. The idioms 'mangiare il carciofo' and 'fare la politica del carciofo' require cultural context to understand fully; they're not commonly used in everyday speech but appear in historical or political discussions.

exampleSentences.italian: Per pranzo, ho preparato i carciofi ripieni.
exampleSentences.english: I made stuffed artichokes for lunch.

exampleSentences.italian: il carciofo
exampleSentences.english: the artichoke (singular)

exampleSentences.italian: un carciofo
exampleSentences.english: an artichoke

exampleSentences.italian: i carciofi
exampleSentences.english: the artichokes (plural)

exampleSentences.italian: dei carciofi
exampleSentences.english: some artichokes

exampleSentences.italian: Tuo fratello è un carciofo! Ne combina sempre una!
exampleSentences.english: Your brother is an idiot. He's always getting into trouble!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to do something bit by bit; to take a long time to accomplish something
to expand territory or take possession of something little by little

grammarNotes: Perdente is a noun that is both masculine and feminine; gender is determined by the article (un/il perdente vs. una/la perdente). The plural for both genders is perdenti. It can also function as an adjective meaning 'losing,' maintaining gender and number agreement with the noun it modifies.
learnerNotes: Perdente refers to both a person who loses competitions and someone unsuccessful in life generally. The adjective form (losing) agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies. Be careful not to confuse sfigato (more colloquial, means both loser and unlucky) with perdente; fallito is even more offensive and should be used cautiously.

exampleSentences.italian: Il perdente ha richiesto una rivincita.
exampleSentences.english: The loser requested a rematch.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi dispiace dirtelo, ma sei e sarai sempre un perdente!
exampleSentences.english: I'm sorry to tell you this, but you are and always will be a loser!

exampleSentences.italian: Il numero perdente
exampleSentences.english: The losing number

exampleSentences.italian: La carta perdente
exampleSentences.english: The losing card

exampleSentences.italian: La squadra perdente è uscita dal campo sotto i fischi del pubblico.
exampleSentences.english: The losing team walked off the field to the boos of the spectators.

relatedExpressions.meaning: someone who generally loses in life; unlucky person (more colloquial)
unsuccessful or failed person (more offensive than sfigato)

grammarNotes: Grossomodo is an invariable adverb composed of two elements: grosso (large) and modo (way/manner). It can be written as one word (grossomodo) or two words (grosso modo). As an adverb, it does not change form and is used to modify verbs or entire clauses to indicate approximation or estimation.
learnerNotes: Grossomodo is a useful adverb for expressing approximations in casual and neutral contexts. Both spellings (one word and two words) are correct, though grossomodo as one word is increasingly common in modern Italian. Be aware that similar adverbs like 'circa' and 'più o meno' are equally common alternatives—choose based on context and formality level.

exampleSentences.italian: Siamo grossomodo a metà strada.
exampleSentences.english: We're approximately halfway there.

exampleSentences.italian: Grossomodo ci saranno quaranta persone questa sera.
exampleSentences.english: There will be more or less forty people this evening.

relatedExpressions.meaning: roughly, more or less (literally: up by down)
more or less (literally: at eye and cross)

grammarNotes: Zerbino is a masculine noun with plural zerbini. All masculine nouns beginning with 'z' take the articles lo (singular definite), uno (singular indefinite), gli (plural definite), and degli (plural indefinite). This article-noun combination is essential for proper Italian usage with z-words.
learnerNotes: Remember that zerbino has a figurative meaning referring to a submissive person who allows themselves to be dominated—this is common in casual speech. Be aware that zerbinotto (the diminutive) specifically denotes a vain, ostentatiously dressed person lacking good taste, quite different from the literal doormat meaning. The z-article pattern (lo, uno, gli, degli) applies to all nouns starting with 'z' or 's' followed by a consonant, so practice this with other z-words.

exampleSentences.italian: lo zerbino
exampleSentences.english: the doormat

exampleSentences.italian: uno zerbino
exampleSentences.english: a doormat

exampleSentences.italian: gli zerbini
exampleSentences.english: the doormats

exampleSentences.italian: degli zerbini
exampleSentences.english: (some) doormats

exampleSentences.italian: Chiedo sempre a tutti di pulire le scarpe sullo zerbino prima di entrare in casa.
exampleSentences.english: I always ask everyone to wipe their shoes on the doormat before entering the house.

exampleSentences.italian: Ti fai trattare come uno zerbino dal tuo capo.
exampleSentences.english: You get treated like a doormat by your boss.

relatedExpressions.meaning: a young dandy or fop; a well-dressed but ostentatious person lacking elegance (diminutive form)
to treat someone like a doormat; to dominate or exploit someone

grammarNotes: Tormentone is a masculine noun; plural form is tormentoni. It derives from the verb tormentare (to torment), reflecting how these repetitive expressions irritate people. Use articles: il tormentone, i tormentoni. Gender agreement applies to adjectives modifying it.
learnerNotes: Tormentone is distinctly colloquial Italian and commonly used in media discussions. It can refer to catchy songs, overused catchphrases, or viral internet content (memes). The word humorously implies that these repeated expressions 'torment' people with their ubiquity—useful context for understanding Italian pop culture references.

exampleSentences.italian: Ma no, di nuovo quel tormentone!? Lo passano in radio ogni cinque minuti!
exampleSentences.english: Oh no, that irritating hit song again?! They play it every five minutes on the radio.

grammarNotes: Dare is a highly irregular -ARE verb despite its appearance. In the present tense, note the accent on dà (lui/lei) but not do (io). It forms the passato prossimo with avere (ho dato) and the imperfetto regularly (davo). Dare extends beyond literal 'giving' to mean 'to cause' in many idiomatic expressions.
learnerNotes: While dare is often a direct equivalent of 'to give,' Italians strongly prefer regalare when discussing gifts, even though dare is grammatically correct. Remember the irregular present tense conjugations, especially the accented dà for third person singular. Dare also functions as 'to cause' in many common expressions (dare fastidio, dare problemi), which may not be immediately obvious to English speakers.

exampleSentences.italian: Gli ho dato una matita.
exampleSentences.english: I gave him a pencil.

exampleSentences.italian: Dammi un attimo per pensare!
exampleSentences.english: Give me a moment to think!

exampleSentences.italian: Diamo da mangiare a questo cane affamato.
exampleSentences.english: Let's give this starving dog something to eat.

exampleSentences.italian: dare una penna a qualcuno
exampleSentences.english: to give someone a pen (hand over)

exampleSentences.italian: dare un regalo
exampleSentences.english: to give a present

exampleSentences.italian: dare una buona notizia
exampleSentences.english: to give good news (communicate)

exampleSentences.italian: dare gli antibiotici a qualcuno
exampleSentences.english: to give someone antibiotics (prescribe)

exampleSentences.italian: dare un premio
exampleSentences.english: to give a prize (award)

exampleSentences.italian: dare indicazioni
exampleSentences.english: to give directions (indicate)

exampleSentences.italian: dare il permesso
exampleSentences.english: to give permission (grant)

relatedExpressions.meaning: to give someone something to eat
to give the thief five years (in prison)

englishTranslation: country house / brothel / confusion / mess / racket
grammarNotes: Casino is a masculine noun derived from casa (house) + diminutive suffix -ino, literally meaning 'little house.' It is invariable in form but has evolved to encompass multiple distinct meanings depending on context. The related adjective incasinato (messy/chaotic) agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies.
learnerNotes: Casino is a false cognate with English 'casino' (gambling establishment)—avoid this confusion! The word carries vulgar/colloquial register and evolved from its historical meaning as a brothel (still considered parolaccia in formal speech). In modern everyday Italian, it's primarily used to mean 'mess' or 'chaos,' making it essential slang for intermediate learners. Note that incasinato is the derived adjective form commonly used to describe someone who is overwhelmed or disorganized.

exampleSentences.italian: Che casino!
exampleSentences.english: What a mess! / What a disaster!

exampleSentences.italian: Che casino per arrivare qui, c'era un incidente in tangenziale.
exampleSentences.english: Getting here was such a nightmare, there was an accident on the ring road.

exampleSentences.italian: Non sento quello che dici, c'è troppo casino qui dentro!
exampleSentences.english: I can't hear what you're saying, it's way too loud in here!

exampleSentences.italian: I vicini hanno fatto casino tutta la notte.
exampleSentences.english: The neighbours made a racket all night.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono troppo incasinato in questi giorni, non posso uscire.
exampleSentences.english: I'm way too swamped these days, I can't go out.

relatedExpressions.meaning: What a mess! / What a disaster!
It's (too) noisy / There's (too) much going on
To make a racket / To cause confusion
To screw up / To cause a problem

englishTranslation: so-so / in short / basically / for goodness sake / come on / so?
grammarNotes: Insomma is an invariable adverb derived from in (in) + somma (sum). It does not conjugate or agree with any noun. Its meaning is highly context-dependent and relies heavily on tone of voice, intonation, and accompanying gestures (such as the hand-swinging gesture) to convey the intended meaning.
learnerNotes: Insomma is a versatile word that learners often find challenging because its meaning depends almost entirely on context, tone, and body language rather than grammatical structure. Pay close attention to how native speakers deliver it—the hand gesture (swinging hand side-to-side) is particularly important for the 'so-so' meaning. Be cautious not to overuse it; while extremely common in speech, it sounds very colloquial and shouldn't appear frequently in formal writing.

exampleSentences.italian: Ti è piaciuto il libro?
exampleSentences.english: Did you like the book?

exampleSentences.italian: Insomma… il finale è stato un po' una delusione.
exampleSentences.english: So-so… the ending was kind of a letdown.

exampleSentences.italian: Ti è piaciuta la bistecca?
exampleSentences.english: Did you like the steak?

exampleSentences.italian: Insomma… si sente che la carne è buona, ma l'hanno cotta un po' troppo
exampleSentences.english: So-so… you can tell the meat is good quality, but they overcooked it a bit

exampleSentences.italian: Ehi, come va?
exampleSentences.english: Hey, how's it going?

exampleSentences.italian: Insomma… potrebbe sempre andare meglio!
exampleSentences.english: So-so… it could always be better!

exampleSentences.italian: Com'è andata ieri sera con Cristina?
exampleSentences.english: How was last night with Cristina?

exampleSentences.italian: Davvero bene! Lei è gentile, simpatica, bellissima… insomma, è perfetta!
exampleSentences.english: Really great! She's kind, funny, beautiful… basically, she's perfect!

exampleSentences.italian: Insomma! Fate un po' di silenzio per favore, non si sente niente!
exampleSentences.english: For goodness' sake! Please be quiet, we can't hear a thing!

exampleSentences.italian: Ma insomma, smettetela di lamentarvi sempre per ogni cosa!
exampleSentences.english: Oh come on, stop complaining about every little thing!

exampleSentences.italian: Insomma, mi dite dove stiamo andando?
exampleSentences.english: Come on, will you tell me where we're going?

exampleSentences.italian: Insomma? Mi vuoi rispondere o no?
exampleSentences.english: So? Are you going to answer me or not?

exampleSentences.italian: E poi? Vi siete baciati o no?
exampleSentences.english: And then? Did you kiss or not?

relatedExpressions.meaning: oh come on / for goodness sake (emphatic version)
well / so / used when pushing for an answer or building suspense
How are you? So-so… (typical Italian response)

grammarNotes: Permesso is a masculine noun derived from the past participle of permettere (to allow). Plural form is permessi. Uses articles: il permesso / un permesso / i permessi / dei permessi. The word has three distinct uses: (1) as a noun meaning permission/authorization, (2) as an interjection to excuse oneself when passing through crowds, and (3) as an interjection when asking to enter a space.
learnerNotes: Don't confuse permesso (noun/interjection meaning permission or excuse me) with the verb form potere (can/to be able to). When asking permission to do something, use potere (Posso uscire?) not permesso. The interjection 'permesso!' is essential for navigating crowded public spaces in Italy—use it when squeezing past people on buses or in cafés. Register matters: plain 'permesso!' works in casual situations, but add 'con permesso,' 'mi scusi,' or 'scusate' for more formal contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Abbiamo chiesto i permessi al comune per iniziare i lavori di ristrutturazione.
exampleSentences.english: We asked the municipality for the permits to start the renovation work.

exampleSentences.italian: I professori non ci danno il permesso di usare il cellulare in classe.
exampleSentences.english: The teachers don't allow us to use our phones in class.

exampleSentences.italian: Le autorità hanno negato il permesso per la manifestazione.
exampleSentences.english: The authorities denied permission for the demonstration.

exampleSentences.italian: Permesso!
exampleSentences.english: Excuse me!

exampleSentences.italian: Permesso, posso passare?
exampleSentences.english: Excuse me, may I pass?

exampleSentences.italian: Permesso, mi fa passare per favore?
exampleSentences.english: Excuse me, could you please let me through?

exampleSentences.italian: Permesso, scusate, devo solo raggiungere il mio tavolo laggiù in fondo.
exampleSentences.english: Excuse me, sorry, I just need to get through to reach my table there at the back.

exampleSentences.italian: Con permesso, devo raggiungere il mio collega per la presentazione.
exampleSentences.english: Excuse me, I need to join my colleague for the presentation.

grammarNotes: Posto is a masculine noun with plural posti. Definite articles: il posto (the place), i posti (the places). Indefinite articles: un posto (a place), dei posti (some places). The word has diminutive (posticino) and pejorative (postaccio) forms that modify the connotation of the place being described.
learnerNotes: Posto is highly versatile and context-dependent; its meaning shifts from 'place' to 'seat' to 'job' depending on the situation. The diminutive posticino softens requests politely, while postaccio expresses disapproval of a location. Pay attention to prepositions: 'in un posto' (in a place), 'nel posto' (in the seat), 'sul posto' (on the spot).

exampleSentences.italian: Ieri siamo stati in un posto meraviglioso appena fuori Roma
exampleSentences.english: Yesterday we visited a wonderful place just outside Rome.

exampleSentences.italian: Questo posto non è adatto ai bambini, è pericoloso!
exampleSentences.english: This place is not suitable for children, it's dangerous!

exampleSentences.italian: Avete posto in macchina per un'altra persona?
exampleSentences.english: Do you have room in the car for one more person?

exampleSentences.italian: Non c'è posto per altri nel mio cuore, solo per te!
exampleSentences.english: There's no room in my heart for anyone else, only for you!

exampleSentences.italian: Riesci a farmi un posticino nella tua valigia? Non so dove mettere i libri che ho preso ieri.
exampleSentences.english: Can you make a little space for me in your suitcase? I don't know where to put the books I bought yesterday.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi scusi, c'è qualche posto in cui bere qualcosa qui vicino?
exampleSentences.english: Excuse me, is there a place nearby where I can get something to drink?

exampleSentences.italian: Stasera ti porto a mangiare in un posticino che fa una pizza strepitosa!
exampleSentences.english: Tonight I'm taking you to a cute place that makes amazing pizza!

exampleSentences.italian: Ieri sera siamo finiti in un postaccio dove servivano cibo immangiabile.
exampleSentences.english: Last night we ended up in a terrible place where they served inedible food.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho prenotato due posti in prima classe sul treno delle 11:45.
exampleSentences.english: I booked two first-class seats on the 11:45 a.m. train.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel secchione di Stefano si mette sempre nei posti davanti per fare bella figura con gli insegnanti.
exampleSentences.english: That nerd Stefano always sits in the front to impress the teachers.

exampleSentences.italian: Qual è il mio posto?
exampleSentences.english: Which seat is mine?

relatedExpressions.meaning: a designated spot for a car
bed space – a place to sleep, often in hostels
a little space (diminutive, used to soften requests)

englishTranslation: to take / to pick up / to catch / to order
grammarNotes: Prendere is mostly regular but has irregular past tense forms (passato remoto: presi, prese, presero). It uses auxiliary avere in most tenses (ho preso), but requires essere in reflexive constructions with gender/number agreement (mi sono preso/a una pausa). Note the stem change in passato remoto and other irregular forms.
learnerNotes: Prendere is extremely versatile in Italian and appears in many everyday contexts far beyond its literal 'to take' meaning. Pay special attention to the reflexive form prendersi (requiring essere auxiliary) versus the standard form. When ordering food/drinks, use prendere instead of English 'have'—this is a common false cognate pattern for learners.

exampleSentences.italian: Devo andare a prendere la macchina dal meccanico.
exampleSentences.english: I have to go pick up the car from the mechanic.

exampleSentences.italian: Possiamo prendere la vecchia macchina da scrivere di papà?
exampleSentences.english: Can we take Dad's old typewriter?

exampleSentences.italian: Prendo il treno per tornare a casa.
exampleSentences.english: I'm taking the train to go back home.

exampleSentences.italian: Domani prendiamo un volo per Shanghai.
exampleSentences.english: Tomorrow we're flying to Shanghai.

exampleSentences.italian: Stanno andando a prendere l'autobus.
exampleSentences.english: They're going to take the bus.

exampleSentences.italian: Potete prendere la metro per arrivare in aeroporto.
exampleSentences.english: You can take the metro to get to the airport.

exampleSentences.italian: Hanno preso la macchina per tornare in Sicilia.
exampleSentences.english: They drove back to Sicily.

exampleSentences.italian: Devo andare a prendere Andrea in palestra.
exampleSentences.english: I need to go pick up Andrea at the gym.

exampleSentences.italian: Passo a prenderti alle 7!
exampleSentences.english: I'll pick you up at 7!

exampleSentences.italian: Puoi venire a prendermi a scuola?
exampleSentences.english: Can you come pick me up from school?

exampleSentences.italian: Prendo una pizza capricciosa.
exampleSentences.english: I'll have a capricciosa pizza.

exampleSentences.italian: Prendiamo anche delle patatine fritte.
exampleSentences.english: We'll also have some fries.

exampleSentences.italian: Mia figlia prende la pasta al pomodoro.
exampleSentences.english: My daughter will have pasta with tomato sauce.

exampleSentences.italian: Tu cosa prendi come antipasto?
exampleSentences.english: What are you having for a starter?

exampleSentences.italian: Cosa prendete da bere?
exampleSentences.english: What are you having to drink?

relatedExpressions.meaning: to pick someone up (on the way)

grammarNotes: Memoria is a feminine noun with plural form memorie. It uses the definite articles la/le and indefinite articles una/delle. The word is a cognate with English 'memory,' making it easy to recognize, though Italian usage includes several idiomatic expressions unique to the language.
learnerNotes: Although memoria closely resembles the English 'memory,' Italian has many rich idiomatic expressions around this word that don't translate literally (e.g., 'memoria di un elefante,' 'scolpire nella memoria'). Pay attention to the gender (feminine) when using articles and adjectives. The phrase 'a memoria' (by heart) is distinct from 'memoria' alone and is commonly used in educational contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Greta ha una memoria fotografica incredibile, ricorda ogni dettaglio!
exampleSentences.english: Greta has an incredible photographic memory, she remembers every single detail!

exampleSentences.italian: Anche se studio poco, ho buona memoria e riesco a ricordare le informazioni importanti.
exampleSentences.english: Although I don't study much, I've got a good memory and can remember the important stuff.

exampleSentences.italian: Possibile che dimentichi sempre dove metti le cose? Non hai proprio memoria!
exampleSentences.english: Do you seriously forget where you put things every single time? You've got no memory at all!

exampleSentences.italian: Mia nonna ha la memoria di un elefante; ricorda ancora tutti i dettagli della sua infanzia.
exampleSentences.english: My grandma has got an elephant's memory; she still remembers every detail from when she was a kid.

exampleSentences.italian: Dopo l'incidente, Marco ha perso la memoria per qualche ora.
exampleSentences.english: After the accident, Marco lost his memory for a few hours.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho trovato il signor Carlo in piazza: era spaesato, ma lentamente ha riacquistato la memoria.
exampleSentences.english: I found Mr. Carlo in the square: he was disoriented, but slowly regained his memory.

exampleSentences.italian: Sicuro di non sapere che giorno è oggi? Devo rinfrescarti la memoria?
exampleSentences.english: Are you sure you don't know what day it is today? Do I need to refresh your memory?

exampleSentences.italian: Il ricordo di quel terribile giorno è ancora scolpito nella memoria dell'intera comunità.
exampleSentences.english: The memory of that terrible day is still etched into the memory of the whole community.

exampleSentences.italian: Ogni volta che guardo questa foto, torno con la memoria a quella splendida estate!
exampleSentences.english: Whenever I see this photo, I think back to that wonderful summer!

exampleSentences.italian: Se la memoria non mi inganna, la vecchia casa dei nonni dovrebbe essere qui.
exampleSentences.english: If memory serves, my grandparents' old house should be around here.

exampleSentences.italian: A memoria d'uomo, non c'è mai stato un inverno così freddo qui.
exampleSentences.english: In living memory, there's never been a winter this cold here.

exampleSentences.italian: Come cavolo si chiamava quel posto dove andavamo sempre d'estate? Aiutami, ho un vuoto di memoria!
exampleSentences.english: What the heck was the name of that place we always went to in the summer? Help me, I'm having a memory lapse!

exampleSentences.italian: Ti ricordi ancora tutti i nomi dei tuoi compagni di classe delle elementari? Però, che memoria!
exampleSentences.english: You still remember all the names of your classmates from elementary school? Wow, what a memory!

relatedExpressions.expression: Avere la memoria di un elefante
relatedExpressions.meaning: To have great memory (literally: to have the memory of an elephant)
To think back to (literally: to return with the memory to)

relatedExpressions.expression: Se la memoria non mi inganna
relatedExpressions.meaning: If memory serves (literally: if memory doesn't deceive me)
In living memory (literally: at man's memory)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural passi. Takes definite articles il/i and indefinite articles un/dei. The word has multiple meanings depending on context: physical steps, figurative moves/progress, pace/rhythm, and geographical mountain passes. Gender agreement applies to adjectives modifying passo.
learnerNotes: Passo is a highly versatile noun with four main meanings: literal steps, figurative moves/progress, pace, and mountain passes. Pay attention to context to determine which meaning applies. Many common idioms use passo with prepositional phrases (a passo spedito, di buon passo) to describe manner of movement, so learn these expressions as fixed patterns. Note that 'passo falso' (wrong move) and 'passo avanti' (step forward) are common figurative uses in business and personal contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai sentito anche tu dei passi dietro la porta?
exampleSentences.english: Did you hear footsteps behind the door, too?

exampleSentences.italian: Il signore del piano di sopra ha il passo davvero pesante; ogni volta che si sposta si sente tutto!
exampleSentences.english: The gentleman above us walks so heavily; every time he moves, you can hear everything!

exampleSentences.italian: Hai proprio un passo felpato, mi hai spaventato!
exampleSentences.english: What a quiet step you have, you startled me!

exampleSentences.italian: Stefania ha incantato tutti con i suoi passi di danza.
exampleSentences.english: Stefania amazed everyone with her dance moves.

exampleSentences.italian: Andrea ha iniziato a muovere i primi passi intorno ai 12 mesi.
exampleSentences.english: Andrea started taking his first steps at around 12 months old.

exampleSentences.italian: Finalmente si è deciso a fare il primo passo e mi ha chiesto di uscire!
exampleSentences.english: At last, he made the first move and asked me out!

exampleSentences.italian: In questo momento non possiamo permetterci passi falsi sul lavoro
exampleSentences.english: Right now, we can't afford to make any wrong moves at work.

exampleSentences.italian: Con questo nuovo farmaco, la ricerca medica ha fatto un grande passo avanti.
exampleSentences.english: With this new drug, medical research has taken a big step forward.

exampleSentences.italian: Dopo aver completato questa fase del progetto, dobbiamo decidere i passi successivi.
exampleSentences.english: After finishing this phase of the project, we need to decide on the next steps.

exampleSentences.italian: Dai, dobbiamo camminare a passo spedito se vogliamo arrivare in tempo!
exampleSentences.english: Come on, we need to walk briskly if we want to get there on time!

exampleSentences.italian: I ragazzi sono bloccati in autostrada, stanno andando a passo d'uomo per il traffico.
exampleSentences.english: The guys are stuck on the highway, moving super slowly because of the traffic.

exampleSentences.italian: I lavori di ristrutturazione procedono a passo di lumaca. Chissà quando finiranno!
exampleSentences.english: The renovations are moving at a snail's pace. Who knows when they'll be done!

exampleSentences.italian: Il nuovo direttore ha portato un cambio di passo nella gestione del museo.
exampleSentences.english: The new director has brought a change of pace to the way the museum is managed.

exampleSentences.italian: Il gruppo sta procedendo di buon passo verso la prima tappa della giornata.
exampleSentences.english: The group is moving at a good pace toward the first stop of the day.

exampleSentences.italian: Dobbiamo accelerare il passo se vogliamo arrivare al rifugio prima che faccia buio.
exampleSentences.english: We need to speed up the pace if we want to get to the hut before it gets dark.

exampleSentences.italian: La crescita del turismo culturale va di pari passo con la valorizzazione dei siti storici.
exampleSentences.english: The growth of cultural tourism goes hand in hand with the promotion of historical sites.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to have a quiet step, to walk on tiptoes
to take the first steps (literally or figuratively)

grammarNotes: Spesa is a feminine noun (la spesa). The plural form is le spese. It takes the definite articles la/le and indefinite articles una/delle. The word is versatile, shifting meaning based on context: the activity of shopping, the items purchased, or abstract spending.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'fare la spesa' specifically means grocery shopping at a supermarket, while 'fare spese' refers to any general shopping (clothes, shoes, etc.). The word spesa shifts meaning dramatically based on context: it can be the activity, the items themselves, or abstract financial spending. Be careful not to confuse it with 'shopping' in English, which is broader and doesn't always translate to spesa.

exampleSentences.italian: Devo fare la spesa per la cena di domani.
exampleSentences.english: I need to do the grocery shopping for tomorrow's dinner.

exampleSentences.italian: Chi va a fare la spesa con la nonna domani?
exampleSentences.english: Who's going grocery shopping with grandma tomorrow?

exampleSentences.italian: Questa spesa è appena sufficiente per il fine settimana.
exampleSentences.english: These groceries are just enough for the weekend.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho dimenticato le borse della spesa in macchina, vai a prenderle per favore.
exampleSentences.english: I forgot the shopping bags in the car, go get them please.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai per caso un gettone per il carrello della spesa?
exampleSentences.english: Do you happen to have a token for the shopping cart?

exampleSentences.italian: Prima di andare al supermercato, facciamo sempre la lista della spesa.
exampleSentences.english: Before going to the supermarket, we always prepare a grocery list.

exampleSentences.italian: Preferisco fare la spesa online, così risparmio tempo.
exampleSentences.english: I prefer to do my groceries online so I save time.

exampleSentences.italian: Ogni mese il sindaco mette a disposizione dei buoni spesa per le famiglie in difficoltà.
exampleSentences.english: Every month, the mayor gives out food stamps to families who are struggling.

exampleSentences.italian: Ragazzi, mi aiutate a scaricare la spesa dalla macchina?
exampleSentences.english: Guys, can you help me unload the groceries from the car?

exampleSentences.italian: Non ho voglia di sistemare la spesa, ci pensi tu?
exampleSentences.english: I don't feel like putting away the groceries, can you do it?

exampleSentences.italian: Oggi pomeriggio esco a fare spese con mia mamma.
exampleSentences.english: This afternoon I'm going shopping with my mum.

exampleSentences.italian: Durante i saldi abbiamo fatto spese pazze!
exampleSentences.english: We went on a shopping spree during the sales!

exampleSentences.italian: Questa spesa non ci voleva proprio!
exampleSentences.english: We really didn't need this expense!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to go on a shopping spree

englishTranslation: cooked / exhausted / in love / baked ham / terracotta
grammarNotes: Cotto is the past participle of cuocere (to cook). As an adjective, it agrees in gender and number: cotto (m.sg.), cotta (f.sg.), cotti (m.pl.), cotte (f.pl.). When used as a noun meaning 'crush' or 'baked ham', it follows standard noun rules. The feminine noun cotta (crush) is commonly used in the expression 'avere una cotta per qualcuno'.
learnerNotes: Cotto is highly polysemous; context is essential to understand which meaning applies. When exhausted, cotto is very colloquial and carries a slightly dramatic tone—use it casually with friends. Note the distinction between the adjective cotto (smitten) and the noun cotta (crush): 'Sono cotto di lei' vs. 'Ho una cotta per lei' both work, but the nuance differs slightly. In grocery shopping, cotto alone refers to prosciutto cotto by ellipsis.

exampleSentences.italian: La bistecca è ben cotta, come piace a te!
exampleSentences.english: The steak is well cooked, just the way you like it!

exampleSentences.italian: Le patate sono state cotte sulla brace.
exampleSentences.english: The potatoes were cooked on the grill.

exampleSentences.italian: Siamo cotti, abbiamo lavorato tutto il giorno nell'orto.
exampleSentences.english: We are wiped out, we've been working in the vegetable garden all day.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono ancora cotto dopo il trekking di ieri, è stato davvero tosto!
exampleSentences.english: I'm still exhausted after yesterday's hike, it was seriously tough!

exampleSentences.italian: Stefano è cotto della sua compagna di classe.
exampleSentences.english: Stefano is completely smitten with his classmate.

exampleSentences.italian: Ammettilo, sei innamorato cotto!
exampleSentences.english: Admit it, you're totally head over heels!

exampleSentences.italian: Tua figlia è stata la prima cotta di Simone.
exampleSentences.english: Your daughter was Simone's first crush.

exampleSentences.italian: Al liceo avevo una cotta pazzesca per Marco, il mio compagno di banco.
exampleSentences.english: Back in high school, I had a huge crush on Marco, my desk mate.

exampleSentences.italian: Quando vai al supermercato, ricordati di prendere anche un etto di cotto.
exampleSentences.english: When you go to the supermarket, remember to grab 100 grams of ham too.

exampleSentences.italian: Come lo vuoi il panino? Con il crudo o con il cotto?
exampleSentences.english: How do you want your sandwich? With cured ham or with cooked ham?

exampleSentences.italian: La casa che abbiamo acquistato ha dei bellissimi pavimenti in cotto antico.
exampleSentences.english: The house we bought have beautiful antique terracotta floors.

relatedExpressions.meaning: overcooked; also a beef stew dish
sweet, thick grape syrup made by slowly cooking grape must
to have a crush on someone

grammarNotes: Feminine noun with plural form 'notizie'. Unlike English where 'news' is uncountable, Italian 'notizia' is countable: singular (la notizia) = one piece of news, plural (le notizie) = multiple updates or 'the news' in general. Indefinite articles: una notizia / delle notizie.
learnerNotes: Remember that 'notizia' is countable in Italian, unlike 'news' in English—you can say 'una notizia' (one piece of news) or 'tre notizie' (three pieces of news). Common adjectives like bella/brutta, vera/falsa, and inaspettata are frequently paired with notizia to describe the type of news. Be aware that 'sul pezzo' is an idiomatic expression meaning 'on top of things' or 'in the know.'

exampleSentences.italian: La notizia della vittoria della loro squadra ha fatto il giro del mondo.
exampleSentences.english: The news of their team's victory spread around the world.

exampleSentences.italian: Durante il telegiornale hanno dedicato un'ampia sezione alle ultime notizie dal fronte di guerra.
exampleSentences.english: During the news broadcast, they devoted a large segment to the latest updates from the war front.

exampleSentences.italian: La giornalista ha diffuso la notizia dell'arrivo di un super ospite all'evento.
exampleSentences.english: The journalist spread news of a special guest arriving at the event.

exampleSentences.italian: Il sito del museo ha pubblicato una notizia sulle nuove mostre in programma.
exampleSentences.english: The museum's website posted news about the upcoming exhibitions.

exampleSentences.italian: La comunità ha appreso con gioia la notizia dell'apertura di una nuova biblioteca.
exampleSentences.english: The community was delighted to hear the news of a new library opening.

exampleSentences.italian: I giornali locali hanno riportato la notizia della scomparsa del famoso scrittore.
exampleSentences.english: The local newspapers reported the news of the disappearance of the famous writer.

exampleSentences.italian: Il ministro ha confermato la notizia riguardante le nuove misure economiche.
exampleSentences.english: The minister confirmed the news about the new economic measures.

exampleSentences.italian: I medici hanno subito smentito la notizia secondo cui il farmaco fosse pericoloso.
exampleSentences.english: The doctors were quick to deny the news about the drug being dangerous.

exampleSentences.italian: Alcuni collaboratori hanno fatto trapelare la notizia prima dell'annuncio ufficiale.
exampleSentences.english: Some collaborators leaked the news before the official announcement.

exampleSentences.italian: Stanno facendo circolare notizie false per screditare il candidato.
exampleSentences.english: They're spreading false stories to discredit the candidate.

exampleSentences.italian: Il nuovo film del regista spagnolo sta facendo notizia per i temi trattati.
exampleSentences.english: The new movie by the Spanish director is making headlines for the topics it addresses.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to be actively looking for stories

grammarNotes: Danno as a noun is masculine: il danno (singular), i danni (plural). The context and article determine whether danno is a noun or the third-person plural present tense verb form of 'dare' (to give). In legal and medical contexts, danno takes specific adjective modifiers that denote the type of damage.
learnerNotes: Danno is a high-value word in legal and medical Italian. Pay close attention to distinguishing the noun (il danno, i danni) from the verb danno (third-person plural of 'dare'—they give). In legal contexts, 'risarcire i danni' and 'chiedere i danni' are essential expressions for any discussion involving compensation or liability.

exampleSentences.italian: Il danno all'antenna è stato causato da un fulmine.
exampleSentences.english: The damage to the antenna was caused by lightning.

exampleSentences.italian: L'incendio di ieri ha causato danni ingenti alle case vicino al parco.
exampleSentences.english: Yesterday's fire caused major damage to the houses near the park.

exampleSentences.italian: La caduta del ramo ha procurato danni alla recinzione del vicino.
exampleSentences.english: The fall of the branch caused damage to the neighbour's fence.

exampleSentences.italian: Certi prodotti possono arrecare danni all'ambiente.
exampleSentences.english: Certain products can harm the environment.

exampleSentences.italian: L'azienda ha subito un danno reputazionale non indifferente.
exampleSentences.english: The company suffered significant reputation damage.

exampleSentences.italian: Il lavoro è stato fatto male e adesso ho perdite in tutta la casa. Chiederò i danni!
exampleSentences.english: The work was done poorly and now I have leaks all over the house. I'll claim damages!

exampleSentences.italian: Dopo il nubifragio, il comune ha promesso di risarcire i danni alle case allagate.
exampleSentences.english: After the storm, the municipality promised to compensate for the damages to the flooded houses.

exampleSentences.italian: Il tribunale ha condannato al risarcimento danni l'azienda che ha licenziato ingiustamente il dipendente.
exampleSentences.english: The court ordered the company that unfairly fired the employee to pay compensation for damages.

exampleSentences.italian: La malattia gli ha causato un danno permanente al braccio sinistro.
exampleSentences.english: The illness caused permanent damage to his left arm.

exampleSentences.italian: In seguito all'incidente, Anna ha riportato un grave danno a carico dell'apparato muscolo-scheletrico.
exampleSentences.english: Following the accident, Anna suffered serious damage to her musculoskeletal system.

exampleSentences.italian: Il medicinale può provocare un danno funzionale ai reni.
exampleSentences.english: The medicine can cause functional impairment of the kidneys.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to pay damages, to compensate for damages

grammarNotes: Sale is a masculine noun with plural form sali. It takes definite articles il/i and indefinite articles un/dei. The word has multiple distinct meanings: the culinary ingredient (salt), and figuratively, wit or common sense. In plural (sali), it typically refers to bath salts or smelling salts rather than multiple types of salt.
learnerNotes: Beware of the false cognate: 'sale' in English means 'vendita' in Italian, not salt! The figurative meaning 'common sense/wit' appears mainly in fixed expressions like 'sale in zucca' and the Latin phrase 'cum grano salis.' In cooking contexts, you'll frequently encounter sale grosso (for pasta water) and the colloquial expression 'aggiustare di sale' when adjusting seasoning.

exampleSentences.italian: Assaggia il sugo e dimmi se è giusto di sale, per favore.
exampleSentences.english: Please, taste the sauce and tell me if it has the right amount of salt.

grammarNotes: Squadra is a feminine noun. Singular forms: la squadra, una squadra. Plural forms: le squadre, delle squadre. It agrees with feminine articles and adjectives in Italian.
learnerNotes: Squadra extends beyond sports into any group working together—from construction workers to emergency responders. Remember it's feminine (la squadra), which affects article and adjective agreement. The phrase 'squadra del cuore' is uniquely Italian, meaning your favorite/beloved team, reflecting the emotional connection Italians have with their sports teams.

exampleSentences.italian: La nostra difesa non è stata abbastanza efficace contro la squadra avversaria.

exampleSentences.italian: Che belle le nuove divise della squadra di pallacanestro!

grammarNotes: Campo is a masculine noun. Singular: il campo (indefinite: un campo); Plural: i campi (indefinite: dei campi). It derives from Latin 'campus' and has multiple meanings depending on context.
learnerNotes: Campo has three main meanings: agricultural field, professional/work sector, and generic sports/activity space. Don't confuse it with 'campagna' (countryside/campaign). When referring to professional sectors, use 'in campo + noun' (e.g., in campo medico = in the medical field). The diminutive 'campicello' can sound either endearing or slightly mocking depending on context.

exampleSentences.italian: Hanno piantato degli ulivi nel campo dietro casa nostra.
exampleSentences.english: They planted olive trees in the field behind our house.

grammarNotes: Ruga is a feminine noun. Singular articles: la ruga (definite), una ruga (indefinite). Plural articles: le rughe (definite), delle rughe (indefinite). Derived from Latin rūga meaning 'fold' or 'crease,' it shares etymological roots with French ride, Spanish arruga, and Portuguese ruga.
learnerNotes: Do not confuse ruga (skin wrinkles) with piega (wrinkles in fabric/clothing). Use piega for clothes: 'Le pieghe della camicia' (the wrinkles on the shirt). The verb raggrinzire or raggrinzarsi means 'to wrinkle,' while the adjective grinzoso describes something as 'wrinkled.' In Venice and certain Italian regions, ruga has an additional regional meaning unrelated to wrinkles.

exampleSentences.english: She has a few wrinkles on her face, but she's still beautiful.

grammarNotes: Scarpa is a feminine singular noun with plural form scarpe. Definite articles: la scarpa / le scarpe. Indefinite articles: una scarpa / delle scarpe. Related augmentative and diminutive forms exist: scarponi (big shoes/boots, using -one suffix), scarponcini (small boots, using -ino + -one), and scarpetta/scarpettina (little shoe/slipper).
learnerNotes: Note that stivali (generic tall boots) differs from scarponi (sturdy, functional boots with rigid soles for outdoor/labour use)—they're not perfectly interchangeable. The idiom 'fare la scarpetta' is culturally important in Italian dining etiquette. Remember scarpa is feminine (la scarpa, una scarpa), which affects article and adjective agreement.

englishTranslation: to be a good deal / it's worth it / it's best to / to agree
grammarNotes: Convenire is a regular -IRE verb with an irregular present indicative stem (io convengo, tu convieni, lui/lei conviene, noi conveniamo, voi convenite, loro convengono). It is typically used in the third person singular, either impersonally (conviene) or with indirect object pronouns (ti conviene, vi conviene). The verb can take infinitives and past participles as complements.
learnerNotes: Convenire has three distinct but related meanings: economic value (worth it/good deal), advisability (it's best to), and agreement (to agree). The third meaning is more formal and used in business/academic contexts; use essere d'accordo for casual conversation. Pay attention to whether convenire is used impersonally (conviene) or with indirect object pronouns (ti conviene = it's best for you), as this affects the nuance. The past participle 'convenuto' is common in formal writing (come convenuto = as agreed).

exampleSentences.english: It's worth it!

exampleSentences.english: Filling up here isn't worth it: it costs 10 cents more per litre.

grammarNotes: Caso is a masculine noun. Its definite articles are: il caso (singular), i casi (plural). Its indefinite articles are: un caso (singular), dei casi (plural). The word is highly versatile and its meaning shifts based on context—from legal/factual situations to hypothetical possibilities to grammatical expressions.
learnerNotes: Caso is a highly polysemous word that requires careful attention to context. It appears frequently in conditional phrases (in caso, casomai, nel caso che) where the subjunctive mood often follows. Be careful not to confuse it with English "case" in grammatical contexts—when Italians discuss grammar cases, they use 'caso' (e.g., caso nominativo = nominative case). The colloquial expression 'un caso umano' is playful and somewhat ironic, typically used with affection rather than genuine criticism.

exampleSentences.italian: Le autorità hanno confermato che si tratta di un caso isolato e non ci sono rischi per la cittadinanza.
exampleSentences.english: Authorities confirmed that it's an isolated case and there's no risk to residents.

grammarNotes: Sacco is a masculine noun: il sacco (singular), i sacchi (plural). The diminutive form sacchetto means 'little bag' and is commonly used for shopping bags. When used as an adverb (un sacco, un sacco di), it remains invariable and does not require gender/number agreement with the following noun, unlike tanto or molto.
learnerNotes: Un sacco di is invariable, making it easier than tanto/molto which must agree in gender and number—use it when you're unsure of noun gender. The expression un sacco (without di) functions as an adverb meaning 'a lot' and is very common in spoken Italian; note it doesn't require the preposition di. Be careful not to confuse sacco (bag/sack) with sacchetto (shopping bag)—the latter is what you'll hear at checkout.

grammarNotes: Gelosia is a feminine noun (la gelosia). The plural form is le gelosie, though it is rarely used. As a feminine noun, any adjectives modifying it must agree in gender and number (e.g., grande gelosia, molta gelosia).
learnerNotes: Gelosia has three distinct meanings: jealousy in romantic relationships, envy of someone's possessions or success, and protectiveness/possessiveness. Pay attention to context to determine which meaning applies. The adjective form is geloso/a (jealous), which is commonly used in everyday conversation: sono geloso (I'm jealous). Note that gelosia also refers to a type of window blind or shutter in Italian architecture, adding a fourth, less common meaning.

grammarNotes: Piano is a multifunctional word with three main parts of speech. As an adjective, it agrees with the noun (piana for feminine singular, piani/piane for plurals). As an adverb, it remains invariable. As a masculine noun, it can be singular (il piano) or plural (i piani). The word derives from Latin planus and has evolved multiple semantic meanings.
learnerNotes: Piano is a false cognate with English 'piano' (the musical instrument)—while it exists in Italian too, the word's primary meanings in everyday speech are 'slowly,' 'flat,' and 'floor.' Pay attention to context: 'parlare piano' means to speak slowly/quietly, not to speak about pianos. The adverbial use of piano often overlaps with 'gently' because slowness and quietness are related actions. When referring to building floors, use 'piano' for the levels (first floor = primo piano), but 'pavimento' or 'terreno' for the ground/pavement itself.

exampleSentences.english: To assemble this piece of furniture, we need a large, flat surface.

englishTranslation: to bear / to endure / to tolerate / to put up with
grammarNotes: Sopportare is a regular -are verb conjugated normally (sopporto, sopporti, sopporta, etc.). It commonly appears in negative constructions (non sopporto) to express strong dislike. The particle 'ne' frequently combines with sopportare in expressions like 'ne sopporta di tutti i colori' where 'ne' represents the accumulated hardships endured.
learnerNotes: Beware the false cognate: sopportare does NOT mean 'support' in English—it means 'tolerate/endure.' Use sostenere instead when you want to physically support something in everyday contexts. The negative form 'non sopporto' is very common and expresses strong dislike or annoyance. Remember that sopportare conveys enduring something difficult or unpleasant, often with resignation or patience.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa mensola non riesce più a sopportare tutti quei libri.
exampleSentences.english: This shelf can't hold all those books anymore.

exampleSentences.italian: Queste piccole colonne sopportano tutto il peso dell'architrave.

exampleSentences.italian: Matteo è davvero indisponente. Lo sopportiamo solo perché lavora bene.
exampleSentences.english: Matteo is really annoying. We put up with him only because he's good at his job.

exampleSentences.italian: Sopporto i suoi scherzi solo perché so che non è cattivo.
exampleSentences.english: I tolerate his jokes only because I know he means no harm.

exampleSentences.italian: Non sopporto la sua risata, è davvero fastidiosa!

grammarNotes: Feminine noun: la credenza (singular), le credenze (plural). Derived from Latin credere (to trust). The word has two distinct meanings: abstract (belief/conviction) and concrete (furniture/cupboard). Both meanings are equally valid in modern Italian.
learnerNotes: This word exemplifies how Italian vocabulary preserves historical layers of meaning. The dual meaning (belief/cupboard) stems from 16th-century court practices where a trusted servant (Mastro Credenziere) would taste food on a cupboard—the furniture inherited the name from this trust-verifying ritual. When discussing beliefs, use the fixed expressions (credenza popolare, credenza antica, falsa credenza) for natural, fluent speech; the cupboard meaning is straightforward but less common in modern usage.

exampleSentences.italian: L'idea che passare sotto una scala porti sfortuna è una vecchia credenza popolare.
exampleSentences.english: The idea that walking under a ladder brings bad luck is an old folk belief.

exampleSentences.italian: Molte credenze antiche legano la qualità del vino alle fasi della luna.
exampleSentences.english: Many ancient beliefs tie the quality of the wine to the phases of the moon.

exampleSentences.italian: Ci sono tante false credenze su ciò che fa bene o male alla salute.
exampleSentences.english: There are a lot of myths about what's good or bad for our health.

exampleSentences.italian: Secondo una credenza diffusa, mangiare carboidrati a cena fa ingrassare.
exampleSentences.english: According to a widespread belief, eating carbs at dinner makes you gain weight.

exampleSentences.italian: Tra gli studenti napoletani è credenza generale che il Cristo Velato si possa ammirare solo dopo la laurea.
exampleSentences.english: Among Neapolitan students, it is a common belief that the Veiled Christ statue should only be admired after graduation.

exampleSentences.italian: Abbiamo restaurato la vecchia credenza della zia Maria, ora sembra nuova.
exampleSentences.english: We restored Aunt Maria's old cupboard, now it looks new.

relatedExpressions.meaning: it is a common belief that
food-tasting service (historical: the ritual performed on a cupboard to verify food safety)

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with regular plural. Singular: il punto / un punto. Plural: i punti / dei punti. The word is highly versatile with multiple concrete and figurative meanings across different contexts (writing, sewing, surgery, sports, geometry).
learnerNotes: Punto is extremely common and appears in numerous idioms, so learning its multiple meanings is essential. The figurative expressions like 'punto e basta' and 'mettere i puntini sulle i' are colloquial and frequently used in everyday conversation. Be aware that 'punto' in sewing, embroidery, and medical contexts all refer to stitches, but the context determines which specific meaning applies.

exampleSentences.italian: Ricordati di mettere un punto alla fine della frase.
exampleSentences.english: Remember to put a full stop at the end of the sentence.

exampleSentences.italian: Il grafico ha scelto di usare il libro come punto focale della locandina.
exampleSentences.english: The graphic designer chose to use the book as the focal point of the poster.

exampleSentences.italian: Ho detto che non si può fare, punto!
exampleSentences.english: I said it can't be done, end of story!

exampleSentences.italian: Ti ho detto che non puoi tornare così tardi, punto e basta!
exampleSentences.english: I told you that you can't come back so late. That's it!

exampleSentences.italian: Ne abbiamo parlato tanto, ma alla fine siamo punto e a capo.
exampleSentences.english: We talked a lot about it, but in the end, we're back to square one.

exampleSentences.italian: Dopo l'ennesima discussione, Silvia ha messo un punto alla sua storia con Diego.
exampleSentences.english: After yet another argument, Silvia put an end to her relationship with Diego.

exampleSentences.italian: Non sopporto più la mia collega, vuole sempre mettere i puntini sulle i!
exampleSentences.english: I can't stand my colleague anymore, she's so pedantic!

exampleSentences.italian: Ho fatto l'orlo con dei punti provvisori, prima di passare alla cucitura definitiva.
exampleSentences.english: I hemmed the fabric using temporary stitches before making the final seam.

exampleSentences.italian: Mia nonna è una maga del punto croce, fa dei ricami bellissimi!
exampleSentences.english: My grandma is a wizard at cross stitch, she makes the most beautiful embroidery!

englishTranslation: plant / sole (of foot) / plan / floor plan
grammarNotes: Feminine noun in singular (la pianta) and plural (le piante). Note the homonym il pianto (masculine, meaning 'crying') which has entirely different meaning and gender. Gender agreement affects all modifying articles and adjectives.
learnerNotes: Pianta has three distinct meanings with no obvious connection: botanical plant, foot sole, and architectural plan. Remember the homonym il pianto (crying) is masculine and completely different. The 'foot sole' meaning extends to shoe sizing (pianta stretta/larga), which is useful for shopping. Practice distinguishing between la pianta (plant/sole/plan) and il pianto (crying) as they sound similar but differ fundamentally in gender and meaning.

exampleSentences.italian: Perché le mie piante appassiscono sempre?
exampleSentences.english: Why do my plants always wilt?

exampleSentences.english: I'm trying to park under a tree so the car stays in the shade.

grammarNotes: Appunto functions as multiple parts of speech. As a verb, it is the first-person singular present indicative of 'appuntare' (to note down, pin, sharpen). As a noun, it can be singular (appunto = observation/remark) or plural (appunti = notes). As an adverb, it emphasizes timing, agreement, or purpose, equivalent to 'exactly' or 'just.' Gender agreement applies only when used as a noun (masculine).
learnerNotes: Appunto is highly versatile; context determines its meaning. As an adverb emphasizing agreement or timing, it's extremely common in spoken Italian—listen for it when natives want to stress 'exactly' or 'just.' The plural appunti (notes) is far more frequent than singular appunto in academic contexts. When making a critique, appunto leans polite; combine with 'piccolo' (small) to soften further.

exampleSentences.italian: Ogni mattina appunto sull'agenda le cose da fare.
exampleSentences.english: Every morning I note down my to-do list in my planner.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi appunto il vostro numero così vi faccio sapere se si liberano dei posti.
exampleSentences.english: I'll note down your number so I can let you know if any spots open up.

exampleSentences.italian: Le ho lasciato un appunto sulla scrivania.
exampleSentences.english: I left her a note on her desk.

exampleSentences.italian: Che bella lezione, ho preso un sacco di appunti!
exampleSentences.english: What a great class, I took tons of notes!

exampleSentences.italian: Il capo ci ha fatto un appunto riguardo la gestione interna dei documenti.
exampleSentences.english: The boss pointed out an issue with how we handle documents internally.

exampleSentences.italian: Vorrei solo fare un piccolo appunto prima di procedere: qualcuno ha considerato i costi?
exampleSentences.english: I'd just like to raise a quick point before we move on: has anyone considered the costs?

exampleSentences.italian: Il cliente ci ha mosso un appunto a proposito dei tempi di consegna.
exampleSentences.english: The client made a remark about the delivery times.

exampleSentences.italian: Bel lavoro! Mi permetto solo un appunto: aggiungerei un esempio per chiarire questo concetto.
exampleSentences.english: Great work! If I may make just one point: I would add an example to clarify this concept.

exampleSentences.italian: Stavo appunto andando a vedere.
exampleSentences.english: I was actually on my way.

grammarNotes: Feminine noun (la coda) that becomes le code in the plural. The diminutive form is il codino (masculine), which changes gender and takes the plural i codini (meaning pigtails). Agreement with adjectives follows standard feminine rules.
learnerNotes: Note the gender shift in the diminutive: coda (feminine) becomes codino (masculine), which is an important irregular pattern in Italian. The verb scodinzolare is specific to describing a dog's joyful tail-wagging—use regular tail movement verbs (agitare, muovere) for other contexts. 'Coda' can refer to a queue in some contexts, though this meaning isn't emphasized in the article.

exampleSentences.italian: I cani hanno iniziato a scodinzolare non appena lo hanno visto.
exampleSentences.english: The dogs started wagging their tails as soon as they saw him.
