englishTranslation: to stink / to smell bad / to seem fishy (figuratively)
grammarNotes: Regular -are verb conjugated like parlare. Pronounced with distinctive double 'zz' (poot-tsah-reh). Often used with preposition 'di' (of) to specify what something smells like. Can be used literally for bad smells or metaphorically for suspicious situations.
learnerNotes: Puzzare is highly colloquial and informal; save it for conversational Italian with friends rather than formal settings. The metaphorical use ('to smell fishy') is very common in everyday speech when expressing suspicion. Note the related noun 'puzza' (stink) and adjective 'puzzolente' (stinky)—these are useful for describing both literal odors and suspicious situations figuratively.

exampleSentences.italian: Questa carne puzza, non è fresca.
exampleSentences.english: This meat smells bad, it's not fresh.

exampleSentences.italian: Mamma mia, che puzza in questa stanza! Apri la finestra!
exampleSentences.english: My goodness, what a stink in this room! Open the window!

exampleSentences.italian: Metti fuori quelle scarpe puzzolenti, non le voglio in casa!
exampleSentences.english: Put those stinky shoes outside, I don't want them in the house!

exampleSentences.italian: Tutta questa fretta puzza, secondo me c'è qualcosa sotto!
exampleSentences.english: All this hurry stinks; in my opinion, there's something going on!

exampleSentences.italian: Questa storia puzza di truffa. Mi raccomando, non dargli i tuoi dati!
exampleSentences.english: This story smells like a scam. Make sure you don't give him your data!

exampleSentences.italian: C'è qualcosa che puzza di marcio in quell'azienda.
exampleSentences.english: There's something that stinks of 'rottenness' in that company.

exampleSentences.italian: Le sue scuse puzzano di bugia lontano un miglio!
exampleSentences.english: His excuses smell fishy from a mile away.

exampleSentences.italian: Quei due parlano sempre sottovoce… puzza di intrallazzo!
exampleSentences.english: Those two are always whispering… something shady is going on!

exampleSentences.italian: Mmm… qui la cosa puzza!
exampleSentences.english: Hmm… this doesn't feel right!

To stink 'like a male goat' (musty and unwashed)

grammarNotes: Simpatico agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: simpatico (masc. sing.), simpatica (fem. sing.), simpatici (masc./mixed plur.), simpatiche (fem. plur.). It typically follows the verb essere (to be) but can also be used with other verbs like riuscire, ispirare, fare, and suscitare when emphasizing different nuances of likability.
learnerNotes: Beware the false cognate: simpatico does NOT mean 'sympathetic' in English. It describes someone genuinely likable and fun, not someone showing sympathy. The subtle use of simpatico in romantic contexts—paired with hesitation—can politely indicate lack of romantic interest while still complimenting someone's personality. When describing places or things, simpatico shifts meaning from 'likable' to 'pleasant' or 'charming.'

exampleSentences.italian: Tuo fratello è proprio simpatico!
exampleSentences.english: Your brother is so likable/fun to be around!

exampleSentences.italian: All'inizio sembra un po' arrogante, ma alla fine riesce sempre simpatico.
exampleSentences.english: At first he seems a bit arrogant, but in the end, he always manages to come across as likable.

exampleSentences.italian: Mi piace il nuovo commesso, ha un viso che ispira simpatia.
exampleSentences.english: I like the new sales assistant, his face just gives off a friendly vibe.

exampleSentences.italian: Il loro cane fa troppa simpatia con quelle orecchie!
exampleSentences.english: Their dog is just so funny with those ears!

exampleSentences.italian: Il protagonista del film suscita immediatamente simpatia nel pubblico.
exampleSentences.english: The film's protagonist immediately wins the audience's affection.

exampleSentences.italian: Allora, che ne pensi di Mauro? – Sì, dai… è simpatico!
exampleSentences.english: So, what do you think of Mauro? – Yeah, I mean… he's nice/fun!

exampleSentences.italian: È stata una cena simpatica.
exampleSentences.english: It was a pleasant dinner.

relatedExpressions.meaning: to come across as likable (focusing on impression after interaction)
to inspire likability (immediate, instinctive positive first impression)
to make someone likable/funny (informal; used for quirky or endearing qualities)
to arouse likability (more formal; used in journalism and reviews)

grammarNotes: Feminine noun: la mossa (singular), le mosse (plural). Can also function as an adjective or past participle of the verb 'muovere' (to move), but primarily used as a noun. Commonly paired with the verb 'fare' (to make/do) in expressions like 'fare una mossa.'
learnerNotes: Mossa has two primary meanings: literal physical movement (usually preceded by adjectives like 'rapida,' 'brusca,' 'involontaria') and figurative strategic action or initiative. The expression 'fare la prima mossa' is idiomatically important in both games and interpersonal contexts, especially dating. Note that 'una mossa di corpo' is colloquial slang best learned for cultural understanding but less frequently used in formal contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: Stavamo passeggiando tranquillamente, ma poi Sergio ha fatto una mossa brusca e il cane è scappato spaventato.
exampleSentences.english: We were strolling peacefully, but then Sergio made a sudden move and the dog ran off scared.

exampleSentences.italian: Con una rapida mossa, i ladri le hanno portato via la borsa.
exampleSentences.english: With a quick move, the thieves snatched her bag.

exampleSentences.italian: Il Signor Mario ha risposto con una mossa del capo, senza dire una parola.
exampleSentences.english: Mr. Mario responded with a movement of the head, without saying a word.

exampleSentences.italian: Cambiare strategia all'ultimo minuto è stata una mossa rischiosa, ma fortunatamente è andato tutto bene.
exampleSentences.english: Changing strategy at the last minute was a risky move, but luckily everything worked out.

exampleSentences.italian: Investire in quella startup è stata davvero una mossa vincente!
exampleSentences.english: Investing in that startup was really a winning move!

exampleSentences.italian: Piero è un grande! Ha concluso la trattativa con una mossa da maestro, ottenendo esattamente quello che voleva.
exampleSentences.english: Piero is awesome! He closed the deal with a brilliant move, getting exactly what he wanted.

exampleSentences.italian: Sono stato io a fare la prima mossa e chiederle di uscire: oggi sono tre anni che stiamo insieme!
exampleSentences.english: I was the one who made the first move and asked her out: today we've been together for three years!

exampleSentences.italian: Luca è un abile giocatore di scacchi; ha vinto la partita in sole quattro mosse!
exampleSentences.english: Luca is a skilled chess player; he won the game in just four moves!

relatedExpressions.meaning: to make a move / to make a movement

grammarNotes: Masculine noun with feminine equivalent taccheggiatrice. Regular plural formation: taccheggiatori (masculine) and taccheggiatrici (feminine). Uses standard definite articles (il/i, la/le) and indefinite articles (un/dei, una/delle). Derived from the verb taccheggiare (to shoplift).
learnerNotes: Note that taccheggiare has two unrelated meanings: shoplifting and a printing press technique. The etymology of the shoplifting sense is uncertain, so don't try to trace its roots. For general theft vocabulary, prefer furto (theft) and rubare (to steal); taccheggiatore specifically means someone who steals from shops, not theft in general contexts.

exampleSentences.italian: La polizia ha arrestato il taccheggiatore mentre usciva dal negozio.
exampleSentences.english: The police arrested the shoplifter as he left the shop.

exampleSentences.italian: Il taccheggio è un reato.
exampleSentences.english: Shoplifting is a criminal offence.

englishTranslation: to happen/to occur/to succeed/to take over a role
grammarNotes: Succedere is an intransitive verb that always pairs with essere (not avere) in compound tenses: è successo. It has two past participles—successo (when meaning 'to happen') and succeduto (when meaning 'to succeed/take over')—which change the verb's meaning and conjugation. The choice between these participles is crucial for distinguishing between the two primary meanings.
learnerNotes: Critical: use essere, not avere, in compound tenses—è successo (correct), not ha successo (which means 'he/she has success'). The past participle successo is a noun when preceded by avere, so context determines meaning. Succedere also means 'to succeed/inherit' in formal contexts (e.g., monarchies), though this usage appears incomplete in the article.

englishTranslation: marching band / gang / crew / stripe / bandwidth
grammarNotes: Banda is a feminine noun following standard Italian patterns. Singular: la banda, una banda. Plural: le bande, delle bande. It is a false cognate with English 'band' when referring to rock/pop groups, which use 'gruppo' or the borrowed word 'band' instead.
learnerNotes: Banda is a false cognate with English 'band'—use 'banda' only for marching bands, not rock/pop groups (use 'gruppo' or 'band' instead). The word has multiple distinct meanings (musical ensemble, criminal gang, casual group of friends), so context is crucial. Common in news and cultural contexts describing Italian traditions and criminal organizations.

exampleSentences.italian: Per tanti anni, mio nonno ha suonato la tromba nella banda del paese.
exampleSentences.english: For many years, my grandpa played the trumpet in the town band.

exampleSentences.italian: La polizia ha finalmente arrestato la banda che ha svaligiato la banca.
exampleSentences.english: The police finally arrested the gang that robbed the central bank.

exampleSentences.italian: Sabato i ragazzi vanno al mare con tutta la banda.
exampleSentences.english: Saturday the kids are going to the beach with the whole gang.

grammarNotes: Pirata is an invariable masculine noun that remains pirata regardless of the pirate's gender; only the article changes (il pirata, un pirata). The plural is pirati. For females, the standard form is la pirata/le pirati, though le pirate and the alternative feminine form piratessa are also widely used and accepted in dictionaries.
learnerNotes: Unlike most Italian nouns, pirata doesn't change its stem to indicate gender—only the article changes. Be aware that pirata extends beyond seafaring contexts to describe various lawbreakers (hackers, hit-and-run drivers, hijackers). As an adjective, pirata describes illegal goods (e.g., CDs pirati = pirated CDs).

exampleSentences.english: The pirate yelled out "Land-ho!"

grammarNotes: Seme is a masculine noun ending in -e. Its plural form is semi. Definite articles: il seme (the seed), i semi (the seeds). Indefinite articles: un seme (a seed), dei semi (some seeds).
learnerNotes: Note that seme has multiple meanings: primarily 'seed' in botanical contexts, but also 'sperm/semen' (synonymous with sperma) in biological contexts—context is essential to understand which meaning applies. The word comes from Latin semen and shares roots with the verb serere (to sow), making it useful for understanding related vocabulary like seminare and seminario. Be careful not to confuse the plural semi with the English word 'semi.'

exampleSentences.italian: Ho piantato il seme e ora aspetto che cresca.
exampleSentences.english: I've planted the seed and now I'm waiting for it to grow.

exampleSentences.italian: La banca del seme è aperta cinque giorni alla settimana.
exampleSentences.english: The sperm bank is open five days a week.

grammarNotes: Stato is a masculine noun. Plural: stati. Use 'lo stato' for singular definite article, 'uno stato' for indefinite, 'gli stati' for plural definite, 'degli stati' for plural indefinite. When referring to government institutions, it's capitalized (Stato); when describing types of states, use lowercase (stato).
learnerNotes: Capitalization matters: 'Stato' (capital S) refers to the government as an institution, while 'stato' (lowercase) describes types of states or conditions. The word appears frequently in Italian politics, news, and official contexts. Remember that 'stato' also means 'condition' in everyday speech, making it one of the most versatile words in Italian.

exampleSentences.italian: Siamo arrivati nello stato di New York proprio il giorno in cui è stato dichiarato lo stato di emergenza.
exampleSentences.english: We arrived in the state of New York on the very day the state of emergency was declared.

exampleSentences.italian: Alla cerimonia di inaugurazione erano presenti tutte le più alte cariche dello Stato.
exampleSentences.english: All the highest state officials were present at the inauguration ceremony.

exampleSentences.italian: Gli aiuti di Stato hanno salvato molte piccole imprese durante la crisi economica.
exampleSentences.english: State aid saved many small businesses during the economic crisis.

exampleSentences.italian: Dopo il colpo di stato, il paese è diventato uno stato totalitario.
exampleSentences.english: After the coup, the country became a totalitarian state.

exampleSentences.italian: La Svezia è considerata un modello di stato sociale.
exampleSentences.english: Sweden is considered a model welfare state.

grammarNotes: Ladro is a masculine noun with feminine form ladra. Plural forms are i ladri (m) and le ladre (f). Articles follow standard patterns: il/un ladro, la/una ladra. The word can also function as an adjective meaning 'thieving' or 'dishonest' (e.g., un idraulico ladro).
learnerNotes: Ladro is commonly used figuratively in Italian to criticize dishonest behavior beyond actual theft—such as overcharging or fraud. Remember the feminine form ladra when referring to female thieves. The related augmentative form ladrone is archaic but may appear in literature; the productive related nouns ladroneria (robbery) and ladrocinio (thievery) are more modern alternatives.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel negoziante è un ladro. Mi ha fatto pagare $50 per questa cianfrusaglia senza valore.
exampleSentences.english: That shopkeeper is a thief. He charged me $50 for this worthless trinket.

relatedExpressions.meaning: To leave in a sly, careless or rude manner
A thief with a distinguished appearance and refined manners
Dressed in a sloppy and unseemly manner
To treat someone in a rude way

grammarNotes: Cornuto is an adjective that must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies. The feminine form is cornuta, and it can be used as a predicate adjective (è cornuto) or an insult. As an insult, it can function as a standalone exclamation or within a full phrase (Sei un cornuto!).
learnerNotes: Cornuto is highly colloquial and potentially offensive—use only when joking with close friends or when recognizing it in Italian media. Beyond romantic betrayal, it functions as a generic insult hurled during road rage or heated arguments, similar to 'asshole' in English. The related expressions (avere/portare/fare/mettere le corna) are essential for understanding Italian gossip and informal speech, but equally require careful, contextual use.

exampleSentences.italian: Povero Marco, non sa di essere cornuto.
exampleSentences.english: Poor Marco, he doesn't know he's been cheated on.

exampleSentences.italian: È cornuta da anni ma continua a stare con lui.
exampleSentences.english: She's been cheated on for years but keeps staying with him.

exampleSentences.italian: Ma dai, lo sanno tutti che la moglie ha le corna!
exampleSentences.english: Come on, everyone knows that the wife is being cheated on.

exampleSentences.italian: Quel poveretto porta le corna ma fa finta di niente.
exampleSentences.english: That poor guy has been cheated on, but he's acting as if nothing happened.

exampleSentences.italian: Hai saputo? Le ha fatto le corna con la vicina!
exampleSentences.english: Have you heard? He cheated on her with the neighbour!

englishTranslation: to rub / to scrub / to trick / to fool / to cheat / to steal
grammarNotes: Regular -are verb with spelling modification: adds 'h' before 'e' or 'i' endings to maintain the hard 'g' sound (io frego, tu freghi, lui/lei frega, noi freghiamo, voi fregate, loro fregano). The reflexive form fregarsi means 'to rub oneself' and is commonly used for actions on one's own body.
learnerNotes: Fregare is highly colloquial and rarely appears in formal or written Italian; strofinare is the more formal alternative for 'to rub.' The verb is context-dependent—meaning shifts from physical scrubbing to deception based on the situation. Be cautious: in the 'trick/cheat' sense, it can range from playful deception to serious fraud, so gauge the tone carefully from context.
